#   Fault Isolation FA Methodology on Multi-Bonded Device

Anne Lorraine Angustia(1), Gilbert Ruiz(2), Arnulfo Evangelista(3)

1,2,3 Global Failure Analysis, Analog Devices, Gateway Business Park, Brgy. Javalera, General Trias, Cavite, Philippines Phone : (+632)8677030, Email :anne.delaon-angustia@analog.com, gilbert.ruiz@analog.com, arnulfo.evangelista@analog.com

#   Abstract

Advancement of technology requires integration of different process nodes which may require multiple bond connections. This paper demonstrates that the traditional FA flow for package-related open or high resistance is already outdated and not applicable for multi-bonded devices. The results of this paper will show the effectiveness of applying the six metaprocess steps, utilizing Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) or simulation, and employing the three-probe measurement methodology. Finally, at the end of the project, an updated Failure Analysis (FA) flow for package-related open or high resistance will be presented showing its effectiveness on sample FA case.

#   Introduction

The rapid evolution of semiconductor technologies has led to the integration of multiple functional components—such as MEMS, analog, and digital circuits—within a single package. This integration often necessitates the use of multi-bonded wire connections to a single external pin, enabling compact and scalable device designs. However, this complexity introduces significant challenges in failure analysis (FA), particularly in identifying package-related open or high-resistance failures. Traditional FA methodologies [1], which were developed for simpler single-bonded configurations, are increasingly inadequate for diagnosing faults in these advanced multi-bonded devices.

In conventional FA flows, open or high-resistance defects are typically identified through curve tracing, fault isolation, and physical inspection. However, in multi-bonded configurations, the presence of parallel conductive paths can mask the electrical symptoms of partial bond failures, leading to inconclusive or incorrect diagnoses. This limitation underscores the need for an updated FA methodology that can effectively localize and characterize faults in complex interconnect structures.

This paper addresses this gap by presenting a comprehensive FA methodology tailored for multi-bonded devices. The proposed approach integrates Six Metaprocess Steps, Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA), simulation techniques, and a Three-Probe Measurement method to enhance diagnostic

accuracy and efficiency. A case study involving a MEMS device with triple-bonded VDD and GND/VBN pins is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of the updated methodology. The results show that this approach enables accurate fault localization and mechanism identification, even in cases where traditional methods fail to detect anomalies. By refining the FA process, this work contributes to more reliable diagnostics and improved yield in advanced semiconductor packaging.

#   I. Background

System application requires integration of different technologies in a single package and may require multiple bond connections to a-single lead or external pin. This will enable us to create flexible and scalable solutions. Together with technological advances, the FA procedures also need to be updated to address those challenges. Figure 1 shows the traditional methodology to determine the failure mechanism of package-related with open or high resistance defects.

The conventional FA procedure [2] will not be able to detect the high resistance defect and may lead to incorrect or inconclusive failure mechanisms. Incorporating the fault localization results and circuit analysis are also useful to prove the high resistance failure. In addition to the updated FA flow, the paper will explain with an actual example of the effectiveness of Six Metaprocess Steps in narrowing the area of interest to determine the failure mechanisms that apply to assembly-related defects and other types of issues.

#   II. Project Description

A MicroElectroMechanical System (MEMS) device is utilized in the project study. This device is composed of MEMS die, analog and digital circuitries which have 3-wire bond connections on VDD and VBN pins. Table 1 describes the behavior if the GND/VBN_AD wire is open with respect to the lead. Since there is no curve trace anomaly detected with anomalous heating or OBIRCH sites on the die during backside fault isolation, the analyst may focus on the die-level analysis which would lead to an unknown failure mechanism.

A sample circuit with 3 bond pads of VDD are connected to a single VDD external pin and 3 bond pads of GND/VBN are connected to a single GND/VBN external pin as shown in Figure 2. An open connection in one of the 3 wire bonds will not be apparent as no curve trace anomaly will be detected.

When the MEMS device is biased and when the GND/VBN_AD bond wire is open:

· The current from Analog/Digital circuit block will flow from GND/VBN_AD bond pad to D5 ESD diode, then to GND/VBN_A bond wire going to GND external pin.

· The current from Analog/Digital circuit block will also flow from GND/VBN_AD bond pad to D8 ESD diode, then to GND/VBN_D bond wire going to GND external pin.

· When the MEMS device is set up using the Optical Beam Induced Resistance Change (OBIRCH), the D5 and D8 ESD diodes will show anomalous resistance changing sites. The same D5 and D8 ESD diodes will show anomalous emission sites when set up using LEM. See Table 2 for actual results.

· Current flows from the Analog circuit block will be the same along GND/VBN_A bond pad going to GND external pin, as well as the current from Digital circuit block along GND/VBN_D bond pad going to GND external pin.

Refer to Figure 3 for the illustration of the current flows from the GND/VBN_AD bond pad going to D5 and D8 ESD diodes to GND external pin. This will explain the OBIRCH and LEM signatures showing current flow on diodes D5 and D8.

#   Three-Probe Measurement for Open Failure

The Three-Probe Measurement [4] is a good technique to ensure proper landing of the probe needles on the area of interest. Refer to Figure 4 for the step-by-step procedure. The 3rd probe needle checks the integrity of the 1st and 2nd probes.

1. On Node 1, land the Probe Needle #1 and Probe Needle #3. Using an Ohmmeter, check if the resistance is zero ohm or low to ensure good contact of the probe needles.

2. Move the Probe Needle #3 to Node 2. Land the Probe Needle #2 on Node 2. Using an Ohmmeter, check if the resistance is zero ohm or low for good contact of the probe needles.

3. Remove Probe Needle #3. Check the resistance between Probe Needle #1 and Probe Needle #2. The resistance measurement is the actual resistance between Node 1 and Node 2.

#   Six Metaprocess Steps

The six metaprocess steps in failure analysis [3], as discussed in Microelectronics Failure Analysis, Desk Reference Fifth Edition, are designed to guide the analyst through a systematic approach to identifying and resolving issues. These steps can be looped back multiple times to narrow down or localize the defect site and finally find the failure mechanism.

1. Existence-Correlation-Causation (E/C/C) Question: This step involves formulating a question that addresses the existence, correlation, and causation of the observed failure. For example, does a specific conductive path exist that correlates with the observed failure?

2. Measurement: The analyst uses various tools and observations to measure effects related to the possible prior cause identified in the E/C/C question. This helps to gather data on the failure.

3. Interpretation: The results from the measurement are interpreted to determine if they support the hypothesis posed in the E/C/C question. This step assesses whether the measured effects align with the expected outcomes.

4. Correlation List: A list of possible prior causes and their secondary effects is created. This helps in brainstorming potential reasons for failure and understanding the relationships between different factors.

5. Selection: From the correlation list, one or more items are selected for further investigation. This involves choosing which potential causes to explore in more detail.

6. Loop Back: This step involves returning to the measurement phase to look for additional effects or to refine the understanding of the failure. The process is iterative, allowing the analyst to continuously refine their hypotheses and measurements until the root cause is identified.

Let's apply the six metaprocess steps to this issue and see how it will help the analyst to define the defect site effectively and efficiently.

#   First Loop

E/C/C Question: Does the reported complaint exist correlate with the bench testing and ATE data, and would this cause this device to be considered as a failure?

Measurement: The device failed to communicate and exhibited a low VDD voltage - an output of Low Drop-Out regulator.

Interpretation: The reported communication failure will not cause a VDD problem, which means that the VDD issue is the one causing the communication failure.

E/C/C Answer: VDD failure will cause a communication issue and other functional failures, this is evident from the results of bench and ATE testing.

Correlation List: Table 3 shows the first cycle correlation list and its predicted or known correlating side effect of the prior cause.

#   Second Loop

E/C/C Question: Does the high resistance in any of the wire bonds connected to VDD and GND/VBN would result in low VDD failure?

Measurement: Simulation results showed that high resistance on GND/VBN_AD would result in low VDD, which would cause communication failure. In addition, Optical Beam Induced Resistance Change (OBIRCH) and Light Emission Microscopy (LEM) showed that the ESD diode between GND/VBN_AD and GND/VBN_A, and GND/VBN_AD and GND/VBN_D are in a forward bias state.

Interpretation: High resistance between the wire bond of GND/VBN_AD would float the ground connection of analog/digital circuits, hence resulting in a low VDD failure. Forward-bias ESD diodes, as shown in Figure 3, would confirm this phenomenon.

E/C/C Answer: Low VDD failure is caused by high resistance between GND/VBN_AD and the lead.

Correlation List: Table 4 shows the 2nd cycle correlation list and its predicted or known correlating side effect of the prior cause.

After the second loop, the final test is necessary to confirm which of the correlating side effects would cause the PPC? At this stage, the last step, like micro-probing or die inspection, is needed to confirm the failure mechanism.

#   III. Results, Learnings and Key Takeaways

Performing a simulation, further understanding of OBIRCH signature or other fault isolation tools, and applying six metaprocess steps would suggest that the mechanism exhibits high resistance on GND/VBN_AD. A multi-bonded device needs to perform localization related to the interconnect before proceeding with die-related analysis, because the defect might not be obvious electrically due to parallel connections. In general, evidence of a wire bond defect can be washed out when proceeding to die-level analysis, which could lead to an inconclusive result. Before proceeding with physical analysis, it is necessary to probe the suspected open node using the Three-Probe Measurement.

#   Conclusion

An updated FA flow was done for package-related open or high resistance failures, as shown in Figure 5. This paper shows that the conventional procedure could not detect package/assembly-related defects with a multi-bonded device. After verifying the electrical failure, it is significant to always check if the behavior is related to the multi-bonded lead. If yes, review all the data gathered and apply the six metaprocess steps or other localization tools to produce a correlation list and select the best likelihood by interpreting the measurement results. This kind of thought process is crucial to determine the mechanism to prevent missing the assembly-related defect site. It is advisable, as part of FA readiness, to prepare the FMEA data related to multi-bonded wire ahead to time instead of running the simulation each time a customer return arrives.

#   AI-based image enhancement improves detection of white bump defects

Raphael Wilhelmer, Roland Brunner

Materials Center Leoben Forschung GmbH, Leoben, Austria
roland.brunner@mcl.at

Tatjana Djuric-Rissner

PVA TePla Analytical Systems GmbH, Westhausen, Germany

Hsien-Wei Ho, Chun-Hsien Lee, Chun-Liang Kuo Advanced Semiconductor Engineering (ASE) Inc., Kaohsiung, Taiwan

#   Abstract

Traditional failure analysis (FA) methods face growing challenges due to the increasing miniaturization and complexity of modern semiconductor devices. In particular, the detection of cracks in the extreme low K layers of flip-chips, utilized in advanced packaging architectures at the back end of line (BEOL), is challenging. To improve detectability of these defects, we propose an AI-based image enhancement workflow, specifically tailored to improve scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM) images. By applying a Deep CNN with Skip Connections and Network in Network (DCSCN) model to low-resolution C-scan SAM images, we are able to improve perceptual quality of images. The approach boosts resolution-dependent analysis like AI-based object detection and classification as well as decreases significantly SAM scanning time. Our work demonstrates that AI-based image enhancement can significantly improve FA workflows, offering a robust and efficient solution for modern semiconductor analysis.

#   Introduction

As the semiconductor industry advances, failure analysis (FA) faces growing challenges due to increased device complexity [1], [2], miniaturization [3], [4] and the adoption of novel device architectures [4], [5]. While these developments vastly increased performance and reliability of semiconductor chips in recent years [2], [4], they also introduce new and more complex failure modes such as interconnect reliability issues or packaging-related defects in the back end of line (BEOL) [6], [7], [8]. In advanced semiconductor packaging, particularly within 2.5D architectures, micro bumps are employed to establish interconnections between stacked dies and interposer during the BEOL process [7], [9]. However, cracks within the extreme low K (ELK) dielectric layers are often formed close to the bumps due to thermal expansion mismatch [9], [10]. As those cracks grow, they may form a delamination [10].

Traditional FA methods, including optical microscopy [11], focused ion-beam (FIB) [12] or electrical measurements [13], are often insufficient for detecting the small cracks and interconnect reliability issues in general. FIB is problematic due to its destructive nature and problems with scalability to large

areas [12], optical measurements struggle in accessing deep and buried structures in 3D stacked devices [11] and electrical measurements face with localization limitations [13].

Meanwhile, scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM) [14], [15] has become an essential tool in semiconductor fabrications, especially to detect voids, delamination or cracks in advanced integrated circuits (ICs) [16], [17]. SAM has the potential to detect deeply buried structures like bump-interconnects and is capable to achieve relatively high throughput rates, however it needs long scanning times in cases when high resolution for complex architectures is necessary or large wafer areas are inspected [18]. Instead, scanning with low resolution often

result in images with low contrast and blurry edges, making it challenging for subsequent resolution-dependent analysis methods like object-detection and classification, which are essential for further automated quantification and statistical failure interpretation, to achieve high accuracy [19].

Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based image enhancement algorithms, like super-resolution [20], [21], can avoid these shortcomings and enable the application of high-resolution SAM to larger areas while keeping scanning time low. Recent developments in image enhancement achieve impressive results by employing modern convolutional neural networks (CNNs) [20], [22], generative adversarial networks (GANs) [21], [22] or diffusion-based algorithms [23], [24]. However, highly generative algorithms, like diffusion models and GANs, also pose the problem of hallucinations i.e. outputs that do not correspond to the physical reality and should be considered as artefacts [21], [25], [26]. For industrial applicability it is necessary to avoid these artefacts, therefore requiring carful model selection and evaluation [19], [27].

In this work we demonstrate how AI-based image enhancement can be utilized for improving SAM C-scan images and subsequent failure analysis workflows. On the example of so-called white-bump defects in flip-chips, we examine the ability of a CNN based approach to increase image quality and improve accuracy of a YOLO object detection algorithm. Even though our work shows how to improve scanning speed of SAM and accuracy of subsequent YOLO object detection, the mentioned approach is applicable to other research areas and resolution-sensitive analysis techniques.

#   Results and Discussion

#   White bump measurements and YOLO object detection

Figure 1 shows a C-scan SAM image of a High-Density Flip-Chip Ball Grid Array (HFCBGA) package with removed lid. When zooming into the image, white bumps, indicating cracks or delamination within the ELK dielectric layer, appear as bright white spots. Due to the small size of the white bumps, measurements require high resolution.

To count and localize white bump defects in the C-scan images, object detection algorithms like You Only Look Once (YOLO) [28] can be employed. YOLO is a modern and fast one-shot object detection algorithm. Compared to conventional sliding-window techniques, it can improve accuracy and drastically decrease evaluation time [29].

In Figure 1, we employ the YOLOv8 algorithm [29], implemented in the Python KerasCV package, for object detection of white bumps. In our experiment a 6 µm/px resolution was necessary to detect all white bumps on the test HFCBGA package with YOLO. However, such high resolutions usually require long scanning times. In our case, scanning the 31 mm by 21 mm large package with 6 µm/px takes around 14 minutes using meander C-scan. Decreasing scanning resolution to 24 µm/px decreases the measurement time to 3 minutes, but also reduces the accuracy of YOLO

object detection. In fact, from nine white bumps on the die, only one was detected in the low-resolution 24 µm/px image, see Fig. 1 and Tab. 1.

To combine the short scanning times of the 24 µm/px scan with the high accuracy of the 6 µm/px scan, image enhancement can be applied before using YOLO. As shown in Fig. 1, enhancing resolution by 4x by applying an AI-based Deep CNN with Skip Connections and Network in Network (DCSCN) algorithm two times, enables us to detect all nine white bumps on the die. In comparison, using simple bicubic upscaling instead of AI-based image enhancement degrades performance by around 20 % to seven detected white bumps, see Tab. 1. Our YOLO object detection is trained on C-scan images of white bumps from one die, containing varying scanning resolutions. The model is tested on a C-scan of a second unrelated die, see also [19].

#   DCSCN-based image enhancement

Deep CNN with Skip Connections and Network in Network (DCSCN) is a modern, CNN-based image enhancement method showing good performance for deblurring and super-resolution of images, trained in a fully-supervised manner [19], [20], [30].

Figure 2 shows the basic training workflow and model architecture of a slightly adapted DCSCN architecture,

including additional CBAM [31] attention. Our workflow begins by down sampling high resolution images via a nearest-neighbor algorithm. In a second step, we incorporate gaussian noise, gaussian blurring and compression artefacts to further degenerate image quality and make the model more effective in real-world situations where degradations can rarely be captured by simple downscaling of an image [32], [33].

Using these degraded images, the DCSCN model can now be trained using a perceptual [22] loss function. Furthermore, different metrics like Peak Signal to Noise Ratio (PSNR) or Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) can be calculated to ensure that the model training converges. Our DCSCN model is pretrained on the DF2K and OST datasets and finetuned on around 300 different C-scan SAM images. Finally, a PSNR of 35.1 and SSIM of 0.92 was reached. For comparison, simple bicubic upscaling reaches a PSNR of 29.8 and SSIM of 0.90.

As shown by [19], a DCSCN trained with this workflow can outperform highly generative models, like GAN and diffusion-models, on simple super-resolution tasks. This performance advantage is primarily attributed to the perceptual loss-based training strategy, which mitigates the generation of unphysical hallucinations often observed in generative approaches.

Additionally, we note that DCSCN image enhancement not only improves the image quality of BEOL structures like white bumps but can be applied to a variety of microelectronic structures like TSVs or bonded wafers, also in the front end of line (FEOL) [19]. This is due to the self-supervised training strategy, which enables the training on large and diverse datasets [19].

#   Limitations of AI-based image enhancement

While AI-based method delivers strong results in enhancing low-resolution SAM images, there are specific limitations to consider. One major constraint is the need for high-quality, domain-specific training data. Training deep models like DCSCN requires large datasets that accurately represent the types of degradations and structures encountered in real-world applications. Variations in noise, texture, and structure across domains can degrade performance if not addressed through careful fine-tuning of the model to these applications. In specialized fields such as microelectronics, collecting enough data for training or fine-tuning can be expensive and time-consuming.

Another limitation is computational cost. Unlike classical methods such as bicubic interpolation, DCSCN involves deep architectures and attention modules, which increase inference time and memory usage. This can hinder deployment in environments with limited resources or where real-time processing is required.

Even though our workflow tries to minimize these problems via self-supervised training and efficient model design, challenges remain and have to be considered during practical implementation.

#   Conclusions

In conclusion, recent advancements in semiconductor technology and manufacturing have introduced new challenges for failure analysis (FA), necessitating innovative approaches to address complex failure modes while keeping analysis time low. In fact, traditional FA methods often fall short due to the high complexity and small features of current device architectures. For example. Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM), while able to detect buried defects in multi-layered devices, struggles with keeping high resolution when scaling to larger scanning areas like whole wafers.

In this work, we demonstrate how AI-based image enhancement can mitigate this problem for the detection of so-called white bumps. By applying a DCSCN based super-resolution model to low-resolution C-scan SAM images, we are able to increase resolution by four times. This also affects subsequent image analysis methods like YOLO object detection. In fact, the accuracy of YOLO object detection increases from 11 % to 100 %, when applying DCSCN image enhancement. Also compared to simple bicubic upscaling, a 23 % improvement in accuracy is observed. Furthermore, the DCSCN shows no signs of unphysical hallucinations like other models [19].

Although we conduct experiments using SAM and subsequent YOLO object detection, similar workflows can be constructed using different FA methods like electron microscopy and algorithms such as semantic segmentation. In fact, we suppose that our workflow can enhance segmentation performance, object detection capabilities or other resolution-dependent analyses in a wide range of practical applications.

#   Advanced Data Imputation Methodology for Handling Missing Values in the Semiconductor Manufacturing Process

Julee Kim, Seokyeong Kim, Soojae Heo, Hyoungjun Kim and Junghwan Lee Samsung Electronics, Hwaseong-si, Gyeonggi-do, Korea, Republic of (South)

#   Abstract

In the development phase of DRAM devices, thousands of processes are carried out, and measurements are conducted. Due to productivity and development efficiency concerns, measurements are conducted on only about 4% of the products. For control and management on the production line, analysis and prediction of in-fab wafers are essential. Therefore we propose specific methodology which predicts missing data of semiconductor in-fab measurement. From only 4% of real measurement data, we managed to fill the absence by developing a missing data imputation method using machine learning. Three major methods were exploited and proposed in this paper: recursive utilization of imputed data, application of target encoding, merged ensemble models. The proposed method would be functional for control and management in production line, which will further contribute to yield development in semiconductor industry.

#   Introduction

In the development of semiconductor devices, data analysis and prediction play a crucial role in identifying potential issues, thereby accelerating development success. Typically, in-fab metrology data obtained during the manufacturing process, such as Critical Dimension (CD) and Optical Critical Dimension (OCD), are utilized for such analysis and prediction. These types of data are commonly used because they are directly linked to the device profile, enabling a fast and intuitive assessment of the current process healthiness.

However, the biggest challenge with this data is the high rate of missing values. For general metrology steps, measurements are performed for only about 6% of the total wafers as shown in Figure. 1. This means that analysis must be conducted with no information available for the remaining 94% of the data. Another major challenge is the absence of data for thousands of metrology parameters. Each parameter has unique data characteristics, requiring the training of independent models.

To address missing data problems, various interpolation techniques have been proposed. Early approaches have primarily relied on classical statistical methods. Multiple imputation (MI) is a statistical technique where missing values are replaced by creating multiple plausible datasets and combining the results to incorporate uncertainty [11]. A

Bayesian approach has been developed by integrating the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithms and a non-iterative posterior computation method based on the Inverse Bayes Formula by Tan et al. [12]. Recent studies have shifted toward data-driven approaches using machine learning and deep learning techniques. For instance, Jerez et al. evaluated various statistical and machine learning methods for imputing missing data, including k-nearest neighbors (KNN), self-organizing maps (SOM), and multilayer perceptrons (MLP) [13]. Their results showed that machine learning-based approaches outperformed statistical methods in the prediction. Yoon et al. [14] used a generative adversarial network (GAN) framework on a dataset with values missing completely at random (MCAR). Based on insights from existing approaches, it was necessary to identify a suitable model for DRAM metrology data, which exhibits time-series characteristics and accumulates information over time.

In this study, we propose a missing data imputation approach using machine learning models, tailored for application in the semiconductor development phase. First, we designed a recursive imputation framework that utilizes previously imputed data as input features for subsequent imputation tasks. Additionally, we constructed an ensemble model by merging multiple machine learning algorithms. The merged ensemble model consists of XGBoost [1], LightGBM [2], and CatBoost [3], it demonstrates superior performance in terms of both speed and accuracy. Finally, we leveraged target encoding techniques [4]. By transforming process recipes and equipment information through target encoding and using them as features, we were able to achieve significantly improved accuracy.

#   Experiments

In this study, we describe several issues faced at the DRAM product development stage: 1) rapid process changes, 2) thousands of missing items, 3) the curse of dimensionality and show how we resolved these issues and increased accuracy.

#   Recursive Utilization of Missing Data Imputation

The in-fab metrology data in semiconductor manufacturing can be considered time-series data. As the fabrication process progresses from fab-in to fab-out, various processes and measurements are performed sequentially. Moreover, DRAM fabrication involves stacking layers, as a result, it is significantly influenced by preceding layers. Therefore, we implemented a sequential missing data imputation approach, starting from the initial measurements after fab-in as shown in Fig. 2. This method allows us to utilize the imputed values from previous layers when imputing missing data for subsequent layers. This approach became the core logic for ensuring the integrity of the model.

![Metrology of the first layerMetrology of the second layerNth layer2.1 ACI1.1 ADI1.1 ACI1.3 ACI2.3 ACIImputed Metrologv datarealpredic2.7 ACISanple anborSauple aanber*ADI (After Development Inspection* ACI (After Cleaning Inspection\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_2c88d39bd7194cb894db6f3b7f19f3f5_4.png)
# Figure 2. Recursive imputation framework structure. Each box denotes a missing data imputation model, while the arrows represent the resulting imputed output data from each model.

As mentioned earlier, semiconductor manufacturing involves stacking layers, and the measurements from preceding layers contain valuable information necessary for imputing missing data in subsequent layers. For instance, in a process where the etching is followed by metal filling, there are measurements for Space Critical Dimension (CD) after etching and Optical Critical Dimension (OCD) for the recess depth after metal etch back. These two measurements are not independent. If the CD is small, it implies less space for metal filling, which would result in a smaller recess value in the subsequent measurement. The direct relationship between such measurements makes the recursive use of imputed data highly beneficial for ensuring accuracy.

We observed that the profile or processing conditions of preceding layers can influence subsequent layers. While a large amount of process and metrology data is available from earlier layers, using all of it poses a high risk of overfitting. To mitigate this, we constructed a database by selectively including only the most influential factors for each layer and item, based on domain knowledge. In other words, our primary approach to feature selection is based on domain knowledge. Although we also apply algorithmic feature selection using the SelectKBest

method [5] during data preprocessing, the domain-driven selection remains the main focus. We conducted an experiment to evaluate the effectiveness of domain knowledge-based feature selection. Specifically, we trained two separate models for comparison. One using features randomly selected from process and metrology data of layers preceding the target layer, and the other using features carefully chosen based on domain expertise. Although both models utilized only prior-layer information, the random selection lacked consideration of process relevance. As shown in Fig. 3, the model incorporating domain-informed features achieved an $R^2$ score of 0.62, a marked improvement over the score of 0.25 from the model using random features, highlighting the importance of informed feature selection.

# Figure 3. Scatter plots comparing measured and predicted thickness for two models: (a) one without feature engineering and (b) one with feature engineering based on domain knowledge. While the plots illustrate the correlation visually, the $R^2$ scores are 0.25 for (a) and 0.62 for (b).

In fact, we do not consider any data from preceding layers to be entirely irrelevant to the target layer. Rather, some features are simply more influential than others. At present, we have constructed a feature set based on domain knowledge, prioritizing features that are considered more important from a causal perspective rather than relying solely on statistical correlations. While this manual selection has proven effective, it raises the question of whether such domain-driven decisions could be automated through algorithmic means. In previous work, we applied Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce the dimension of the input data while preserving the most significant sources of variation. [6][7] However, we observed that this compression led to information loss, which resulted in a lower $R^2$ score as shown in Table 4. This highlights the need to explore more effective and interpretable methods for feature extraction or selection that preserve critical process information while minimizing noise.

#   Merged Ensemble Models

One of the challenges encountered while designing the model was the presence of missing values across thousands of metrology parameters. Furthermore, for practical application, not only accuracy but also speed was crucial, that is, missing imputation had to be performed daily for thousands of items. At the beginning, we focused on finding an appropriate model using single-model approaches. Random forest, an ensemble method that averages predictions from multiple randomly constructed decision trees, was primarily used. This approach

was motivated by its strong generalization performance, ease of hyperparameter tuning, and robustness to noise, which collectively help mitigate overfitting [8] [9]. In addition, we explored alternative regression approaches suitable for tabular data, including gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT)-based models such as XGBoost. Deep neural networks were excluded from consideration, as previous research indicates that they generally do not achieve superior performance on tabular datasets [10].

While GBDT-based models consistently exhibited strong performance, we observed that the most suitable model varied depending on the target variable. For example, LightGBM achieved the best results in imputing missing CD values, whereas XGBoost performed more effectively for certain OCD measurements as shown in Table 1. To address this, we constructed an ensemble model that combines XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost. The model is trained independently for each metrology target variable, allowing for tailored features per target. This approach maintained stable accuracy when dealing with the task of imputing thousands of missing values, providing modest gains over the single-model approach. Additionally, we regenerated the model daily using only the most recent 180 days of data. During the development phase, the characteristics of the data changed constantly due to continuous changes in the processes. This meant that the features present in past data could not be found in future data, indicating that the data's characteristics were constantly shifting. Therefore, we considered past data to be noise for current missing value imputation and opted for a refresh-based learning approach rather than cumulative learning.

#   Application of Target Encoding

In the features used for model training, PPID (Process Program Identification), reticle ID, and equipment chamber information are categorical data. Initially, we attempted to apply one-hot encoding but faced the curse of dimensionality problem due to the excessively large number of features. Accordingly, we conducted model training using only numeric data. To integrate information related to the processing equipment, Fault Detection and Classification (FDC) data was utilized. FDC data refers to the various types of data collected and analyzed to detect and classify faults or anomalies in semiconductor manufacturing equipment and processes. Especially in the context of semiconductor manufacturing, Radio Frequency (RF) time data, one of the FDC data types which is related to equipment Preventive Maintenance (PM), is crucial for maintaining optimal equipment performance and overall efficiency. RF time data refers to the cumulative time that a piece of equipment has been operating with RF power applied. This represents the internal environment of the equipment, since excessive RF time can lead to equipment degradation and decreased productivity. This implies that when the internal environment of the equipment is not optimal, the process may deviate from the intended recipe. Therefore, we considered that FDC data such as RF time could have a direct impact on the process profile and included it in the training. However, the inclusion or exclusion of FDC data did not result in a significant difference in the $R^2$ score. This is presumed to be due to the raw nature of the FDC data. To make effective use of this data for

model training, additional preprocessing such as feature extraction appears to be necessary. This aspect has not yet been experimentally investigated.

Therefore, we returned to the original problem of how to incorporate categorical data and decided to adopt a target encoding approach. Target encoding replaces each categorical variable with the mean of the target variable for each group. We believed that this encoding method was well-suited for the dataset in the DRAM development phase, and it led to a significant improvement in accuracy. PPID contains information on how to proceed with the process, and the process target is fixed that directly related to the device profile. Thus, replacing categorical values with the group mean value, which represents the process target, is logically natural and results in higher accuracy as shown in Fig. 4.

![5.7kProcess1MeasuredThicknessProcess 2Process 3Process 4-5.4kSample numberw/ Target Encodingw/0 Target EncodingThicknessThicknessPredictedPredictedSample numberSample mumber※unitA\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_e3e34ebc92f94990bc1435cf6376dd66_6.png)
# Figure. 4. Comparison of the results with and without the application of target encoding. (a) Real measured data of metrological thickness. (b) Predicted data without target encoding. (c) Predicted data with target encoding.

Furthermore, we performed additional experiments by incorporating features derived from a more detailed characterization of the factors affecting in-fab metrology data using domain knowledge. Whereas target encoding typically involves grouping based on a single categorical feature, we applied a method that performs grouping and encoding based on a combination of multiple categorical features selected based on domain knowledge, which is Mixed Target Encoding. For example, equipment data typically includes information about which processing equipment or chamber was used, which is important since the processing environment can vary across different equipment. However, the internal conditions of the same equipment may also change over time, and the wafer's position within the chamber can further influence the process outcome. Thus we grouped data using a combination of slot number and equipment chamber and encoded each group using the mean of the target variable. When multiple wafers are loaded into the equipment simultaneously, the process environment can differ between the front and rear position, potentially affecting the process profile. To reflect this effect in the learning process, we incorporated such positional information through the proposed encoding method. Additionally, we grouped the processing start time with the chamber data. This grouping reflects temporal shifts in the

equipment environment. It allows the model to learn how chamber conditions change over time. Although the results did not show significant difference as shown in Table 5. This suggests that the target variable, OCD metrology, may lack clear equipment-specific characteristics. Alternatively, the dataset may be too small to learn diverse features. It is necessary to secure a large dataset.

#   Results and Discussion

We prepared three datasets, each representing a different metrology type: CD, OCD, and Thickness (THK). For each type, a representative variable was selected as the target variable y. The feature sets included both numerical and categorical variables. Feature selection was performed in two stages. First, features were selected based on domain knowledge specific to each y, followed by the application of the SelectKBest method to retain the top 50 features for model training.

For dataset splitting, we applied shuffling to the training and validation sets but not to the test set. This decision was made due to the nature of DRAM data, where process recipes tend to remain consistent within the same time window. Shuffling the entire dataset could result in test samples with identical process paths being included in the training data, which would compromise the validity of model evaluation. To prevent this, the data were sorted chronologically, and the most recent 20% were assigned as the test set. The remaining 80% were shuffled and then split into training and validation sets at a 7:1 ratio.

The number of samples in each dataset is as follows: 3,107 for OCD, 7,096 for CD, and 6,437 for THK. Table 1 summarizes the $R^2$-scores of each model on the respective datasets. While GBDT-based models demonstrate strong performance, the optimal model varies depending on the target variable y. The ensemble of the three GBDT-based models yielded the highest overall performance, suggesting improved stability and robustness across different y.

#   Conclusions

The ensemble model proposed in this study demonstrates both high speed and a reasonable level of accuracy in imputing missing values across thousands of metrology parameters on a daily basis. The model incorporates not only statistical methodologies but also domain knowledge specific to semiconductor manufacturing processes, enabling the development of a solution well-suited to real-world industrial applications. Currently, the imputed data are being actively utilized across a range of areas, including analysis, prediction, and trend anomaly detection. Our approach offers a practical and applicable method for handling missing data in complex manufacturing environments like semiconductor fabrication, where massive and diverse metrology data are continuously generated.

Through this study, we have proposed a missing data imputation framework tailored for such high-complexity environments and demonstrated its practical usability. However, as the model prioritizes efficiency in its current design, there remain limitations in accuracy when conducting more fine-tuned data analysis. Therefore, further work is required to enhance model accuracy for more detailed analytical applications. Future work may involve expanding the dataset to more thoroughly evaluate the performance of mixed target encoding for categorical features, as previously discussed. It would also be worthwhile to conduct additional experiments on metrology data that are particularly sensitive to variations in the facility environment. Furthermore, incorporating feature extraction techniques such as autoencoders could facilitate the identification of salient features for model training, which may contribute to dimensionality reduction and help address overfitting.

#   Non-Destructive Defect Localization based on Anomaly Detection in Acoustic Signals using Autoencoders

Lorenz Heinemann, Sebastian Brand, Michael Kögel, Frank Altmann
Fraunhofer Institute for Microstructure of Materials and Systems, IMWS, Halle, Germany

#   Abstract

Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM) is a critical non-destructive technique for detecting buried defects in semiconductor devices [1]. However, interpreting the complex acoustic data requires expert knowledge, especially as microelectronic structures grow increasingly intricate. This study presents a novel, unsupervised approach for defect detection in SAM data using an autoencoder neural network trained exclusively on intact reference samples. The method exploits reconstruction error as an indicator of signal anomalies, identifying potential defects without prior knowledge of their characteristics or the need for defective training samples. The resulting similarity parameter facilitates intuitive visualization of outlier regions through overlay on high-resolution SAM images. This enhances defect detection sensitivity and operator support, making SAM more accessible for less experienced users and highly promising for automation in production environments. While the method effectively highlights signal deviations, it may also flag non-defect-related anomalies such as sample tilting. Nonetheless, it significantly advances automated and operator-independent semiconductor failure analysis by enabling reliable detection of structural anomalies through learned representations of intact signal patterns.

#   Keywords

Non-destructive Testing (NDT), Acoustic microscopy, Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM), Microelectronic failure analysis, Autoencoder, Neural Network, Unsupervised Learning, Unsupervised Defect Detection, Anomaly Detection

#   Introduction

In the field of semiconductor failure analysis, Scanning Acoustic Microscopy (SAM) is a crucial non-destructive technique for detecting and localizing buried defects [2]. Currently, significant expert knowledge is required to appropriately interpret and analyze the acoustic data, as their characteristics are influenced by a variety of factors. Each scan pixel corresponds to a full time-domain signal, which is reduced to a single pixel value based on a specific signal feature to enable intuitive visualization and evaluation. The selection of

an appropriate reduction method is key to representing the relevant signal information and is therefore essential for assessing the sample's condition under the given analysis. Due to the increasing complexity of the internal structures of modern microelectronic components and systems, the level of expertise required for successful analysis has become a critical factor—one that could greatly benefit from sophisticated automation methods.

In recent years, data, signal and image analysis using neural network architectures has gained increasing attention in the field of failure analysis. It is now possible to train relatively simple network structures capable of automatically detecting and correctly classifying defects such as bump fractures and delaminations based on acquired acoustic microscopy data [3]. However, a persistent challenge in training classifiers lies not in the overall quantity of data—since techniques like SAM can generate thousands of signals from a single sample—but in the absence of labeled examples for the wide variety of possible defect types. In practice, sample sets often consist mainly of intact examples, with only a limited number of defective cases, leading to an incomplete representation of all possible defect types. This significantly hinders defect detection, as conventional supervised learning approaches rely heavily on labelled example data. Consequently, there is a pressing need for methods capable of identifying defects without prior knowledge of their characteristics—or even their existence.

The present work addresses the investigation of a novel approach for detecting outliers in acoustic signals obtained from acoustic microscopy data for defect detection. A key feature of the proposed method is that the training data exclusively consists of data acquired from reference (intact) samples, and no prior knowledge of possible defects is required. To achieve this, an autoencoder neural network is employed to learn the typical signal characteristics of defect-free samples. After training, the network is used to estimate the similarity of signals from unknown samples, where deviations in reconstruction are interpreted as potential defects. This enables the detection and localization of structural anomalies without the need for defective reference data or retraining. The approach is evaluated in the context of semiconductor failure analysis and demonstrates improved sensitivity, automation potential, and usability for non-expert operators.

#   Materials and Methods

#   Recorded Acoustic Microscopy Data and Samples

Acoustic microscopy data was recorded in the time domain using a high frequency scanning acoustic microscope (SAM). The study focuses on nonmolded flip chip samples, with one designated reference sample and one additional sample with possible defects for prediction. The samples were scanned using a 200-MHz transducer with a focal length of 3.2 mm. Echo signals were digitized at a sampling rate of 1 GS/s and an amplitude resolution of 8 bits. The transducer was mounted on a commercial 3-axis scanner to acquire full-field time-domain scans of the sample surface. A Scan of one sample is displayed in Figure 1.

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_737371f9f6c04b189f239bf8cac4e21b_3.png)
# Figure 1: SAM-Scan of the sample with possible defects.

#   Preprocessing of Training Data

Preprocessing and model development were implemented in Python using the Keras deep learning framework. The primary challenge in preparing the dataset was the variability in signal lengths resulting from different acquisition setups or scanned structures. Since convolutional neural networks require a fixed input size, simple padding approaches would have limited the model to a maximum input length. To address this, all signals were divided into fixed-length segments of 128 samples. This value was selected based on the temporal characteristics of the acoustic pulse.

Given a transducer center frequency of 200 MHz and a bandwidth of 10%, the pulse duration is approximately

$$ \frac{1}{f} = T \rightarrow \frac{1}{20 \text{ MHz}} = 50 \text{ ns} $$

which corresponds to 50 samples at the 1 GS/s sampling rate. A segment length of 128 samples was selected to accommodate more than two complete echo pulses, ensuring comprehensive capture of their temporal features. This length is optimized for the current experimental setup and can be adjusted accordingly if different transducer parameters or sampling rates are used.

During training, multiple random segments were extracted from each signal to ensure that the autoencoder learns representative features from all parts of the signal, independent of any fixed starting point. For prediction, each signal was divided into a minimum of three and up to

#   2(signal_length/segment_length)

segments, depending on its duration. These segments were equally distributed across the signal, allowing for partial overlap where necessary. If a signal was shorter than the segment length, it was padded with its zero-value baseline to meet the required input size. This ensures consistent input dimensions while enabling the model to handle signals of varying lengths and preserve coverage across the entire signal. Each segment was subsequently padded with zeros on both sides. This allows the convolutional kernel to slide across the entire input, including edges, reducing feature bias toward the signal centre.

#   Autoencoder ML-Network Structure

The neural network used for anomaly detection is an autoencoder based on a one-dimensional convolutional architecture. Autoencoders are unsupervised learning models trained to reconstruct their input data through a compressed latent representation [5], making them well-suited for outlier detection since signals that deviate from the learned distribution yield higher reconstruction errors.

Several alternative network structures were tested in addition to the Conv1D architecture. Preliminary experiments indicated that Conv1D networks performed better than simple multilayer perceptron (MLP) architectures, particularly in capturing local temporal patterns. These investigations were exploratory and not extensive enough for a conclusive quantitative comparison, and a systematic evaluation with defined metrics is noted for future research.

The final Conv1D-based network architecture consists of multiple layers, starting with two Conv1D layers (filters: 32, 64 and kernel sizes: 8, 4) with a dropout layer in between for regularization. Due to the use of kernels, padding must be defined so that signal information at the borders of the segments is not underrepresented. For this autoencoder, the same value is padded to maintain the original dimensional size. The ReLU activation function was chosen for all layers. The encoder compresses the input signal after a flatten layer into a latent space of dimensionality 16, which was empirically determined as a balanced trade-off between compression and reconstruction accuracy for the given segment size. The decoder mirrors the encoder structure to reconstruct the input from the latent representation.

Conv1D layers have been effectively used in signal-related autoencoder models for recognition tasks, demonstrating their ability to capture local temporal features in 1D signals [6]. Furthermore, similar latent dimensions (around 16) have been reported as optimal in related acoustic signal denoising studies, supporting the architectural choice [7]. The final structure of the autoencoder is displayed in Figure 2.

![EncoderDecoderDropoutDropoutConv1DConv1DFlattenOutputLatent SpaceInpu(Compressed Representation\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_a08ccb5821e5447d92cfe7325f8410b4_0.png)
# Figure 2: Structure of the used Autoencoder for Signal-Reconstruction.

#   Training with References

The network was trained on signals derived from a user-defined reference region of a SAM scan. The region was manually selected based on known defect-free areas and can encompass either the full 2D scan or specific subregions. From this region, the time-domain signals were extracted and processed as described in the preprocessing section.

All training data were segmented into fixed-length input samples and passed through the autoencoder. During training, the network learned to reconstruct the characteristic waveform of each segment, effectively modelling the underlying structure of non-defective acoustic responses.

It is important to note that the autoencoder is dependent on the specific signal shape and associated signal characteristics. While different transducers may capture comparable information content, their signals differ in representation, leading to distinct waveform shapes. These waveform differences arise from physical factors such as transducer design. Consequently, a trained autoencoder is transducer-dependent. For the same reason, the autoencoder is also dependent on the sample type, as variations in structural properties alter the signal shape. In addition, variations in the scanning focus can cause similar issues: changes in focus affect the shape of the recorded waveform, potentially degrading model performance if the focus conditions during inference differ from those used during training. These dependencies are well known and also occur in other machine-learning-based approaches for acoustic microscopy data, as they stem from fundamental changes in the input signal representation [1].

As a result, a separate model is generally required for each transducer-sample combination and, ideally, for consistent scanning conditions such as focus.

Training can be resumed or expanded at any time by introducing new reference signals, allowing for iterative improvement and adaptation.

#   Prediction on Samples

Predictions were performed on individual time-domain signals acquired from the samples. Each signal underwent the same preprocessing steps as the training data, including segmentation and zero-padding.

The processed segments were sequentially passed through the trained autoencoder. For each segment, the network produced a reconstructed version of the input signal. The reconstruction error, defined as the difference between the input and the reconstructed signal, was computed for each segment. This error served as a measure of familiarity: segments well-represented in the training data resulted in low reconstruction errors, while unfamiliar or anomalous signal patterns produced higher errors due to insufficient representation in the training-data. The highest reconstruction among all the segments from the decomposed time-signal was selected. By focusing on the maximum error, the method ensures consistency regardless of signal length, allowing localized defects in shorter signals to still be detected clearly. This segmentation and evaluation procedure is illustrated in Figure 3.

#   Results and Discussion

The objective of the present work is the development and evaluation of a machine learning-based method for the automated analysis of time-resolved acoustic microscopy signals in the context of non-destructive defect detection in microelectronic components. Specifically, the study investigates the potential of autoencoder neural networks to identify structural anomalies based solely on data acquired from intact reference samples, without requiring prior knowledge of possible defect types. The focus lies on the ability to detect and localize outliers in complex signal structures, thereby supporting failure analysis workflows through targeted highlighting of abnormal regions. The following section presents and discusses the results obtained using the proposed method and the corresponding datasets.

#   Defect Detection Performance

The proposed method demonstrates strong performance in identifying anomalies within time-resolved acoustic signals. Figure 4 illustrates the detection capability using a flip-chip sample with known defect structures. Graph 1.1 shows the signal segment used for training, which includes both the

surface echo and the interface echo. By training the autoencoder exclusively on this reference segment from an intact sample, the network learns to model the typical signal behaviour of defect-free structures. Once training is complete, the autoencoder can be used to analyse previously unseen samples. Graph 2.1 presents the prediction on the same Signal-Segment, while Graph 3.1 displays the corresponding reconstruction error. The low reconstruction error in intact regions and elevated error at defect locations confirm the method's ability to localize deviations from the learned signal pattern.

To evaluate robustness, two additional Signal-Segment-Choices were tested. Graph 2.2 shows the prediction based on a shorter segment of the signal, and the reconstruction error in Graph 3.2 indicates that the autoencoder still maintains accurate anomaly detection. In Graph 2.3, only the interface echo is used for prediction, and the corresponding reconstruction error (Graph 3.3) again highlights the defect with high confidence. This confirms that the method remains effective when focusing on signal regions where the anomaly is present—in this case the interface echo. In contrast, relying solely on the surface echo would fail to reveal the defect, as it contains no relevant disturbance.

![TrainingPrediction3.13.2\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_85fc0787b7bb42cd92e369fe2147c5c1_0.png)
# Figure 5: Outlier detection performance using different training regions. Graphs 3.1 and 4.1 show the region of interest used for training (white box). Graph 3.1 uses a reference scan from an intact sample, while Graph 4.1 uses a defect-free region from a defect-containing sample. The corresponding predictions on the full signal, shown in Graphs 3.2 and 4.2 (white dotted box), confirm the model's ability to detect anomalies regardless of whether training was based on complete reference scans or localized defect-free areas. The colored heatmap in Graph 3.2 and 4.2 shows only the corresponding reconstruction error. It is not an overlay with a SAM-Image.

Figure 5 presents the results of training conducted on two distinct regions, as illustrated in Graphs 3.1 and 4.1. Graph 3.1 shows the region of interest used for training, extracted from a reference scan of an intact sample. In contrast, Graph 1.2 displays the training area selected from a defect-free region within a sample that contains defects elsewhere. The corresponding predictions, shown in Graphs 3.2 and 4.2, demonstrate the model's capability to detect outliers on the defect-containing-sample using different training data. These findings indicate that the model can be effectively trained either on entire reference scans or on defect-free regions within defective samples.

#   Detection of Non-Defect Anomalies and the Need for Expert Interpretation

Across multiple samples, consistent outlier signals were observed at chip edges, laser-marked regions, and in areas suspected to be affected by slight die tilting or excess mould compound. These anomalies were particularly prominent near die edges when the surface echo was included in the analysed signal segment (Figure 4 Graphs 3.1 and 3.2), and diminished when excluded (Figure 4 Graph 3.3).

The observed deviations are primarily attributed to acoustic interactions at structural boundaries, including scattering and refraction effects caused by sharp topographies and material transitions. In the case of laser markings, although such features

may appear in training data, the variability in engraving geometry and surface roughness introduces inconsistent signal patterns. Similarly, geometric tilts and excess mould compound lead to subtle but systematic changes in the signal envelope due to altered acoustic path lengths and damping behaviour. While these factors do not represent functional defects, they result in reconstruction errors because they deviate from the learned patterns of intact samples. As the model does not perform semantic classification, it flags these irregularities as potential anomalies. This sensitivity is beneficial for identifying structural deviations but also highlights the need for domain expertise. Because these non-critical features may be misinterpreted as defects, expert knowledge remains essential for accurate assessment and to prevent false conclusions.

#   User Feedback and Interpretability

Despite the promising detection performance, the analysis revealed that user feedback remains essential for effective deployment of the method. In particular, flagged regions due to die tilting, surface texturing, or other packaging-related variances require contextual interpretation to avoid false positives. The algorithm is therefore best utilized as a pointer system, guiding the user's attention to areas with elevated anomaly scores while leaving the final defect assessment to a trained evaluator. This interaction model aligns with the goal of increasing automation without removing expert oversight, making the method particularly suitable for hybrid workflows in semiconductor failure analysis.

#   Conclusion

This paper presents the development and evaluation of a machine learning-based approach for the automated analysis of time-domain acoustic microscopy data with the goal of non-destructive defect detection and localization in microelectronic components. The method is based on the use of autoencoder neural networks trained exclusively on intact reference data, enabling the identification of structural anomalies as signal outliers—without requiring prior knowledge of defect types or manual labelling.

The potential of the approach is demonstrated through its application to a real-world sample set containing defect bumps, where these irregularities were successfully highlighted. The results show that the method offers high sensitivity to deviations in complex signal structures, providing valuable support for failure analysis workflows. In particular, the approach enhances usability for non-expert users by automatically guiding attention to regions of interest, while still requiring contextual interpretation for final classification. The findings confirm the feasibility of reconstruction-based outlier detection in SAM signals and suggest that the integration of such techniques into existing analysis environments can significantly increase efficiency and objectivity in early defect screening.

Future work may focus on refining the interpretability of the output and improving the localization accuracy of detected anomalies, for instance through attention mechanisms or hybrid models combining autoencoders with spatial context information. Additionally, the model structure itself could be optimized by leveraging pre-trained networks rather than training an autoencoder from scratch each time, which could reduce computational cost and improve performance by transferring learned features from related tasks. A further consideration is that the current approach is dependent on both the transducer type and the sample type, as differences in signal shape require separate models for different transducer-sample combinations - an aspect that could be addressed in future research to develop more generalizable solutions.

Two main directions for improving generalization can be envisioned. One approach is to retain the original signals and address variation by training multiple autoencoders, combined with a classifier that automatically selects the most suitable model for each measurement. The other approach is to normalize the measurements themselves, for example by applying deconvolution techniques to remove setup-dependent transfer properties, resulting in a unified signal representation that is less sensitive to differences in the measurement configuration.

#   A step towards automation in failure analysis by FIB-SEM 3D tomography and AI segmentation

Pascal Limbecker, Rong Wu, Thomas Woyack Globalfoundries LLC & Co. KG, Dresden, Saxony, Germany pascal.limbecker@globalfoundries.com

Heiko Stegmann, Daniel Plencner, Roland Salzer

Carl Zeiss Microscopy GmbH, Oberkochen; Carl Zeiss AG, Munich, Germany heiko.stegmann@zeiss.com

#   Abstract

In recent decades, automation has not played a significant role in the field of failure analysis. The process of searching for a defect in a single field return sample involves a multitude of manual analysis steps, applying different methods and FA techniques. However, regarding mass data FA and constructional analysis, as is practiced in high-volume foundry fabs or in the context of a substantial number of RMA samples, automation can result in significant resource savings and improved tool utilization. The recent advancements in FIB-SEM instruments, when employed in conjunction with programmable tool kits, have resulted in the acquisition of reliable, high-resolution, automated slice and view cross-section data sets. The generation of a 3D model out of the data sets facilitates a comprehensive evaluation of the defects by enabling an assessment from multiple directions. This paper explores the subsequent step in the process of automatic defect detection. We demonstrate a variety of approaches to automatically detecting defects using conventional image processing and artificial intelligence based segmentation.

#   Introduction

In the competitive high-volume semiconductor foundry business, yield, quality and cost are key to gaining competitive advantage. In addition to in-line metrology and defect scanning, mass failure analysis of base line product wafers is important to generate defect Pareto charts (Fig. 1) for continuous yield improvement, by eliminating the major yield detractors. Hundreds/Photon Emission, plus several thousands of Bitmap and Logic failures are analyzed using FIB-SEM slice and view or top-down polishing and SEM inspection. A lot of manpower and tool time are required. Over the past decades, visitors to failure analysis laboratories have often asked the operators if they could imagine a computer taking over their job at some point. The typical answer was “Not really, you need the human eye and mind to detect a defect in a cross-section or top-down SEM image”.

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_6c1bd3e8da384e7982343be489ae2490_11.png)

However, the evolution of automation, artificial intelligence, deep learning and improved FIB-SEM performance over the last years has changed the mindset.

With current FIB-SEM tools, you can navigate to the area of interest using CAD alignment on full wafers, wafer pieces or single dies. Enabling Bitmapping (Memory) and scan diagnosis (Logic) will narrow down the failure location to a small area for slice and view application. The calculation of a physical bit address or logic net can be already automated, using the available SORT and Scan diagnosis data set (Fig. 2).

# Figure 2. GDS snapshot with calculated signal trace after Logic Scan diagnosis.

OBIRCH (Fig. 3 Left), Photon Emission or Lock-In Thermography typically also provide a very precise failure location. Because top-down inspection by delayering multiple

dies is very time consuming, further physical analysis is mostly done by manual FIB slice and view (Fig. 3 Right).

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_c1a0a63994ce47a780e5b461729149f7_1.png)
# Figure 3. Left: GDS – OBIRCH overlay image. Right: SEM image of a FIB cross section.

The maximum area to be investigated by slice and view is typically not larger than 15x15 µm – usually smaller. Since it is not known in which layer the defect is located, you must decide on the direction of the cut. There is a risk that the defect will be missed in the selected direction [1].

#   Automated SEM / FIB slice and view

With recent FIB-SEM generations, the image series of the target volume can be acquired fully automated. Using such FIB-SEM tomography data acquisition for root cause analysis at defect sites isolated by volume diagnosis techniques has been demonstrated in [1].

![4n-品AAABAAnAAAAAAA\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_0471557266c54344a3fc964b06bf523a_6.png)
# Figure 4. Fiducial patterns on the top ROI.

In the real logic analysis failure case study presented here, an open interconnect was found and localized to within a 10 x 10 µm $^{2}$ area (Fig. 2). A FIB-SEM tomography dataset was acquired in a ZEISS Crossbeam 550L FIB-SEM instrument, using the Atlas 3D software. This software is capable of autofocus, autostigmation and ROI centering using special fiducial patterns [2].

The data acquisition extended over the entire 10 x 10 µm $^{2}$ area and to a depth of 5 µm. Before data acquisition, a 11 x 11 x 1 µm $^{3}$ platinum layer was ion beam deposited on top of the area. A set of diagonal and straight fiducial lines was FIB cut into the platinum layer and covered with an ion beam deposited carbon layer of the same size. A large trench was FIB milled in front of the targeted region to make it accessible for the subsequent repeated FIB slice milling and SEM imaging. The fiducial lines appear as notches in the cross-section thus produced (Fig. 4).

The nominal FIB slice thickness was set to 5 nm. High resolution SEM imaging of each slice was done at 5 nm pixel size on a 10 x 1 µm $^{2}$ sub-area of the cross-section that covered the complete layer stack of the circuit, but not the surrounding areas, as these were not of any interest. Both SE (Secondary Electron) and BSE (Backscattered Electron) were stored simultaneously in order not to lose any information. Slight slice thickness variations and lateral drifts during data acquisition are unavoidable and lead to distortions of the sample structures in the resulting 3D dataset. To counteract, the notches serve as references for periodic measurement and correction of slice thickness, as well as for correction of lateral drift during data acquisition and for periodic electron beam tuning [2].

Set-up and starting of the data acquisition required 45 min of operator time. The data acquisition itself was performed unattended and took 15:30 h. Traditional slice and view inspection of the defect would have taken an estimated 2-3 h. However, as the tomography data acquisition runs unattended, tool utilization can be maximized by collecting the data when nobody uses the tool otherwise, for example overnight.

#   Data set post processing & visualization

After acquisition, all sequential images must be registered perfectly to each other to create a precise 3D model. To this end, a translational alignment by cross-correlation to remove residual image to image drifts was applied to the dataset, and it was interpolated to a constant slice thickness of exactly 5 nm using the thickness of each slice measured during acquisition. Both post-processing steps were done in the Atlas software. The final dataset consisted of 1702 SE and 1702 BSE images of 1987 x 408 pixels each, covering a volume of 9.94 x 2.04 x 8.51 µm $^{3}$.

A quick manual review of the BSE image sequence immediately revealed a patterning issue in the first metal layer almost in the center of the region of interest (Fig. 5). The SE images did not provide any further information and were not used for the remainder of this work.

![250nm\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_56e3b6ecd0b84bbb896cf6fa04f7ed8d_15.png)
# Figure 5. Detail of one of the backscattered electron images of the FIB-SEM tomography dataset showing a pattern defect in the first metallization layer.

The quality of the dataset can be assessed in all directions from virtual slices extracted in XZ and YZ directions and is quite impressive. The virtual top-down image (XZ direction, Fig. 6) can hardly be distinguished from a real top-down image acquired after delayering by manual polishing or Plasma FIB. For better interpretation of the data by the process engineers that requested the analysis, a 3D visualization is very helpful. The prerequisite for such a visualization is a segmentation of the individual structural components. This is straightforward with artificial intelligence-based segmentation [3]. It consists of defining the required number of segmentation classes, then annotating a limited number of training images according to these classes, training the model on these annotations, and finally using the trained model to segment the full dataset or other datasets obtained with the same acquisition conditions.

Annotation of the dataset and the computation intensive training of the segmentation model with these annotations was done with the ZEISS arivis Cloud service. Ten classes were annotated in a subset of the tomography images (here, 25 out of 1702): The five metal layers M1 to M5, Si substrate, contacts, NiSi and poly-Si; and everything else as background. These annotations were then used to train a model that segments the dataset into these components. The training uses a U-net with EfficientNet B0 [4] as encoder and Pixelshuffle [5] as decoder. The encoder is initialized with imagenet-pretrained weights. The number of training epochs was 1200. The learning rate was 3e-4 for the first 70% of epochs and 4e-5 for the remainder of epochs. The batch size was 3. The training algorithm returns several measures of quality, here we are specifying the Intersection over Union (IoU) that was 0.8 at the end of the training. For segmentation of the full dataset with the obtained model as well as for visualization, the ZEISS arivis Pro desktop software was used. (were). The result contained spurious small, artificial segments with considerably smaller volumes than the correct segments. They could easily be removed by filtering out all segments with unrealistically small volumes before

rendering. Figure 7 shows a volumetric rendering of the BSE dataset (a) and a rendering of the segments (b, Si substrate not shown). Figure 8 presents the segmented metal layer 1 (M1) with the defect in detail. Applying the model to a second dataset obtained from a different sample with a substrate to M6 layer stack and a similar open interconnect defect, but overall denser structures produced too many artifacts to be useful, indicating that the model did not yet generalize well enough to be applicable to different datasets acquired at partially different conditions.

In the case study presented, the data acquisition time was long compared to a manual slice and view process. However, the total acquisition time is mainly determined by the ratio of voxel size to the volume image and can be considerably reduced if more information about the defect to be inspected is taken into consideration: The more precisely the location of the defect is known, the more the acquisition volume can be reduced. Furthermore, if the expected size of the defect is roughly known, the voxel size can often be increased to an extent that minimizes acquisition time while maintaining sufficient 3D resolution to characterize the defect. With the dataset acquired here, in hindsight we estimated that the acquisition time may

have been reduced to below 3 h without compromising the information content of the dataset for failure analysis.
