#   Automated Defect Detection

The next step towards automation is automated defect detection in FIB-SEM tomography datasets. For 2D electron microscopic images, automatic defect finding is a current field of research [6], but the authors are not aware of existing work on automatic defect localization in 3D EM data of semiconductor devices. We have begun to examine various aspects and challenges of the topic and highlight these in this paper.

Finding a defect of known nature, but unknown shape and size in a complex 3D interconnect structure, as in our case, is more

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_671776023efa410180802c8e50992cee_6.png)
# Figure 9. Left: cross section SEM image. Right: CAD image from the same location.

challenging than typical 2D applications, such as the classification of different defect categories in SEM images of interconnect line arrays [7]. However, like in the 2D case, reference-based and reference free methods can be considered. These two categories can be further subdivided into using conventional, machine learning or deep learning methods. With the reference-based approach, the addition of the third dimension raises the question of whether the comparison of the experimental with the reference volume shall be made on the 2D slices of both volumes, or whether a direct comparison of the 3D structures is made. We have explored data processing with conventional slice-by-slice data comparison, and deep learning data processing, both within the reference-based approach.

The first reference-based approach is to compare the experimental 3D model including the defect with a second, defect-free FIB-SEM tomography model generated from a reference location on the same or a reference die. As the sample region investigated is a different one in most cases, it is evident that this method would be excessively time-consuming. Consequently, this method was not explored.

The second approach is to use the CAD layout of the same volume as the ground truth and to detect defects by searching for structural differences between the expected (CAD) and the measured (FIB-SEM tomography) data (Fig. 9). To obtain the required ground truth image stack from the CAD layout, there is no function in Synopsis Avalon GDS layout viewer to automatically extract 2D image slices from a defined area. Therefore, a semiautomated approach was used to save consecutive, binary layout cross section shots with 5 nm distance in Y direction, corresponding to the slice thickness of the FIB-SEM data set. Windows Power Automate allows defined mouse clicks on the button to jump to the next slice followed by saving a screenshot from the layout cross section view.

The prerequisite for meaningful slice-to-slice comparison of the datasets is that only matching slices are compared. For each

![|图表|切片编号|CAD|FIB-SEM tomo|\n|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|\n|XY|850|60|60|\n|YZ|450|40|40|\n|XZ|10|0|0|](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_6fa971efba7941eeb7a7894d53a8a934_12.png)
# Figure 10. Mean gray values of each slice image in the FIB-SEM tomography (red) and the CAD datasets (blue), plotted over the slice number, for the XY, YZ and XZ slices. Grey rectangles highlight the slice ranges where the defect is located. The plots give no clear indication of a defect signature.

![|通道|值域|\n|:---:|:---:|\n|XY|0.4-0.9|\n|YZ|0.65-0.9|\n|XZ|0.5-1.0|](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_986c2b4e2bfe4284b7b4c4cccc0449ef_0.png)
# Figure 11. Normalized cross-correlation error between each slice of the FIB-SEM tomography dataset and the corresponding slice of the CAD datasets, plotted over the slice number, for the XY, YZ and XZ slices. Grey rectangles highlight the slice ranges where the defect is located. The plots also give no clear indication of a defect signature.

image in one stack there must be a matching one in the other stack with the same structural content, except for the possible defect. Otherwise, differences between the two images of a pair of slices arising from mismatches in slice position and scale or from skew in one of the images may be mistaken for defect signatures. Such mismatches can be eliminated by registering the datasets to each other in 3D by an affine transformation that comprises rotation, translation, scaling, and shearing in X, Y and Z. However, the real device structures are slightly larger than in the layout, and locally they deviate somewhat arbitrarily from the layout in terms of their individual scale, shape and position (compare Fig. 9). Affine registration between image pairs from both datasets thus does not provide sufficient 3D registration. For better adaption of the CAD volume to the experimental one we tried an elastic (non-rigid) 3D registration using an optical flow estimator (optical flow tv1 function in the Python library scikit-image). The FIB-SEM dataset was scaled by a factor of 0.5 before that to reduce computation time. It should be noted that the parameters of the registration algorithm need to be carefully adjusted to avoid overfitting, that is, the reference structures being deformed in the defect region to mirror the shape of the defect in the experimental structures.

Once the two volumes were registered, a 3D Median filter (2 pixel) was applied to the experimental one to decrease noise, it

was then binarized by grey value thresholding, remaining spurious noise up to a size of 3 pixels was removed, and an erosion operation (2 pixel) was applied to decrease the size of the structures to make them match the width of the CAD structures better. We then explored detecting a defect signature using three conventional, gray value based methods: A) Comparing the mean gray values within each slice pair. B) Calculating the cross-correlation between the two images of each slice pair. Both A and B were applied to the XY, YZ and XZ slices of the volumes. C) Performing image arithmetic that makes use of the CAD data to mask structures in the experimental data.

Figure 10 shows the mean gray values of each XZ, XY and YZ slice pair plotted over the slice number (method A). The slice ranges where the defect is located are highlighted in light gray. No significant difference between the mean gray values between experimental data and reference is discernible in these ranges. There is no indication of a defect signature in the shape of the curves. The same is true for the cross-correlations between the slice pairs (method B). In the plots of the normalized cross-correlation error over the slice number in Fig. 11, there is no indication of a deviation that could be attributed to the defect.

The reason for the lack of a defect signature in these gray value-based measures become clear if you look at the difference between two slices. Figure 12 shows the difference between an XZ slice from the FIB-SEM dataset extracted at the M1 layer that contains the defect, and its CAD counterpart. White pixels represent the deviations of the real structures from the CAD layout structures. It is evident that despite the extensive post-processing, the contribution of the defect to the gray value distribution is relatively small. The real structures do not perfectly match the reference structures because deviations from the layout in production and residual image registration errors outweigh the effect of the defect on the gray values.

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_e7551a18d52a4d669871fe3c3e1e3d11_7.png)
# Figure 12. Difference between two corresponding XZ slices from the M1 layer of both datasets, showing the defect (compare Fig. 6).

![ADCDEG\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_a36fdc3175d6402eb381f340cf2d2684_0.png)
# Figure 13. Image processing steps to detector a defect structure in the FIB-SEM tomography image stack. A) raw BSE image, B) binarized BSE image, C) CAD slice, D) difference between B and C, E) D multiplied with C, F) E after asymmetric erosion and dilation, G) overlay of A (blue) and F (red).

For method C, we continued with the difference between the binarized measured data and the CAD data (Fig. 13 A to D). As mentioned above, it includes ghost structures due to the deviations between the experimental and the layout data (Fig. 13 D). To get rid of those features, we assumed that the CAD ground truth represents a minimum subset of the experimental data in terms of structure sizes. In other words, wherever the

![自T\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_4b75c960a8a94aa6b8163b5738cc3aa8_3.png)
# Figure 14. Detail of a virtual top-down image of first metal layer showing a defect in the center marked in red, extracted from the post-processed dataset in XZ.

CAD data shows a structure, a corresponding structure should be found in the measured data, unless there is a defect of the type of missing structure. Hence, we can ignore data where the CAD is not predicting anything, such as these ghost structures. This was achieved by a simple additional step: Multiplication of each difference image with the corresponding CAD image (which is > 0 where structures are present and 0 where there are no structures). The result is shown in Fig. 13 E. After a subsequent asymmetric dilation and erosion step to remove remaining small artifacts and noise, the defect is segmented (Fig. 13 F). Figure 13 G shows an overlay of the experimental image with the defect mask.

This simple approach provides good results. The reconstructed XY-view shows the found defect areas marked in red, which matches their location very well (Fig. 14). Some false positives are visible, but since they are usually present in one or two adjacent slices only, it would be easy to ignore them in a subsequent automation step. It should be noted that this algorithm only works for the investigated defect class (opens) and would not detect additional features that are not in the CAD, such as particles. Furthermore, as described above, the registration and correct scaling of the CAD to the experimental data is crucial. For further refinement of the method, feedback loops using AI models are a promising approach to achieve this in a fully automated process in a better way than the elastic alignment method used here.

Nevertheless, it would be ideal to have a method that is robust against the deviations of the produced sample versus the CAD layout, but still sensitive to the deviations caused by a defect, without depending on extensive data pre-alignment.

To this end, we explored a deep learning-based method: D) Using a pre-trained feature extractor to find differences in higher-level image features. The key challenge is selecting features (at an appropriate scale) that are invariant to deviations between actual structures and reference design, while remaining sensitive to defects in the actual structures. Method D did not yield results different from those using conventional approaches A and B. The deviations between actual structures and reference design are also evident in such higher-level image features. To overcome this, the feature extractor would need to be fine-tuned with supervision indicating which deviations are expected, and which correspond to defects. Another possible approach would be to apply the feature detector (or image arithmetic approaches like the one described above) to synthetic data generated from the CAD images by a 2D image-to-image GANs [8]. The model would need to learn to generate the ghost structures that are not present in the CAD data. This approach was not pursued and is reserved for future work.

# Figure 16. 3D rendering of the segmented M1 layer of the layout dataset, colored by segment volume.

Finally, we investigated yet another deep-learning based method: E) Using a deep learning-based segmentation model to analyze geometric relationships between the different segments. The idea behind this approach is that features such as the remaining segments of an open interconnect (compare Fig. 6) should be discernible from the intact interconnects in the same metal layer by inspecting properties such as the relation of aspect ratio and volume of these segments. This method would allow reference-free defect detection if the pristine distribution of the analyzed segment properties is already known. As this was not the case with our dataset, a reference-based approach was used by segmenting the corresponding layout image stack as well and then comparing the distributions of the segment properties from both datasets. Training a segmentation model on the binary CAD images annotated for the same ten classes as with the experimental backscattered

electron dataset resulted in a lower IoU of 0.7 (25 training images, 1200 epochs). Segmentation of the full CAD image stack with this model resulted in segmentation artifacts that were partly too large to be removed by filtering out unrealistically small segments. Improving this would require adding more images with annotations to the training data, which we will reserve for future work. To explore method D with the available data, we reduced the segmentation classes for both the experimental and the CAD data to only two: All metal layers and background. Training with these reduced annotations resulted in IoU values of 0.96 (experimental) and 0.99 (CAD). Segmentation of the full CAD dataset segmented with this simplified CAD segmentation model was artifact-free, providing 138 segments in the M1 layer. Segmentation of the experimental dataset with its simplified segmentation model resulted in a very good segmentation that nevertheless still contained small erroneous segments that needed to be removed by filtering out the segments with unrealistically small volumes. After the filtering, the M1 layer consisted of 138 segments as well. Such filtering can maybe be avoided in future work by appropriate noise filtering of the data before segmentation.

Method E showed potential for automatic defect detection. Figure 15 shows a scatter plot of the segment aspect ratios against their volume, both normalized to their maximum values, for the M1 layer of the segmented experimental and CAD layout data. Each dot in this scatter plot corresponds to a unique segment. Two outliers can be identified in the side ratio over volume distribution of the experimental compared to the CAD dataset. Figure 16 presents a view of the M1 segmentation of the CAD data. Figure 17 shows the same for the experimental dataset. Here the segments corresponding to the two outliers are marked by their bounding boxes - the two remaining halves of the open interconnect. We conclude that outliers in the experimental segment properties distributions that are not present in the layout data indicate defects, at least in our case where the defect type, an open interconnect, was known from the initial logic analysis.

![皖AV21r\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_c8011ae0fce34bd08595c2209292bc6d_7.png)
# Figure 17. 3D rendering of the segmented M1 layer of the experimental dataset, colored by the segment volume. The open interconnect halves corresponding to the two outliers in Fig. 14 are highlighted by their bounding boxes.

The distributions in Fig. 15 differ in their details due to the discrepancies between layout and produced sample. Therefore, finding incomplete small interconnects by visual inspection of the scatter plots is difficult and not automatic. However, with improved segmentation by using more training data, it should be possible to exploit not only major outliers but also minor differences between experiment and reference by suitable algorithmic comparison of one distribution with another.

As an alternative approach that was not investigated in this work, one can extract features from the experimental dataset (or from the difference between registered experimental and reference datasets), and identify defects using unsupervised anomaly detection on these features. This way, one can find defects with shape that deviate from other structures in the sample. We aim to follow this approach in future work.

Yet another, but reference-free approach that may be investigated in the future is classifying open and intact interconnects in the experimental dataset, like the approach used to detect open vias in [3]. Both interconnect types, open and intact, are labelled by a human operator in a training dataset, a deep learning segmentation model is trained on it, and the trained model is used to segment the experimental datasets, which would then directly detect open interconnects. For the time being, this approach was not pursued, as the amount of training and validation data available was not sufficient.

#   Conclusions

The results achieved with automated slice and view 3D tomography dataset using the latest generation of FIB-SEM systems in combination with Zeiss Atlas 3D software are quite impressive. Virtual slicing in all directions, especially the top-down view, helps significantly for interpretation of defect type and root cause finding. In addition, auto slice and view can save resources and maximize the tool utilization, e.g. overnight or over the weekend.

An automated defect detection using the recorded tomography dataset is much more challenging than expected. The five approaches based on comparison with CAD data: A, B, C (conventional gray-value based) and D, E (deep learning-based methods) so far are not yet capable of reliable identifying defects without extensive data pre-processing or manual data exploration. This can be attributed to the inherent structural disparities between the CAD and FIB-SEM data sets. In future work more training data is needed to improve deep learning segmentation and refine the models. Nevertheless, the necessary hardware and software are available, and sufficient computing power is in place for model training. It is only a matter of time before automation in failure analysis becomes a reality.

According to the statement David Albert: “Use computer power versus people power to solve problems. Save the people power for the difficult signatures (problems)” [9]

#   Advanced method for 3D FIB tomography AI supported on SRAM I/O circuit block with missing data bits problems.

Domenico Mello, Guillaume Fiannaca and Filippo Marinelli
EM Microelectronic, a Company of the Swatch Group, Marin, Switzerland
domenico.mello@emmicroelectronic.com

Heiko Stegmann, Flavio Cognigni and Giulio Lamedica
Carl Zeiss Microscopy, Oberkochen and Milan
heiko.stegmann@zeiss.com

Angelica Accorinti and Marco Rossi
basic and Applied Sciences for Engineering (SBAI)
technology Applied to Engineering of Sapienza (CNIS)
Sapienza University of Rome, Italy

#   Abstract

Supported by new algorithms based on Artificial Intelligence (AI), FIB µ-tomography has recently been added to the arsenal of Physical Failure Analysis (PFA) methods. This paper shows the efficiency of these methods to solve difficult device development problems. We present 3D reconstruction of a failing I/O circuit block of an SRAM. The tomography unequivocally demonstrated that the problem was not attributable to process or line defects. It was only through the study of the 3D model that a solution to this difficult case could be achieved, prompting the developers to revise their silicon sizing parameter optimization for minimum size deviations.

#   Introduction

In microelectronics, due to continuous shrinkage and evolving technology nodes, some tools traditionally used for material science were also established in the field of failure and defects analysis. This is the case with transmission electron microscopy (TEM), which is mandatory for imaging smaller and smaller structures in samples [1], up to the atomic resolution achieved with aberration-corrected TEM.

However, such high resolution would be completely useless when one needs to explore a portion of a circuit, a net, or a block in search of the defect causing the electrical malfunction. To get a global view it is often more effective to get the big picture, ideally in three dimensions, rather than resolving individual atoms. This is where FIB-SEM-based techniques come into play, particularly 3D tomographic imaging where focused ion beam slicing is combined with SEM imaging [2].

Despite the great success this technique has achieved in life science and material science, it is establishing itself slowly in the semiconductor world. It is obvious that the bigger the acquired volume is, the more problems arise during data acquisition [3]. In addition, the larger the datasets acquired, the

greater the post-processing issues. Initially, both soft- and hardware were not supporting reconstructions of large volumes [4]. Particularly for the segmentation step that is prerequisite to efficient data inspection and quantification, traditional methods based on histogram-based thresholding [5, 6] were unable to provide appreciable results. There was, therefore, a risk that after the acquisition phase, the defect signature might be significantly reduced or even lost without delivering a useful result.

Today, the situation has completely changed thanks to dedicated procedures for data acquisition, assisted by AI-based algorithms for the image post-processing and analysis. It should be noted, though, that these post-processing techniques require a large amount of computing power, which continues to be a problem for the processing of large datasets [7, 8]. This paper considers a failure in a column decoding block in Volatile Memory (SRAM) in 110 nm technology. Initial fault isolation failed, so that the integration of the entire block needed to be evaluated to understand the nature of the failure. This work made use of a 35 µm x 14 µm x 10 µm volume with a resolution sufficient to discern internal objects in the order of 100 nm, which presented a challenge for both the acquisition and post-processing phases.

#   Results and discussion

Microcontrollers are some of the most used devices. They were implemented in many applications in various semiconductor markets. It is a component that contains in one small chip the logic part (CPU), volatile memory (SRAM), nonvolatile memory (NVM), one or more timers, an oscillator, and input - output (I/O) ports. The device considered in this work had data read/write problems in the SRAM. The defective device was diced and mounted in a ceramic (PGA144) package for electrical characterization. The initial measurements revealed missing data bits in the failing devices after programming. In some columns of the Input/output (IO) section, a 0 was always read out when it should have been a 1.

Once the programmed code was verified, attention shifted to the circuit block that controls IO.

Using further electrical characterization, the physical failing block was identified, but there was no relationship with possible defectivity events that happened during the manufacturing process. Furthermore, parametric tests performed in the same area gave no evidence for a critical parameter that could explain the failure mode or drive the physical failure analysis. In addition, traditional fault isolation methods were not able to provide candidate areas to investigate.

In the hope of identifying a physical defect that could explain the problem, a morphological characterization of the entire circuit was performed. The traditional approach, which is commonly referred to as slice and view, is to visually follow the evolution of the structures during iterative FIB cross-sectioning and SEM imaging in areas that the failure analyst deems anomalous. This process is both labor-intensive and time-consuming, and it offers no assurance of successfully identifying the defect. In fact, the matching between the layout and the physical results often is not very accurate due to geometrical discrepancies, which makes it difficult for the failure analyst to simultaneously follow the morphology of the cross-section structures and the succession of layers in the layout during ion beam erosion. In addition, the analyst must pay special attention to all possible artifacts that may occur when stopping and starting the cutting process.

On the other hand, FIB-SEM tomography does not come without its own risks. The sample volume of interest is destroyed during the tomography process, so that there is no chance of recovering data should the dataset quality turn out to be inadequate because of drift, charging, defocus, or other problems. Poor data quality can result in the block not being able to be reconstructed, especially when using traditional post-processing approaches.

In recent years, however, there has been rapid development in methods for capturing and processing tomography data sets, driven primarily by hardware improvements, significantly enhanced data acquisition methods, and the introduction of algorithms based on artificial intelligence. Today, these modern approaches are often preferable to traditional slice-and-view techniques for several reasons: They offer superior qualitative results, provide greater accuracy when compared with layout, the structures can be observed in all directions, and, importantly, ensure a complete volumetric view of the sample. This reduces the risk of overlooking regions where critical defects may be hidden and remain undetected during slicing.

When performing tomography on a circuit block, the process can be divided into two key phases that must both be successfully completed to achieve an optimal result: the acquisition phase and the post-processing phase.

#   Challenges in Acquisition and Stabilization of FIB-SEM 3D Datasets for Defect Analysis

The first major challenge in the acquisition phase was that, since there was no clear indication of the layer where the defect was to be expected, it was not possible to perform dedicated sample preparation to reduce its strong surface topography [5]. Only a thin layer of gold was sputtered on the sample surface to reduce residual charging as much as possible.

The FIB-SEM 3D data acquisition was carried out using a ZEISS Crossbeam 550L FIB-SEM instrument, and the Atlas 3D software system [9]. A 14 × 35 × 1 µm $^{3}$ platinum layer was ion beam deposited on top of the target area shown in Figure 1. A set of diagonal and straight lines was FIB cut into the platinum layer, and then covered by an ion beam deposited carbon layer of the same size of 14 × 35 × 1 µm $^{3}$. A large trench was FIB milled in front of the volume of interest (VOI) to make it accessible for the subsequent repeated slice milling with the FIB and imaging with the SEM. For slicing the volume of interest, a FIB probe of 30 kV and 700 pA was used. The SEM probe used for imaging was 2 kV and 1 nA. SEM pixel size was 10 nm, as was the nominal slice thickness set for the data acquisition. Backscattered electron (BSE) and secondary electron (SE) images were recorded simultaneously, which in summary resulted in 3312 images (times 2 channels) and a total acquisition time of 49 h, covering a volume of about 14 × 35 × 10 µm $^{3}$.

![9-8\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_bba7c1cdaeb648b6b21127ef0257d6ea_9.png)
# Figure 1: (a) layout of the area acquired (b) optical picture of the top side of the device with area of interest reported in the red box.

A critical aspect in this type of 3D data acquisition is the long-term stability of the microscope and electron-optical system. For an optimal result, several error sources must be considered and optimized both during image stack acquisition and post-processing. The most important such phenomena are:

· Fluctuations of the slicing distance (z-direction) between individual images in the stack,

· Drift in the imaging (x-y) plane.

· Shift in imaging conditions (focus and stigmation).

Due to the relatively long acquisition times of such datasets, typical sample drift speeds of a few nanometers per minute can cause severe distortion of the resulting image stack that requires

to be corrected during acquisition. In this case, the mentioned lines were used as fiducials for measurement and dynamic correction of slice thickness during data acquisition, as well as for correction of lateral drift and for periodic electron beam tuning. [9, 10]. To this end, the cross-sections of the fiducial lines are scanned at regular intervals, the current z position of the cross-section determined from that, and the forward feed of the ion beam is corrected whenever necessary to keep the slice thickness constant. The reference marks are particularly valuable not only because they allow automatic focusing and correction of astigmatism in certain intervals ensuring optimal image resolution. They can also be used as references for image stack registration during post-processing.

However, with the sample investigated in this study, it was not possible to achieve stable drift correction because the surface topography of the sample introduced lateral position correction artefacts during the image series acquisition. The last metal level on the sample surface consisted of regularly arranged truncated pyramids with a width of 3 µm, length of 5 µm and height of 1 µm. Because of these surface features, the fiducials did not form straight lines but had a wavey shape. Therefore, when milling forward, the fiducials moved up and down following the shape of these truncated pyramids instead of developing linearly as they would on a flat surface. The tracking algorithm misinterpreted these movements as excessive drift and corrected them, which eventually lead to the algorithm losing track of the fiducials whenever they changed direction due to the shape of the sample surface. To mitigate this issue, several manual re-centering steps were necessary throughout the acquisition. However, periods affected by incorrect shifts still occurred and had to be corrected during post-processing. As the specific layers where defects might occur were unknown, it was not possible to perform mechanical polishing to flatten the sample surface. For future work, ways to level such strong surface topography without altering the sample need to be explored, such as filling it with a suitable resin.

#   Post-Processing and Deep Learning-Based Segmentation for 3D FIB-SEM Data Reconstruction and Analysis

All 6624 images taken during the acquisition were included in the reconstruction. The first step of the processing was denoising with a Non-linear means (NLM) filter. NLM replaces a pixel's value with a weighted average of all pixels in the image. The weights are determined by the similarity between small patches centered on those pixels. NLM is effective at preserving fine details and textures while reducing noise.

Figure 2 compares a detail of one original image (a) and the denoised version (b). In this work, a Python script in which the NLM kernel size was set to 21 and the $\sigma$ parameter to 0.03 was used. This step is crucial as it facilitates the following processes of image stack registration and segmentation. Registration was challenging due to the shift issues encountered during the acquisition phase. These shifts are obvious when viewing an yz plane of the original data set, shown in Figure 3a. The discontinuities introduced by manual adjustments during

acquisition are clearly visible. Typically, a post-acquisition image registration (alignment) step is necessary to remove small misalignments between individual slices in the x-y plane before the 3D dataset can be reliably analyzed. Most image processing tools offer the ability to register images based on image-to-image correlation. However, these algorithms often "lock onto" dominant features, making them ineffective when significant shifts or abrupt jumps - such as those caused by manual corrections during acquisition - are present, introducing strong distortions in the final reconstruction.

![GB\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_5503d5d9c3b94900b2524d152bb2e4b3_6.png)
# Figure 2: (a) Original picture of the dataset compared with the same denoised by NLM filter (b).

![q\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_1eeaef8130a14094b52f0fbd3762d70a_8.png)
# Figure 3: yz view of the original dataset (a) before and (b) after the registration process.

This issue can be addressed by applying a correction based on reference markers intrinsic to the sample structure. Here, proper image registration was achieved by correcting x and y shifts separately, each on a different reference structure. The required image translations in x direction were determined from the x shifts of the central FIB-produced fiducial lines, and the translations in y direction from the y shifts of the bottom of the field oxide, as shown in Figure 4. A simple Python script was employed to calculate the necessary shifts and to apply them as isometric translations to the image stack. In some blocks,

however, one or both reference features were no longer visible. In those cases, metal lines within the structure were used as alternative references.

Figure 3b shows the result of the image registration. After this step, the dataset was ready for the subsequent segmentation step.

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_6de200f85a4040c994f30d711a149a9b_2.png)
# Figure 4: Marks used for alignment in x and y.

To understand advancements in AI applied to image processing and analysis, it is important to define key concepts. AI broadly refers to computer systems that mimic human intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is a subset of AI, where computers learn from data without explicit programming. Deep learning (DL), a further subset of ML, uses neural networks - interconnected layers of nodes inspired by brain neurons - to process information. Among neural networks, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are the most used in image processing. The U-Net architecture is particularly prominent in the field of image segmentation and analysis, known for its high performance even with limited training data, mainly due to the presence of skip connections that help preserve spatial information during feature extraction and reconstruction.

A Deep Learning (DL) semantic segmentation model was trained using the software ZEISS arivis Pro. In DL based image segmentation, convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are used to learn correlations among adjacent pixels in the image. CNNs utilize small patches that are moved over the image, which allows for localized analysis and improved accuracy and efficiency. In our case, the U-net CNN architecture [11] was used. Its recent success can be attributed to its effectiveness in segmenting images that significantly reduced the amount of training images that need to be annotated by the user. The model was trained on 20 images in which we annotated 150 objects per class i.e., metal layers including the poly line. Each metal layer was then highlighted in the analysis step. Then, the model was used for segmenting the dataset within the arivis Pro pipeline. Segmentation results are shown in *Error! Reference source not found*.

The annotation process, a crucial step in training deep learning segmentation models, involves manually highlighting the features to be segmented. In the arivis Pro environment, this process is enhanced by an AI-assisted annotation tool that enables a streamlined point-and-click annotation workflow.

The relationship between the manual annotations and the resulting model predictions is illustrated in Figure 6 for three representative images.

![annotationspredictions0292\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_1827ca8fe65749c387abd6b6f156ff8d_0.png)
# Figure 6: Using arivis Pro environment for annotation, training, and segmentation, the development of customized DL models becomes possible with only a limited number of annotated images and objects. For illustrative purposes, three representative images are shown in the figure

Figure 7 shows a 3D rendering of the segmentation result for the defective block. The segmentation enables efficient defect screening, as all components of the block are visible in the 3D visualization. Each part can be inspected in detail - either individually or in the context of neighboring structures - and from any viewing angle. In contrast, simply browsing through the 2D image stack would not provide the same level of comprehensive spatial understanding, increasing the risk of overlooking critical details. Moreover, for the same block, it is possible to perform a highly detailed construction analysis, including critical dimension measurements. This can be done either directly from the segmentation or, as shown in Figure 8, using virtual 2D slices extracted from arbitrarily oriented planes.

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_aff74ff47a3845d08b4bd3ce83f53bf7_3.png)
# Figure 7: 3D rendering of the- $\mu$-tomography of the failing I/O circuit block. Each layer was isolated using masking boxes and color-coded to enhance structural differentiation.

In addition to that, as the segmentation represents the physical manufacturing results, it can be compared in detail with the layout, and it can furthermore be used as an input for improving process simulations.

![(a) (b)\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_7d028e5250ac4b1294fdb63c86025df9_6.png)
# Figure 8: Views of the same transistor extracted from the dataset in two perpendicular directions.

In the dataset discussed here, no physical defects were found. This result prompted the designers to reconsider the parameters used for their simulation of the whole SRAM block. Time- expensive Monte Carlo simulations are needed to find accurate simulation parameters to match simulations of minimum-size devices typically present in an SRAM to the dimensional measurements obtained from the produced device. Here, in particular the sigma enhancement value used during Montecarlo simulations needed to be re-evaluated. It was finally confirmed that the previously used sigma enhancement was too optimistic. With the latest set of simulations and the newly determined parameters, a good matching between silicon behavior and simulations was finally obtained.

#   Conclusion

This work demonstrates the potential of advanced 3D FIB-SEM tomography, enhanced by AI-based post-processing and deep learning segmentation, as a powerful tool for addressing complex failure analysis and design validation challenges in microelectronic devices. The successful reconstruction and analysis of a SRAM I/O circuit block with missing data bits, despite acquisition difficulties and the absence of clear defect indicators, highlights the effectiveness of modern imaging pipelines that integrate fiducial-based corrections, denoising, and deep learning-driven segmentation.

The segmentation and 3D visualization enabled precise defect screening, critical dimension measurements, and comprehensive comparison with layout data. Importantly, the tomography results ruled out process-related defects, shifting the focus to simulation parameters.

The workflow presented, spanning acquisition, image correction, semantic segmentation, and structural verification, sets a benchmark for next-generation physical failure analysis. It opens new paths for integrating 3D imaging into design feedback loops and underlines the relevance of AI-enhanced microscopy in microelectronics development, especially when traditional fault isolation methods fall short.

#   Intelligent Assistants for the Semiconductor Failure Analysis with LLM-Based Planning Agents

Aline Dobrovsky

University of the Bundeswehr Munich, 85579 Neubiberg, Germany
aline.dobrovsky@unibw.de

Konstantin Schekotihin

University Klagenfurt, 9020 Klagenfurt, Austria konstantin.schekotihin@aau.at

Christian Burmer

Infineon Technologies AG, 85579 Neubiberg, Germany. christian.burmer@infineon.com

#   Abstract

Failure Analysis (FA) is a highly intricate and knowledge-intensive process. The integration of AI components within the computational infrastructure of FA labs has the potential to automate a variety of tasks, including the detection of non-conformities in images, the retrieval of analogous cases from diverse data sources, and the generation of reports from annotated images. However, as the number of deployed AI models increases, the challenge lies in orchestrating these components into cohesive and efficient workflows that seamlessly integrate with the FA process.

This paper investigates the design and implementation of an agentic AI system for semiconductor FA using a Large Language Model (LLM)-based Planning Agent (LPA). The LPA integrates LLMs with advanced planning capabilities and external tool utilization, allowing autonomous processing of complex queries, retrieval of relevant data from external systems, and generation of human-readable responses. The evaluation results demonstrate the agent's operational effectiveness and reliability in supporting FA tasks.

#   Introduction

The semiconductor industry underpins modern technology, producing essential components for diverse applications. Ensuring the correctness of device functionality is critical, making Failure Analysis (FA) a key process in semiconductor manufacturing. FA systematically investigates non-conformities to identify their root causes and suggest corrective actions, supporting risk assessment and quality assurance. FA engineers require extensive expertise in science, engineering, and analysis processes, navigating vast technical data, including test results, microscopy images, and historical cases. Traditional knowledge-management systems, like databases, wikis, or file shares, demand significant manual effort, underscoring the need for AI-driven solutions to efficiently retrieve, synthesize, and present relevant information, enhancing decision-making and productivity in FA.

The rapid advancements in AI and Natural Language Processing (NLP) have opened new possibilities for enhancing complex, data-driven tasks across various industries. Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently emerged as powerful tools, capable of understanding human language and generating human-like text. By accessing and using human knowledge, they have the potential to significantly improve decision-making processes even in highly specialized fields. However, general-purpose LLMs lack the domain-specific knowledge required for meaningful responses in FA, including knowledge about specific analysis methods and laboratory equipment, and domain-specific LLMs, like SemiKong [1], are still premature. As a result, modern solutions utilize semantic search and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [2], to enhance their capabilities by using various prompting techniques [3]. Experiments in the FA domain already demonstrated the benefits of these methods in improving the efficiency of information retrieval and decision-making processes [4]. Nevertheless, these approaches still rely on a predefined pipeline and lack the flexibility to adapt to the specific needs of users. They also require a significant amount of data to be encoded and stored in a vector database, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive.

This paper, therefore, explores the novel approach of LLM-based agents, which integrates LLMs with planning capabilities, memory, and tool utilization, such as database information retrieval, search machines, and even AI models, like object detectors or image classifiers. The LLM serves as the “brain” of an agent, decomposing complex queries into multiple tasks and resolving them step-by-step through reasoning and autonomous tool use. In particular, the suggested LLM-based Planning Agent (LPA) utilizes LLM-based ReAct planning [5] as the core component to implement an AI assistant. To answer complex and ambiguous natural language questions from users, the system automatically identifies required information sources, synthesizes retrieval requests, analyzes obtained information, and generates textual responses. To retrieve the required data, we equip the LPA with several tools available on the cloud infrastructure of an FA lab, such as programming interfaces allowing search over documents on shares, wikis, and job logging databases, or access to other AI components, like image classifiers. The tests and evaluation

demonstrated that the agent is capable of autonomous, robust operation in a productive environment. It successfully interprets complex technical queries and autonomously uses reasoning and external tools to produce a textual answer suitable for an FA engineer. These achievements illustrate the potential of the LPA concept in a practical use case, namely supporting FA.

The paper is organized as follows: After an introduction to LLMs and intelligent agents, we detail the technical design, development, and implementation of the LPA application. Next, we evaluate agent's performance in generating high-quality responses to FA queries. Finally, we conclude with key findings and recommendations for future research.

#   LLM-based Planning Agents

LLMs represent a significant advancement in NLP, leveraging the transformer architecture [6] to process and predict text based on patterns learned from extensive corpora. These models, with billions of parameters, excel in language understanding and generation tasks. Key milestones in their development include bidirectional transformers for contextual encoding [7], encoder-decoder architecture for text-to-text tasks [8], and GPT-3 autoregressive model [9]. Nevertheless, LLMs often show limited performance for specific domains, like semiconductor FA, where domain-specific knowledge is crucial for effective problem-solving.

To address this, several strategies have been developed to enhance LLMs' capabilities. Instruction fine-tuning [10, 11] further enables LLMs to follow natural language instructions and adapt for domain-specific tasks. Similarly, in-context learning or prompt-based learning becomes an increasingly popular alternative to the computationally intensive fine-tuning [12]. These methods automatically augment user input with textual prompts, like in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) [13], as well as specific techniques, such as few-shot or Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [14]. For example, CoT prompts decompose complex problems into intermediate steps, significantly improving performance on reasoning tasks. Zeroshot CoT variants, such as appending “let’s think step by step” to prompts, have also shown efficacy [15] in various tasks. Factors like the number of reasoning steps in CoT prompts further influence effectiveness, with more steps benefiting complex tasks [16]. However, both fine-tuning and prompting are based on specific preprogrammed pipelines, which may not be flexible enough to adapt to the specific needs of users and require much maintenance efforts to reflect changes in the data and software landscape of an FA lab.

To address this issue, recent advancements in AI have facilitated the convergence of the classical concept of intelligent agents [17] with the transformative capabilities of LLMs. Intelligent agents are fundamentally characterized by their ability to perceive their environment and respond in a manner that aligns with predefined objectives. In the FA context, goal-oriented agents are particularly relevant as they

leverage search and planning mechanisms to reach desirable goals, e.g., interpreting the states of a sample and corresponding analysis tasks. The belief-desire-intention architecture further enhances this paradigm by incorporating the internal goals of an agent, such as assisting an AI engineer in solving a problem [18]. However, the applicability of these solutions in mission-critical enterprise environments remains to be thoroughly validated. Key challenges include seamlessly integrating tool handling with LLMs, such as combining database queries with the natural language processing capabilities of LLMs, accurately assessing tool functionalities to prevent unintended consequences (e.g., accidental database modifications or email dispatches), and implementing robust mechanisms for error handling during tool execution failures [19].

![graph TD\n    A[Select appropriate tool for executing the planned action] --> B[LLM]\n    B -->|Actions| C[Environment]\n    C -->|Observations| D[Result from tool execution]\n    B -->|Reasoning/Thinking| B](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_d3d0f3bef5524953817e8a2e90b4590b_7.png)
# Figure 1: General schema of the ReAct approach [5] to planning as iterative task generation

In literature, LLM-based Planning Agents (LPA), still do not have a common architecture and might include different sets of components [20, 21, 22, 23]. In this paper, we consider the following LPA core components: (1) Plan Generation, where the agent decomposes high-level tasks into executable subtasks and formulates a step-by-step plan; (2) Action Matching, which involves selecting appropriate external tools to execute the subtasks; (3) Memory, enabling the agent to retain information across multiple interactions; and (4) Feedback, allowing the agent to refine its plan based on internal reflection or external outcomes.

Figure 2 shows an abstract agent design with the selected components. The system employs two planning approaches for FA applications. The first approach, online replanning, generates a complete plan and adapts it dynamically based on feedback after each step. This approach aims to ensure consistency and avoid endless loops by incorporating criteria for valid answers. The second approach, iterative task generation with a ReAct agent, interleaves reasoning and action execution, utilizing environment feedback to refine subsequent actions. This method, inspired by factual question answering. ReAct [5] is one of the most influential and widely adopted

planning methods. It employs a thought-action-observation framework, which defines an iterative process involving action selection, execution, retrieval of observations, and the use of these observations to plan subsequent actions. The overall workflow is illustrated in Figure 1. The ReAct approach has demonstrated superior performance across various tasks compared to standalone LLMs, as it effectively integrates real-time information retrieval through web interaction tools with advanced reasoning capabilities.

LPA actions are usually implemented as a set of tools that a planner can use to interact with the environment, like APIs for retrieving FA data or AI models for specific FA tasks. Tool descriptions must be manually curated for effective integration into prompts, following practices from [24]. Feedback from tools is processed to ensure compatibility with the agent's reasoning context.

#   Technical Design and Implementation of the LLM-Based Planning Agent

This section outlines the design and implementation of the Proof-of-Concept LPA, detailing the core design decisions and system architecture. Given the novelty of LPA systems and the lack of industrial examples, a flexible and iterative approach was chosen, especially for prompt design, which required extensive prototyping. The final application was refactored into a modular, object-oriented Python program. Each tool is encapsulated as a class; prompts, logs, and domain-specific data

are stored in structured directories. A global settings file manages model selection and paths. Prompts are stored as editable text files, dynamically filled with runtime values and FA-specific knowledge. Logging is implemented for system, user-facing, and evaluation outputs to ensure full traceability. The application is built using the LangChain framework, chosen for its flexible support of agent-based architectures and modular design.

#   Agent Initialization

Agent initialization begins with model selection via the global configuration. Models used in our implementation include Mixtral 8×7B (32k) [25], LLaMA3-70B (8.2k), and LLaMA3-8B (8k) [26]. A temperature = 0 is used to ensure deterministic responses of an LLM.

Listing 1: Definition of ElasticSearch as LangChain tool

query_elastic_failure_analysis_jobs_database_tool = Tool(name="query elastic failure analysis jobs database", func=elasticsearch_tool.
query_elastic_failure_analysis_jobs_database, description="Useful if you need to retrieve information ab failure analysis jobs, specific devices/products and tasks a findings of previous analyses. This tool allows searching specific information in the elastic database contain information about all failure analysis jobs. It returns sea results of the database query. Input is a text with a w formulated specific question or search instruction specify what information to search for

Tool integration follows a structured three-step process: (1) the tool logic is encapsulated in a callable function, (2) the tool is wrapped as a LangChain tool with a name and a natural language description (used by the LLM for selection), and (3) it is added to the agent's tool list. All tools accept a single text input. To ensure robustness, each tool class includes a method to verify availability by checking connectivity and authorization, so that only operational tools are included at runtime. This prevents execution errors and avoids confusion in tool selection. Once tools and models are initialized, the agent can be created and launched using LangChain's AgentExecutor, which orchestrates the reasoning loop and tool invocation.

Prompt handling uses modular templates with curly brackets for runtime values (e.g., input) and uppercase markers (e.g., ELASTICFIELDS) for previous domain-specific insertions. Templates are loaded and formatted at runtime using LangChain utilities, supporting reuse and maintainability.

Intent Classification optionally precedes execution to tailor prompts based on user queries. The LLM assigns one of five predefined categories: (0) root cause or next analysis step suggestion, (1) general failure modes, (2) similar job identification, (3) related general information, or (4) no classification possible. Tested on 20 labeled queries, the classifier performed well overall but showed some ambiguity-related errors.

#   ReAct Agent Implementation

The ReAct agent is implemented using LangChain's ReAct prompting framework, extended for domain-specific adaptation and increased robustness in production-like environments. Two general prompt versions are supported: the standard LangChain ReAct prompt and a custom variant based on intent classification. Only zero-shot prompting is used in this work. Early tests with few-shot prompting, which included sample ReAct loops, resulted in degraded output quality. LLMs often copied irrelevant example details (e.g. job IDs), corrupting the results. In contrast, zero-shot prompts with clear instructions and domain context proved more stable and effective.

The ReAct prompt uses placeholders for the user input, tool names and tool descriptions. These are dynamically populated with the user's query and the list of available tools (name, input type, description). The prompt follows a structured, iterative format of Question, Thought, Action, Action Input, Observation. Each interaction is stored in an agent scratchpad, which accumulates the full reasoning history to guide subsequent steps. A final response is generated only when the LLM decides that sufficient information has been gathered.

The agent is executed via a custom wrapper that constructs the ReAct chain using the selected prompt, LLM and tool list. LangChain's AgentExecutor manages the Thought-Action-Observation loop until a final response is produced. Parameters such as timeout, maximum iterations, and parsing error behavior are configurable. A callback handler records each step

for later analysis. The complete control flow is illustrated in the sequence diagram (Appendix 5).

Model-specific issues were observed during testing: while Mixtral handled the standard ReAct prompt correctly, LLaMA3 models failed to stop at the “Observation” keyword, probably due to tokenization differences. This broke the loop logic. A variant using “Response” was introduced, along with a mechanism to conditionally switch stop sequences depending on the model.

#   Listing 2: Excerpt from an exemplary agent scratchpad with inserted information

Thought: I need to find similar failure analysis jobs that have a short between a signal and a power domain, and ....

Action: query elastic failure analysis jobs database
Action Input: ""short between signal and power domain""
AND ""bent down lead"" AND ""lead frame""

Observation: ['"" {'Projectnr': '...', → 'Package': '', ... 'No delamination seen .

To handle long execution loops, the agent logic has been modified to avoid context window overflow. By default, LangChain appends the full scratchpad at each step, which may exceed the context window. To prevent this, the scratchpad is dynamically trimmed to half the available context window. This required overriding LangChain's default agent creation function to ensure stable operation.

#   Online Replanning Agent Implementation

The online replanning agent was implemented from scratch using LangChain components and defined in a dedicated class. Unlike the ReAct agent's reactive loop, this architecture follows a structured plan-act-replan cycle, with separate LLM prompt chains for each stage. Following optional intent classification, the system uses a planning prompt to generate an initial step-by-step plan via a dedicated planner chain. Both zero-shot and few-shot styles were tested. Each step is then executed by a simplified ReAct-style execution agent, which receives the current task and prior observations. The result is appended to the execution history.

After the completed action execution, a replanner chain revises the remaining steps based on newly acquired observations. Past steps are preserved and excluded from modification, achieved through careful prompt engineering. This loop continues until the plan is completed or a 15-step limit is reached. The current step in the plan is explicitly maintained across iterations. To reduce LLM inconsistencies, planner and replanner outputs are formatted as enumerated lists. Due to the absence of structured output support at implementation time, step parsing is handled via regular expressions. Although effective, this remains brittle and should be replaced with structured output parsing in future versions.

A key challenge was ensuring that only future steps are altered during replanning, requiring precise prompt instructions. Another recurring issue was the generation of overly detailed, human-centric steps (e.g., manual electrical testing, documentation), which are unsuitable for an agent's autonomous execution. As in the ReAct agent, accumulated observations are truncated to half the context window to avoid overflow. After completion, a final evaluator prompt synthesizes the answer from the latest observation, prior steps, and an output directive tailored to the use case from intent classification. The full agent loop is illustrated in the sequence diagram (Appendix 6).

#   Transparency and Robustness Additions

To ensure production readiness, the agent includes measures for robustness, transparency, and short-term memory support.

Error handling covers all critical failure points, including file I/O, LLM API access (e.g., outages), and external tool responses. Exceptions are logged and handled gracefully, either continuing with reduced functionality or halting with a controlled message, depending on severity.

Logging operates on two levels. A technical log records system events, warnings, and errors in a timestamped rotating CSV file. A parallel user-facing log records intermediate observations, including step, type, content, and references, structured for display and downstream analysis.

Short-term memory enables later reasoning steps to access earlier tool outputs. A dedicated memory class stores observations as structured CSV entries, retrievable by type. To remain within LLM context limits, retrieved entries are trimmed to fit half the context window.

These mechanisms enhance the system's stability, traceability, and suitability for integration into real-world engineering workflows.

#   Technical Design and Implementation of the LLM-Based Planning Agent's Actions

Agent actions are realized through external tools, typically invoked via internal APIs to access information or perform computations beyond the agent LLM's pretrained scope. Tool selection must balance functionality and context length, while ensuring data security through internal services only. Three categories were integrated: knowledge retrieval tools, an ML-based analysis tool, and explicit reasoning tools.

#   FA Knowledge Retrieval from ElasticSearch

ElasticSearch is used to query Infineon's internal FA job data, providing structured access to historical iFAct job records and documents. Two tool functions were implemented: one retrieves jobs by JobID, the other enables general querying from natural language. Queries are expressed in ElasticSearch's Query DSL (a JSON-based domain language) and executed using the Python client via es.search(index='..., body=query).

For general queries, a single LLM-driven tool was implemented instead of separate tools per field. This enables complex, multifield queries and avoids agent prompt bloat. The LLM receives a task prompt, a list of valid fields, and field explanations to construct DSL queries. The output is parsed from unstructured text into JSON and used for API calls. Returned results are cleaned of metadata and unnecessary strings to save context space. If the DSL syntax is incorrect, a repair mechanism triggers up to two LLM-based retries using the original prompt and error feedback. This design allows flexible, contextual querying while keeping prompts compact, a key trade-off in production-grade LPAs.

Listing 3: Example of complex query that was generated within a normal program flow for the question “What is the failure mode ‘Fused Wire’ related to?”

```
"{ "query": {
               "bool": { "must": [{"match":
              {"ImageLabel": "Fused Wire"}}]}],
               "size": 5,
               _source": ["Projectnr", "ImageLabel",
               "JobSummary"] }"
```

Listing 4: Example of a generated description explaining the generated query

"Description: This query searches for documents where the "ImageLabel" field contains the phrase "Fused Wire". It returns the top 5 results, including the columns 'Projectnr', 'ImageLabel', and 'JobSummary'. The 'JobSummary' column may provide more information about the failure mode and its context."

#   General Knowledge Retrieval from Confluence Pages

Confluence is Infineon's internal wiki system containing specialist FA knowledge and product data. The tool enables keyword-based search via the Confluence Query Language (CQL) using the Atlassian Python API. For each user query, text and site search return relevant page IDs, from which titles and body content are retrieved. An LLM then evaluates each page's relevance to the original question. Only relevant pages are summarized and returned as observations, reducing context usage while preserving meaningful content. A mode excluding known evaluation-answer pages is available for test scenarios.

Integration of a Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipeline A Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) service, developed in a parallel thesis project [4], was also integrated. It enriches LLM responses by injecting relevant content of retrieved, domain-specific documents into the prompt. The service indexes FA-specific documents and is accessed via FastAPI using simple GET requests. RAG was tested both as a standard

agent tool and as a preprocessing step to enrich the query prior to agent execution.

#   Machine Learning Action: Image Retrieval and Mold Void Checking

To demonstrate ML integration into the LPA workflow, a mold void detection model was added as a tool. It analyzes scanning acoustic microscopy (SAM) topscan images of TDSO-packaged devices, returning bounding boxes and confidence scores. The tool chain includes (1) image retrieval from the iFAct API, (2) pre-processing with a split-image service, and (3) model inference via API. Only SAM images labeled as “top” or “front” are selected. Inputs are base64-encoded images; outputs are post-processed to summarize voids by confidence range. Since the model is trained only on TDSO packages, a warning is issued for incompatible images. This tool illustrates how ML services can be orchestrated within LLM-agent workflows, extending capabilities beyond text-based retrieval.

#   Reasoning Actions with Prompting: Abductive and Practical Reasoning

Two explicit reasoning tools were implemented to complement the agent's implicit reasoning: abductive reasoning (inferring likely root causes from partial observations) and practical reasoning (suggesting next analysis steps). Both are implemented as prompt-based tools and can access prior observations via the agent's short-term memory. Each tool loads a reasoning prompt, optionally appends previous observations, and prompts the LLM to generate structured reasoning outputs. Two prompt variants were tested: (a) simple prompts requesting hypotheses or recommendations, and (b) explanatory prompts guiding the LLM through step-by-step reasoning, including rating hypotheses or assessing action consequences. Both were evaluated in ablation studies.

For abductive reasoning, the LLM receives prior observations and is instructed to generate 1–3 hypotheses for possible failure causes. A structured prompt version additionally guides the LLM to rate each hypothesis from 0 to 10 based on how well it explains the data. For practical reasoning, the LLM receives prior hypotheses and findings and is asked to recommend concrete, goal-driven next analysis steps. A prompt provides additional structured information including general FA workflows and harmonized task names. This modular prompting approach enables the LPA to perform explicit, interpretable reasoning steps, supporting transparency, testability, and integration of domain knowledge into the agent's decision-making.

#   Evaluation

To assess the performance and robustness of the implemented LLM-based planning agent (LPA), we conducted extensive ablation studies across different configurations. The goals were to evaluate (1) technical robustness, (2) answer quality compared to gold standards, and (3) the impact of various architectural and tool choices.

#   Experiment Setup and Execution

A total of 15 representative FA-related questions were used. All configurations are shown in Table 1. While the full combinatorial space would result in 1,296 configurations (19,440 runs), only scientifically interesting combinations were selected. Configurations without core retrieval tools like ElasticSearch or Confluence were excluded, as their absence would clearly degrade performance. Answer quality was evaluated automatically using a Mixtral 8x7B model prompted to score the generated output against gold standard answers on a 1–5 Likert scale. All test executions and evaluations were fully automated. Each run was logged in an evaluation CSV, including configuration details, tool usage, the test question, the gold answer, the evaluated score, and the score reason. Invalid runs (e.g., tool or model failures) were rerun. The final logs were structured into tables and pivot charts for grouped analysis across configurations. Over 2000 valid runs were performed in total.

# Table 1: Overview over tested component configurations

|Component|Tested Variants|
|---|---|
|Model|Mixtral 8x7B, Llama3 70B, Llama3 8B|
|Agent|ReAct, online replanning zero-shot, online replanning few-shot|
|Intent classification|with intent classification, without intent classification|
|Short-term memory|with memory, without memory|
|Abductive reasoning|simple abductive reasoning prompt, explanatory abductive reasoning prompt, no distinct abductive reasoning tool|
|Practical reasoning|simple practical reasoning prompt, explanatory practical reasoning prompt, no distinct practical reasoning tool|
|Retrieval augmented generation tool|with RAG tool, without RAG tool|
|Retrieval augmented generation preprocessing|with RAG preprocessing, without RAG preprocessing|


#   Experiment Results

Key findings from the evaluation are summarized below. All scores represent average values over the 15 representative FA-related questions.

· ReAct outperformed online replanning in both runtime and answer quality. ReAct averaged 3.5 minutes per run vs. 14 minutes for online replanning. The best ReAct setup without RAG but with intent reached 3.25 (avg. 2.63), compared to 3.07 (avg. 2.83) for the best online replanning configuration.

· Mixtral 8x7B outperformed Llama3 70B in ReAct setups; Llama3 70B performed slightly better in online replanning.

● Intent classification improved performance and was present in all top configurations.

● Short-term memory and reasoning tools (abductive, practical) showed no consistent benefit.

● RAG improved answer quality, especially as preprocessing. The best configuration reached 3.6 (avg. 3.14), but added 3 minutes runtime.

● Llama3 8B underperformed with a best score of 2.47 (avg. 2.13) and was excluded from RAG tests.

The best-performing configuration across all experiments, achieving a best average answer quality of 3.6, was: ReAct agent, Mixtral 8x7B, intent classification, short-term memory, no abductive reasoning, simple practical reasoning, and RAG integration as preprocessing.

Overall, answer quality is mixed but promising for a PoC, with many partially useful answers indicating feasibility. Considering technical robustness, all configurations executed reliably. Failures due to service unavailability or timeouts were detected by log checking and resolved. The system consistently produced answers, or correctly indicated when time or iteration limits were exceeded. This confirms the implementation is robust enough for deployment, practical use and user-facing evaluation.

#   Experiment Discussion

The evaluation confirms the technical feasibility of LPA-based support for failure analysis. While average answer quality was moderate (2–3), top configurations reached up to 3.6, demonstrating that useful responses can be generated. However, answer quality remains sensitive to both prompt formulation and the availability of relevant information.

Although many runs were conducted, the significance of the results should be interpreted with caution. All prompt-based components are highly dependent on the exact wording and structure of their prompts; thus, the results reflect the performance of specific prompt implementations rather than the general effectiveness of the component types. Furthermore, in the initial experiments, question characteristics, such as clarity and the retrievability of relevant information, had a greater impact on answer quality than configuration changes. This highlights the importance of better knowledge integration and more comprehensive test coverage.

The LLM-based evaluation method proved scalable for large test sets but remains inherently brittle and subjective. Future work should incorporate user studies and well-defined ground truth data to validate practical utility. Developing a benchmark dataset with diverse, real-world FA questions and expert-validated answers would significantly enhance the robustness of future evaluations.

#   User Interface Creation and Cloud Deployment

To make the LPA application accessible to engineers, a simple user interface was developed using Streamlit, a lightweight

Python framework for web-based applications. The interface enables users to submit questions, monitor agent progress, and inspect results.

# Figure 3: Screenshot of the Failure Analysis Agent application: UI after finishing the processing, displaying the whole trajectory including the answer.

Upon launch, users can optionally activate RAG preprocessing via checkbox, trading off improved answer quality against increased runtime. A text field accepts natural language questions; execution begins via a button press. During runtime, users are shown intermediate steps from the agent's reasoning trajectory using LangChain callback handlers. Each action/observation pair can be expanded for inspection. After execution, the full reasoning trajectory and the final answer are displayed. Below, a structured table presents intermediate outputs for each tool. Informative error messages are shown for tool or model failures (e.g., unavailable LLM or disconnected tools). If critical LLM components fail, execution halts with a message. Tool unavailability is reported, and partial processing continues. A built-in feedback mechanism allows users to rate answers (1–5) and leave optional textual feedback. All entries (question, answer, config, tool status, rating, comment, timestamp) are logged anonymously for evaluation. This minimal but functional interface enables hands-on experimentation and evaluation in realistic usage scenarios and prepares the groundwork for future usability studies. Further screenshots are included in the appendix.

To demonstrate productive applicability, the LPA application was deployed on Infineon's internal cloud platform. Deployment was conducted via an internal GitLab repository. Secrets (e.g., credentials) and configuration paths were defined as environment variables and accessed in the application via os.environ. To enable concurrent agent sessions, UUIDs were appended to filenames to prevent file conflicts. Logging and data files were transferred via OpenShift CLI using oc cp commands. This deployment served both as a working

prototype for users and as a showcase for internal stakeholders, proving the LPA's technical deployability within enterprise IT environments.

#   Conclusion and Future Work

This work demonstrated the feasibility of applying Large Language Model-based Planning Agents (LPAs) to support semiconductor FA. A fully functional PoC agent was designed, implemented, and deployed within Infineon's IT infrastructure, integrating LLM reasoning, external tool use, and autonomous task decomposition. The agent processed complex technical queries and delivered structured, human-readable responses.

Developed through a structured, waterfall-aligned methodology, the system addressed FA-specific requirements and integrated productive tools, including databases and proprietary services. Evaluation showed moderate average answer quality, with the best configuration using the ReAct agent, Mixtral 8x7B, intent classification, and RAG preprocessing. The agent proved technically robust, but performance was sensitive to prompt formulation and available knowledge.

Despite the novelty of the LPA approach, integration into existing infrastructure succeeded. Challenges such as prompt brittleness and tool interoperability were mitigated through modular design, iterative prototyping, meticulous error handling, and externalized configuration. The deployed application includes a user interface and logging mechanisms to support practical usage and transparency.

Overall, this PoC lays the groundwork for applying LPAs in FA and similarly complex domains, enabling not only advanced information retrieval, but also automation of high-level reasoning tasks in knowledge-intensive environments.

Future Extensions and Scalability: Future development should expand the agent's capabilities by integrating more tools and implementing additional reasoning actions. A key direction is incorporating domain-specific background knowledge, either through prompt design or fine-tuning. Multi-agent setups, where LLMs collaborate or critique each other, could enhance performance but raise resource concerns. Human-in-the-loop mechanisms may further improve reliability. For full scalability, secure user management and concurrent operation must be addressed.

Added Focus on User Experience and Evaluation: Usability testing with FA engineers is essential to refine the interface and interaction flow. Observations of real-world use and structured evaluations should inform system adaptation. Additionally, creating a benchmark dataset with realistic FA queries and expert answers would enable consistent, objective performance assessment.

Expected Advances in LLM-Based Planning Agents: As LLMs evolve, newer models with built-in planning capabilities

or models that are fine-tuned on FA data may significantly boost agent performance. Ongoing research into agent architectures, reasoning strategies, and tool orchestration will be key. Sharing frameworks and evaluation methods across domains can accelerate the maturity and adoption of LPA systems in industrial contexts.

#   Listing 7: Zero-shot OnlineReplanning planning prompt template, inspired by [27]

For the given question, come up with a step by step plan.

This plan should involve individual questions, that if answered correctly one after another, → will yield the correct answer. Do not add any superfluous steps.

The result of the final step should be the final answer. Make sure that each step has all, → the information needed. Do not skip steps.

Output the plan in a list format like this: [1...,\n 2. ..., \n 3...,\n ...]

User question: {input}

#   Listing 8: Prompt template for replanning in OnlineReplanning

For the given question, you came up with a step by step plan.

This plan involves individual questions, that if answered correctly one after another will, → yield the correct overall answer. The result of the final step should be the final, → answer.

Check if, with the learnings from the past steps, the plan is still valid to answer the
, → question or if the future steps to be adapted. You can change existing future steps,
, → add new future steps or delete unnecessary future steps. Do only include new future
, → steps that can be solved via information processing, including finding information,
, → summarizing information, reasoning and similar actions. Include the relevant technical
, → terms in the steps. Remember your main goal is to find information to help the user
, → answer their question. You must not include steps that need practical analysis, , → investigation or in general conducting or performing analysis actions on a real device , → or in the laboratory.

If you add future steps add only absolutely necessary steps. Make the plan as short as

, → possible, with as few steps as possible, between 5 and maximum 10 steps overall. If, → you think you can already answer the question based on the previous results from the, → past steps, remove all future steps from the plan.

The user question was this: {input}

Your original plan was this: {plan}

You have received these past results: {past_steps}

#   Next step: {next_step}

Update your plan accordingly. The overall plan must have less than 11 steps. Update only, → steps not done yet. Just copy the previous steps before the next step from the, → original plan into the new plan. Do not change the previous steps. Do not add anything, → to the previous steps. Each of the previous steps is only one sentence with only the, → step. Only output all the plan steps and no additional information.

Output the plan in a list format like this: [1. ..., \n 2. ..., \n 3. ..., \n ...]
