#   Conclusions

The successful identification of the missing Thin Film Resistor (TFR) defects across the three case studies highlights the critical importance of a comprehensive and structured failure analysis (FA) approach in uncovering elusive circuit-level continuity issues. Across all cases, the root cause was traced to missing Thin Film Resistors (TFRs).

Through the combination of circuit analysis, microprobing, advanced fault isolation techniques (OBIRCH, LEM, and Thermal analysis) and Physical Failure Analysis (Parallel lapping and FIB cross-sectioning), the physical defects were localized and confirmed. These findings validate the robustness of the deployed failure analysis approach and emphasize the critical role of integrating electrical characterization, fault isolation, physical analysis, and inspections in uncovering the defects from complex yield and test failures.

#   Case Study: Nanoprobe Verification of EOS Induced Resistor-Capacitor Oscillator Frequency Shift Failure

Randal Mulder, Yuting Wei

Silicon Laboratories, Inc.; 400 West Cesar Chavez, Austin, TX 78701randy.mulder@silabs.com

#   Abstract

A customer began experiencing numerous failures at their production line test resulting in a line down situation. Evaluation of the customer's failing boards identified the problem was caused by a ~5% frequency shift for the resistor capacitor oscillator (RCO) circuits for an IC chip on the customer's board.

This paper will demonstrate how an unexpected standard deprocessing result first indicated EOS as a possible root cause of the oscillator frequency shift failure even though the leakage tests did not indicate an EOS issue. It will then be shown how nanoprobe analysis of the oscillator circuit was able to confirm that EOS was the primary failure mechanism. Confirmation and corrective action by the customer eliminating the EOS problem validated the analysis results.

#   Introduction

A customer began experiencing failures at their production line test resulting in a line down situation. The failure mode was determined to be a ~5% frequency shift for the oscillator circuits in the IC chip. Failing devices from the customer were returned for analysis.

Production testing of the returned failures confirmed the failure mode. The oscillator circuits were exhibiting a ~5% frequency shift. The failing devices did not fail any additional tests in the test program. The chip had three different resistor-capacitor oscillator (RCO) circuit types that were exhibiting the frequency shift problem which are shown in Figure 1. The three oscillators were located closely together at the bottom right corner of the device.

The non-destructive investigation exhibited the following characteristics:

● Optical Microscope, X-ray and CSAM inspection results were negative showing no anomalies.

● Devices were curve traced with results showing no IO, Functional or VDD supply pin leakages.

● Bench testing IDD values for the VDD supplies did not indicate any internal leakage issues.

● A functional FA evaluation board was used to evaluate the devices programmed to exercise the oscillator circuits while measuring the IDD values

for the VDD supplies. All functional IDD values were within normal value ranges.

● Backside Optical Beam Induced Resistance Change (Obirch) and Light Emission Analysis (PEM) performed while exercising the failing oscillators were negative.

![团322222222网3\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_182230442a784c4e9cbc6848aa03c621_19.png)
# Figure 1a: General device floor plan. Device failed three resistor capacitor oscillator (RCO) circuits for a 5% higher frequency shift. All three oscillators were located in close proximity (White Box) at the lower right corner of the chip.

![2\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_a556c769699d4eecb31b383d353d1be4_21.png)
# Figure 1b: Close-up of the chip area containing three resistor capacitor oscillator (RCO) circuit blocks located together at the bottom right corner of the chip.

Once the production test, non-destructive inspections, curve trace and bench testing, and backside Obirch/Light Emission were completed, an evaluation of the results was performed to determine the most likely root cause candidates. The results of the electrical evaluation did not indicate an EOS or ESD related issue because no excess leakage was detected for the VDD supplies, signal pins or IO pins. The shift in frequency pointed more to a processing problem in manufacturing. To understand what manufacturing problem could affect the performance of the Resistor Capacitor oscillator circuits, an understanding of how the oscillator is designed, constructed and functions had to be acquired to determine what must be investigated in the circuit to find root cause of the failure.

#   The Resistor Capacitor Oscillator

The Resistor Capacitor Oscillator (RCO) circuit is a standard circuit in most analog and mix signal (digital/analog) devices. Information on their purpose, design, and function is readily available on the internet. The purpose of the oscillator is to provide a consistent, controlled, stable signal needed for synchronization and control for other analog circuits [1]. An oscillator converts energy from DC power into an AC signal. The signal produced is a periodic signal usually a sine wave, square wave, or triangle wave at a specific frequency that does not require an input signal from another circuit. These signals are defined by their frequency and amplitude, which can be precisely controlled to suit specific applications. Oscillators are found in a wide array of electronic products, including clock, radio, and computer ICs. They are the base circuit of electronic systems, serving as timing references that enable circuits to synchronize and function properly.

Basic overviews of the RCO circuit design and function are available online at numerous locations. This paper references an excellent overview from the source Electronics-Tutorials [2]. The basic RCO circuit consists of an amplifier and a resistor-capacitor (RC) feedback network that produces oscillation due to the phase shift between the stages of each section (Figure 2). The amplifier produces an 180° phase shift between the amplifier output and the amplifier input signal. The feedback network is designed as a resistor-capacitor network to provide the required feedback. This configuration is used to produce an RCO circuit.

Frequency selective RC coupled amplifier circuits are easy to build and can be made to oscillate at any desired frequency by selecting the correct values of resistance and capacitance. For an RCO circuit to maintain oscillation, sufficient feedback with the correct phase (positive in-phase feedback) must be provided with the voltage gain of the amplifier being used to provide addition loop gain into the closed-loop circuit to maintain oscillations. This allows the circuit to oscillate continuously at the selected frequency.

![+VccPhase 0Phase 180°OutpuInputAmplifierwith GainPhase Shift=180FeedbackNetwork\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_7bc802a038c04915b6a3ccee31e9e3db_5.png)
# Figure 2: Block diagram for an RCO circuit showing the circuit consists of an amplifier and a feedback network [2]. Amplifiers shift the phase of the input signal 180° and the feedback network is required to shift the feedback signal back to the input an additional 180° resulting in a net shift of 360° (or 0°).

The RC phase shift network requires a minimum of three RC stages cascaded together to obtain the required value at the oscillation frequency. The amount of actual phase shift in the circuit depends upon the values of the resistor (R) and the capacitor (C), at the chosen frequency of oscillations with the phase angle ($\varphi$) being given as [2]:

$$ X_c=\frac{1}{2\pi fC}\qquad R=R,\\ Z=\sqrt{R^2+(X_C)^2}\\\varphi=\tan^{-1}\frac{X_C}{R}\end{aligned} $$

Where:

● $X_C$ = Capacitive Reactance of the capacitor

● R is the Resistance of the resistor in ohms

● f is the Oscillator Frequency in Hertz

For a RC phase shift network with three segments, the R and the C values for a desired oscillator frequency are chosen that each segment will provide a 60° phase shift as shown in Figure 3. By joining together three of these RC network segments together in series a total phase shift in the circuit of 180° at the chosen frequency is produced at the output of the network. This creates the basic “Resistor-Capacitor Oscillator” or Phase Shift Oscillator as the phase angle is shifted by a specific amount through each stage of the circuit.

![C1C3C2InpuOutputR1180°180°120\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_803160e5665d445fa795ec10a688ee00_0.png)
# Figure 3: Schematic of a three segment RC phase shift network [2]. Each segment consists of a resistor and a capacitor with values that produce a 60° phase shift to the to the input signal. At the network output, with three 60° phase shifts, the total phase shift for the signal is 180°.

For integrated circuit (ICs) chips, the RC phase shift network is combined with an Operational Amplifier to form an Op-amp Phase-lead RCO circuit. The oscillator circuit consists of a negative-gain operational amplifier and a three section RC phase shift network previously describe that produces the 180° phase shift. The phase shift network is connected from the op-amps output back to its “inverting” input as shown below (Figure 4).

![Positive FeedbackCCC120°+V60°0°180°VoUTAv=29+R-VOv3-Stage Phase-lead NetworkAmplification180° Shif180°Shift\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_50ce08a07803475795ac08f6b085124a_3.png)
# Figure 4: Schematic of Op-amp Phase-lead RCO circuit Circuit which combines a three-segment phase-shift network and negative gain operational amplifier [2]. The Op-amp must provide a 180° phase shift and enough gain to compensate for amplitude loss through the phase-shift network.

The desired frequency for these oscillators in IC chips is predetermined due to the overall requirements of the device design. The resistor and capacitor values in the phase-shift network are specified by the desired frequency. The resistors are polysilicon resistors manufactured in the “front-end of line” silicon of the IC chip; and the capacitors are “Metal Oxide Metal” (MOM) capacitors manufactured in the “backend of line” metallization layers. The polysilicon resistors are designed to have the same value ($R_1 = R_2 = R_3$); and the MOM capacitors are also designed to have the same value ($C_1 = C_2 = C_3$) then the frequency of oscillations produced by the RCO circuit is simply given as [2]:

$$f_r = \frac{1}{2\pi RC\sqrt{2N}}$$

Where:

● $f_r$ is the oscillators output frequency in Hertz.

● R is the feedback resistance in Ohms.

● C is the feedback capacitance in Farads.

● N is the number of RC feedback stages.

This RCO circuit summary shows that any damage, defect or manufacturing processing issues of the poly-resistors (or the MOM capacitors) that changes the values of these passive components will change the value of the oscillator frequency, phase or both. Component values must remain precise over time requiring a well-controlled manufacturing process. Reliability of the component materials must be high to maintain the values over time as the device is used in stressful environments. Any damage, defects, or drifting of the values for the passive components will result in the RCO circuit not maintaining the proper frequency or ceasing to function altogether.

#   Physical Failure Analysis

Based on the production test failure mode, the non-destructive electrical evaluation of the failing device results, and review of the RCO circuit design and function, it was determined that the best course of action was to focus the physical failure analysis (PFA) on the resistors and capacitors of the oscillator circuits. Any defectivity, damage or processing issue would result in frequency failure for the oscillator circuits with the more likely candidate being the poly-silicon resistors.

#   Delayering and Inspection:

The standard operating procedure (SOP) for failure analysis when provided multiple failing devices with the same failure mode is to perform top-down layer by layer deprocessing of the device with optical microscope and SEM inspection of the failing circuit(s) at each layer for damage, defects or processing issues that might occur during the manufacturing of the device. If the top down deprocessing finds no problems or anomalies in the circuit, then an investigation of the capacitors and poly-resistors would be performed to determine their integrity by nano-probe analysis.

Oscillator circuit 1 shown in Figure 1 was chosen as the primary circuit to investigate because its location on the chip is farther from the chip edges which would provide a better planar, layer by layer, delaying result. A good, planar, delaying result allows for most if not all the circuit area to be uniformly inspected (or nanoprobed) without introducing deprocessing artifacts that may make the investigation more difficult.

The first failing device #1 was removed from its package. Mechanical polishing was used to delay the chip layer by layer with optical microscope inspection of the failing oscillator circuit. Careful inspection of the metal layers of the MOM capacitors for the oscillator circuit did not reveal any anomalies. At the contact layer, optical microscope and SEM inspection showed the anomalous material in the transistor buffer adjacent to the poly-resistors and additional anomalies in the polysilicon resistor block itself (Figure 5–8). The device was sent for TEM analysis to identify the nature of the anomalies in the poly-resistor block being of primary interest.

#   TEM Analysis Results:

The failing device #1 was sent for TEM analysis on one of the defect locations in the poly-resistor block. Due to resource limitations and area, only one location could be chosen for the analysis. Figure 9 shows an SEM image of the anomaly of interest in the poly-resistor block at both low and high kV. The TEM image results show the material is comprised of Metall metallization extending down into the ILD0 layer possibly contacting the polysilicon resistor at that location (Figure 10). No processing issues were observed for the poly-resistors. It was hypothesized that the cause might have been due to EOS burn-out. The resulting heat from an EOS event would be sufficient to melt the underlying oxide allowing Metal 1 metallization to penetrate the ILD0 oxide layer.

![SEM Low kVa)SEM High kVTEM X-SectionLocationb\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_5ce9737e4f674a12a5fac8cfe4d8cf53_0.png)
# Figure 9: SEM images at one of the anomaly locations in the poly-resistor block at a) low kV and b) high kV shows the anomaly is not surface material but embedded into the ILDO above the poly-resistors. The TEM cross section location is shown.

![bMetalBarrier\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_9a5838ebfdf64369a9ddbb040b14affb_2.png)
# Figure 10: a) TEM cross section image of the anomaly shows it is residual Metal 1 metallization that penetrated the ILD0 layer. EDS mapping b), c) confirms the material consists of metallization and barrier metal from the Metal 1 layer.

EDS Spectrum Analysis was performed on the anomaly. The results confirm that the anomaly consists of only Metal 1 metallization and barrier metal. No foreign elements were found (Figure 11).

![Cps/eV40Metal/Barrier35Peaks30125MetalMetalBarrierO20S1510-5\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_46031e8f3de54db6ac10e420bb94c920_5.png)

#   TEM Analysis Summary

· Metallization was observed in the ILD layer which may indicate EOS burn-out at the upper layer.

· No obvious process anomaly was revealed in the poly resistors.

#   EDS Spectrum Analysis Summary

· Metallization element extrusions were observed which may have resulted from burn-out.

· No foreign element was found.

· Anomaly comprised of only Metal 1 elements.

The TEM Analysis result pointing to EOS was unexpected and surprising. Production test, the initial electrical evaluation, and Obirch / Photo Emission Microscope (PEM) analysis did not give any indication of EOS damage. If an EOS event did occur, a high current condition would propagated through the circuit area resulting in excessive heating of the oscillator circuit blocks.

An EOS breakdown location had to be identified for confirmation of the failure mechanism to convince the customer. The results for the TEM only identified the symptoms of an EOS event. Therefore, a second failing device was chosen for deprocessing to silicon substrate. Hydro Fluoric acid was used to remove the metal layers of the device to expose the silicon substrate. SEM inspection observed EOS damage in the oscillator circuit in the circuitry just below the poly-resistor block (Figure 12). A third device was also deprocessed to silicon substrate. It also showed EOS damage at the same circuit location (Figure 13).

![Iransistor BufferHeaDameePoly-resistorBlock...EOSBreakdown\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_5c781124db3a49d5967ebf8f8c87da66_0.png)
# Figure 12a: SEM image of the second failing device deprocessed to silicon substrate shows EOS damage in the oscillator circuit just below the location of the poly-resistor block.

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_3dbd63c31426419aabda87421f3e4978_2.png)
# Figure 12b: Close-up SEM image of the second failing device deprocessed to silicon substrate showing the EOS damage in the oscillator circuit just below the location of the polyresistor block.

![0000090000000900\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_c4df8fe533564c7ea6dd89f5b7974527_4.png)
# Figure 13a: Optical microscope image of a third failing device deprocessed to silicon substrate showing EOS damage in the oscillator circuit just below the location of the polyresistor block.

![](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_666d6b7bedc1423d976b0144e987013e_6.png)
# Figure 13b: SEM image of the third failing device deprocessed to silicon substrate showing the EOS damage in the oscillator circuit just below the location of the polyresistor block.

At this point in the analysis, there was now a high level of certainty that EOS was the root cause of failure for the oscillator frequency shift even though production testing and electrical evaluation had not indicated it; and that the customer was damaging the devices in the manufacturing line. For the customer to accept the findings, the EOS damage had to be tied to the frequency shift of the oscillators.

It is well known that the sheet resistance for polysilicon resistors is affected by heat. Numerous studies can be found showing how temperature affects poly-silicon resistance over time based on doping concentration and doping type [3], [4], [5]. However, most of these studies are only concerned with temperature ranges that include normal operating temperatures and conditions; or what temperatures a device will experience during a reliability test for qualification were temperatures might range from -40°C to 150°C (Figure 14).

However, under the conditions of an EOS event, temperatures at a localized breakdown point are high enough to reach the melting point for silicon (1,414 °C (2,577 °F)), silicon dioxide (1,610°C (2,930°F)), and metallization (1,084°C (1,983°F)). The heat then radiates out and dissipates throughout the chip. Therefore, it's reasonable to assume that polysilicon resistors exposed to very high temperatures for a short period of time can have the sheet resistance values of the polysilicon permanently shifted. For this hypothesis to be proven, nanoprobe analysis would have to be performed on the polysilicon resistors to measure the resistance for the failing oscillator.

#   Nanoprobe Analysis

#   Nanoprobe Sample Preparation:

A fourth failing device was submitted for nanoprobe analysis of the poly-resistors. The device was removed from the package and delayering was performed down to the top of the contact layer for nanoprobe analysis. Optical microscope inspection of the oscillator circuit observed a slight irregularity at the middle top of the poly-resistor block (Figure 15). SEM inspection at the location observed an irregular shaped area of material that was at first thought to be residual material from the delayering (Figure 16). The device was cleaned, and the sample was re-inspected with the SEM, but the material remained indicating it was not residue material on the surface of the sample but embedded in the oxide. The anomaly has a darker contrast and the contacts for the two poly-resistors show less contrast indicating a leakage path to ground bleeding off charge; and shows the anomaly extends from the contacts of the two poly-resistors into the contacts for the Well-tie.

#   Nanoprobe Measurements:

The device was mounted in an AFP nanoprobe system [6]. Initial topographical imaging of the anomaly area produced an image that had image quality similar to what was seen in the SEM (Figure 20). The anomaly was re-imaged several more times and the image remained consistent indicating a hardness to the material. The contacts for the top two middle poly-resistor segments are not visible for probing so verifying the leakage to the Well-ties was not performed.

Individual poly resistor segments were nanoprobed and measured for their resistance values for the failing device and for a reference device. The resistor segments chosen for measuring were the segments at each corner of the block (Top Right Edge (TRE), Top Left Edge (TLE), Lower Right Edge (LRE), Lower Left Edge (LLE)) and one segment in the Middle Middle (MM) (Figure 21).

![-\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_95bb5990a254444587b668d8551c5807_0.png)
# Figure 20: AFP topographical image of the anomaly shows an image very similar to what was seen in the SEM. Repeated AFP scanning gave a consistent image with no smearing indicating that there was a material hardness for the anomaly.

![TransistorBufferTLETREMMPoly-ResistorsLLELRE\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_f0a88bc4f11242578676f3895db1d69d_2.png)
# Figure 21: Optical microscope image of device #4 showing the location of the poly-resistor components that were measured for both the failing device and reference device.

Each poly-resistor segment has four contacts at each end of the segment. Four probe tips were used to measure each poly-resistor segment (two probe tips at each end 1,2 and 3,4) (Figure 22). The probe tips were landed on the outside contact at each end. Low voltage was applied across probes 1 and 2 while measuring current. Force was slowly applied to tips 1 and 2 to drive them into the contacts while monitoring the current to minimize tip to contact resistance. When adding force no longer caused the current to increase, tip to contact resistance had been minimized, and the process was stopped. This process was then repeated for probe tips 3 and 4.

![-一一一一---------------3<N\n](1/parseimages/imgParseSvr_img_9c49f4332ad245389a0cb637b2b40130_5.png)
# Figure 22: Image of a single poly-resistor segment from the poly-resistor block. To measure resistance, two nanoprobe tips are landed on the outside contacts at each end of the resistor. A small voltage is applied for probes 1 and 2 and current measured. Force is applied on the probe tips into the contacts minimizing probe tip to contact resistance and maximizing current. The process is repeated for probe tips 3 and 4.

After probe tip to contact resistance had been minimized for all contacts, voltage was applied to tips 1 and 3 (with 2 and 4 floating) and the current flowing through the poly-resistor segment was measured (Figure 23). Each poly-resistor component measured was swept from -1.1V to 1.1V in steps of 0.05V. The current was measured at each step and plotted (Figure 24). The resistance of the poly-resistor segment was calculated using Ohm's Law: $V = I \times R$ (or for this case $R = V / I$). The current value (I) measured at the voltage value $V = 0.5V$ was used to calculate the resistance value (R) of the poly resistor segment. This nanoprobe procedure was repeated for each designated poly-resistor segment for both the failing device and a reference device. The results are shown in Table 1. The results for poly-resister segments were average for both the failing device (Table 1a) and reference device (Table 1b) and compared (Table 1c). The calculated results indicate that the poly resistor segments on average had a resistance value that was ~50 ohms higher (5%) for the failing device than what was measured for the reference device. This resistance difference equates to the ~5% frequency shift measured for the oscillators at production test.

calculated based on Ohm’s Law (V = I x R) or for this case (R = V / I).

It was now obvious that the anomaly was ILD0 oxide that had  melted during the EOS event and resolidified resulting in the  anomalous material seen in Figures 15 - 19. Buffered Oxide  Etch (BOE) was used to etch away the oxide and expose the  polysilicon layer. The time interval used is usually sufficient  to clear away all the ILD0 oxide for a normal device. In this  case, the etching resulted in only partial removal of the  anomalous oxide (Figure 25). Oxide that is harden by  excessive heating due to EOS is much more difficult to  remove with BOE than original native oxide. The device was  then deprocessed to silicon substrate using straight Hydro  Fluoric Acid. Optical microscope inspection observed  transistors in the transistor buffer with burnt appearance for  source/drain active due to high current is common for EOS  failures (Figure 26).

Figure 25: SEM image of the fourth device after deprocessing  to the poly layer with BOE shows the ILDO oxide at the  anomaly location was difficult to remove, indicating that  heating had hardened the oxide.

98

EOS breakdown in the circuit area below the poly-resistor  block was not observed like the previous two devices 2 and 3 (Figure 26). However, based on the observations of the  analysis for this device, the preponderance of the evidence  indicated that the EOS breakdown occurred at the edge of the  top two middle poly-resistors to the adjacent Well-tie. Because the source/drains of the transistors in the transistor  buffer are connected directly to the poly-resistors through  Metal 1 metallization, EOS current was pulled through  transistors’ source/drain active resulting in the burnt  discoloration of the active silicon. With these physical  analysis results and the nanoprobe results, the analysis was  concluded with the determination that EOS damage was the  root cause of failure. The RCO circuit at location 2 was  checked for an additional failing unit and EOS damage was  also found at that location also.

Figure 26: Optical microscope inspection of the fourth device  after deprocessing to silicon substrate shows heat damage  discoloration to multiple transistor source/drain active in the  transistor buffer above the poly resistor location (red circle). These transistors are connected directly to the poly resistors  through Metal 1.

The results were unexpected based on the failure mode that  showed no excess pin or IDD leakage. However, review of  layout produced a hypothesis. This is a mix signal device. Deep N-wells are used to isolate functional blocks from  crosstalk noise from adjacent circuits throughout the chip  especially for the analog (Figure 27). Some of the analog  circuit blocks are not directly supplied by the external DC  supply for the chip but by a secondary “AC” supply circuit  which converts the external DC supply voltage to a limited  reduced supply voltage and current for the analog circuits. Therefore, there is some isolation of the analog circuits from  the external VDD supplies. If those internal analog circuits  are exposed to Charge Device Model (CDM) ESD charging  which then produces EOS damaged internally when  discharged, then leakage current may not be detected because

it is contained within the deep n-well isolation of the  circuit(s).

Figure 27: Image from Figure 1b with the locations of the  deep N-well blocks shown. Many of the circuit areas have  their own deep N-wells resulting in significant isolation.

Results Verification

The failure analysis results were sent to the customer  identifying EOS as the root cause of the oscillator circuit  failures. The customer replied that their production had  recently moved to a new production line and had recently  started producing failures. An evaluation of the customer’s  ESD/EOS mitigation procedures was performed and found  not to be insufficient. The ESD mitigation was improved, and  the failures no longer occurred verifying that the ESD/EOS  was the root cause of the oscillator failures.

Summary

This paper showed how a customer was having a problem  with functional oscillator failures at the end of line due to a  frequency shift. Initial electrical evaluation of the failing  units did not indicate any issue with EOS breakdown such as  higher current values for the VDD supplies or the  functional/IO pins. The expectation for the functional failure  was to find a wafer fab manufacturing processing problem for  the oscillator’s resistors or capacitors. Failure analysis  standard operating procedure for multiple failures first  required a standard deprocessing and inspection of one the  failing devices which resulted in finding EOS damage at the  circuit location. This prevented a longer, more tedious failure  analysis result saving time and expense. Circuit review and  nanoprobe analysis were used to confirm that heating from  the EOS event caused the performance of the functional  circuit to shift resulting in failure in the customer’s  application. 8D root cause analysis identified the problem  was poor ESD/EOS mitigation for customer’s production line  which was then corrected solving the problem.

Effectiveness of Photon Emission Microscopy in Identifying Intrinsic Device  Reliability Issues and Aiding Design Debug

Amrutha Sampath, Kristofor Dickson, Carey Wu

NXP Semiconductors, Austin, Texas, USA  Amrutha.sampath_1@nxp.com

Abstract

Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM) is a popular failure  analysis technique capable of detecting photons emitted from  defective circuitry and helps pinpoint the failure location. This  technique has helped identify open defects, polysilicon gate  defects, gate oxide-related failures, electrostatic discharge  failures, metallization failures, logic state detection, memory bit  failures, and leakage failures. In this paper, we discuss how  photon emission microscopy can be a valuable tool in  identifying and understanding intrinsic device reliability issues. We examine how emission intensity, measured by processing  photon emission images using a Python script and an opensource computer vision tool, can be used to estimate the relative  number of trapped charges compared to leakage over time  under applied stress. Through case studies, we show how  photon emission microscopy (PEM) can reveal interactions  between design processes and different IP blocks within a

microelectronic chip. Finally, we highlight how PEM’s high

sensitivity can aid in design debugging by uncovering potential  vulnerabilities that could affect future tape-outs.

Introduction

Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM) is a vital tool in Failure  Analysis (FA) for detecting defects in microelectronic devices [1,2]. It works by capturing photons emitted during electronhole recombination or intra-band electron transitions in silicon. These emissions typically occur when transistors switch states, such as charging or discharging capacitive loads, or during brief  events where current flows from Vdd to Vss through saturated  devices. For instance, in an inverter circuit, both PMOS and  NMOS transistors can be simultaneously active during a narrow  region of the voltage transfer curve. This allows current to flow  directly from VDD to GND [2,3], creating a high electric field  in the channel’s pinched-off region. Energized carriers in this  field emit visible and near-infrared photons.

PEM involves comparing the photon emissions of a failing  device with those of a known-good reference unit under  identical test conditions. Accurate interpretation of these  emissions requires a solid understanding of circuit behavior. Transistors typically emit light during switching but should  remain dark when static and outputs are discharged. Figure 1  illustrates common emission scenarios and how they can be  interpreted.

Previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of PEM  in isolating die-related failures, including open defects, polysilicon gate defects, gate oxide failures, electrostatic  discharge failures, metallization failures, logic state detection  failures, memory bit failures, and leakage failures [4-6]. This  paper emphasizes how analyzing emission intensity from PEM  images can reveal intrinsic device reliability issues and assist in  design debugging.

Figure 1: Guide to recognize how light emission occurs based  on voltage characteristics of a transistor [2].

Advanced FINFET technologies, though more robust than  planar CMOS MOSFET technology, possess key reliability  challenges [7].  These include issues caused by interface defects  acting as charge traps due to intrinsic device degradation  mechanisms, such as Hot Carrier Injection (HCI), Bias  Temperature Instability (BTI), and Time-Dependent Dielectric  Breakdown (TDDB) [8]. The physics behind HCI is that the hot  carriers in the channel near the drain-pinch-off region gain a  considerable amount of energy due to high electric fields, break

Copyright © 2025 ASM International®All rights reserved.

www.asminternational.org

ISTFA 2025: Proceedings from the 51st International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis Conference

November 16–20, 2025, Pasadena, California, USA

https://doi.org/10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2025p0101

the silicon-hydrogen (Si-H) bonds at the interface, and generate  interface-trapped charges [8]. BTI is a time-dependent  degradation mechanism that causes shifts in transistor  parameters with aging. Ions that tunnel through the gate oxide  at high temperatures trap charged carriers that flow between the  source and drain, resulting in the formation of a narrower  transistor channel due to charge loss and degradation of device  performance. BTI can be categorized as Negative BTI (NBTI), where a negative bias voltage is applied to the gate of the  transistor, and Positive BTI, where a positive bias voltage is  applied to the transistor. Several past publications have covered  these reliability mechanisms extensively [7,8].

This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of PEM in  identifying intrinsic device reliability issues in FINFET  technologies through three case studies. Case study 1 identifies  a high current-consuming NMOS issue, showing how emission  intensity analysis, utilizing a Python imaging script, can  quantify trapped charges and correlate them with current  leakage under stress. Case study 2 explores PEM's role in  design debugging across various power modes, highlighting its  sensitivity in understanding design-process interactions in  SOCs. Emission intensity comparisons of different IPs at  process corners reveal how process variations affect current  consumption. Case study 3 showcases PEM's precision in  design debugging, equivalent to analog and mixed-signal  simulation, emphasizing the need for fault-injection-proofing  of I/O pads to prevent reliability failures.

Case 1

This case involves a device subjected to a High-Voltage Stress  Test (HVST), during which all I/O pins were pulled up to the  supply voltage. Following the stress test, the unit exhibited  increased current consumption on the I/O bank power supply. Optical Beam Induced Resistance Change (OBIRCH) analysis  revealed no discernible differences between stressed and  unstressed units. However, Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM) analysis—conducted using a Mercury Cadmium  Telluride (MCT) camera with an 1800 nm filter and a constant  emission acquisition time—revealed elevated emission  intensity at a specific NMOS device in the stressed units. This  NMOS device was part of the ESD high-current applicable  circuitry.

The emission intensity, analyzed using a Python-based imaging  script and computer vision techniques, is presented in Figure 2. Additional emission images were captured using the MCT  camera with various optical filters and a fixed 60-second  acquisition time for both stressed and unstressed units. These  images, shown in Figure 3A, were analyzed to assess how  average emission intensity varied across different wavelength  spectra. The results indicated that average emission intensity  increased with broader wavelength ranges. Notably, the NMOS  device of interest in the stressed unit exhibited significantly  higher emission intensity, further indicating elevated leakage  compared to the unstressed unit.

Further PEM analysis, using the MCT camera with the 1800 nm  filter applied during the stress period, demonstrated that the  emission intensity increased with the duration of stress. This  behavior suggests charge trapping in the NMOS device. Figure  4 illustrates this trend: the unit stressed for x+5 hours exhibited  higher emission levels than both the unit stressed for x hours  and the unstressed unit. This is represented as a histogram  plotting pixel density versus emission intensity. Here, pixel  density refers to the number of pixels per unit area in the image, while emission intensity corresponds to the number of photons  detected by the MCT camera at the device of interest. The  histogram reveals that a peak at lower emission intensities  corresponds to reduced photon emission—and thus lower  leakage—in unstressed units. Conversely, a peak at higher  emission intensities indicates increased leakage in stressed  units.

Figure 2: PEM images acquired using MCT camera with an  1800 nm filter, comparing stressed and unstressed units under  a constant emission acquisition time. Computer vision-based  analysis revealed increased emission intensity at the high  current-consuming NMOS device in the stressed unit, indicating elevated leakage compared to the unstressed unit.

Figure 3a: PEM images captured using an MCT camera with  various optical filters applied, under a constant emission  acquisition time, for both stressed and unstressed units.

Figure 3b: Computer vision-based analysis on the emission  images showed that average emission intensity increased with  broader wavelength spectra. The NMOS device of interest in  the stressed unit exhibited significantly higher emission  intensity, suggesting greater leakage than in the unstressed  unit.

Figure 4a: PEM images obtained using an MCT camera with  an 1800 nm filter and a fixed 60-second emission acquisition  time when the unit was being stressed.

Figure 4b: The corresponding pixel density versus emission  intensity plot showed that the emission intensity from the high  current-consuming NMOS device increased with stress  duration, indicating the presence of trapped charges.

Thermal bake experiments were conducted on the stressed unit  to determine whether the behavior of the high-currentconsuming NMOS could be attributed to charge trapping. The  results showed a significant reduction in current following the  bake, with leakage decreasing by up to 80%. These findings, illustrated in Figure 5, suggest that the stressed units can be  nearly fully recovered through thermal treatment. The NMOS  in question is a high-current ESD protection device with a  stacked structure and larger geometry, which helps explain its  significant contribution to the externally measured leakage.

Figure 5: IV curves of the stressed unit before and after baking  demonstrate partial recovery, with reduced current  consumption at the I/O pin correlating with increased bake  temperature and duration.

This analysis highlights an intrinsic reliability concern related  to trapped charges and the effects of Bias Temperature  Instability (BTI) in high-current-consuming NMOS devices. Specifically, NFET Positive Bias Temperature Instability (PBTI) degradation is associated with electron trapping in high-

k metal gate stacks. Photon emission analysis played a crucial  role in identifying this issue, which was found to be partially  reversible through baking. The underlying mechanism was  further validated through aging simulations, which ultimately  led to circuit design modifications aimed at mitigating future  charge trapping.

Case 2

This case study utilizes Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM) to  evaluate current consumption in a device operating in lowpower mode and to investigate how process variations influence  the current drawn by specific IP blocks and power supplies. When the device was programmed into low-power mode, it was  observed that units fabricated using a Fast-Fast (FF) process  split consumed approximately 10 mA more current than those  manufactured with Typical-Typical (TT) material.

PEM analysis was conducted on both FF and TT units using  identical emission acquisition times, as illustrated in Figures 6A  and 6B. The study revealed that IP blocks 2 through 9 exhibited  higher current consumption in the FF unit compared to the TT  unit. These observations were then evaluated against the  original design expectations.

Figure 6a: PEM images of FF and TT units in low-power mode, captured using identical emission acquisition times and  thresholds, revealed increased current consumption in the FF  unit. Notably, IPs 2 through 9 exhibited higher emission  intensity in the FF unit compared to the TT unit. The power  switching transistors within IP_2, highlighted in red, showed  significantly greater emission than expected by design.

Figure 6b: The pixel density versus emission intensity plot  further confirmed that the FF unit had a higher concentration  of pixels with emission intensity above 80, indicating elevated  leakage. The average emission intensity in low-power mode  was 102.048 for the FF unit, compared to 80.46 for the TT unit, as determined through computer vision-based analysis.

Further analysis of the emission images, using consistent pixel  value threshold settings, revealed an anomaly in IP_2. While  design expectations predicted similar emission intensity—and  thus identical current consumption at the power switches in  IP_2—between FF and TT units, the PEM image showed  substantially higher emissions at the power switches in IP_2 on  the FF unit.

Simulations for each process split predicted a 7-mA difference  in current consumption between FF and TT units. However, actual silicon measurements showed a 10-mA difference. Additional PEM analysis of the power switches in IP_2  revealed that Low-Vt (LVT) power switching (PSW) transistors  exhibited significantly higher emission intensity than StandardVt (SVT) PSW transistors in the FF unit. Advanced power  simulation and silicon modeling revealed a more than 15× difference in current consumption between LVT and SVT PSW  transistors, highlighting a silicon-to-model mismatch.

This strong dependence on process variation—specifically the  Vt-type of power switching transistors—prompted a  recalibration of power and current consumption expectations in  low-power modes. It also supported design debugging efforts, leading to modifications in the Vt-type of power switching  transistors used in certain IP blocks.

Emission analysis of the highlighted region confirmed that the  LVT power switching transistor exhibited a higher emission  intensity value (252.98) compared to the SVT power switching  transistors (96.784) under identical test conditions [9]. This  analysis confirmed that the LVT power switching transistors  were responsible for the additional current leakage observed in  FF units operating in low-power mode, contrary to initial design  expectations.

Figure 7: PEM images captured using an MCT camera with an  1800 nm filter showed that LVT PSW transistors had an  emission intensity of 252.98, compared to 96.784 for SVT PSW  transistors under identical conditions. This discrepancy  contributed to the higher-than-expected leakage observed in FF  units.

Case 3

This case involves a device that experienced latch-up when a  negative current stress pulse was injected through a  multifunctional I/O pad. Latch-up typically occurs in bulk  CMOS integrated circuits (ICs) when an unintended lowimpedance path forms between the power supply and ground. This condition is often triggered by the interaction of parasitic  NPN and PNP bipolar transistors, which together form a  parasitic PNPN (or NPNP) structure. Common causes include  poor VDD connections to N-well ties or excessive spacing  between those ties.

In this case, the latch-up behavior deviated from typical  patterns, as it involved the output of a low-dropout regulator (LDO) and was triggered by the injection of negative current or  voltage on a multiplexed I/O pad. The root cause was traced to  a combination of insufficient decoupling capacitance on the  affected supply and an inherent design vulnerability. Experimental results demonstrated that adding a sufficiently  large capacitor to the supply effectively prevented latch-up.

Further analysis focused on the interaction between the  negative stress applied to the multiplexed I/O pad and the

LDO’s regulation behavior. As shown in Figure 8, emission

intensity increased at the NMOS transistor of the transmission  gate (T-gate) connected to the LDO with increasing levels of  negative voltage injection, indicating stress-induced  degradation at that node.

Analog mixed-signal simulations revealed that the T-gate, connected to the sensitive nodes of the LDO, became  conductive when a negative voltage was applied to the  multiplexed I/O pad. This caused the LDO to over-regulate (Figure 9). When the injected current or voltage exceeded -2.5  mA or -0.711 V, the sensitive nodes of the LDO were pulled  toward a negative voltage, disrupting regular operation. As a  result, the SYS LDO, which typically regulates to 1.8 V, temporarily shifted to a higher output voltage—emission  intensity analysis closely aligned with simulation results, confirming a critical design vulnerability. Specifically, the  absence of a pull-down transistor at the T-gate output was

identified as a flaw. This issue was subsequently corrected to  mitigate reliability risks (Figure 10).

These findings highlight the importance of designing  multifunctional I/O pads to be resilient against fault injection. Ensuring that multiplexed I/O pads are fault-injection proof is  essential for maintaining device reliability under stress and  protecting against potential security threats.

Figure 8: PEM images revealed an increase in emission  intensity at the NMOS transistor of the transmission gate (Tgate) connected to the LDO as the magnitude of the injected  negative voltage on the multiplexed I/O pad increased.

Figure 9: Analog mixed-signal simulations modeling the  negative voltage stress confirmed that the T-gate connected to  the LDO becomes conductive when a negative voltage is  applied to the multiplexed I/O pad.

 Abstract

unknown Figure 10: The case study revealed that the absence of a pulldown transistor at the T-gate output caused unintended conduction under stress. Adding the missing pull-down transistor resolved the issue and improved reliability.

 Conclusion

Conclusion

This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of emission intensity analysis in identifying intrinsic device reliability issues and design vulnerabilities.

Case Study 1 highlighted how emission intensity analysis of PEM images across varying stress durations, combined with thermal bake experiments, successfully identified charge trapping in a high current-consuming NMOS device exhibiting Positive Bias Temperature Instability (PBTI) failure mechanisms.

Case Study 2 showed that emission intensity analysis across different process corners provides valuable insights into power consumption at the IP level. In particular, it revealed that in low-power mode, Low-Vt (LVT) power switching transistors consumed significantly more current than their Standard-Vt (SVT) counterparts, pinpointing a key contributor to the unexpectedly high-power draw observed in Fast-Fast (FF) process split material.

Case Study 3 demonstrated the sensitivity and diagnostic power of emission analysis in uncovering a design flaw triggered by negative current or voltage injection on a multiplexed I/O pad. The analysis led to the identification and correction of a missing pull-down transistor, mitigating a critical reliability risk.

Overall, emission intensity analysis using Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM) images, captured with Meridian DBX Mercury Cadmium Telluride (MCT) camera under consistent conditions (emission acquisition time, VDD, and optical filter), proved to be a powerful technique for uncovering intrinsic reliability issues, understanding device behavior under varying power modes and process conditions, and identifying latent design weaknesses. All analyses were performed using focused photon emission images processed through Python imaging scripts and open-source computer vision libraries.

Innovative Pattern Modification for Hard Failure Diagnosis  Using Dynamic Laser Stimulation

Kan Sun, Hao Hu, Soon Woei Chong, Wan Abdul Rahman, Rahul Babu Radhamony, Wilson Cheng Hoe Lee

Qualcomm Global Trading Pte. Ltd.  No. 6 | Serangoon North Ave 5 S(554910), Singapore  Email : kans@qti.qualcomm.com

Silambarasan Karuppannan

Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.  5751 Pacific Center Blvd, San Diego, CA 92121-4203, USA  Email: skaruppa@qti.qualcomm.com

Abstract

Dynamic Laser Stimulation (DLS) has been predominantly  utilized for debugging soft failures, which are characterized by  the presence of a shmoo wall/passing window. However, its  application has been limited when addressing hard failures, which lack any passing window and on the other hand, hard  failures are notoriously difficult to analyze for advance tech  node due to the absence of effective fault isolation methods  when Photon Emission Microscopy (PEM) analysis provides no  clues. This study proposes a novel methodology to extend the  applicability of DLS to hard failures by transforming them into  soft failures through a detailed analysis of error cycles within   the shmoo plot, thereby enabling the use of DLS for a broader  spectrum of failure types. The paper presents a comprehensive  analysis of the proposed method, including 2 case studies that  demonstrate its efficacy in various scenarios. The results  indicate a significant improvement and offer new insights in the  ability to diagnose and rectify complex hard failures in  advanced semiconductor devices.

Keywords—DLS, PEM, Pattern Modification, Hard Failure

Introduction

Dynamic Laser Stimulation (DLS) has emerged as a key  technique in the field of semiconductor failure analysis, particularly for localizing soft failures. DLS operates by utilizing  laser-induced thermal/photon effects to alter the electrical  characteristics of a device under test, thereby identifying failure  points through changes in the device's operating status (Pass/Fail)[1][2]. This method has proven highly effective for  soft failures, which are typically characterized by the presence  of a shmoo wall—a graphical representation of a device's  performance across varying voltage and frequency  conditions[3][4]. However, the application of DLS will be  significantly limited on hard failures due to the absence of any  passing window across the testing specifications. On the other  hand, hard failures will become increasingly challenging  especially when it is lack of precise diagnostic result and PEM  provides no clues[5]. Traditional fault isolation techniques often

fall short in addressing these failures, as they do not exhibit the  same thermal sensitivity that DLS exploits in soft failures. Consequently, there has been a growing need for innovative  approaches to extend the capabilities of DLS to encompass hard  failures.

Methodology

The proposed methodology facilitates the transformation of hard  failures into soft failures by analyzing error cycle behavior  within shmoo plots and strategically modifying test patterns. By  selectively enabling or masking specific error cycles based on  error count behavior across the specification range, a pass  window can be constructed. This enables DLS analysis to be  conducted using the modified pattern, allowing for effective  failure isolation and subsequent physical failure analysis (PFA).

Figure 1: Methodology

For the failures exhibiting gross error counts across  specification, a selective enablement of specific error cycles can  be employed to establish a functional pass window. As  illustrated in graphical representation of a shmoo plot in Fig. 2, certain error cycles observable only at lower voltage levels with  error count A and absent at higher voltages with error count B—can be selectively enabled, thus transforming a hard failure to  soft failure.

Figure 2: Selectively Enable Error Cycles

For the failures with only a few error cycles at certain operating  conditions, as shown in graphical representation of a shmoo plot  Fig3, where only 2 error cycles are observed at higher voltage  side. We could mask out the 2 error cycles within the test pattern. This modification results in a new test pattern containing A–2  error cycles at the lower voltage side and introduces a pass  window at the higher voltage side.

Figure 3: Selectively Mask Error Cycles

Case studies

Case 1: Selective Enablement of Specific Error Cycles

This case presents a logic Stuck-at-Fault failure, where the logic  diagnosis provided massive callouts and PEM analysis revealed  no abnormal emission spot. Error counts analysis of the failure  shmoo indicated distinct error count distributions across voltage  regions. A detailed comparison of error cycles identified two  specific failing cycles present only at lower voltage range, which are the 43111 and 43112 highlighted in red in table1.

Table 1. Error cycle analysis

The test pattern was subsequently modified to enable  comparison exclusively at these two error cycles, while  masking all others, thereby enabled the DLS technique for  further analysis.

Figure 4: Case 1 Shmoo analysis for modified pattern

With the modified pattern with pass/fail window, DLS analysis  was performed based on the two error counts enabled pattern and  a distinct laser sensitive site was identified at one of the  diagnostic callout locations.

Figure 5: Case 1 DLS analysis

Subsequent PFA was performed target on DLS laser sensitive  site and transistor nanoprobing observed gross high Ioff at DLS  identified cell. Further investigation with planar view  Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) imaging confirmed  Electrical Induced Physical Damage (EIPD) at the affected  transistors.

Figure 6: Case 1 Nanoprobing and PSTEM result

Case 2: Selective Masking of Error Cycles

In this case, the device exhibited a hard failure signature during  MBIST (Memory Built-In Self-Test) testing and consistently  failing across all voltage and frequency conditions. However, only a few error counts were observed at specific specification  points. Memory diagnosis indicated a  sparse row failure but  PEM analysis did not reveal any abnormal emission sites.

Figure 7: Case 2 Diagnostic callouts & PEM analysis

Shmoo analysis showed the persistent presence of only 2 error  cycles at higher voltage range. The test Pattern was subsequently  modified by masking these two specific error cycles and the  modified shmoo able to achieve a desired passing window at  higher voltage range.

Figure 8: Shmoo analysis for original and modified pattern

Subsequent DLS analysis was conducted using the modified test  pattern, revealing multiple laser sensitive sites in Fig. 9.

This confirmed the effectiveness of the pattern modification  methodology in localizing the failure mechanism for further  investigation.

Figure 9: DLS analysis based on the modified pattern

Physical failure analysis and nanoprobing showed a resistive  short between wordline and ground trace. Subsequent  Secondary Electron Microscopy(SEM) inspection observed  abnormal metal profile caused metal to via bridging.

Figure 10: Nanoprobing and Abnormal metal line profile

Summary

In this work, we developed a systematic methodology that  effectively transforms certain hard failures exhibiting error cycle  variation into soft failures. This advancement enables DLS to  address a broader range of failure types, particularly those  traditionally classified as hard failures. This methodology allows  us to isolate issues where standard Electrical Fault  Isolation(EFI) methods are challenged and enhancing EFI  capability for Root Cause Analysis.

 Understanding the Latent Impact of Residual Particles in 3D NAND

Understanding the Latent Impact of Residual Particles in 3D NAND

 Authors

 Abstract

3D NAND memory, featuring vertically stacked memory cells to enhance storage density and performance, serves as a critical component in modern data storage solutions and AI applications. In this paper, we investigated the electrical impact of memory hole (MH) mis-formation defects in a multi-tier three dimensional (3D) NAND memory technology. Despite being confined to local word lines (WLs) and source lines (SLs), such defects cause a global impact to all the memory cells in the same plane by slowing down their program speed. Specifically, the bit line potential of victim cells is disturbed when quick pass write (QPW) program technique is implemented. Such disturb originates from the interaction between source line and global bit line through the aggressor memory cells. Based on the failure mechanism, several approaches were proposed to improve the screen efficiency for these defects, which could otherwise become latent system failures.

 Introduction

Introduction

Random residual particles are inevitable during manufacturing processes  [1]  and the most common failure mode induced in 3D NAND technology is leakage between word lines, memory holes, and source lines. Test protocols to catch such failures are well established. Once such a failure is detected, a standard approach is to mark those defective blocks as "bad blocks", by means of floating the compromised WLs, when operating other defect-free blocks in the same plane, i.e., sharing the same bit lines with defective blocks, as shown in Figure  1 (a). Typically, the above-mentioned defect will not cause global NAND functional failures due to its in-situ electrical impact.

However, a large residual particle can introduce a MH misformation type of defect with massive WL-WL shorts and WL-SL shorts. Figures  1 (a)-(b ) demonstrate a typical MH misformation defect from a BiCS (Bit Cost Scalable) 6 th generation die. Such a defect could cross multiple blocks. In contrast to typical WL-WL and WL-SL defects, the MH mis-formation would cause extended impact, although in a subtle manner, on neighbor, defect free (victim) blocks during programming. This MH mis-formation defect raises concerns due to its latent nature and the risk of causing uncorrectable errors at system level, even if those defective blocks are treated as "bad blocks" as suggested by the traditional approach. In the main text, we focus on the aggressor-victim mechanism triggered by MH misformation defects, detailing how the bit line potential is disturbed at each stage of the program sequence, which leads to both slow-to-program and over-programmed cells. Based on our findings, we also propose effective screening methods to increase the detection rate of cells exhibiting abnormal VT. The investigations in this paper can be generalized to any 3D NAND technology.

 Failure Mechanism

Failure Mechanism

As shown in Figure  3 , during a program operation, the three different stages of programming each use a different bit line voltage. VSS is applied during the programming phase (stage-1), αVCC (0 < α < 1) is applied during QPW (stage-2), and VCC is utilized for inhibition (stage-3).

(1) Vth of cell is far away from VH for stage-1. VSS will be applied to the bit line so that a large electrical field between the WL and channel can be generated to program the cell.

(2) Stage-2 cells are referred to as QPW cells whose threshold voltage is in between VL and VH  [2] . The main purpose of introducing a QPW scheme and VL level is to slow down the

 References

program speed for the last few programming pulses before VH  is reached. The sacrifice of programming time would end up  gaining a tighter Vth distribution, crucial for better device  reliability performance [3]. For QPW cells, medium voltage

level αVCC (0<α<1) is applied to the bit line to reduce the  electrical field between silicon channel and WL. A lower α  results in relatively faster program speed, whereas a higher α  results in relatively slower program speed.

(3) For stage-3, when cells have already reached the target Vth, referred to as VH in the following text, VCC will be applied to  the bit line. In this scenario, the memory hole channel potential  will be coupled to VPGM, the voltage applied to the control  gate of selected memory cells during programming, to avoid  further program disturb [4].

Figure 2: Vth distribution of victim cells after one TLC  programming sequence at 90°C. F state, a higher VT state, showed clearly lower tail and upper tail compared with the RT  distribution.

Further analysis showed that victim cells exhibited remarkable  lower and upper tail only when QPW scheme was applied, as  shown in Figure 4. It suggests that the aggressor cells  originating from mis-formation induce worse disturb when the  bit line is biased at αVCC.

Figure 3: Schematic of NAND memory cell programming  scheme. Bit line potential starts from VSS, then ramps up to αVCC, and end up with VCC through the program sequence.

Based on Figure 1(b-c), a simplified schematic composed of a  pair of aggressor-victim cell is illustrated in Figure 5. For the  aggressor cell, in presence of the massive defect, a substantial

number of WLs are electrically shorted. The WL potential is  mostly driven by the source line through either direct leakage  or coupling as the connection to WL drivers is cut off when

programming the victim cells. SL is typically biased at γVCC (γ~1) during program for better channel pre-charge and  boosting. The attacker cell disturbs the bit line potential by  forming a leakage path from the common source line through a  series of memory cells to the bit line at the top. The attacker  strength from SL to bit line is proportional to VSL-Va, where  Va is the overall Vth of the attacker cells, as shown in Figure 5.  The Vth of the attacker cell along WLs is typically low as any  program attempt on those cells would fail due to the massive  WL leakage. We can thus ignore the interaction between bit line  and SL.

Figure 4: F state Vth distribution of victim cells at 90°C with  and without QPW scheme.

At stage-1, the bit line potential is grounded to enable a faster  program speed as shown in Figure 6-1. The aggressor cell  shows negligible impact to the victim cell program speed at this  stage. This phenomenon aligns with the fact that despite a subtle  leakage between VSL and VSS, the bit line potential at the  victim cell location only experiences a negligible fluctuation. Most of the voltage drop is across the tall and thin poly-silicon  channel of the aggressor cells. Considering the ongoing effort  towards WL stacking, the above statement will hold for future  NAND generations.

Figure 5: Simplified aggressor-victim model based on MH misformation defect. Besides massive WL to WL leakage, most of

the WL of attacker memory cells are affected by source line  potential as well through either direct bridging or coupling.

During stage-2, bit line potential is in between VSS and VCC  to slow down the program speed. The bit line bias method  differs from stage-1 in that the bit line is driven with reduced  strength. Therefore, the global bit line potential is more  vulnerable to disturb from aggressor cells, especially when  VSL-Va is larger than αVCC (0<α<1). The leakage current  from VSL will charge up the bit line potential above αVCC, significantly reducing the program speed of victim cells. Higher  temperatures lead to a reduction in Va, thereby exacerbating  disturb effects, which is consistent with the data in Figure 2.

Figure 6-1: Aggressor-victim scheme for programming cells.

It was found that certain amount of victim cells after QPW  would turn to over program cells, indicated by the upper tail, as  shown in Figure 6-3. The upper tail belongs to victim cells  suffering less bit line potential disturb, which are typically far  from defective bit line address. Accordingly, the Vth movement  during QPW is not entirely prohibited, in contrary to the slowto-program scenario where the Vth almost gets frozen. However, extra program pulses, thus a higher final VPGM, are  required to push Vth over target VH. Since the program speed  for a given program pulse is proportional to (VPGM-Vchannel), a  higher final Vth and thus a wider distribution are anticipated.

Figure 6-2: Aggressor-victim scheme for slow-to-program  QPW cells.

However, during stage-3, once the victim cells reach VH, the  aggressor impact reduces significantly. As shown in Figure 6-

4, the bit line potential ramps to VCC, which is comparable to  or even higher than the VSL and VSL-Va. The leakage path  from the aggressor is cut off under this bias configuration. The  bit line potential around the victim cell could then hold at VCC  to ensure an effective channel boosting.

Discussion

Given its randomly occurring nature, latent electrical signature, and detrimental impact at system level, effective screening is  critical to address the mis-formation type defect.

Figure 6-3: Vth evolution for victim cells in QPW region.

The first method is to increase the distance between VL and  VH, as shown in Figure 7(a). From the failure model discussion, the key impact of the aggressor cells is to slow down/freeze the  Vth movement of victim cells during the QPW stage If VL is  set too close to VH, most of the victim cells are nevertheless  capable of being programmed to VH just as normal cells. On  the contrary, if VL is far from VH (shown as VL_far in Figure  7(a)), a greater portion of victim cells would either be stuck at  QPW stage or end up being over programmed. As shown in  Figure 7(b), reducing VL dramatically widened the distribution  of victim cells, which would otherwise show normal error  counts and program status.

Figure 6-4: Aggressor-victim scheme for inhibition cells.

Another approach to address the MH mis-formation defect is to  increase the source line voltage during programming. As  discussed earlier, the aggressor strength during QPW stage is  closely related to VSL-Va. A higher VSL is capable of charging  up the bit line potential to a higher level and thus holding more  cells within the QPW stage. The effectiveness of increasing  source line bias is shown in Figure 7(b).

Figure 7: (a) Illustration of Vth movement for good and victim  cells upon VPGM pulses. (b) F state distributions collected at  90°C from a victim block showing the effectiveness of proposed  screen methods of reducing VL and increasing source line bias.

The aggressor-victim scenario and proposed screen methods  discussed in the main text apply to both triple-level cell and  quad-level cell (QLC) NAND technologies. For QLC cells, the  disturb occurs during both foggy/fine stages once QPW scheme  is utilized.

Conclusions

Memory hole mis-formation is a common failure mode for  multi-tier 3D NAND architecture and will remain given the  constantly growing WL layers [5]. Despite being a local  physical defect, it exhibits extended electrical interference on  good memory cells especially during program via modulating  the global bit line potential. Here we discussed the underlying  mechanism of such latent aggressor-victim behavior along with  targeted screen proposals.

713127.

[4] Y. Kim and M. Kang, “Down-coupling phenomenon of  floating channel in 3D NAND flash memory,” IEEE

Electron Device Lett., Vol. 37, No. 12 (1996), pp 1566–1569, doi: 10.1109/LED.2016.2619903.

[5] S. I. Shim, J. Jang, and J. Song, “Trends and Future  Challenges of 3D NAND Flash Memory,” in 2023 IEEE  International Memory Workshop (IMW), Monterey, CA, USA: IEEE, (2023), pp. 1–4, doi: 10.1109/IMW56887.20

Effective Fault Isolation Beyond 2nm Programmable Logic by Dynamic LIT

Lay Lay, Goh

Altera Corporation, San Jose, California, USA

lay.lay.goh@altera.com, (408) 797 9293

Jiajun, Wu

Altera Corporation, San Jose, California, USA

jiajun.wu@altera.com, (415) 810 9061

Abstract

This paper outlines a comprehensive fault isolation (FI) and  physical failure analysis (PFA) process for advanced backside  power delivery silicon technology. In the FI stage, it highlights  the effectiveness of dynamic LIT (lock-in thermography) in  isolating functional failures within a 2nm process on the  programmable logic subsystem. By utilizing a customized test  pattern and a direct tester docking mechanism, the LIT camera  can detect heat propagated from transistors within a lock-in  environment. This work also emphasizes a novel de-processing  technique for accessing the active diffusion layer through the  backside power delivery metal stack.

Introduction

Delivering power through the backside is crucial for advancing  transistor scaling, allowing chip designers to enhance transistor  density while maintaining resources to achieve unprecedented  levels of power and performance [1]. This innovative power  delivery approach presents new challenges for fault isolation  and failure analysis, particularly in functional fault isolation  using conventional optical tools. The complexity of failure  debugging and defect isolation has increased due to  metallization on both sides of the wafer. As demonstrated in  Fig. 1 below, photon and laser-based fault isolation (FI) techniques are now less effective, as signals are obstructed by  the front-side metal stack. To address these challenges, modified conventional and novel debugging techniques have  been developed to effectively localize hard defects and address  speed path issues [2].

Figure 1: Backside power delivery silicon limits optical FI.

Background and Technique

Dynamic LIT has emerged as a partial substitute for emission  microscopy (EMMI) in photon collection for logic state  imaging and power mapping. LIT is based on the principle  theory of thermal wave propagation which is generated as a  result of a harmonic temperature excitation [3]. Therefore, the  amplitude and phase of heat propagating through an opaque  layer depends on the stimulation frequency, distance of the  buried defect to the surface and the thermal parameters of the  propagated material layers. Although a significant loss of  resolution is anticipated, it can be mitigated using the Lock-In  feature synchronized with the test trigger. The diffractionlimited spatial resolution of LIT can be further improved by  applying a solid immersion lens (SIL) [4].

In these functional case studies, the power rail of the logic  subsystem is not externally accessible and must be set through  the test vector. For this reason, the tester setup was modified to  dock with the LIT system. The power rail is alternated between  minimum and maximum at specific frequencies using a script. defining trigger pin, loop count, Vdd and phase duration, as  illustrated in Fig. 2.

Figure 2: Scripting to define key parameters for dynamic LIT.

Loop count

Vdd level

Phase duration

VLevel High

www.asminternational.org

ISTFA 2025: Proceedings from the 51st International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis Conference

November 16–20, 2025, Pasadena, California, USA

https://doi.org/10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2025p0115

Loop count is programmed by users where 60-120s is a  reasonable analysis time. The value of Vdd using VLevel low  and high is written respectively in the script. The phase duration  defines the frequency of the modulation. Fig. 3 shows a  modulated power rail. This setup is intended to modulate VCC  from 0V to 1.0V, with phase duration of 0.05s for each of the  low and high voltage periods. Total time is 0.1s per cycle, equivalent to 10Hz.

Figure 3 Modulated VCC power rail from 0V to 1.0V.

Figure 4: LIT system detects trigger pin’s frequency. Small  frequency offset from 10 Hz is normal and does not affect the  acquisition.

The LIT system detects and synchronizes with the trigger  frequency (Fig. 4) to identify hotspots, accumulating their  intensity over a specified period of time. Small frequency  detection fluctuates in a range of ±4%, which does not affect  the acquisition during voltage modulation.  Once a hotspot is  localized, physical failure analysis (PFA) methods, including  dry etch, wet etch, and plasma focused ion beam (PFIB) milling, are employed to expose physical defects. The two case  studies below demonstrate fault isolation using dynamic LIT  and PFIB de-processing on both frontside and backside metal  stacks.

Results and Discussion

Case study 1: DR failures

DR (data register) failures were reported in the Configurable  RAM logic block. The initial attempt using front side dynamic  LIT by looping the failing read/write test pattern was  unsuccessful without the power modulation, Fig. 5. The second  attempt by modulating VCCL at 10Hz successfully localized a  hotspot near the address line buffer region in Fig. 6.

Figure 5: With only looping of the failing test pattern without  power modulation, no hotspot was detected within the region  of interest (red box).

Figure 6: Localized hotspot detected within the region of

interest when VCCL is modulated at 10 Hz by SIL lens.

The device was de-processed from the front side by removing  the carrier Si and epoxy using SF6 dry etch. After that, the Si  was parallel lapped and PFIB de-layered using Dx chemistry (Thermo Scientific PFIB system) to locate the anomaly based  on the hotspot location. Metal bridging was found at Metal 4, Fig. 7.

Figure 7: Metal 4 bridging in DR buffer region.

Case study 2: BBRAM Voltage Sensitive Failure

BBRAM (battery backed ram)_leakage was reported where the  device consumed higher dynamic power. The leakage was seen  in µA while nA leakage current is expected. The subsystem is  dependent on VCCBAT power rail, thus this rail was modulated  for frontside dynamic LIT. Voltage modulation at 1.0 to 1.1V  did not yield any hotspot. When the voltage was elevated to

1.15-1.20V, a prominent hotspot was detected at the power  multiplexer region. The hotspot was further magnified using a  SIL lens which gives 25x optical resolution to further pinpoint  the location, Fig. 8.

Figure 8: Localized hotspot detected at Power MUX region  using 10x lens.

The Si was de-processed from the back metal stack using PFIB. Conventional Dx delayering using XeF2 in PFIB is time  consuming and causing planarity issues due to unique structure  in between the metal stack. Instead of using XeF2, DE chemistry (Thermo Scientific PFIB system) and Iodine assisted mill were  introduced into BM4-BM3 removal and cleanup process. Planar BM2 exposure is key for successful BM2-BM0  delayering. Once BM3 is fully removed, there is a need to  backfill the region of interest with insulator deposition to  smooth out the surface. Hence, re-planarization step is created

in the flow. The backfilled area will be re-exposed using XeF2  assisted mill. BM2-BM0 delayering was performed using the  conventional Dx chemistry. The PFIB recipe was developed  based on the package layer material, thickness and density to  precisely remove back metal (BM) layers. Several parameters  like column setting (C), scanning conditions (S), detector setup (D), pattern (P) and tilt (T) were characterized to achieve the  consistency of layer removal for each step. Figure 9 illustrates  the steps to access each layer by repeating the exposure, removal and cleanup process using different settings of ion  voltage (kV) and current (nA).

Figure 9: BM removal recipe was developed and deployed as  a System Preset in the Thermo Scientific PFIB system.

SEM inspection was performed at each layer and an anomaly  was found in the backside diffusion Via layer. Physical damage  affecting a VCCBAT trace segment was observed, spiking into the  Gate region, as illustrated in Fig. 10.

Figure 10: Electrical induced physical damage observed in  the hotspot region.

Conclusions

The cases above explored the effectiveness of the Dynamic LIT  technique in frontside fault isolation for silicon technology with  backside power delivery. Using the ATE direct dock setup and  scripting, this approach focuses on modulating the internal  power rail to improve hotspot sensitivity and intensity in Lockin mode. Localized hotspots can be detected even through a 14-layer metal stack. Additionally, a novel physical failure analysis (PFA) de-processing flow and recipe using DE and Iodine  assisted mill was developed for frontside and backside metal  de-layering, ensuring consistent results.
