Ultra-high speed/High timing-resolution Electro-optic probing using streak  camera

Xiangguang Mao, Tomonori Nakamura, Kenta Nakamura, Akari Kato, Mitsuyoshi Yoneda, Takayoshi Kaneoka, Fuminori Niikura, Ayumu Yoshimi

Hamamatsu Photonics K.K. Hamamatsu City, Japan   shoko.mo@sys.hpk.co.jp

Abstract

Electro-optic (EO) probing is a widely used technique in failure  analysis (FA). Conventional EO probing techniques use  digitizers or oscilloscopes to accumulate data over extended  periods to obtain waveforms, making the EO probing method a  time-consuming technique for FA. This paper presents a novel  approach to use a streak camera in conjunction with ATE (Automated Test Equipment) to capture waveforms in a short  time with extremely high time resolution.

Introduction

With the continuous advancement of high-speed memory  technologies, particularly in the domain of Double Data Rate (DDR) memory, testing methodologies must evolve to keep  pace. The latest DDR6 standard achieves data transfer rates of  up to 12,800 MT/s, corresponding to a clock period of  approximately 156 ps. These ultra-fast transitions present  significant challenges for signal acquisition and analysis. To  accurately capture these fast signal transitions, such as rising  and falling edges of the clock, or invertor delay or inverter jitter, a sampling interval of less than 10% of the signal’s clock period  is recommended. For DDR6 and similar high-performance  interfaces, this translates to a required sampling rate of at least  65 GS/s.

Another inherent challenge in EO probing is the extremely  weak intensity of reflected light, necessitating signal averaging  over millions of cycles.[1][2]

To address these limitations, Hamamatsu has developed an  advanced Ultra-EOP (U-EOP) system that integrates a streak  camera with Automated Test Equipment (ATE). By exploiting  the high time resolution of the streak camera and adjusting the  test loop repetition rate to exceed 1 MHz, up to 40 MHz, the UEOP system enables waveform capture within a narrow  acquisition window with exceptional time resolution. The  average time will be ten times shorter when the loop repetition  is 1 MHz and 100 times shorter when the loop repetition is more  than 10 MHz compared to conventional high-speed  oscilloscope. This paper presents the system architecture and  experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of U-EOP.

System Setup and Working Principles

Hamamatsu has developed a U-EOP system that integrates a  streak camera into a failure analysis (FA) tool. A simplified  system diagram is shown in Figure 1. The system uses a low

noise 1300nm light source (LS) to probe the target transistor  within a semiconductor device. During transistor operation, variations in the depletion layer thickness and free carrier  concentration alter the intensity of the reflected light. The UEOP unit, equipped with high-speed photodetectors (PDs) and  electro-optic (EO) converters, transforms the modulated nearinfrared (NIR) light into visible light, which is then directed to  the streak camera.

The light signal is focused onto the photocathode of the streak  tube, where photons are converted into electrons in proportion  to the light intensity. These electrons are accelerated toward a  phosphor screen, producing a visible image [3]. A low-noise  CMOS camera captures the phosphor screen image, from which  the U-EOP waveform, which contains detailed operational  information, is extracted.

Figure 1: System Diagram of U-EOP

Figure 2. illustrates the system setup, which consists of a UEOP system, a conventional EOP system, a system controller, and the laser scanning optics from a standard iPHEMOS  system. Communication between the tool and the tester is  managed via two signals. The first is a synchronous signal that  drives the sweeping circuit within the streak camera. This  signal’s frequency can be customized at the factory to match the  user's tester, with a configurable range from 38 MHz to 74  MHz. In the present system, a frequency of 40 MHz is  employed, resulting in a scan repetition interval of 25 ns. Therefore, the test loop period must be an integer multiple of  25 ns to ensure synchronization. The second signal is a trigger  signal used to initiate the test sample.

Experimental Results and Discussion

Figure 3(a). illustrates the experimental system setup used in  this study. To evaluate the digitizing speed and time resolution  of the proposed system, the emission from a DistributedFeedback (DFB) laser diode was measured. Custom-designed  circuit boards were used to drive the laser diode and regulate  the thermoelectric cooler integrated within the device, ensuring  thermal stability during operation. The external appearance and  emission pattern of the laser diode are presented in Figure 3 (b).  The laser power was modulated at frequencies of 2 GHz and 12  GHz using a synthesizer, serving as a substitute for probing an  actual silicon device.

A synthesizer and pulse generator were employed to drive the  system in place of an Automated Test Equipment (ATE), allowing controlled and repeatable signal generation for  performance assessment.

(a)

(b)

Figure 3: (a) Experimental System Setup, (b) Appearance and  Emission spot of DFB-LD

Figure4. presents the experimental results obtained from the  EOP, F-EOP, and U-EOP systems when measuring 2 GHz  signals. The conventional EOP system, equipped with a 10 GS/s  digitizer [4], faces limitations when analyzing 2 GHz signals  due to its relatively coarse time resolution. The F-EOP system  improves upon this with a 32 GS/s digitizer [4], achieving a  time resolution of 31.25 ps. The U-EOP system offers  significantly finer resolution at 2.78 ps, enabling the detection  of subtle waveform features that are not discernible with  conventional systems.

While the F-EOP system is sufficient for characterizing signals  at 2 GHz, the U-EOP system offers superior time resolution, making it well-suited for high-precision waveform analysis. However, this enhanced resolution comes at the cost of a  reduced acquisition window, approximately 4 ns, which is  significantly narrower than that of the conventional EOP  system.

To overcome this limitation, we recommend a two-step  approach: first, use the conventional EOP system to identify the  region of interest (ROI); then switch to the U-EOP system for  detailed waveform inspection within the identified ROI.

To support accurate ROI identification, the system includes a  timing alignment function. During initial installation, users are  advised to employ a tester to generate a single pulse with an  interval shorter than 2 ns, the shorter the interval, the more  precise the alignment. This procedure enables accurate  synchronization between the F-EOP and U-EOP signals. Once  the timing offset is determined, it is stored in the software  configuration. A one-click compensation feature allows users  to automatically apply the offset, ensuring consistent timing  alignment throughout operation.

Figure 4: Result of EOP/F-EOP/U-EOP with 2 GHz signal  Figure 5. presents the results of the 12 GHz modulation  experiment. By adjusting the sweep speed of the streak camera, the U-EOP system demonstrates a significant enhancement in  time resolution, up to a tenfold improvement. This optimization  enables the U-EOP system to achieve an effective digitizing

rate of up to 3703 GS/s, positioning it as one of the fastest  digitizing solutions available for high-speed waveform  analysis.

Figure 5: Result of U-EOP in different range

Conclusion

The U-EOP system demonstrates exceptional time resolution  capabilities, making it well-suited for testing current DDR6  memory technologies and scalable for future, more advanced  memory generations. To fully leverage this high time  resolution, it is essential to minimize the test loop duration. However, achieving such short loop periods presents a  significant challenge in system design and integration. Addressing this constraint will be critical for maximizing the  performance and applicability of the U-EOP system in nextgeneration memory testing.

CAD Alignment Methodologies for Accurate and Reliable Optical Fault Isolation  at Sub-5 nm Process Technologies

Rudolf Schlangen, Arpan Bhattacherjee, Christopher Nemirow, Nirakar Poudel, Srilakshmi Nallapati, William Lo

NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara, CA USA

Rupa Kamoji, Madhav Shanbhag

Synopsys Inc., Mumbai, India

Abstract

The continued scaling of semiconductor technologies below  5 nm has created significant challenges for CAD (computeraided design) alignment for optical and LSM (laser scanning  microscope) images. Besides increasing the gap between  optical resolution and feature size, shrinking geometries drive  the need for ever greater alignment accuracy. DesignA

technology co-optimization (DTCO) scaling has imposed a

280nm

shift toward uniform, feature-scarce layouts, breaking  traditional alignment approaches based on oxide diffusion (OD) features. We still observe significant imaging contrast, even  within dense logic, but the contrast does not corelate to one  individual CAD layer, but rather a complex convolution of  multiple CAD layers. All optical fault isolation (OFI) techniques are affected, but laser voltage probing (LVP) is  disproportionately impacted due to its requirement of precise  probe placement before meaningful data acquisition can begin. The resulting productivity hit has already been felt for 5 nm but  is significantly worse for 3 nm. The result is prolonged defect

5nm, 8-track

localization efforts and extended analysis cycles. In this paper, we will present two novel techniques that we are investigating

B

for precision CAD alignment of sub-5 nm ICs: CAD based

210nm

image simulation and decap LVI. We will describe the  techniques, provide examples, and discuss the results and future  work.

Introduction

Laser voltage probing (LVP) remains an essential OFI  technique for design debug, reliability improvement, and yield  ramping activities [1]. Accurate CAD alignment is a  prerequisite for LVP because accurate probe placement is

5nm, 6-track

required before useful and trustworthy waveforms can be  acquired. This is in distinct contrast to other techniques such as  photon emission microscopy (PEM) or soft defect localization (SDL) where data acquisition can already be started after only  coarse alignment. Accurate alignment is then required only if  useful OFI signatures are detected and can often be performed  off-line (i.e., without consuming valuable system time). Furthermore, the OFI signature locations themselves, along

with CAD layout and diagnosis results, help facilitate  alignment.

Figure 1 shows an example of the impact of DTCO driven fin  depopulation and cell height reduction on OD uniformity for a  5 nm process. The OD layer in logic of an 8-track (8T) design

is shown in Fig. 1A) while Fig. 1B) shows a 6-track (6T) design. Distinctive layout features in the 8T design are created  by the mix of 2-fin and 3-fin cells. These features provide  reliable image contrast for precise optical alignment, as shown  in Fig. 2. However, increasingly stringent design rules driven  by DTCO scaling have imposed a shift towards the uniform, feature-scarce layouts seen in the 6T design, where only 2-fin  cells are possible. As shown in Fig. 3, that change has  eliminated the usefulness of the OD layer for precise CAD-toimage alignment within areas of dense logic, making the task  much more difficult and time consuming.

Fortunately, as shown by the LSM image in Fig. 3, distinct  image contrast still exists w/in logic for 6T designs. The cut  metal-diffusion (CMD) CAD layer matches this contrast best, as shown in Fig. 4. A major drawback, however, is the  significantly greater (approx. 7x) number of polygons in the  CMD layer compared to the OD layer. This results in  significantly longer polygon transfer times from the CAD  server to the OFI system. This major impact on productivity can  be avoided by transferring a bitmap of the CMD layer instead  of polygons, but not all OFI systems currently support this  capability.

For the 3 nm process (Fig. 5) the CMD match has been severely  degraded, to the point where it has lost much of its usefulness, and we cannot see any other single CAD layer that shows a  reliable match to LSM images within logic.

To try to address this problem, we are investigating two  advanced precision CAD alignment techniques. The first is a  novel methodology utilizing synthesized microscopy images  generated directly from one or more layers of the CAD layout. The use of simple heuristics instead of full  optical/electromagnetic simulations is likely good enough for  3nm and is expected to help make the technique fast and  efficient enough for real-time use in OFI scenarios. The second  technique is based on decap (decoupling capacitor) LVI (laser  voltage imaging). Modulating the VDD rail highlights all the  standard-cell decaps within the field-of-view (FOV). The  relatively large size of the decaps, their prevalence in leadingedge ICs, and the nature of their LVx response makes them  nearly ideal as alignment beacons [3, 4]. We anticipate that  these techniques will become useful and productive options in  the near future, in addition to the existing techniques of clockbased LVI and navigation fiducial insertion.

CAD-Derived Image Simulation

For all simulated images in this paper, we simply use a Gaussian  blur, with user adjustable standard deviation (σ). This  capability is already integrated into a special version of Avalon. Boolean operations with weighting factors for each layer can be  applied (currently, offline, but planned for integration into  software) to combine multiple layers.

Figure 6 shows a simple example for a region of logic in a 5 nm, 6T IC. A single, derived CAD layer, CMD_MERGE was used  for the simulated image. CMD_MERGE is a layer derived from  the CAD CMD layer. It was obtained by defining  CMD_MERGE = RESIZE CMD 3 in the “Define Synthetic  Layers” panel in Synopsys’ Avalon software. In  CMD_MERGE, smaller, closely spaced rectangles in the CMD  layer are merged into larger, more complex polygons.

The match is remarkable, especially given the use of only a  single CAD layer and the simple heuristics. One obvious  discrepancy between the two images is in the pitch of the bright  horizontal stripes running throughout the images. In the LSM

We fully realize that CMD (and, hence, CMD_MERGE) does  not directly correspond to a physical layer in the actual IC. However, since we are using simple heuristics, we started with  CAD layers that have previously been found to provide a good  match to LSM image features. We are investigating whether  using CAD layers corresponding to actual physical structures  helps improve the simulation results.

We also understand that the raw CMD (and CMD_Merge) layer  already provides a good match to 5 nm, 6T LSM images and  simulated images may only be beneficial within large areas of  dense logic. However, the larger dimensions and more obvious  correlation of the various features (such as the NWELL  contrast) allows us to better identify the important CAD layers  and how to combine them for best results. We expect that these  learnings will transfer to geometries where this correlation is  less obvious (e.g., 3 nm).

Figure 7 shows a 3 nm example. Again, only the  CMD_MERGE layer was used. Again, the match is remarkable  considering the simplicity of the simulation. And, again, we  expect that bringing in additional CAD layers will further  improve the result. We discuss our results from combining  multiple simulated layers in the next section.

Once the algorithm for generating the simulated images for a  particular technology node is well defined, the plan is to fully

automate and incorporate that algorithm into Avalon. The goal  is to make the use of simulated images seamless and compatible  with existing alignment methodologies based on use of  traditional CAD layers (such as OD and CMD, etc., Fig. 6).

Combining Multiple Simulated Layers

While single layer CMD_MERGE simulation has shown strong  visual correlation to the LSM image for 5 nm/6T as discussed  earlier, we tried to further improve the correlation by combining  simulated images generated for different physical layers in the  chip. We simulated CAD layers for MD, M0, POLY, NW, PP, NP, M1 and qualitatively correlated these results to the LSM  image. As shown in Figure 8, simulated MD, and M0 layers

Figure 7. 3 nm process CAD image simulation example. A) LSM image, 1064 nm, 3.3 NA SIL, Horizontal  Polarization, ~20 µm horizontal FOV. B) Image  simulation based on CAD CMD layer. C) CAD CMD layer  used for B), rendered with 0-pixel minimum [2].

show the best correlation to the LSM image within logic areas, where a mix of simulated poly, OD and NW correlated better  with the tap-cell area of the LSM image (highlighted arrow in  Fig. 8A, D and E). After many iterations and visual correlation, which is subjective, we chose sigma of 85 to better reflect the  blur factor of the actual LSM image. The Gaussian blur’s full  width at half maximum (FWHM =2.35 x 85 ~200 nm) closely  matches the resolution for 1064 nm LSM image based on the  Rayleigh criterion (0.61 x 1064 nm / 3.3 =197 nm).

We performed linear combination of these images with various  weight factors based on each image’s visual correlation with the  actual LSM image. In the final image produced, each pixel is a  weighted average of corresponding pixels from the layers used  for the combined image. The weights were always adjusted to  sum to 100%. The aim was to match the original LSM image as  closely as possible. Figure 9 shows the result of the linear  combination of various layers for a 5 nm 6T IC. Despite  combining various layers with different weights, we still cannot  accurately reproduce the contrast in the tap cells and some other  details of the actual LSM image, but the overall correlation is  significantly better than to any individual CAD layer.

This approach of using just the linear combination of the CAD  layers has its limitation as this method still cannot completely  reproduce every detail and features of actual LSM image. The  actual LSM image is produced by a complex interaction of the

high NA, coherent laser light with various layers in the DUT  containing sub-resolution features and grating structures. There are PP and NP layers with different doping and straining, which  lead to different light absorption and possible birefringence  effects. Moreover, there are diffraction, multilayer interference, and polarization effects occurring in the actual device. Our  model of linear combination of simulated layers overlooks all  of these physical phenomena. The complete explanation of the  LSM image will likely require a more comprehensive  electromagnetic and optical simulation.

However, for now we only need to match enough of the image to ease the CAD alignment process (Fig. 10). Using the  simulated LSM images does not preclude the use of other CAD  layers in steps 8 and 9 which may provide a better match to  certain LSM features. Our aim is to fully software integrate and  make seamless the generation, transfer, rendering, and  alignment of simulated layers to actual LSM images. In other  words, make the simulated images behave like any other CAD  layer in Avalon. Doing so would substantially enhance the  productivity of fault isolation engineers, especially during LVP  procedures.

Decap LVI

The second alignment technique we are investigating is the use  of decap LVI modulation [3]. It has been previously reported  by Niu, et al., that modulating the power rail of an IC highlights  the decap cells in LVI maps, and that such maps are useful for  CAD alignment [4]. Figure 11 demonstrates that this is still a  viable technique for 3 nm ICs. Figure 12 is a schematic of the  FETs in a decap cell showing how they are electrically biased. The FET-based standard-cell decaps use the same transistors as  logic cells. Therefore, modulating VDD modulates the charge in  the gate channel, producing an LVI response. For the 3 nm  process, only pFETs are used as decaps. The nFETs are  disabled by having all terminals tied to ground. Hence, the use  of the DCAP CAD layer ANDed to the NW layer for alignment  in Fig. 11 (DCAP_NW = DCAP AND NW). The strongest  decap modulation occurs when two larger decap cells abut on  their pFET side (creating the wider polygons). The shorter  decaps modulate weakly due to the low fraction of active pFETs  contained in the smaller cell. The modulation visible w/in logic  is thought to be due to laser-logic-state-imaging (LLSI) [4].

The main barrier to practical application of this technique is the  need to modulate VDD with sufficient amplitude at high enough  frequency to be detectable. The lower frequency limit is set by  the LVX electronics with 10-20 kHz cut-on frequency being  typical. For the test vehicle used, a function generator driving  an off-the-shelf current amplifier was adequate [Accel TS250  current amplifier https://accelinstruments.com/]. For product  IC on ATE, other means are required. Some possibilities are  discussed in [4]. Ideally, VDD is modulated with the IC powered  up and looping the LVX test pattern to allow real-time  alignment.

If real-time modulation on ATE is not possible, one potential workaround is to first acquire reference LSM images off-line  using a benchtop setup. The well-aligned reference images  could then be imported into the CAD layout and used in the  same way that the simulated images would be used for  alignment (Fig. 10). For this scheme, a DUT board is needed  that allows the VDD rail to be powered using a current amplifier  with sufficient ampacity, e.g., a latch-up test board with  multiple current amplifiers ganged together. Alternatively, a  system-level board could be used by injecting a modulation into  the voltage regulator VSENSE line to induce a VDD modulation.

The obvious drawback to this scheme is the need to  predetermine the ROI over which to acquire the aligned LSM  images. The extra overhead in both time and equipment setup  required is also a major drawback.

Conclusions/Future Work

Two advanced CAD-to-image alignment methodologies were  presented: CAD based image simulation and decap LVI. These  methodologies are meant to address fault isolation challenges at  sub-5 nm technology nodes caused by the increasingly large  gap between optical resolution and shrinking IC geometries. No  ideal CAD alignment methodology exists for these leadingedge nodes and both introduced methodologies will require  further development before they can be considered practical  and productive. For CAD-derived image simulation, the match  between LSM and simulated images is already significantly  better than the correlation to any individual CAD layer, but  there is still much room for further improvements. For this  paper, we focused on the image simulation and correlation aspect, and further work is needed to enable seamless import, thresholding and CAD alignment using the simulated images.

Given that different CAD layers can have different scaling with  regards to their corresponding structures within the chip, not all  layers should be simulated in the same way. Additionally, given the complex convolution of many CAD layers forming the LSM  image, we believe that the heuristics for individual layers and  layer weighting factors are best derived with the help of image  correlation optimization algorithms. We hope to motivate  further investigation and investment along those lines with this  paper. If the simulated image quality can be improved

sufficiently, it could open the door to further productivity gains  based on auto-focus and auto CAD alignment procedures, which have not been reliable in the past and are impossible  today without enhancements like image simulation.

For Decap LVI, we continue to investigate ways to modulate  VDD on ATE and work with vendors to reduce the cut-on  frequencies of their detectors. We anticipate that in the near  future, these two techniques will join the existing techniques of  clock LVI and insertion of navigation fiducials as available  options for precision CAD alignment and help reduce time to  results and help extend the usefulness of OFI systems within  future technology nodes.

Laser Probe Techniques with Adaptive FPGA Device

Zhi Hao Ko

Advanced Micro Devices Singapore Pte Ltd, 5 Changi Business Park Vista, Singapore 486040  Email: zhihaok@amd.com

Amitesh Kumar, Jobin Thomas Valliyakalayil

Liquid Instruments Lyneham, ACT, Australia 2602

Email: amitesh@liquidinstruments.com, jobin@liquidinstruments.com

Abstract

This paper introduces an accessible implementation of laser  probe (LP) techniques using a single adaptive fieldprogrammable gate array (FPGA) device. Through several case  studies, we demonstrate different integration methods and  improvements over conventional ways. First, we investigate  two alternative implementations of frequency-domain mapping (FM): one using a software-defined lock-in amplifier, and  another using a dual boxcar averager module. Second, we  explore a time-domain mapping (TM) technique implemented  with the dual boxcar averager. Third, we introduce a  customized solution to enhance signal quality in combination  with a software-defined lock-in amplifier. Lastly, we examine  the use of artificial intelligence (AI), specifically neural  networks (NN), to improve LP signal acquisition during realtime signal processing. These approaches reduce barriers to  innovation by eliminating the need for substantial upfront legal  or financial commitments between collaborating organizations.

Introduction

A field-programmable gate array (FPGA) is an integrated  circuit that can be programmed and reconfigured by the user  after manufacturing, enabling custom digital logic designs. Due  to their high-speed parallel processing capabilities, FPGAs are  particularly suited for applications that require rapid data  handling and high efficiency, especially in real-time data  processing [1]. Modern FPGA variants often integrate both hard  and soft intellectual property (IP) cores, further enhancing their  functionality. Examples of these integrated solutions include  system-on-chip (SoC) architectures with embedded processors, radio-frequency (RF) and digital front ends optimized for highspeed real-time RF signal processing, and neural processing  unit (NPU) designed to accelerate artificial intelligence (AI) algorithms and machine learning model training.

The ability to partially reconfigure an FPGA enables users to  simultaneously access a suite of software-defined instruments, supporting high-speed data acquisition, signal processing and  visualization, waveform generation, and real-time control

applications [1]. This feature allows users to build custom test  configurations with low-latency, lossless interconnects, significantly reducing complex cabling and related signal  impairments. Instruments running in this mode can be daisychained to build sophisticated signal processing pipelines. Additionally, instruments can be hot swapped i.e. added or  removed dynamically, without disrupting the operation of those  already running. Figure 1 shows the block diagram of the FPGA  with reconfigurable block A that can run any of the bit streams  while in operation.

Figure 1: Basic premise of partial reconfiguration with hotswap switch fabric.

An innovative hybrid front-end design [2] performs frequencydependent signal blending from multiple ADCs, offering  exceptional low-noise performance across a wide frequency  range - from acoustic to radio frequencies as shown in Figure 2.

Advanced users can implement custom functionalities  developed using hardware description language (HDL) and  python-based application programming interface (API). This  capability to integrate user-defined code with software-defined  instruments offers users unlimited potential for innovation and  the ability to handle complex experiments effectively.

Accessible Implementation in Laser Probing

The integration of applications such as laser probing and its  derivative techniques typically relies heavily on original  equipment manufacturer (OEM) solutions, with proprietary  knowledge constraining open innovation. Furthermore, the  initial legal and financial agreements required between external  organizations can be complex and laborious, significantly  hindering the innovation process. This challenge equally  impacts collaborations between government and academic  institutions.

In response, this paper explores a more accessible user-friendly  approach designed to be compatible with any commercial laser  scanning microscope (LSM) equipped with a low-noise laser  and an appropriate bandwidth detector. Most commercial LSMs  provide at least one photon detector output, which conveys  electrically stimulated reflections from the device under test (DUT); an analog auxiliary input used to translate signals into  greyscale image pixels; and an external synchronization input  for laser-instrument synchronization (Figure 3).

Figure 3: Commercial Laser Scanning Microscope (LSM) external I/O with default LP and FM configuration.

Default LP and FM configurations provided by LSM OEM are  usually paired with standalone instruments such as  oscilloscopes and spectrum analyzers for respective techniques. The implementation of TM further necessitates an additional  lock-in amplifier instrument with a boxcar averaging capability, usually as an add-on option. Our proposed approach  significantly simplifies this setup, requiring only a single  adaptive FPGA device and two physical connections: one to the  photon detector output and another to the analog auxiliary input (Figure 4). Notably, laser synchronization is not used under this  configuration due to LSM software limitation. Once hardware  connections are established, the instruments can be switched  entirely via software. We will now discuss the implementation  of LP and its derivative techniques in more detail.

Figure 4: Simplified implementation of LP techniques versus  the default OEM configuration (crossed out), by replacing all  three standalone measurements instruments (spectrum  analyzer, oscilloscope and lock-in amplifier) with a single  Adaptive FPGA Device.

Frequency-domain Mapping (FM)

FM is typically the initial technique used to align laser images  with die layouts and to ensure precise optical focusing, which  is critical for optimal signal acquisition.

Our first FM implementation utilizes a software-defined lockin amplifier deployed on the adaptive FPGA. The lock-in  amplifier includes a phase-locked loop (PLL) option capable of  generating a sine wave synchronized with the DUT sync pulse  signal. If phase information is required, the DUT sync pulse can  be optionally connected directly to the FPGA device; otherwise, an internal oscillator is sufficient (Figure 5). The final  configuration involves setting the desired experiment frequency  either in the internal oscillator or within the PLL module and  selecting rectangular or polar coordinates, depending on  whether phase information or amplitude-only FM is desired (Figure 6). The result is a high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) FM  signal that supports fast scan rates with reduced raster areas.

Thus, optimal optical focusing can be achieved by observing  live FM scan results and adjusting the optical focus on-the-fly. Figure 7 (upper row) shows sequential FM images captured  during a focusing maneuver. To attain an optimal focus, both  the P and N type active regions must exhibit their global  maximum contrast values. A contrast graph, plotted from the  dotted rectangular region shown in Figure 7 (upper row), appears in Figure 7 (bottom row). This graph quantitatively  depicts contrast variations along the P and N active regions. Image number 4 qualifies as having optimal focus because it  meets the criterion of global maximum contrast in both the P  and N type active regions. This statistical approach has  potential applications in automation processes for future work.

It should be noted that optimal FM performance is achieved  when the target frequency is periodic - such as a clock or a  flattened HHLL-based scan pattern - with a duty cycle of  approximately 50%. Deviations from a 50% duty cycle  introduce additional harmonics, negatively impacting system  performance and reducing the overall SNR [6].

Figure 5: Physical Hardware connection between the adaptive  FPGA device and LSM.

The second FM implementation utilizes a software-defined dual  boxcar averager. The baseline boxcar is set to the null clock  location, and the pulse boxcar is set to the active clock location  in the time domain (Figure 8). The dual boxcar requires more  than 2000 averages to achieve a decent SNR and can attain a  fast scan rate depending on the test pattern length, frequency, and permissible laser power. Figure 9 shows a comparison of  results obtained from different FM implementations. In general, FM using a dual boxcar averager exhibits a busier background  compared to the lock-in amplifier method because it captures  all activity within the gated time domain, whereas the lock-in  amplifier method exclusively captures activity at the target  frequency (Figure 10). Users can select the appropriate FM  implementation based on their specific objectives.

Time domain Mapping (TM)

To implement TM [4][5][6][7] with the adaptive FPGA device, no changes were made to the hardware connections as per  Figure 5. Only the software-defined instrumentation is switched  from the Lock-In Amplifier to the dual boxcar averager module. Configure the pulse boxcar to capture the desired signal  location and the baseline boxcar to no signal location. Finally, align the laser pixel delay with the boxcar averaging time, as  shown in Figure 11.

Figure 11: Example of time domain waveform diagram for TM  setting. The trigger (blue) is provided by the tester. The baseline  boxcar (short yellow) is set on location with no signal, and the  pulse boxcar (tall yellow) is set on the desired location to  investigate.

TM is particularly effective for tracing transistor activity  signatures of aperiodic signals or low-duty-cycle periodic  signals, such as those generated by compressed scan patterns. Figure 12 shows TM applied to a scan cell under test, with input  and output buffers at SI and SO. A missing TM signal is  detected starting from within the scan cell at the output section  and extending to SO buffer B. This anomaly is further examined  using LP, which reveals that the scan cell output was stuck.

Figure 12: TM result image on good and fail unit. Missing TM  signal starting from the scan cell output region to the output  buffer B on the failure unit compared to good unit. LP signal

on the scan cell output marked as “+” showing it is stuck

comparing to good unit.

TM has also proven valuable for accurate probe placement [4], offering a faster alternative to traditional, time-consuming  multi-point acquisition methods [8] and mitigating issues  caused by laser misalignment when the LP laser wavelength  differs from the imaging laser wavelength. However, the  throughput of TM is inherently slow, requiring at least three  orders of magnitude of averaging cycles. Typically, TM is  performed using a reduced scan window, and it is advisable to  optimize the test pattern length for maximum efficiency.

Moving Average Filter

In this section, we demonstrate that a custom solution can be  deployed to meet unique measurement requirements. Specifically, we show a simple implementation of FM using a  lock-in amplifier operating in tandem with a customized realtime moving average filter in cloud compile module [Figure  13].  No physical wiring is required between the two softwaredefined instruments, as all connections are configured  internally within the FPGA’s physical interconnect fabric.

The moving average filter can be implemented by equation:

Where x(t) is the discrete time series input signal, y(t) is the  output signal and n is the number of consecutive signal samples. The equation is converted into HDL code, compiled into a  bitstream file, and is then ready for deployment [3].

Figure 13: Tandem configuration of software-defined  instruments. The output A of lock-in amplifier is connected to  input A of cloud compile which contained the custom solution  of moving average filter.

This simple filter is computationally lightweight, requiring only  an accumulator, subtractor, and bit-wise shift. As a result, it  operates with very low latency and is well-suited for real-time  applications. The latency between the input and output of the  moving average filter is measured at 224 ns, corresponding to  70 clock cycles of the 312.5 MHz FPGA-based clock [Figure  14].

Figure 14: The latency between input and output of both lockin amplifier and moving average filter is around 222ns with  50Mhz FPGA based clock. Red line is the input, while the blue  line is the output of the moving average filter.

This moving average filter reduces the noise amplitude by a  factor of √2n. In our implementation n=8, so the noise amplitude  should be reduced to 1/16 or equivalently, the signal amplitude  is amplified by 16 times its original value. The moving average  filter output and input is measured to be 360mV and 22mV  respectively, around 16.4 times. This performance matches the  theoretical expectation [Figure 15]. With the improved SNR  provided by the moving average filter, the laser power can be  reduced, or faster scan times can be achieved by decreasing the  pixel dwell time while maintaining comparable results.

Figure 15: Comparison of the moving average filter output and  the original output from lock-in amplifier; The output voltage  is 360mV and 22mV respectively.

Neural Network (NN) Denoise

The reconfigurable and parallel-processing architecture of  FPGAs is well-suited for neural network (NN) processing. It  provides low latency inference performance suitable for a wide  range of real-time signal processing applications, such as signal  denoising, classification, and closed-loop control.

In this case study, we use an autoencoder NN for signal  denoising, serving as front-end signal processing before feeding  into software-defined instruments, such as oscilloscope, lock-in  amplifier and boxcar averager. An autoencoder is a type of  neural network designed to efficiently learn compressed  representations of input data. It accomplishes this by employing  a network architecture that compresses data into a smaller latent  space representation before reconstructing it back to its original  input size.

Autoencoder

A 32-data-point sliding window algorithm is used to transform  serial time-series data into 32 parallel data formats before  feeding into the NN. A four-layer autoencoder is configured as  shown in Figure 16. The first three layers have latent spaces  configured as 16-2-16, each using a Tanh activation function, while the final layer employs a linear activation function to  funnel the decoded data into a single output. The autoencoder  is trained using randomly generated, zero-mean, normaldistribution white noise data.

Figure 16: A four-layer autoencoder structure on a sliding  window of temporal data.

With the current FPGA resource constraints, the NN input  sampling rate is limited to 305 kSa/s, hindering further

exploration in real case studies, as our test setup and laser probe  detector bandwidth are incompatible. Nonetheless, we  conducted a series of software simulation tests to study the  autoencoder NN behavior, using randomly generated white  noise with a normal distribution added to a square waveform  signal of 0.5 amplitude.

Metric

To evaluate the denoising performance, we employed the  standard deviation difference (SDD), which measures the  standard deviation of the difference between the processed  signal and the ground truth, instead of using the mean square  error (MSE). The SDD metric provides a more consistent  representation of the denoising results compared to the ground  truth across various scenarios unlike the MSE metric. Figure 17  demonstrates that MSE misinterprets the autoencoder’s  performance, indicating it is eight times better than a median  filter (8.9975 vs 0.9347), which is misleading, as the median  filter more closely resembles the ground truth. In contrast, the  SDD metric accurately reflects actual performance, showing  that the median filter achieves a lower SDD (lower the better) compared to the autoencoder (0.1551 vs 0.3814).

Figure 17: Comparison of SDD and MSE metric between a  median filter and autoencoder.

Offset

A negative offset of 5 data points is observed in the autoencoder  output relative to the ground truth [Figure 18]. This offset is  noticeable only in simulation, where no processing delay is  factored in. In practical applications, this negative offset can  generally be disregarded because instrument delays will be  significantly longer, and ground truth data for direct  comparison will be unavailable. A 5-data-point offset is applied  throughout this case study.

Figure 18: Comparison of original autoencoder output with  negative offset, and the corrected version.

Sampling

To test how well the autoencoder performs under different  sampling rates or data densities, we defined the sampling rate  as the number of samples taken per signal pulse. In LP  applications, the sampling rate is generally set between 50 and  200 samples per signal pulse to achieve a reasonable resolution  for analysis, depending on the test setup frequency and the  capabilities of the oscilloscope. The results show that the  autoencoder benefits from increased data density but begins to  plateau above 400 sampling/pulse [Figure 19].

Figure 19: The performance of the autoencoder with different  sampling rate. *Lower SDD is better.

Noise level

In this experiment, we tested the autoencoder under varying  noise input levels. The noise was defined and generated based  on the standard deviation of a random normal distribution. The  results show that the autoencoder performs better under low  noise conditions [Figure 20] and begins to struggle dramatically  as the noise level increases.

Figure 20: The performance of the autoencoder with different  noise levels. *Lower SDD is better.

NN Layer

Different NN layer counts and latent space sizes were tested  with the autoencoder structure.  The results show that the  autoencoder performs better when the latent space is  compressed to the smallest allowable size, which is 2 in this  case. Performance improves as the number of NN layers  increases from 3 to 5, but it declines when the number of layers  increases from 5 to 7 layers.

Figure 21: The performance of the autoencoder with different  NN layer counts and latent spaces. *Lower SDD is better.

Average vs Autoencoder vs Median filter

The autoencoder was tested against median filters with average  under a high-noise input scenario, using a normal distribution  with a standard deviation of 2. The results show that the median  filter outperforms both the average filter (noisy input) and the  autoencoder by a significant margin.

Figure 22: A comparison of performance between autoencoder, average and median filter.

Autoencoder Experiment Summary

To summarize, the autoencoder can perform reasonably well  under conditions of high data density and low noise levels. However, the experiment shows that the autoencoder is not  suitable for deployment as a front-end signal denoising solution  when the input noise exceeds a standard deviation of 0.25 in a  normal distribution. A median filter with averaging is more  appropriate for this application, as it can accommodate a  broader range of input data densities and noise levels. Future  research could focus on alternative training datasets or feedback  NN structures – such as recurrent neural network (RNN).

Conclusions

This paper presents an accessible implementation of laser probe  techniques using a single adaptive FPGA device, demonstrated  through real-world use cases. The FPGA device extends beyond  a simple reconfigurable test and measurement instrument. It  serves as a customizable signal processing solution, fostering  innovation to accommodate a wide spectrum of unique testing  requirements. The live NN concept still holds significant  potential in real-time signal processing; a more capable FPGA  could mitigate current sampling rate limitations. Additionally, other NN models should be explored to achieve improved  performance.

The demonstrated application implementations represent lowhanging fruit and lay the groundwork for further innovation – not only in advanced optical fault isolation methodologies but  across the broader domain of failure analysis techniques  methodologies.

Detection Efficiency Improvements on Automated Soft Defect Localization Using  Array-based Image Reconstruction

Benny Hsu, Arun Karunanithi, Kent Erington, Calder Wilson

Advanced Micro Devices, Inc., Austin, TX, USA

Abstract

Efficient and accurate fault isolation (FI) is crucial for  determining the root cause of integrated circuit malfunctions. One of the challenges is long data acquisition time and accuracy  for soft defect localization (SDL). This paper proposes a novel  approach for soft defect localization (SDL) data collection and  processing, enhancing the accuracy and efficiency of the data  acquisition process. Our approach utilizes an array-based image  reconstruction methodology alongside an automated SDL  workflow for improved site detection accuracy of both weak  and strong sites. In this study, we demonstrate the effectiveness  of our approach using simulated SDL runs and a real test case, showing significant improvements in site coverage and  detection capabilities when compared to traditional continuous  averaging approach. The newly proposed methodology  facilitates a more comprehensive and practical SDL workflow  and analysis time.

Introduction

Electrical fault isolation (FI), is a crucial process for  investigating the root cause of integrated circuit malfunctions. FI techniques typically utilize the electrical or functional testing  of the device combined with external stimulus to isolate the  point of failures, which can be favorable since it is less intrusive  and is less likely to permanently alter the DUT.

Among many non-destructive FI techniques, soft defect  localization (SDL) is widely used to detect marginal failures or  timing-sensitive paths where the device under test (DUT) is  marginally compromised but not to the point of complete or  permanent failure [1]. The core mechanism of SDL technique  is the implementation of a 1340 nm laser to generate localized  heat that temporarily alters the electrical properties of  transistors. The DUT undergoes a continuous test loop that  outputs either a pass or fail condition while the laser scans over  the DUT surface in a raster pattern. The pass/fail result is  recorded according to the laser scan pattern to recreate a gray  scale SDL image. This image reveals the sections of the  circuitry that are more susceptible to the effect of localized  heating. SDL boasts high modularity as it can fit diverse types  of tests as long as there is a pass-fail boundary within the test's  parameters.

SDL Acquisition Time Challenge

Since each pixel in a 2D SDL image represents a combination  of multiple test results, SDL acquisition time is directly  proportional to factors such as scan area, test loop time, image  resolution, and the number of captured frames. In test cases

involving long test times or large areas of interest (AOI), acquisition time can easily grow from hours to days, making  large area SDL scans inefficient or even impractical [2] [3] [4]. The issue is further exacerbated by growing die size, device  complexity, and shorter product development cycles. Therefore, minimizing SDL scan time is critical for enhancing  efficiency and practicality. In the pursuit of shorter image  acquisition times, the challenge lies in managing the troika of  compromises involving the number of frames, scan area, and  image resolution. These factors greatly depend on the  experience of the analyst, the tool employed, and the DUT  being examined.

To address the challenge of SDL acquisition time, our team  recently proposed a novel solution featuring an automated SDL  workflow referred to as software automated intelligent laser  scanning (SAILS) [5]. This approach incorporates a refined site  detection algorithm that identifies SDL sites early in the  acquisition process and introduces a region of interest (ROI) mask to include only these sites. As a result, the downstream  scan area and acquisition time are significantly reduced, leading  to increased data acquisition efficiency. However, the current  automation relies on a single continuous averaging dynamic  laser stimulation image for site detection. While this approach  demonstrates good accuracy and a significant reduction in scan  area for detecting strong sites, detecting weak sites remains  challenging. Additionally, the current workflow requires setting  up the site detection algorithm sensitivity manually before the  data acquisition process - an area with room for improvement. Setting the value too high leads to good detection of strong sites  as well as a significant reduction in scan time but poses a higher  possibility of missing weak sites. Lowering the threshold to  identify weak sites introduces a higher number of false  positives, which in turn negatively impacts both the signal-tonoise ratio (SNR) and overall acquisition time.

In this article, we introduce an innovative data acquisition  methodology and a refined automated SDL workflow with the  goal of enhancing automated site detection for both weak and  strong sites. To evaluate the performance of our new approach, we have conducted simulated SDL runs that quantify its  effectiveness and site detection coverage, and one case of a real  SDL scan that demonstrates its performance.

Array-Based Image Reconstruction

Methodology for Site Detection

The SDL scanning process utilizes a laser to scan the area of  interest (AOI) in a raster pattern, capturing pass-fail results and  continuously averaging values into a single 2D SDL image  where pixel values are the failure percentage of the test when  the laser is at that given location. In this work we refer to the

laser interaction signal intensity as the shift in fail percentage. The continuous averaging of the standard SDL method is a lossy process since it discards individual pass/fail (binary) frames and only presents a single continuous averaging frame. As such, further algorithmic site detection improvements are limited simply because only a single reference image is available.

To address this issue, we introduce an array-based image reconstruction methodology that aims to ensure lossless data capture by preserving all the individual binary frames for further analysis. In this array-based image reconstruction methodology for site detection, each individual frame is captured and subjected to a reconstruction process, resulting in the production of numerous reconstructed frames. Subsequently, the processed reconstructed frames are processed and merged to form a single ROI mask. This ROI mask is depicted as a red enclosure, as illustrated in Figure  1 .

 Site Detection Algorithm

Site Detection Algorithm

The site detection algorithm begins by applying a smoothing filter to the input frame, effectively suppressing high-frequency noise. Next, the frame undergoes an element-wise comparison in which each individual element is compared to a specific value, known as the threshold, T. This threshold represents a certain percentile of the entire image, with A denoting the input frame. Since the SDL site could be both passing and failing sites, the comparison works on both sides of the distribution. As the result of this comparison, a binary frame is created according to the following rule:

(1) Binary frame(i, j) = { 1, if A(i, j)  >  T 1, if A(i, j)  <  1 -T 0, otherwise }

This process generates a binary frame where each pixel is assigned to a value of 1 if its intensity in the input frame, A, exceeds the threshold, T or less than 1 -T; otherwise, it is assigned a value of 0. Finally, morphological transformations are applied to create a grouping effect that eliminates gaps between close pixels to better approximate the true shape of the site. The same site detection workflow is used in both the array-based and continuous averaging approaches, with the difference being the number of frames the algorithm has operated on. For the continuous average approach, the algorithm runs once and generates one ROI mask out of a single input image (continuous averaging frame), while in the array-based approach, the same algorithm runs multiple times on the reconstructed frames.

 Methods

Methods

 1. Statistical Analysis

1. Statistical Analysis

In this study, our objective was to evaluate the performance improvement of the array-based method in comparison to continuous averaging on site detection accuracy and coverage.

The simulated SDL dataset comprises a single circular site with a diameter of 15 pixels, arbitrarily positioned within a 200x200 pixels frame.

The site intensity is determined using a standard distribution, where the probability of high values (1 in a binary image) is centered around 50%. The simulated site consists of two concentric probability circles: The inner circle is eight pixels wide and has X% higher chance than 50% to give either a 0(dark site) or 1(bright site). The outer circle is between 8 and 15 pixels wide and has half the chance compared to the inner circle to change from the 50%, as shown in Figure  2 . This probability is referred to as "site intensity" in the subsequent discussions. Probabilities ranging from 4.8% to 22.6% were selected for data generation. To create simulated images that are more representative of actual SDL images, a final 3x3 averaging filter was applied to all binary frames to smooth out the site boundaries. A total of 100 datasets were generated, with 50 sets featuring a single bright site and 50 with a single dark site for each site intensity variable.

In each simulated SDL run, six frames were generated representing the initial frames captured for site detection and ROI mask generation. In the continuous averaging, a single average frame was created by averaging all six binary frames.

In contrast, the array-based approach utilized the original six binary frames for site detection. The focus of this experiment is to compare two approaches for site detection accuracy. In this case, site coverage, representing the percentage of the known site area (with a diameter of eight pixels) present within the ROI mask, is represented by the following equation:

(2)   (%) =   ℎ ℎ  

                                         

                                        

The ideal scenario entails high site coverage even when the ROI mask area is low. Area ROI mask is defined as the percentage of pixels in the mask compared to the full frame. Area ROI mask values of 5%, 10%, 20%, and 35% were selected to compare the two approaches.

Results

1. Statistical Analysis

The motivation for developing this workflow is to increase the site detection accuracy and coverage while reducing data acquisition time. Figure 2(right) shows one of the ROI masks generated using the array-based approach with a 5% area constraint. In this case, site coverage is 100% as the inner circle is fully covered by the ROI mask.

Figure 3 presents the results of the simulation, comparing the  ROI mask coverage versus simulated site intensity for the two  approaches under various area constraints of 5%, 10%, 20%, and 35%. The figure consists of four statistical charts, each  displaying the site coverage distribution and variation using  boxes and whiskers.

In each chart, the X-axis represents the simulated site intensity, while the Y-axis corresponds to the ROI mask coverage. Within  the charts, the continuous averaging is depicted by the blue box, whereas the array-based is represented by the tan box. The  charts illustrate that under tighter area constraints, the  probability of missing the site increases, specifically when the  site intensity is as low as 4.8% and 7.2%. This increased  likelihood is indicated by the extended distribution observed in  the charts. The results suggest that when dealing with weak  sites, detection becomes more challenging, as it is easier to  identify random locations with statistically higher intensity  values. At higher site intensities, a considerably tighter and  higher overall coverage distribution can be observed, accompanied by a few outliers.

Logically, one might assume that increasing the ROI area  would improve the chances of detecting the site. While this  assertion holds true to some extent, based on the observed  increase in the lower quartile (Q1) and lower whisker across all  four charts, it is notable that outliers with low coverage still  persist. In some cases, the presence of these outliers does not  show any improvement, indicating that merely increasing the  ROI area might not be a fix-all solution for site detection.

When comparing both approaches, the array-based approach  has better site coverage across all area constraints since it has a  higher median and tighter distribution. It also appears that from  a practical standpoint, it is better to implement a 5% area ROI  mask to allow for a fast scan to detect sites with intensity up to

11.8%, and a 35% area ROI mask for weaker sites.

2. Experimental Analysis

Figure 4 presents the experimental results of actual SDL performed on a DUT. The left side of the figure displays the six-frame average with laser power set at 100% and 33%, while the right side illustrates the generated ROI masks with a 5%frame area, using two different approaches. When the laser power is at or above 40%, both approaches are capable of generating ROI masks with 100% site coverage. The primary difference between the two approaches becomes apparent when the laser power is reduced to 33%; array-based ROI mask displays a site coverage of 28%, while continuous averaging yields 0% (as indicated in the table in Figure 4).

Although this experiment demonstrates that the array-based  approach generates better outcomes for weak site detection, further case studies are necessary to confirm these findings. A  variety of factors, such as AOI drift, optical focus, and image  resolution, may significantly affect the image SNR and overall  quality. Nevertheless, the experimental results in this study  indicate that the array-based approach provides higher site  coverage compared to the traditional approach.

Based on the statistical data presented above, a revised  automated SDL workflow is used that consists of three stages. In the first stage, a normal full area ROI is used to acquire the  initial six frames necessary for site detection. Subsequently, the  frames are processed to generate two ROI masks, one with a  5% area and another with a 35% frame area. The 5% area ROI

mask is applied first to enable rapid frame acquisition for strong  sites. Once the strong site(s) has been captured, the process  switches to the 35% area ROI mask to acquire frames for weak  site(s). Figure 5 depicts the correlation between the number of  captured frames and normalized acquisition time. Assuming  that 10 frames sufficiently identify both strong and weak sites, the traditional approach would necessitate a total of 10 units of  time. In contrast, the double ROI mask approach allows the  acquisition of 35 frames for strong sites and 15 frames for weak  sites in the same amount of time, resulting in a substantial  enhancement in acquisition efficiency and overall site  identification, as illustrated by the purple line in the graph.

Figure 4: Six-frame averages at 100% and 33% laser power  levels (left) and their corresponding 5% frame area ROI masks (right), with site coverage comparisons under different site  intensities (bottom table).

Figure 5. Capture Frame vs. SDL Acquisition Time for  Different ROI Masks: Utilizing a combination of 5% and 35% ROI masks within the data acquisition workflow that maximizes  site detecting for both strong and weak site(s).

Conclusions

We have proposed and demonstrated a novel approach for SDL  data collection and processing that enhances both the accuracy  and efficiency of the data acquisition process. The effectiveness  of this new approach was assessed through simulated SDL runs,

revealing significant improvements in site coverage across a  variety of area constraints. Notably, our approach shows a  marked improvement in weak site detection capabilities  compared to the traditional approach. Experimental studies  further validate the feasibility of the new site detection  approach across various site intensities.

The proposed methodology offers a more effective means of  processing data, yielding multiple benefits over the  conventional technique such as site coverage and weak sites  detection accuracy. It facilitates a true automated SDL  workflow that could accommodate both weak and strong sites  and introduces prioritization to maximize acquisition  efficiency. Moreover, this methodology holds potential for  integration not only in SDL but also in other imaged based FI  techniques such as laser assisted device alteration (LADA) or  thermally induced voltage alteration (TIVA). This study  demonstrates enhanced performance with minimum shift of  mindset on data acquisition and analysis, paving the way for  future advancements that continue to enhance the performance  and capabilities of fault isolation techniques.

Electrical Failure Analysis of Speckled Shmoo and Shmoo Striping Failures

Amrutha Sampath, Kristofor Dickson, Dan Bodoh, Chik Hooi Liew

NXP Semiconductors, Austin, Texas, USA  Amrutha.sampath_1@nxp.com

Abstract

As System-on-Chip (SoC) designs grow increasingly  complex—driven by advanced clocking architectures, asynchronous independent clock domains, and continued  device scaling—there has been a noticeable rise in failures that  manifest as speckles or stripes in shmoo plots. This paper  explores the root causes of these distinctive failure patterns and  offers insights into the underlying mechanisms.

We investigate a range of timing-related failure modes, including clock skew, excessive signal delays, and issues from  signals crossing asynchronous clock domains. Particular focus  is placed on metastability caused by inadequate glitch  management. Many of these failures stem from marginalities in  circuit design or manufacturing processes.

The discussion begins with basic shmoo signatures linked to  setup timing violations and progresses to more complex  scenarios. To pinpoint the causes of speckled shmoo failures, we apply various electrical failure analysis techniques. A case  study is presented involving a sub-10nm device that exhibits a  speckled shmoo failure, tied to a Streaming Scan Network  Transition Delay (SSN-TD) pattern, where two independent  clock domains interact to produce a unique failure mode. Finally, waveform data captured using 785 nm and 1064 nm  lasers is compared to highlight performance differences  between the two wavelengths.

Introduction

Soft failures occur when a device does not behave as expected  under certain operating conditions, often due to variations in  voltage, frequency, or temperature. To analyze such failures, engineers rely on shmoo plots—visual representations that map  pass/fail behavior across a range of environmental and  operational parameters, such as voltage and frequency. Shmoo  plots help identify the boundaries of reliable operation and  reveal regions of marginal functionality, offering valuable  insights into the robustness of a design. Figure 1a shows a  classic speed-versus-voltage shmoo plot for a given device. The  gradual curve along the pass/fail boundary indicates the  functional speed limit as a function of supply voltage. As we  move from right to left and as clock speed increases, a setup  timing violation occurs somewhere in the device, associated  with the slowest data path exercised with that particular test. Increasing supply voltage reduces propagation delay, and  therefore, we see that the device can operate at high clock

frequencies as VDD is raised. Figure 1b illustrates the setup  time criteria and explains how a setup violation can occur. The  lower-right corner of the plot typically flattens out as the clock  slows down, revealing the minimum achievable operational  voltage floor (Vmin). Below this floor, certain logic cells  become metastable, or latches refuse to transition properly.

Figure 1: a) The most common Shmoo plot is a Speed versus  voltage graph, shown below. It reveals where the pass/fail  boundary for the device under test exists.  b) This figure  illustrates the setup time criteria and explains the parameters it  depends on.

Soft failures often manifest as shifts in the shmoo plot  boundaries compared to typical distributions, such as slower  speed walls or elevated Vmin values. Signatures extracted from  these plots can be correlated with specific failing test vectors,

www.asminternational.org
