November 16–20, 2025, Pasadena, California, USA

https://doi.org/10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2025p0140

enabling engineers to quantify performance improvements  through targeted design changes. As shown in Figure 2, the  effectiveness of these fixes—whether aimed at improving  power efficiency or speed—can be assessed by analyzing the  thickness of failure bands within the shmoo region of interest.

II: Understanding Shmoo Plot Signatures

Within shmoo plots, distinct patterns often emerge that provide  valuable insights into underlying issues. One such pattern is  the speckled shmoo, characterized by scattered failing points  near the pass/fail boundary. These speckles typically indicate  marginal failures caused by subtle defects or complex timing  violations, such as glitches, metastability in flip-flops, or noise  coupling. Figure 3 illustrates a good example of a speckled  shmoo. For most cases, the speckles appear randomly or move  slightly within each plot. Diagnosing these failures is  particularly challenging, as the failure rate can fluctuate  unpredictably between 0% and 100% at a fixed test condition. This variability complicates efforts to establish a stable bias  point for techniques like Soft Defect Localization (SDL) or  Laser-Assisted Device Alteration (LADA) [1,2].

Figure 2: Shmoo plots can be color-coded to highlight specific  test fail signatures. By identifying each fail mode and resolving  its root cause, subsequent design revisions can achieve either  lower power consumption at the same frequency or higher  frequency at the same power level.

.

Figure 3: Example of a speckled signature in a voltage-versusclock-period shmoo plot. These failures are pseudo-nondeterministic and typically result from glitch propagation, metastability, or cross-domain clocking issues.

Speckles in a shmoo plot represent rare, pseudo-nondeterministic failures—events that occur only under highly  specific conditions. These failures are typically caused by glitch  propagation, metastability, or issues related to clock domain  crossings that lead to a temporary timing violation. Figure 4  illustrates a speckled failure resulting from a glitch generated  by simultaneous input switching to an XOR gate. In each  instance of failure observed in the shmoo, the glitch  successfully propagated downstream and arrived at a flip-flop  precisely at the same time as the rising edge of the clock. This  timing alignment caused the flip-flop to capture incorrect data, but only when the glitch and clock edge coincided. These are  classic examples of special-event failures, where the interaction  of design behavior, process variation, and timing creates a  narrow and unpredictable window for failure to occur.

Figure 4: a) Another example of a speckled signature in a  voltage-versus-clock-period shmoo plot. b) Speckled shmoo  failure caused by a glitch aligned with the clock edge. The root  cause was traced to a glitch at the output of a multiplexer, triggered by the interaction between design and process.

Another example of a speckled failure is shown in Figure 5. In  this case, the root cause was traced to an asynchronous clock  domain crossing event that occurred during a memory Built-In  Self-Test (BIST) operation. Such failures arise when signals  transition between clock domains operating at different  frequencies without proper synchronization. Despite  advancements in synchronization techniques and  improvements in design rule checks at modern process nodes, cross-domain clocking issues continue to be a significant source  of non-deterministic failures in shmoo plots. Improper  synchronization can lead to metastability, glitch propagation, and timing inconsistencies—particularly during complex test  sequences such as the March Test Algorithm. In this instance, a  glitch was captured at the rising edge of the clock due to a  synchronization fault, resulting in a speckled failure mode.

Figure 5: Speckled shmoo failure caused by a signal crossing  asynchronous clock domains. A glitch was captured at the  rising clock edge due to a synchronization fault.

Another notable failure signature is the shmoo stripe, which can  appear as distinct bands of failures across the plot. These stripes  may be voltage-dependent, emerging at specific voltages across  all frequencies, or frequency-dependent, repeating at certain  intervals within the operating voltage range. The causes of  shmoo stripes vary and often involve more complex timing  violations than those previously discussed. These may include  issues related to test methodologies such as Launch-on-Shift (LOS) combined with Scan Enable (SE) skew, metastability in  level shifters or latching circuits, test configuration problems  like Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) instability, or errors in tester  timing equations. In some cases, asynchronous clocks bleeding  into adjacent domains can also produce stripe patterns. While  synchronizing or phase-locking the involved clocks may help  mitigate these issues, such fixes can sometimes obscure the root  cause rather than resolve it [1,2].

To further illustrate the complexity of stripe-related failures, we  examine scenarios where aggressive clocking conditions  introduce subtle mismatches between launch and capture paths. Figure 6 illustrates a case where failing stripes emerged due to  a 10% delay mismatch between the launch and capture clocks. While a simple setup violation would typically produce a solid  speed wall, the presence of stripes in this case suggests that the  root cause is glitch generation or timing instability. This  distinction is important: stripes indicate a repeatable but  conditionally triggered failure, often resulting from intricate  interactions between the design and the test environment.

Figure 6: Failing shmoo stripes observed during IP testing at  aggressive capture clock speeds. The stripes were caused by a  10% delay mismatch between launch and capture clocks, suggesting glitch generation or timing instability.

Building on this,  horizontal shmoo stripes are occasionally  observed when plotting one power supply against  another. These patterns are typically attributed to boundary  crossing level shifter logic, which experiences metastability  issues within specific voltage regions. An example of this  phenomenon is shown in Figures 7A and 7B. This issue arises  from circuit design choices and is typically observed outside  normal operating boundaries. However, such circuits—and the  associated failure signatures—are highly susceptible to  threshold voltage (Vt) shifts, particularly those caused by aging  mechanisms such as Hot Carrier Injection (HCI) and Negative  Bias Temperature Instability (NBTI). In severe cases, these  shifts can result in significantly widened failure bands that  eventually encroach into the customer operating region. For  instance, Figure 8 illustrates a stripe caused by a thresholdsensitive latch that failed to enable the PLL at a specific voltage. The investigation revealed that the latch was not properly  activated due to the absence of clock signals from the VoltageControlled Oscillator (VCO), which was ultimately traced to a  design bug preventing correct latch operation in bypass mode.

Figure 7a: Horizontal shmoo stripe observed when plotting  internal core VDD versus GPIO VDD.

Figure 7b: This failure was traced to a metastable bias region  in a level shifter, caused by a Vt mismatch and circuit  instability.

Figure 8: Horizontal shmoo stripe caused by a thresholdsensitive latch that failed to enable the PLL at a specific  voltage.

In contrast, vertical shmoo stripes in the clock period axis are  most often attributed to test pattern configuration errors, but on  rare occasions can be caused by design IP clocking scheme  integration errors. For instance, during shmooing, timing  equation misconfigurations can cause one clock domain to scale  incorrectly relative to other active domains. Figure 9A  illustrates such a case. Resolving these issues typically involves  identifying the variables responsible and troubleshooting the  test program for configuration errors.

Another class of stripe-inducing failures arises from issues  related to Phase-Locked Loop (PLL) configurations. Improper  initialization, voltage sensitivity, or incorrect lock timing can  all lead to stripe patterns in shmoo plots. Figure 9B illustrates a  case where failing stripes were observed at voltages below  nominal levels and were attributed to a high capacitive load on  a critical signal in the VCO startup circuit, resulting in slow  transitions. An additional finding during this analysis was that  insufficient wait time for PLL lock could result in speckled  failures—highlighting how even minor misconfigurations can  have a visible impact on shmoo behavior.

Figure 9: a) Vertical shmoo stripe caused by a test  configuration error related to timing across clock domains.

b) Failing shmoo stripes caused by PLL configuration, design, and initialization issues.

III: Case Study

To demonstrate how these failure mechanisms manifest in realworld scenarios, we present a case study involving a sub-10nm  technology device that exhibited speckled failures in the shmoo  plot during Streaming Scan Network Transition Delay (SSNTD) testing. As shown in Figure 10, these failures appeared  when the functional/shift clock was swept across the PLL clock, revealing a timing-sensitive interaction between two  asynchronous clock domains.

To better understand the context of this failure, it’s essential to  first consider the scan methodology used. To address the  limitations of traditional scan access methods, the Streaming  Scan Network (SSN) methodology was introduced [3–5]. Traditional scan access methods presented challenges, including inefficient test times, high planning overhead, and  difficulties in physical design and timing closure. The SSN  architecture enables simultaneous testing of multiple cores  using a bus-based scan distribution system, where each core is  equipped with a Streaming Scan Host (SSH) to manage data  flow. This approach is particularly valuable in modern SoCs, where the number of cores continues to increase while the  number of available chip I/Os remains limited. By facilitating  concurrent core testing, SSN significantly improves test  efficiency and scalability [3–5].

Figure 10: Speckled failures appeared when the functional/shift  clock was swept across the PLL clock, revealing a crossdomain timing issue.

LADA analysis was performed as the next step to isolate the  root cause of the speckled failures. As shown in Figure 11, LADA revealed a passing signature at a Low-Dropout  Regulator (LDO) responsible for biasing I/O pads. When the  laser targeted this region, the speckles disappeared (Figure 12), indicating a possible connection between I/O biasing and the  observed failure mode.

Figure 11: LADA identified a passing signature at the LDO, which biases I/O pads.

Figure 12: Speckles disappeared when the laser targeted the  LDO, confirming its role in I/O-driven failure behavior.

Scan diagnosis failed to provide suspects but did identify failing  capture flops of interest. Laser Voltage Probing (LVP) showed  that the capture flop’s output Q incorrectly transitioned from 0  to 1 during the capture cycle of interest (Figure 13A), while the

data-in port remained static throughout the failing Load/Unload  sequence. This indicated the error originated earlier in the  overall test sequence. Both LVP (1064 nm) and VLP (785 nm) were used to enhance signal clarity. As shown in Figure 13B, VLP reduced crosstalk on the Scan Enable (SE) signal, while  LVP offered a better signal-to-noise ratio for Q and SI signals. This comparison underscores the trade-offs in wavelength  selection when probing advanced nodes [6, 7].

Figure 13: A) LVP (1064 nm) showed an incorrect 0→1  transition on Q at the capture edge, with SE affected by  crosstalk. B) VLP (785 nm) reduced SE crosstalk but showed  lower SNR on Q/SI compared to LVP.

Figure 14:  LVP waveforms in comparison with the Simulation  confirm that the data signal was incorrectly high during failure.

Further investigation traced the incorrect data at the flop’s input

to a MUX selection error upstream in the associated cone of  logic. Figure 14 shows that the flop was high during the failure, and Figure 15 confirms that this transition occurred much  earlier in the SSN test. As shown in Figure 16, the MUX select

signal originates from logic controlled by a different clock  domain, which is derived from the PLL clock. Because the  MUX control signal came from a different clock domain, its  behavior was unpredictable, allowing the wrong data to  randomly propagate to the flop depending on the phase and  timing of the two independent clock distribution trees. The  incorrectly selected input to the MUX was driven directly by an  I/O pad.

Figure 15: Erroneous data transition traced to a MUX in a  much earlier scan Load/Unload cycle.

This finding ties back to the initial LADA results, which can  now be explained by the laser perturbing the LDO and altering  the I/O pad reference levels. This change affected the value  driven to the active input of the MUX, eliminating the speckled  failures. Ultimately, this confirmed that the root cause was a  design flaw that allowed a control flop to be clocked from the  wrong domain, resulting in asynchronous data transitions and  corruption (Figure 17).

Figure 16: MUX select signal, driven by a different clock  domain, caused incorrect input selection.

Figure 17: Root cause: design bug in clock gating allowed  unintended cross-domain clocking.

Conclusion

This paper presents a detailed investigation into the root causes  of speckled and striped failures observed in shmoo plots—an  increasingly prevalent issue in advanced SoC designs. Through  systematic analysis, we correlate specific shmoo signatures  with a range of contributing factors. These include timing  violations caused by design errors, insufficient wait time for  scan enable signals, clock skew between launch and capture  paths, metastability in level shifters, unwanted glitch  propagation from edge misalignments, invalid Phase-Locked  Loop (PLL) configurations, and tester timing equation  inaccuracies. Additionally, subtle design-process interactions  and fabrication defects were found to induce marginal failures, which in some cases exhibited partial or full recovery.

A key contribution of this work is a case study on a sub-10nm  device exhibiting speckled failures during Streaming Scan  Network (SSN) testing. The root cause was traced to an  asynchronous clock domain crossing, where a MUX select  signal, driven by a separate clock domain, erroneously  propagated incorrect data to a capture flop. This was enabled by  a hardware design flaw in the clock-gating scheme and not  related to the SSN architecture. Root cause analysis was  achieved using advanced Electrical Failure Isolation (EFI) techniques, including Laser-Assisted Device Alteration (LADA), Laser Voltage Probing (LVP), and Visible Light  Probing (VLP), which revealed the timing-sensitive nature of  the failure. A comparative analysis of probing wavelengths  further highlighted trade-offs between crosstalk suppression  and signal-to-noise ratio.

The methodologies outlined in this study demonstrate the  effectiveness of combining shmoo analysis with EFI techniques  in isolating and understanding marginal failures in advanced  SoC designs. By focusing on asynchronous clock domain  interactions, the study underscores how subtle design flaws—such as unintended clock gating paths—can lead to data  corruption under specific timing conditions. The findings  emphasize the importance of domain-aware test pattern  development and rigorous clock architecture validation in sub10nm technologies. Ultimately, this work contributes to a  deeper understanding of failure mechanisms in modern  semiconductor devices and offers practical guidance for  enhancing design robustness and test coverage.

Electrically Active Defect Localization using X-ray-Induced Voltage Alteration (XrIVA)

Andrea L. Rodarte, Edward I. Cole Jr.

Sandia National Laboratories, Albuquerque, NM USA  alrodar@sandia.gov

Joel Long

Model World, LLC., Albuquerque, NM USA

Abstract

Recent advances in packaging and design of integrated circuits (ICs) have embraced techniques such as 3D stacking, heterogeneous integration (HI) and backside power delivery to  maximize processing power while maintaining a small physical  footprint. These developments have posed difficulties for the  failure analysis (FA) community as many standard defect  localization techniques are not compatible with the new  construction. This research describes a defect localization  technique using high-intensity x-ray beams of varying energies. The technique is analogous to light-induced voltage alteration (LIVA), wherein electron-hole pairs are introduced to a device  biased in a static state using a constant current source. The  recombination of carriers at defect sites changes the power  consumption of the device which is spatially mapped to create  an x-ray-induced voltage alteration (XrIVA) image that can be  used to identify defect sites in the IC. We demonstrate the  technique on a Sandia fabricated device and investigate the  potential for use with 3D HI devices by showing the penetration  of different x-ray energies to generate XrIVA images.

Introduction

Modern IC designs have recently shifted toward development  of HI and stacked devices to provide added functionality while  retaining a small footprint [1]. In addition, new chip designs  introduce large numbers of metal layers for signal routing as  well as backside power delivery [2]. As these systems become  more common, the FA community must develop new  techniques for defect identification. Traditional laser-based  techniques such as thermally-induced voltage alteration (TIVA) and light-induced voltage alteration (LIVA) cannot penetrate  the layers of metallization necessary to identify defects deep  within stacked devices. Thermal imaging has the potential for  identifying defect sites that dissipate heat, but localization  within a stack is not straightforward, and the technique does not  identify defects that are open or dissipate minimal heat. At this  stage, the FA community does not have sufficient tools to  perform FA on stacked die.

To address these limitations, we developed XrIVA, a technique  analogous to LIVA using high intensity x-ray beams. For x-ray  techniques to produce real-time effects that can be mapped, the  intensity of the x-ray beam must be sufficient to induce enough  electron-hole pairs to alter the power consumption of the target  under test with dwell times that allow for scans that are not time  prohibitive. This research has been performed using a modified  Sigray AttoMap™, which allows for high intensity beams of  three energies and a focus spot size of approximately 10 m. A  version of this tool has been used to demonstrate timing shifts  and fault isolation in ICs using x-ray assisted device alteration (XADA) [3-5].

XrIVA follows the rationale of its laser-based cousin LIVA, which uses the integrated circuit under test as its own current to  voltage amplifier. Using x-rays as a source of minority charge  carriers in silicon is inherently less efficient than using optical  wavelengths due to silicon’s low absorption cross-section for xrays. This work aims to turn that flaw into an advantage as we  develop a tool for use with stacked silicon devices with multiple  layers of metallization.

Test Setup

Previous research has shown the potential of x-rays to induce  current in silicon photovoltaics, a technique known as x-ray  beam-induced current (XBIC). The early reports used high  fluence synchrotron beamlines, but lab-based systems promise  similar results if the intensity of the beam is sufficient [6,7]. The  Sigray AttoMap™ XRF incorporates several innovative  features that distinguish it from other XRF machines and  make it ideal for research in this area. The tool utilizes Sigray’s  patented x-ray source technology, which produces significantly  higher brightness compared to conventional XRF systems. This  high-intensity source enables higher electron-hole pair flux  generation yielding faster data acquisition and defect  sensitivity. The proprietary mirror lens objectives focus the xray beam to a tightly controlled spot size, enabling high spatial  resolution imaging. The AttoMap™ achieves spot sizes as  small as 8–12 μm, depending on the target material and energy. These objectives also minimize beam loss, ensuring that the  maximum x-ray intensity is delivered to the sample, which is  critical for applications requiring deep penetration. The

The AttoMap™ is equipped with  a multi-target source that can hold up to four different x-ray  targets simultaneously. Figure 2 shows the test setup used for these experiments. In this  system the x-ray source containing the targets remains  stationary while the sample sits on an xyz movement stage with  a minimum 5 µm step size. The targets used in this research are  chromium, copper and molybdenum, which have characteristic  x-rays of 5.4 keV, 8.0 keV and 17.4 keV, respectively. Figure 3  shows the x-ray emission spectra from each of the targets, courtesy of Sigray. X-rays from the source are focused on the  sample through one of the four available optics. The x-ray  optics can be aligned to an optical camera for sample  positioning. The SDD is lowered to the sample to collect x-ray  fluorescence data for elemental identification and mapping.

Figure 2: Experimental setup inside AttoMap™ chamber (top). Schematic of experimental setup (bottom).

The device under test (DUT) is placed in a board that allows it  to be powered into a static state drawing minimal current. The  AttoMap™ has feedthroughs that allow power supplies to be  controlled outside of the x-ray chamber. The DUT is powered  through a Keithley 238 source measure unit. The supply is used  as a constant current source for analysis, with the voltage  compliance set to prevent accidental overvoltage to the sample. XrIVA images are produced by monitoring the IC operating  power supply voltage. Variations are amplified using an Ithaco  1201 voltage amplifier in AC coupled mode. The signal from  the AC coupled amplifier is connected to a LabJack DAQ  integrated into the AttoMap. The output from the LabJack DAQ  is collected by the Linux interface of the Sigray™ software  which allows for an external program to spatially map a  grayscale image (XrIVA signal) that correlates with the optical  navigation image and x-ray fluorescence data collected.

Figure 3: X-ray spectra from 5.4 keV Cr (orange), 8.0 keV Cu (blue) and 17.4 keV Mo (green). Data courtesy of Sigray.

Figure 4 shows an example of an XrIVA image collected by  scanning a commercial off the shelf (COTS) comparator. This  comparator exhibited an extremely strong response to 532 nm  laser stimulation under minimal power, producing strong LIVA  images. The device was decapsulated to expose the active wire  bonded surface. The device was scanned using a fly scan in  which the stage is moved in a raster pattern over the region of  interest (ROI). The user defines the total dimensions of the  scan, the step size and the dwell time of each pixel. The program  adjusts the speed of stage movement and collects data at  intervals corresponding with the correct step size. A shutter  controls the beam exposure on the DUT.  The shutter is opened  at the start of the scan and closed at the conclusion. During the  scan, the x-ray fluorescence spectra and DUT voltage data are  collected for each step. For Figure 4, the device was scanned  using the 5.4 keV chromium target set to maximum power of  30 W (25 kV and 1200 A), using a dwell time of 100 ms per  pixel. The XrIVA image shows a sensitive location on the IC  that corresponds with the LIVA images collected on the part  using a 532 nm laser.

Figure 4: COTS comparator optical image (left) and XrIVA  image collected using 5.4 keV x-rays (right). Location of XrIVA  signal identified on the optical image with a red circle.

Scans of the comparator using the 8.0 keV copper target yielded  similar results. By changing testing parameters, it was  determined that shorter dwell times helped to further localize  defects until the dwell became too short for the software to  accurately collect voltage data. At dwell times under 50 ms the  data began to appear to smear because of the DUT’s limited  bandwidth response to electron-hole pair generation. Figure 5  shows an example of the comparator’s response at a different  static state scanned at shorter dwell times. Longer dwell times  also changed the response of the device, as increased time led  to a sustained response from the part that persisted for several  seconds after exposing the sensitive area. Repeated scans also  created the potential for a persistent response to x-ray exposure.

Figure 5: XrIVA images collected for a different comparator at  50 ms, 25 ms and 5 ms dwell times using a 5.4 keV x-ray source. (Same FOV as Figure 4).

Figure 6 shows a scan completed over the comparator using

8.0 keV x-rays. This was a repeated scan at full power (30 W (25 kV and 1200 A)) using a dwell time of 100 ms. As the xray beam passes over the sensitive area the power consumption  of the part begins to deviate and continues to be unstable for a  period (~1 minute) before returning to normal. This is observed  by a band of noise stemming from the initial XrIVA signal  region. Repeated scans also can result in an increase in nominal  power demand from the DUT. Annealing the device at 120 °C  for 15 hours returned the power to its original state. Preventing  changes or persistent response in the device can be achieved by  shortening the dwell time per pixel or reducing the intensity of  the x-ray beam (lowering the current applied to the target  material).

Figure 6: Comparator scan region optical image (left) and  XrIVA image (right). Device scanned using 8.0 keV x-ray beam.

Results

For defect localization demonstration, an ASIC fabricated at  Sandia’s MESA fab was selected. This ASIC ball grid array, wire bonded 12.5 x 12.5 mm2 chip is in a 0.35-micron  technology with 5 layers of metal. This failed device was  chemically etched to expose the die surface for LIVA analysis. Figure 7a shows a region of the failed device scanned using the  LIVA technique. There are defect areas with LIVA contrast  observed in the bus under the top layer of metal circled in blue. Figure 7b shows the same region scanned using a 5.4 keV x-ray  beam. In addition to using the optical image for orientation we  map the Ti XRF signal to verify x-ray location. Defects  generating XrIVA signals can be seen in the same regions as  observed under LIVA, circled in green. It should be noted that  while LIVA produces a number of additional signals due to

metalization and exposed transistors, XrIVA only registers a  signal in the defect areas. These experiments show that XrIVA  signals do, in fact, correlate with LIVA defect locations. Future  work can include destructive analysis to correlate XrIVA  signals to defective elements of the circuit.

Figure 7: Defective ASIC scanned using A) LIVA using a  532 nm laser and B) XrIVA using a 5.4 keV x-ray beam.

A selected region of the device was scanned using all three  targets to show that a XrIVA signal is observed from 5.4, 8.0  and 17.4 keV x-ray beams, shown in Fig. 8. The top of the  figure shows an optical image of the scanned region in black  and white. The red overlay shows the Ti fluorescence collected  during the ROI scan. The XrIVA maps collected for each x-ray  beam are shown with observed signals circled. It is noted that  signals are not in the same location for each scan, future work  will include determining why different energy x-rays highlight  different defect regions. The maximum possible intensity of  each target is different and during this experiment it was  determined that the 17.4 keV beam had a lower overall intensity (~0.35X) than the other targets and required longer dwell times  for maximum signal generation. Scans in Fig. 8 were all  completed using the same dwell time and the 17.4 keV signal is  thus weaker than the other two. Further experiments were  completed using only 5.4 and 8.0 keV beams while the intensity  issues of the 17.4 keV beam were investigated.

Figure 8: XrIVA images collected on defective area using Cr (5.4 keV), Cu (8.0 keV) and Mo (17.4 keV) x-ray beams with  100 ms dwell time.

Figure 9: Experiment collecting XrIVA signals using 5.4 and

8.0 keV x-ray beams on bare die and through 50 and 100 µm Si  layers.

With top down, bare surface defect localization demonstrated  we moved to investigate the potential of x-rays for use with 3D  and HI devices. To mimic a stacked device, thinned pieces of  silicon were prepared at 50 and 100 µm thicknesses. These  pieces were placed over the defective region of interest and  scanned to ascertain through silicon XrIVA signal generation. Figure 9 shows the results of the experiments using the 5.4 keV  and 8.0 keV x-ray beams to create XrIVA images. The scanned  region of interest is shown on the optical image with a red box. Both x-ray energies reveal defects on the bare die in the scanned  region. When a 50 µm piece of silicon is placed on top of the  ROI both energies continue to show defects though the signal

is significantly reduced in the 5.4 keV image. It is noted that the  location of the defects appears to shift with the 8.0 keV beam. With a 100 µm Si layer the signal from the 5.4 keV beam is  gone, though the 8.0 keV signal is still present.

Discussion

Results from these experiments indicate that the conditions of  the DUT will inform the x-ray energy selection or XrIVA  measurements. Silicon’s ability to absorb lower energy x-rays  leads to a greater XrIVA response with short dwell times, however, lower energy x-rays have limited penetration depth in  materials. Figure 10 shows the attenuation of 5.4, 8.0 and

17.4 keV x-rays in silicon. Devices with substantial material  between the surface and active circuitry will be more difficult  to probe using lower energy x-rays. Dwell time can be adjusted  to account for attenuation but scan time increases, making  higher energy x-rays such as the 17.4 keV beam more useful.

Figure 10: Attenuation of 5.4 keV (red), 8.0 keV (green) and

17.4 keV (blue) x-ray beams through varying thickness of  silicon.

These experiments were conducted with the IC in a static, low  power state. The Sandia radiation hardened devices did not  show any significant change in power consumption with  repeated scans as the COTS comparator did. Commercial  devices show that exposure to x-ray beams can change the  functionality of the device, so care must be taken to understand  the damage threshold for each individual part  type/configuration examined. In most cases an overnight anneal  at 120°C has returned the part to its original state, but this  should be done cautiously to avoid annealing the defect under  examination.

Conclusions

We have demonstrated the XrIVA technique of using highintensity x-ray beams to generate real-time images for defect

localization. The response of test ICs indicate that the high  absorption of 5.4 keV x-rays allows for fast scans and strong  signals on devices with exposed surfaces. Encapsulated or  backside processed parts will likely require higher energy xrays for greater penetration depths and adjusted scan times.

Future work for this technique includes characterizing the  feasibility of using 17.4 keV beams for defect  identification/localization through silicon and encapsulation  materials. Experiments were conducted on older technology  nodes and future work will include testing state of the art  technologies including backside power delivery and advanced  nodes for defect localization.

Performance of a 3D Magnetic Inverse for Fault Localization

F. C. Wellstood

Department of Physics, University of Maryland, College Park, MD and Neocera Magma LLC, Beltsville, MD

N. Lettsome, J. Patel, J. Sabath

Neocera Magma LLC, Beltsville, MD

A. Cawthorne

Trevecca Nazarene University, Nashville, TN and Neocera Magma LLC, Beltsville, MD

T. Venkatesan

University of Oklahoma, Norman OK and Neocera Magma LLC, Beltsville, MD

Abstract

We examine the performance of a new magnetic inverse  technique that can process an image of the z-component of  magnetic field generated by a multi-layer current path and  obtain the path that the current follows in three dimensions (3D). We processed hundreds of simulated images of the field  from paths with 1-10 segments on 1-3 layers for which the exact  true values of all path parameters were known. Each image  included randomly sampled gaussian noise with a standard  deviation of σB = 0.1 nT in each pixel, typical of the MAGMA  SQUID imaging system [1,2]. A range of typical path and  image parameters were used, including sample-sensor  separations z between 20 µm and 1 mm, segment lengths ℓ from  50 µm to 2 mm, and current I between 100 µA and 2 mA. We  find that the vertical and lateral resolution are comparable, proportional to the depth z of the current path, and inversely  proportional to the total signal-to-noise ratio So/N of the image. For So/N  >108, the vertical and lateral resolution was typically  better than z/1000. Since audio frequency magnetic fields can  penetrate unhindered through opaque insulating or thin  conducting layers, this implies that low-noise magnetic imaging  has the potential to achieve sub-micron vertical and lateral  localization of circuit paths for depths z

≤

1 mm.

Introduction

For fault localization [3] in encapsulated chips and multi-layer  packages, a user will typically know which input/output leads  or pins have a short circuit fault. The challenge is to find the  precise location where the fault occurs. To determine the fault’s  location using magnetic imaging, ac current at a frequency of a  few kHz is supplied to the input/output pins and a fine-scale  image is acquired of the resulting ac magnetic field above the  surface of the sample. Since audio frequency magnetic fields  can penetrate unhindered through optically opaque layers, including thin metal layers, magnetic imaging can be  accomplished non-destructively, without the need to remove  intervening material. By using a magnetic sensor based on a  Superconducting Quantum Interference Device (SQUID) [1], images with exceptionally low magnetic noise can be obtained [4-9]. Low noise is important because it enables the observation

of relatively weak currents (0.1 mA scale) at the relatively large  depths of modern packages (mm scale).

The Standard Approach and Its Limitations

While direct inspection of a magnetic image can reveal useful  information about the possible locations of a fault, we can  obtain much better information by processing the image. The  standard approach to analyzing magnetic images for failure  analysis is to use the standard 2D FFT magnetic inverse [4-9]. This inverse can convert an image of the z-component of  magnetic field Bz into an image of current density, thereby  revealing where the current is flowing. This approach has some  significant strengths: it is fast, simple to apply, and generates an  output current density image that is sharper than the original  magnetic image and can be directly compared to a computerassisted design (CAD) layout of a circuit, thereby facilitating  the localization of faults.

Despite widespread use, the standard 2D FFT magnetic inverse  has significant limitations. The most serious limitation is that  this technique assumes that the current that is generating the  field only flows in a single two-dimensional (2D) plane that is  parallel to the plane of the image. In consequence, the technique  can only produce accurate images of current density if that  current is flowing in a single layer at fixed depth below the  sensor. Second, even if all the current is flowing in a single  layer, the inverse does not determine the depth z. Instead, a user  must provide a value for z before the technique can be applied. This is particularly problematic for fault isolation - the depth z  of a fault may be the key unknown that a user is trying to find. Third, while the 2D FFT inverse can yield images of current  density that are sharper than the original magnetic field image, the resolution improvement is modest, as we discuss below. Finally, the technique will blindly convert any image of the zcomponent of magnetic field into a 2D image of current density, even if the currents in the sample are not actually flowing on a  single layer. As a result, users can apply the technique to  situations where it will deliver inaccurate results, such as when  current is flowing on multiple layers. Nothing prevents the  technique from being applied in situations where it should not  or warns a user when the results cannot be trusted.

Non-uniqueness of 3D Path Solutions

Given the limitations to the standard 2D FFT magnetic inverse, it is natural to seek alternative techniques that can convert a  magnetic image into accurate current paths in 3D and perhaps  overcome some of the other issues noted above. However, it is  well-known that it is impossible to extract a unique solution for  current flow in 3D from a 2D image of the magnetic field Bz  that it produces. In addition, measuring additional components  of the field, or acquiring images at different distances z, does  not improve the situation. The fundamental problem is that  different distributions of current in a volume can produce  identical magnetic fields outside the volume. For example, consider (1) a long thin-walled metal tube with circular crosssection, and (2) a long solid circular metal cylinder with the  same outside radius as the tube. If the same total current flows  uniformly in the tube and the cylinder, their 3D current  distributions will obviously differ (no current flows in the  hollow interior of the tube), but the magnetic field distribution  outside the tube will be identical to that outside the cylinder.  Note that the above discussion does not mean that it is  impossible to find a 3D solution for the current distribution. Instead, it means that many different solutions are possible, all  of which are physically consistent. Finding a unique solution  requires applying suitably strong constraints, such that all  possible solutions, but one, are eliminated. For the standard 2D  FFT magnetic inverse, this constraint is supplied by requiring  that current is conserved and the current flow is in 2D. Upon  further examination, it does not appear possible to simply  replace these assumptions with ones that would allow the FFT  technique to be extended to 3D. Instead, we have developed a  completely different approach that applies sufficiently powerful  and realistic constraints to allow unique 3D path solutions to be  obtained for situations that are of interest to fault localization.

Constraints

By necessity, our 3D Solver must apply constraints that limit  the possible paths that will be considered. If the constraints are  too restrictive, no solutions will be possible, while if the  constraints are not sufficiently restrictive, many solutions will  be possible. The following set of constraints appears to be  sufficient for our purposes.

First, we require the path to be constructed only from one or  more straight wire segments. Second, each segment extends in  either the (positive or negative) x or y directions (Manhattan  geometry). Third, each segment has negligible width and  thickness. Fourth, each segment has a length ℓ that is larger than  a specified cut-off value, typically in the 20 to 50 µm range for  the results shown below. Segments that are too small may  produce a magnetic field that is negligible compared to the  noise, and could be added to a path solution, if not forbidden by  this constraint. Fifth, the different segments in a path may be at  different depths z, but we assume that all are placed inside a  specified sample volume. Sixth, our current version of the 3D  Solver is limited to not more than 10 segments. An upper limit

on the number of allowed segments is necessary to ensure  unique solutions. The limit of 10 was chosen to ensure that  solutions can be obtained in a reasonable amount of time and to  simplify the programming. Seventh, for the results discussed  here, we assume that each segment carries the same current I. This reduces the number of path parameters and simplifies the  programming and path search. Eighth, we assume that we have  a magnetic image that shows the z-component of the magnetic  field, measured at known, regularly spaced, locations (the  pixels) on a 2D xy-grid (the image plane) that is at depth z= 0. Since current flow in the z-direction does not produce a zcomponent of the magnetic field, this means that we can ignore  the contribution to the field of any z-vias in a path. We define  the matrix

                            

as the measured z-component of the magnetic  field field at pixel (i,j), where i is the row number and j is the  column number. Finally, we have included an option that allows  us to have disconnected or connected paths. For the connected  path option, we assume that two wires that are at different depth  z are connected by z-vias if the (x,y) coordinates of the output  of one segment are equal to the (x,y) coordinates of the input of  another segment.

Obviously, not all circuits will satisfy these constraints, so we  will not be able to solve all magnetic images when they are  applied. The limit to just 10 segments is quite restrictive. Nevertheless, we have found that this still allows a surprisingly  wide variety of situations to be modelled. Since each segment  can be a

Single connected paths, as well as multiple  disconnected paths, and paths with sections that spiral, or cross  and overlay other sections are all allowed. Note also that this  count only includes lateral (x or y) segments and does not  include z segments (z-vias); there can be up to 9 additional z  segments in a connected path with 10 lateral segments.

Our Approach to Finding 3D Path Solutions

Our basic approach to extracting a 3D path from a magnetic  image is to generate a trial path, calculate the test field the path  produces, and then vary the path and the path parameters until  we find a good fit between the test field and the original  magnetic image.

Figure 1 summarizes the main steps in our 3D Solver. After a  magnetic image

                            

and the pixel size ∆x are input at step 1, the user can set default values for some of the parameters that  control the search process, such as the maximum and minimum  possible values of a segment’s depth z. At step 3 (see Fig. 1), the image is examined to locate the largest and smallest  magnetic field, as well as other details. Based on this  examination, a

The examination and selection may  be handled manually or automatically, at the user’s discretion. The sequence of steps 5, 6, 7, 8, and back to 5, forms the main  search loop (see Fig.1). The routine continues around this loop, incrementing the number of segments n→n+1 each time, and  adjusting the path parameters until finding a good fit or  reaching the maximum number of segments. The routine  eventually stops and outputs the best fit path as well as other  useful information, such as the final residual field image, and  whether the best fit image is in good statistical agreement with  the original image.

We emphasize that the output path is the best fit path that the  routine finds. This path may generate a field that gives a good  fit to the data (successful search), or it may not (an unsuccessful  search). These two cases are distinguished using the χ2 statistics  of the fit, which are also recorded.

There are several reasons why the path search may fail. First, if  the true path does not obey the constraints that the routine  imposes, then the search will typically fail. In this situation, the  constraints will need to be modified. Second, steps 3 and 8 are  particularly difficult and critical. The segments are selected at  these steps, and, if this is not done correctly, the routine will  typically fail. Third, minimizing χ2 in step 5 can be difficult and  time-consuming. If there are n segments in the path, then at step  5 there will be 4n+1 parameters that are varied simultaneously. A 10-segment path will have 41 parameters. Finding the global  minimum in a space with 41 dimensions is, in general, a  difficult problem, and there is no guarantee of success. Finally, if the noise in the image is too large, the smaller and more  distant segments may not be distinguishable. In this case, the  best fit path may give a good fit, but it will be missing fine scale  details that occur in the true path. In this situation, we have  reached the signal-to-noise limit of the data; an image with  higher So/N is needed to resolve finer scale features.

Generating Simulating Magnetic Field Images

To test the performance of the 3D Solver, we used it to extract  path solutions from hundreds of magnetic images. While at first  sight it may seem preferable to evaluate the performance using  real magnetic images, this is impractical. In addition to the large  cost and time involved in fabricating and imaging a large  number of suitable test samples, we would need to know all the  sample parameters very accurately. As we demonstrate below, the technique can extract path parameters to an accuracy of 1

155

part per million (ppm) or better if the signal-to-noise ratio is sufficiently high. Large sets of real samples with a range of such accurately known parameters are not available. In contrast, it is trivial to generate large sets of simulated images with accurately known path parameters that span a wide range. Our simulated images include realistic levels of noise and could, in principle, include other artifacts that appear in real images (such as sensor tilt, sample rotation, etc.). In this way, we were able to compare the exact true values for all the path parameters to the parameters extracted using our 3D Solver. Further validation on real samples is needed, but this will not require a prohibitive number.

For convenience, each simulated image was square, with the number Nx of pixels on each side ranging from 64 to 256. The pixels were centered on a square xy-grid with step size ∆x in the x and y directions. We placed the origin of our xyz coordinate system at the center of the image, i.e. the image plane and SQUID sensor were at z = 0 and the sample was below this. The z coordinate of all current segments was negative. However, for convenience, we generally ignore this minus sign in the following discussion and refer to the depth z of a segment as positive.

To create simulated magnetic images, we first generated paths. The procedure varied but typically was as follows. We first chose the number n of segments in the path. From predetermined sets of allowed values, we then choose the pixel size ∆x, the number of pixels Nx along each side of the image, and the current I.

We next select the type (+x, -x, +y or -y) of each of the n segments in the path. This could be a random selection or predetermined such that a family of closely related paths will be generated. For paths with several segments, a random selection of each segment type gives paths that appear to be random walks in 2D. Such paths are not typical of real samples, and for this reason we used a selection procedure that was not completely random. For example, in Sets #2 and #3 (discussed below), we did not allow a +x segment in a path to be immediately followed by a -x segment. As another example, in set 4 (discussed below), we alternated between y and x segments.

For each segment, we next chose the depth z below the imaging plane from a range of allowed values, typically between 20 µm and 2 mm. The coordinates (x1, y1) of the input of the path's first segment were then chosen to lie inside the image. This location may be chosen randomly, or from a set of allowed values, or assigned a predetermined value. The length of each segment was then chosen from a range or set of allowed values, with the length being less than zero for a -x or -y segment and greater than zero for a +x or +y segment. From the length and type of each segment, and the coordinates of the input of the first segment, we construct the coordinates of the input of each of the remaining segments. This completes the construction of a path in which all segments are connected. Simple modifications allow for the construction of disconnected paths.

For each path, we simulated a magnetic image by summing at each pixel the z-component of the magnetic field from each segment in the path. We then added randomly sampled gaussian noise to each pixel. For an x-segment that carries current I from its input at (x,y,z) to its output at (x+ℓ,y,z), the z-component of magnetic field at pixel (i,j) is:

For the results reported here, all images were of the field from single paths that were simply connected (no split, divided or parallel sections). In sets #2 and #3, some of the paths had input or output segments that started or ended outside the region covered by the image. This is typical of real images; current is usually supplied to a sample by input and output leads that extend beyond the sample.

Second Set of Images

Set #2 had 100 images of the magnetic field from paths with two connected lateral segments (x-segment or y-segment). In  each path, the current was the same in each segment, but the  segments could be at different depths z. If the segments were  on different layers, they were connected by a z-via. Since a zvia does not produce a z-component of magnetic field, their presence does not influence the image, and we do not include  them in our segment count. The selection and range of image  and path parameters was similar to that used for Set #1, with  two exceptions. First, the path input or output could be chosen  to lie outside the region covered by the image. Second, we  chose the two segments to carry current in the same direction,or in orthogonal directions, but not in exactly the opposite  direction. Thus, we did not consider paths that folded back on  themselves, such as a +x segment followed by a -x segment. The 3D Solver could process such paths, but they form an  interesting distinct class that we do not consider here.

 Third Set of Images

Third Set of Images

Set #3 had 100 images of the magnetic field from paths with three connected lateral segments. Most of the path and image parameters were the same as in Table  1  (see Table  2  for the parameters that were different). The type of each segment (x or y) was chosen at random, which resulted in 8 types of paths: xxx, xxy, xyx, yxx, xyy, yxy, yyx, and yyy. As with set #2, we did not include any paths in which one segment was immediately followed by a segment carrying current in the opposite direction. Thus, for example, all the segments in a yyy path carried current in the same direction. Otherwise, the choice of the direction of current flow was random.

In creating each path, we assumed there were three current carrying layers, with adjacent layers separated by 50 µm. We chose the layer at random for each segment, except when a segment was immediately followed by a segment of the same type, in which case we placed the two segments on different layers. The depth of the top layer was chosen at random, and this gave us paths in which some segments were as close as about 49 µm and as far as 1.13 mm (see Table  2 ). The magnitude of the length of each segment was chosen at random in the range from 20 µm to almost 1 cm.

Examining the resulting magnetic field images of our 3segment paths, we see a large variation in their appearance. Figures  6  and 7  show ten examples. As with our other magnetic images, red, white and blue correspond to a positive, zero, and negative z-component of magnetic field, respectively.

Figure  6  shows four examples in which a clear indication is visible of each segment in the path. Figure  6 (a) shows a loopshaped pattern. The input is a +y segment (on the left), that connects to a +x segment, that in turn connects to the output -y segment (on the right). The input to the path appears to be outside the image. Figure  6 (b) shows a small n-shaped pattern generated by a positive y-segment (on the right), which connects to a negative x-segment, which in turn connects to a negative y-segment. The three segments appear to be at the same depth z. In Fig.  6 (c), three distinct -y segments are visible, with the middle segment giving a noticeably larger and sharper field profile, consistent with being at a lesser depth than the other two segments. Finally, Fig.  6(d)  shows an s-shaped pattern. The input is a -x segment (upper right part of s-shape),

It is not immediately obvious how a path with just 3 segments could produce such an image. Figure7(b) looks like the field from a single-x segment that is rotated slightly away from the x-axis. Figure  7(c ) clearly shows the field from an +y segment and a -x segment, but there is no obvious sign of a third segment. In this case, there is an output -x segment that is just outside the image. The image in Fig.  7 (e) has a relatively low signal-to-noise ratio of 3.08x10 5 (the lowest in set #3) and appears as a single, slightly rotated, negative y segment. Finally, Fig.  7 (f) shows an L-shaped pattern with a clear -x segment and a long +y segment, which is extending outside the image. There is just a hint of a +y segment connecting to the right end of the -x segment, which would form the path input.

With one exception, we were able to find 3-segment path solutions for all the images shown in Figures  6  and 7 . This included the Paths #9, 23 and 32 (see Figs. 6(a) 7(d) and 7(f)), where segments extended, or were entirely outside, the region of the image. The exception was Path #30 (see Fig.  7 (e)), which produced a good fit to a 2-segment solution, discussed below. Overall, we were able to obtain good 3-segment path solutions for 78 of the 100 images in Set #3. In addition, 11 images could be solved with 2-segment paths  (Paths #1, 11, 30, 40, 52, 62, 63, 71, 74, 93 and 99) , 4 images could be solved with 4 segment paths (Paths #5, 10, 49, 73), and 2 images required 5 segments (Paths #2 and 95).

Finding the path for the remaining 5 images in Set #3 proved to be much more challenging. In two cases (Paths #48 and #91) a segment extended far outside the image, or was entirely well outside the image, and we were only able to find path sections within the image. We were also not able to solve three other cases (Paths #51, #86, and #96). The combination of parameters resulted in images and residual fields that frustrated the routine. We could identify one or two likely segments but could not find a complete path that gave a good fit to the data. Improvements in the routine will be needed to handle these cases.

The images with 2-segment path solutions had a segment that was too small to resolve. The ability to detect a segment depends on several factors, including the length and depth of the segment, the pixel size, the number of pixels, the current, the signal-to-noise ratio in the image and the presence of other segments.

Table  3  summarizes key information about the missing segments in seven of these paths. It is not a surprise that Path #52 is missing an x segment: it is the shortest segment we allowed (20 µm), its path carries the smallest current allowed (125 µA) and it is at the greatest depth (z=1.131 mm). The 2-segment solution has simply replaced these two segments by a single longer y segment. The results for Path #93 are even more revealing. Here a missing 30.1 µm long x-segment is connected a 100 µm long x segment, which is in turn connected to a 27.4 µm long y segment. The missing x segment is actually longer than the y segment and they are at the same depth. The routine had no trouble finding the y segment because it was not hidden by another segment of the same type. Again, the 2-segment solution has simply replaced the two segments of the same type by a single longer segment.

Discussion

Our results on lateral and vertical resolution are remarkable for  their small size. We note that there are ultimate limits to what  can be achieved using magnetic imaging [11] and our results do  not violate these limits. To put our results in perspective, we  note that the spatial resolution of the standard 2D FFT magnetic  inverse is limited to roughly δx = δy = z/5 (see Fig. 3). A  detailed discussion of this result can be found in Ref. [10].  The results presented here suggest the potential to improve this by  more than an order of magnitude, while simultaneously  obtaining vertical resolution. These improvements in

performance could significantly improve the utility of magnetic  imaging for fault localization. In particular, it could allow other  techniques, such as x-ray microscopy, to focus on a relatively  small volume of interest.

Our present version of the 3D Solver has some significant  limitations. Not all paths can be found. There are several  distinct issues that can cause a path search to fail. First, if the  signal-to-noise ratio is too small, one or more segments may be  partially or completely hidden in the noise. In this case, a user  could try re-imaging the sample using a larger drive current, a  longer averaging time or a closer separation. Second, if the  search routine finds a local minimum of χ2 (see Step 5 in Fig. 1), it can become trapped and fail to find the true best fit. Sometimes, local minima can be avoided by making small  changes in the segment parameters, or by adjusting the  constraints. However, since there is no universal technique for  finding global minima [12], there is no guarantee that the global  minima will always be found for this class of problems. We use  a Nelder-Mead search and have not explored other techniques. Third, if the true path does not obey all the constraints imposed  by the Solver, the routine will be unable to find the correct  solution. The only option would be to modify the constraints. This could be easily done in some cases (allowing more than 10 segments, for example) but impossible in others (allowing a  continuous distribution of current flow). Finally, if the Solver  examines a residual image (see step 8 in Fig. 1) and is unable to  correctly identify the next segment, the path search may fail. The present routine is not very sophisticated in its ability to  identify segments and there is much room for improvement. We  have mitigated this issue somewhat by allowing the user to  perform this step manually, if they choose, but success requires  the user to exercise good judgement.

Another important characteristic of our approach is the time to  obtain a path solution. The 3D Solver results presented above  were obtained on two desktops and one laptop computer, each  running an Intel I9 CPU with 32 GB to 64 GB of memory and  8 to 24 processors. All field values and parameters were 64-bit double-precision floating point numbers. Minimizing χ2 (see  step 5 in Fig. 1) is the most computationally intensive step. It  requires us to repeatedly generate test images with

        2

pixels  while searching in the 4n+1 dimension parameter space for a  path with n segments. Elementary consideration of the  properties of the Nelder-Mead search suggest that the search  time will scale as the number of pixels

Neocera MAGMA Although most of these run-times were well above the red dashed curve, we nevertheless see a clear increase in the runtime with the number of segments. The shaded blue area shows the range of runtimes that capture most of our results, extending from the fit curve given by Equation  [6]  to an order of magnitude larger. Extrapolating the shaded region far beyond our 10-segment results, we suggest that 100 segments may be solvable in 1 day to 1 week, assuming that a suitably modified version of the 3D Solver was available.

Modifications to the search process and the use of parallel processing may greatly reduce the time to obtain solutions. However, further consideration of Equation  [6]  suggests another approach to handling images with a large number of segments. If the image could be cut into two separate pieces, with half as many segments in each, each sub-image could be solved 8 times faster. With two sub-images, this would speed up the overall process by a factor of 4. In addition, this would effectively circumvent our 10-segment limit, allowing our current routine to solve paths with more segments.

Finally, we note two strengths of our approach that may not be obvious. First, although our simulations used parameters that are appropriate for SQUID-based magnetic field imaging, the 3D Solver could be applied to magnetic images obtained using other techniques, including quantum-diamond microscopes [13] or scanned giant magnetoresistance sensors  [14] . Although these systems have higher magnetic noise than a SQUID, they are well-suited for fine-scale imaging of currents flowing near an accessible surface of a sample. Second, our approach naturally incorporates constraints and is easy to modify. We have run versions of our 3D Solver that allow each segment to carry a different current, that use segments with non-zero width, that allow the entire image to be rotated by an arbitrary angle, or that allow for non-square images and pixel spacing that differs in the x and y directions. In principle, the choice of constraints would be determined by known features of a sample. For example, a circuit with a non-Manhattan layout could use modified constraints that allow segments that make a 45 o angle with respect to the x or y axes. We have not implemented such modifications, but they appear feasible.

 Conclusions

Conclusions

We have described results from a new magnetic inverse technique that processes images of the z-component of magnetic field generated by a multi-layer current path and obtains the path that the current follows in 3D. Compared to the standard 2D FFT magnetic inverse now in widespread use, our results suggest the potential to improve the lateral resolution of magnetic imaging by more than an order of magnitude, while simultaneously obtaining vertical resolution. Such capabilities would significantly improve the utility of magnetic imaging for fault localization in multi-chip modules and other chip packages. The ability of the routine to find the path, and the resolution obtained, depends on the signal-to-noise ration of the image and many other details. Not all images will be solvable. Further analysis of real and simulated magnetic images is underway to better understand the capabilities and limitations of this technique and help us develop improvements to the routine.

Investigating Decap LVP for On-Die Dynamic Voltage Droop Measurement

William Lo, Nicholas Callegari, Puneet Gupta, and Bruce Cory

Advanced Technology Group, NVIDIA, Santa Clara, CA, USA  wilo@nvidia.com

Nirakar Poudel, Srilakshmi Nallapati, Jessica Yang, and Rudolf Schlangen,

Silicon Failure Analysis Lab, NVIDIA, Santa Clara, CA, USA

Abstract

Laser voltage probing of decap fill cells in standard-cell logic  is explored for on-die measurement of dynamic voltage droop  and other applications. These FinFET based decaps offer  unprecedented access to the local power grid for making noncontact noise measurements because they are widespread in  modern CMOS logic ICs. Compared to logic cells, their  waveform interpretation is simplified because they are nonswitching and less impacted by signal crosstalk. Examples of  this novel use of decaps will be provided for 5 nm and 3 nm test  vehicles. Possible methods for voltage calibration will be  discussed and some examples provided. Other potential  applications of decap laser voltage probing and imaging will  also be discussed.

Introduction

Measuring local on-die voltage droop is an important and  ongoing problem for high performance integrated circuit (IC) chips such as graphics processing units (GPUs) and central  processing units (CPUs). Voltage droop caused by, e.g., current  surges during high-speed switching activity, can affect the  timing and jitter of following events. Similarly for voltage  overshoots which occur when heavy workloads are terminated. Figure 1 shows an example of the effects of voltage droop on  clock timing. VMIN and VMAX testing is necessary, in part, to  ensure proper chip functionality in the presence of this noise. Minimizing this noise is a primary driver for the adoption of  backside power distribution and integrated voltage  regulators [1, 2].

Due to chip design and workload complexity, simulation tools  are incapable of capturing the full details of dynamic voltage  droop events in an operating IC. This can lead to excessive  guard banding that results in lost performance in many  situations even as unanticipated failures occur in others. A  common scenario is failures caught under production test  conditions but not system test conditions due to the abnormally  high and closely timed switching activity used to speed  production test.

One method for measuring on-die voltage droop is to use high  bandwidth mechanical probes and focused ion beam (FIB) created probe points. The impact of probe loading on  measurement accuracy can be a concern in some situations: The

best mechanical probes have tip capacitance of 50 fF (GGB  Industries, Model 35) or more while interconnect capacitance is  typically only 0.2-0.3 fF/µm. The need to create probe points  limits the usefulness of this approach.

Non-contact techniques to measure voltage droop have been  reported by others. Rusu, et al., used a mercury cadmium  telluride (MCT) camera to measure static photon emission from  custom nFET (n-type field-effect transistor) based voltage  transducers [3]. Stellari, et al., used time resolved emission (TRE) to measure dynamic noise by probing the photon  emission from off-state leakage current of CMOS logic  gates [4]. Converting photon emission intensity to voltage  required careful calibration entailing close control of chip  temperature due to the temperature sensitivity of the off-state  leakage. The lack of currently available TRE systems and the  weak photon emission from non-defective logic gates in  leading-edge ICs renders this technique effectively obsolete for  most failure analysts.

It’s also possible to use LVP to make non-contact voltage noise  measurements. LVP is a well-established, widely available  technique for capturing waveforms of internal chip activity [5]. Voltage noise amplitudes can be 100s of mV, well within the  range of LVP detectability. The main challenge is voltage

calibration due to the weak (~100-1000 ppm/V) LVP modulation, the complexity of the laser interaction with the FETs, and the AC coupling used in the detection electronics, needed for low-frequency noise rejection. AC coupling also prevents the direct measurement of DC voltage droop. Typical detector frequency response is ~50 kHz -7 GHz. Some tool vendors offer low-frequency detectors with, e.g., 1 kHz -50 MHz bandwidth. (For best results, these low bandwidth detectors are best paired with light sources exhibiting low noise over the same range.)

One method (method 1) for extracting voltage noise information using LVP is illustrated in Fig.  1 . The envelope of a fast clock signal reflects the voltage droop at the node probed. The main advantage of this approach is the simple voltage calibration based on the assumptions that the full amplitude of the clock pulses represents the applied VDD (i.e., static voltage droop is minimal) and that LVP measurements are linear with voltage (discussed further in the next section).

Two obvious drawbacks of this approach are the limited sampling rate, determined by the clock frequency, and the need to have an appropriate clock probe node at the location of interest with clock signal running over the time span of interest. Another drawback, at least for more advanced nodes, is susceptibility to signal cross talk from nearby logic cells.

Another method (method 2) for detecting noise with LVP is to measure a slow clock or logic signal. Voltage noise can then be captured on the static portions of the waveform. The waveform in Fig.  2 , for example, shows voltage noise visible on the low portion of the trace. Like the first method, signal cross talk can complicate waveform interpretation. Due to the complexity of the LVP interaction, voltage calibration can be more difficult than with method 1 (discussed in more detail in the next section).

In this paper, we introduce a third method (method 3) for making voltage noise measurements using LVP that avoids some of the drawbacks with methods 1 and 2. This novel method is based on probing standard-cell decaps (decoupling capacitors) that are used as fill and for power supply filtering in modern CMOS ICs. The prevalence of decaps in these ICs provides unprecedented access to the local power grid.

Additionally, their LVX interaction, design, and placement make them better isolated from surrounding logic and therefore less susceptible to crosstalk.

In the rest of this paper, we will first review LVx signal modulation for FETs in CMOS logic and apply this understanding to decaps. We will then show decap noise measurement examples and discuss methods for voltage calibration. We finish by briefly discussing other applications of decap LVx.

 LVX Signal Modulation Review

LVX Signal Modulation Review

Here we review the interaction of the laser with the FETs in a CMOS inverter. Inverters are fundamental logic elements in CMOS ICs and common LVX probe nodes. The primary source of interaction is through free-carrier modulation and the plasma-optical effect  [5] . The basic principles discussed also apply to the FETs in more complex cells. We focus the discussion on the pFET of the inverter, but it applies equally well to the nFET. Finally, for simplicity, planar FETs are illustrated, but the general behavior of the free carriers with which the laser interacts also holds for fin and gate-all-around FETs.

Figure  3A  shows an inverter in its output-high state. The pFET gate inversion layer is fully formed, and the drain depletion region is unbiased and at its minimum width. From experiments with 5 nm and 3 nm process test vehicles, pFET laser reflectance is at its peak. Figure  3B  shows the inverter switched to its output-low state. The pFET gate inversion layer has dissipated, and the drain depletion region is now fully biased and at its maximum width. Experimentally, pFET laser reflectance is at its lowest.

In both Fig.  3 (A ) and (B) transient VDD droop is illustrated by the purple traces and the effect of this noise on the reflected laser beam is illustrated by the green traces. Note that in practice, the laser spot size (Rayleigh Criterion: ~200 nm for 1064 nm wavelength with a 3.3 NA SIL) is much larger than the FET dimensions and simultaneously overlaps the source, gate, and drain of the FET. As a result, the LVX signal arises from the combined effects of charge modulation in both the FET gate and drain.

Figure  3  (C) illustrates an LVP waveform acquired from the pFET when it is driven by a clock signal. The amplitude of the transitions (orange arrows) involves laser modulation from both the gate inversion layer (forming and dissipating) and drain depletion region (shrinking and growing). We ignore the transient effects of the switching current and channel pinch-off, which only impacts the shape of the waveform edges but not the waveform amplitude. VDD noise occurring when the pFET is in one of its fully switched states (green arrows) only involves a single source of laser modulation: gate inversion layer when the pFET is on or drain depletion region when the pFET is off. Experimentally, these sources of modulation are found to have different relative strengths and, at least for our 5 nm process test

 References
