vehicle, different polarity (as illustrated). Thus, for the 5 nm process used, the two modulation sources reinforce to increase the LVX signal amplitude

The complexity of the LVX interaction makes it difficult to calibrate the voltage noise captured on the static portions of an LVP waveform (i.e., method 2 above). Naively, calibration would be based on capturing a full VDD switching event in the same waveform (i.e, the falling edge on the left side of the waveform in Fig.  2 ). Assuming voltage linearity, the noise amplitude could then be compared against the amplitude of this switching event, which represents VDD. However, given that the laser modulation sources are not identical during switching vs the fixed states of the FET, this procedure is not valid unless the relative contributions to switching of the two modulation sources is known.

Since method 1 is based on only using the full transitions of fast clock pulses to capture voltage noise (see Fig.  1 ) voltage calibration is trivial if the LVP voltage response is linear. LVP voltage linearity is not guaranteed, however, and must be experimentally verified  [6] . This can be done by voltage sweeping and collecting waveforms at the different VDD, or by using a spectrum analyzer to measure the peak intensity of a clock signal  [7] . Note that duty cycle distortions affect the spectrum analyzer measurements, so care must be taken to ensure that clock duty cycle does not vary significantly over the range of measurements. Figure  4  shows the results of the latter technique for our 5 nm and 3 nm process test vehicles, confirming linearity of the LVP response over a usefully wide range.

 Decaps, LVx, and Voltage Transduction

Decaps, LVx, and Voltage Transduction

Standard-Cell Decaps Standard-cell decaps are typically used as fill and for local power grid noise filtering  [8] . These decaps use the gate capacitance of FETs to store charge by connecting the source and drain of the FET to one voltage rail and its gate to the opposite rail, as shown in Fig.  5 . The CAD layout of a 5 nm,

 References

8-track decap is shown in Fig.  6 . The finFETs in the decaps have identical front-end-of-line structures as those used for logic.

The number of transistors used for decaps in a modern CMOS logic IC is a significant fraction of the total transistors available, making them widespread in the IC. Figure  7  shows an example of their distribution within a region of logic in a 5 nm test vehicle. They are available in various sizes and automatically placed to fill otherwise empty areas. They can often be found clustered together.

 LVX and Voltage Transduction

LVX and Voltage Transduction

Like the FETs in CMOS logic elements, decaps can modulate light via the free carriers in the gate channel region and the plasma optical effect. However, since decaps do not normally switch (with the exception of power gating) power rail modulation is the only way to generate an LVX response. In terms of electrical biasing, a comparison of Figs.  5  and 8  shows that the pFET/nFET in a decap is equivalent to the pFET/nFET in an inverter with output state high/low, respectively. In principle then, decaps are able to transduce voltage noise the same way that a data or clock buffer can (e.g., method 2, Fig.  2 ).

Power rail modulation can be externally induced through the power supply of the IC. Thermal frequency imaging (TFI) and laser logic state imaging (LLSI) both make use of this mode of operation  [9] [10] [11] . Figure  9  shows an LVI map obtained by modulating VDD by ~200 mV at 50 kHz. The decaps (teal rectangles) in the field-of-view (FOV) are clearly highlighted. The ability of decaps to generate an LVX response when the power rail is modulated in this way was noted by Niu, et al.  [11] .

Internally induced modulation such as that arising from voltage noise generated by normal chip activity should also be detectable. Figures  10  and 11  show that this is indeed the case. The decap LVI modulation visible in Fig.  10  (teal rectangles)  168 Downloaded from http://dl.asminternational.org/istfa/proceedings-pdf/ISTFA2025/85212/165/715086/istfa2025p0165.pdf by guest

 References

was generated by voltage noise caused by clock activity. It is  weak relative to the modulation in the surrounding logic due to  the noise’s low amplitude and duty cycle, which is clear from  the decap waveforms in Fig. 11.

One notable feature of the decap LVI signal is that both nFETs  and pFETs modulate in-phase. This is in distinct contrast to the  out-of-phase nFET vs. pFET modulation in a CMOS pair, which gives rise to the characteristic 4-lobed pattern observed  for clock buffers (Fig. 10, red rectangle).

The in-phase modulation of the FETs in decaps minimizes  signal crosstalk since the laser can be positioned in the middle  of the decap cell for probing, furthest away from any  surrounding logic. Probing logic requires the laser to be

positioned directly on either the pFET or nFET of the cell to  minimize signal cancellation. The increased susceptibility to  crosstalk from neighboring logic that results is apparent in  Fig. 11, where the clock buffer waveform shows evidence of  1100… data modulation.

Two other properties of decaps that make them less susceptible  to probing crosstalk are the ready availability of larger decap  cells (see Figs. 7, 9, and 10) and their possible clustering in a  region of interest (Fig. 10, white circles). Both allow the laser  beam to be positioned further away from surrounding logic  when probing.

Voltage Droop Measurement Examples

Some of the capabilities and advantages of decap probing are  demonstrated in the following examples. Figure 12 shows  decap and clock buffer pFET measurements taken while scan  shifting two different data patterns at 32 MHz clock frequency: 0011… (top pair) and 0000… (bottom pair). For the 0011  pattern, two features of the waveforms are notable: First, the  clock buffer waveform (green) exhibits crosstalk from the  0011… data stream while the decap waveform (yellow) does  not. Second, the decap waveform shows that the magnitude of  the voltage droop associated with the rising edges of the clock  is greater than that of the falling edges. This feature is consistent  with the fact that chip activity is clocked off the rising edges. Neither of these features are observed when clocking the  0000… data stream.

Figure 13 shows measurements taken with the same program, except with only a burst of four pulses clocking the 1100 data. This allows features such as the ‘static’ droop and the voltage  bounce to be captured, which are otherwise not possible to  capture or not present in the steady state. Note that since LVP  does not have DC sensitivity, true static droops are not  detectable. However, static droop is expected to develop and  stabilize a short time after the start of any sustained activity as  the power grid responds to the new load requirements. The  transition to this new steady-state level can be accurately  captured in the decap waveform, as demonstrated in Fig.  13.

different data streams were used: 0011… (top pair) and  0000… (bottom pair).

Interesting features to note about the clock buffer waveforms in  Fig. 13 are: First, the shape of the voltage bounce feature differs  from that of the decap waveform. The nFET is in the on-state  following the last clock pulse and is thus biased the same way  as the decap (Fig. 8). Since the LVX response for both arises  from modulation of the gate inversion layer, the nFET  waveform should closely resemble the decap waveform during  this period. It is clear, however, that the voltage bounce feature  on the nFET waveform is much less prominent compared to the  decap waveform. The pFET of the clock buffer, on the other  hand, is in the off-state during this period, so laser modulation  is caused by modulation of the drain depletion region. As a  result, the pFET waveform is not necessarily expected to match  the decap waveform (even after accounting for the inversion).

Second, the clock buffer waveforms do not return to their  baseline level within the ~250 ns span captured after the last  clock pulse. This suggests that effects with longer time  constants are at play for the clock buffer but not the decap. One  possibility is self-heating due to the burst of clock activity, which would not impact decaps. (Note that the temperature  sensitivity of LVX is exploited in TFI [9, 10].)

Figure 14 shows that decap probing is also possible with 3 nm  finFETs. There are two interesting differences compared to  5 nm: First, 3 nm standard-cell decaps only make use of the

pFET’s gate capacitance. The nFETs are disabled by tying their  terminals to VSS. This means that maximizing signal strength  requires probing directly on the pFETs rather than probing the  middle of the decap cell.  As a result, susceptibility to crosstalk  from surrounding logic increases compared to 5 nm. Fortunately, pairs of decaps abutting along their pFET sides are  commonly found (Fig. 15, white arrows). Probing at these  locations offers the best isolation and signal strength. The decap  waveform shown in Fig. 14 was acquired at such a location.

Second, unlike the 5 nm clock buffer waveforms shown in  Figs. 11-13, the 3 nm clock inverter waveforms shown in

Some applications, however, require determining the voltage  amplitude of the droop events. Therefore, in the rest of this  section we outline several potential voltage calibration  techniques that are being investigated.

Calibration w/ Clock Waveform

The first technique involves calibrating a decap waveform by  comparing droop features to corresponding features captured on  an accompanying clock waveform. The full VDD switching

events captured on the clock waveform provides the voltage  scaling. Figure 17 shows an example of how this technique  would be applied in practice. The waveforms are scaled so that  corresponding droop features match (dashed lines). The full  800 mV VDD transition is then used to create a voltage ruler. This same ruler is now used to measure the droop in the decap  waveform.

1 Scan Chain

This relatively simple procedure applied to the 3 nm waveforms  shown in Fig. 17 is valid under the assumption that only charge

2 Scan Chains

modulation in the gate inversion layer contributes to the clock  waveforms. (See discussions around Fig. 14.) This is the same  modulation mechanism for the decaps, making a direct  comparison of the waveforms possible. This technique also  depends on voltage linearity of the LVX response (see Fig. 4).

For the 5 nm clock waveforms shown in Figs. 11-13, the fact  that voltage droop is captured on both the high and low periods  indicates that charge modulation in the FET gate and drain both  contribute to the waveform. Calibrating the decap waveforms  then requires that the relative contribution of each modulation  mechanism be determined. If each mechanism is linear with  voltage, then comparing the amplitude of similar droop events  captured on the high and low periods of the waveform should  allow this determination. Calibration then follows the same  process as above, but the scaling for the decap waveform must  be adjusted accordingly. As a simple example, assume equal  contributions of gate and drain modulation to the clock  waveforms shown in Fig. 17. Then the voltage ruler for the  decap waveform must be scaled by 50%, giving ~200 mV of  droop instead of ~100 mV.

Additional care must be taken in situations where temperature  variations can occur due to LVX’s temperature sensitivity. Non-steady state waveforms such as shown in Fig. 13 are likely  to have a thermal component that may need to be considered. One other source of error is static voltage droop: A DC droop

Calibration Using Externally Induced VDD Modulation

The second voltage calibration technique is illustrated in  Fig. 18. VDD to the device under test (DUT) is DC biased at its  nominal value with a small modulation burst added. An external  oscilloscope is used to probe VSENSE to measure the amplitude  of the modulation in the DUT. Timing of the modulation is  synchronized to the test pattern and it is switched off for the  droop measurement period of interest. Assuming voltage  linearity of the decap modulation and flat frequency response  of the LVX detector electronics, the droop amplitude can then  be directly compared to the amplitude of the calibration  waveform.

Vdd

This technique has the advantage of not requiring custom  circuitry to be inserted into the DUT (beyond a VSENSE pin, which may already exist). However, it may be difficult to  modulate VDD with sufficient amplitude at a high enough  frequency to pass the lower frequency cut-on of the LVX  detector since the DUT power distribution network (PDN) is  normally designed for stability. Several possible methods to do  so are described by Niu, et al. [11]. Differences in the LVX  detector frequency response to the likely slow calibration  modulation and the faster noise modulation needs to be  accounted for. Finally, the limited record length for the  oscilloscope waveforms (typically, 1000 for the Tektronix  scopes used in the FastAcq mode) means that separate  acquisitions for the slower calibration modulation and the faster  droop events are required to be able to resolve the droop details. In this case, care needs to be taken to account for any sample  and/or laser power drift before the two waveforms can be  compared.

Custom Calibration Circuitry

The third technique requires a custom circuit, illustrated in  Fig. 19, to be inserted into the DUT. The circuit consists of an  inverter with decap load(s) on the output. The inverter must be  programmed to toggle during the test program and this  switching event must be captured in the decap waveform along  with the noise event of interest. Again, assuming voltage  linearity of the decap response (which can be experimentally  verified here by capturing switching events at different VDD) noise amplitude can be directly compared to the amplitude of  the VDD switching event.

Decap LVP Waveform

This technique bypasses the need to externally modulate the  power rail but requires planning to design and place the custom

ΔVdd

circuitry. It also eliminates one of the main advantages of using

PeriodNoise Measurement Period

Calibration

decap-based transducers: their widespread placement which  allows broad access to the power grid. Taking advantage of  existing power gating infrastructure to toggle the bias across the  decap fill cells is a possible alternative to using the custom  circuit described which would address these issues.

Calibration Against Another Available Voltage Sensor

The final technique we will mention is to cross-calibrate decap  measurements against voltage measurements made by other  means, e.g., in-circuit systems [12]. Comparing measurements  where they overlap in capability (e.g., overlapping range of  frequency response) would provide the calibration for events  captured by the decaps outside this range. Figure 20 shows an  example where the waveform acquired using a bench  oscilloscope from a VSENSE pin is used to cross-calibrate the  LVP decap waveform.

In this example, the decap waveform was scaled such that the  slower slopes were matched as best as possible. This choice was  based on the assumption that the slower transients are less  filtered by the power grid between the device level (where the  LVP waveforms are acquired) and the higher metal layers (where the VSENSE signal is tapped). This choice is best  validated through voltage noise simulations and/or successful  debug results.

Results and Discussions

Calibration accuracy

Without an independent means to accurately measure or  otherwise determine the actual voltage droop at the device level  where a decap waveform is acquired, it is difficult to assess the  accuracy of any calibration scheme. The best we can do at this  time is check for calibration consistency.

Figure 21 shows the results of calibrating the decap waveform  shown in Fig. 20 by using a clock waveform (i.e., the first  calibration technique). A maximum droop of ~320 mV is found  compared to the ~270 mV determined by calibrating against  VSENSE (Fig. 20). The 17% difference is reasonable, given the  uncertainties in the calibration methodologies used.

Other Limitations

Measuring the voltage droop under heavy functional workloads  is often of greatest interest to chip architects. This requires  system-level testing (SLT) and involves high-power  dissipation, both of which are problematic for non-contact  probing, LVP included: With SLT setups, it is often difficult to  generate a synchronized trigger signal and to efficiently loop a

functional program. High power dissipation is problematic  because use of SIL necessitates complete removal of the

V_SENSE LVP DECAP

standard thermal solution and thinning the DUT backside to ~50 µm remaining silicon. Even water spray cooling may not  be adequate in these test scenarios. It may be possible to design  custom decap probe structures that are large enough to allow  lower magnification air-gap optics to be used with a fullthickness die and transparent heat spreader. Given the  significant number of FETs used for decaps in a leading edge  IC and given that the decap probe structures would still be  useful for power filtering, there would be few drawbacks.

Logic Waveform Interpretation

The decap waveforms show that many of the features  commonly observed in logic waveforms are caused by voltage  droop and not by laser invasiveness, thermal effects or other  effects intrinsic to FET operation, LVP physics, or the LVP  signal acquisition process. For example, the decap waveforms  in Figs. 11-13 shows that the roll-off at the top of the risingedges and the bottom of the falling-edges in the corresponding  clock waveforms are due to voltage droop. Similarly for the  sloping tops and bottoms of the waveforms. Decap probing  offers a simple way to extract voltage noise information that can  be helpful for logic waveform interpretation.

Decap LVI For CAD Alignment

Not surprisingly, CAD alignment is getting more difficult as  geometries continue to shrink [13]. Not only are the smaller  features more difficult to optically resolve, but the alignment  accuracy required is increasingly stringent. Niu, et al., suggested the use of decap LVI for CAD alignment by  modulating VDD [11]. Figure 15 shows an LVI map  highlighting the decaps in logic in a 3 nm test vehicle. The  excellent match to CAD demonstrates that this technique  remains viable, provided a means to modulate the power rail of  product IC on ATE is available.

 Summary/Conclusions

Summary/Conclusions

 Abstract

We introduced a novel technique for making voltage droop measurements based on LVP of decap fill cells in CMOS ICs. In the process, we reviewed the LVP signal modulation mechanisms for CMOS FETs and demonstrated its remarkable and fortuitous voltage linearity over a wide, useful range of values. We provided several examples of the measurements that are possible to make with this technique. Potential voltage calibration methodologies were discussed. Two were demonstrated and compared and shown to match reasonably well, especially considering the uncertain methodologies used in these early investigations. Limitations to the technique were also discussed. These include lack of direct DC measurement sensitivity and difficulty handling the heaviest functional workloads due to inadequate thermal solutions and/or issues with efficient test pattern loop generation. Finally, other applications of decap LVX such as LVP waveform interpretation and CAD alignment were presented.

 Abstract

Voltage noise is an important, recurring problem, especially for high-performance computing. Despite its limitations, decap LVP offers the only remaining practical way to make local, non-contact, dynamic voltage droop measurements in flip-chip ICs. As such, it deserves further investigation which we hope to have motivated with this paper.

Acknowledgments

 References

Novel looping methodology for Laser Voltage Probing of stuck-at and at-speed  fails in SSN Architecture

Nirakar Poudel, Srilakshmi Nallapati, Rudolf Schlangen

Logic Fault Isolation, NVIDIA, Santa Clara, CA, USA

Karthik Sundararaman, Kunal Jain, Vishal Agarwal

DFT, NVIDIA, Santa Clara, CA, USA

Abstract

Streaming Scan Network (SSN) is a new Design for Test (DFT) architecture that addresses the testing challenges of complex  integrated circuits by enabling concurrent testing of multiple  cores with limited Input/Outputs (IOs), ensuring reduced test  times, simplifying physical design, and timing challenges. SSN  architecture poses major challenges for Laser Voltage Probing (LVP) and Soft Defect Localization (SDL) for at-speed and  stuck-at tests. The loop setup strategies that work for older DFT  architectures are no longer applicable for SSN based products. We present a unique solution in which we use retargeted  looping patterns specific to a failure in a particular IP and utilize  chip internal signals as the trigger for LVP. Our LVP loop  consists of 1000x consecutive load, capture, unload events  followed by SSN End while our SDL loop consists of one load, capture and unload event followed by SSN END. Our approach  has helped us achieve LVP looping efficiency of >95%, reduction in dynamic power consumption by >80% and  improve LVP loop speed by 3x compared to looping constructs  used in previous DFT architecture for a similar IP. We also  demonstrate SDL looping using chip internal signals rather than  ATE for pixel clock and pass/fail signal generation, which can  improve SDL speed by ~9x for our test case. We hope that our  paper will help others to ease FA within the SSN architecture  and foster a debate regarding further improvements.

Introduction

The continuous drive for technology shrink, increased design  complexity and reduced IO availability for testing has driven  the need for ever higher test-compression and optimization [1]

[2]. Nvidia chip design heavily relies on replication of certain  core IP blocks, making SSN test with on-chip-compare a well  suited DFT architecture since all identical IPs can reuse the  same input data [3].

DFT pattern release is costly, and in the previous chip  generations that used a different compression architecture we  compromised by using the same pattern set for logging and FA  looping. We were able to setup the required looping for Laser  Voltage Probing (LVP) and Soft Defect Localization (SDL) manually, on the fly  [4]. We could quickly identify and set loop  start and end points for a failing stuck-at or at-speed pattern  from the production set.

With SSN, production testing and logging are performed using  full chip patterns to test all core-IP blocks simultaneously, sharing the same bus bandwidth. While this maximizes  throughput and significantly reduces production test time, it  makes manual identification of IP-specific test-loops and on the  fly looping setup almost impossible.

For FA, we usually do not want to loop the full chip  concurrently. Rather, we target only the one failing IP that  needs to be analyzed by configuring the test and selecting test  patterns specific to the IP of interest. Full chip looping  significantly increases dynamic power consumption and  increases chances of sample damage due to thermal runaway. Full chip looping also substantially slows LVP and SDL loops.

In collaboration with our DFT team and Siemens, we have  developed a way to create FA looping patterns for a specific IP  via retargeting from the production master pattern set. The  SSN test-sequence requires executing SSN-END after every  payload pattern, including retargeted patterns for FA looping. Depending on the size of the targeted IP, the SSN END portion  can constitute ~50% of the overall loop length when executing  the targeted load, capture unload just once. Just one execution  of payload and SSN End results in poor looping efficiency and  long LVP acquisition time to reach sufficient signal to noise  ratio (SNR). In addition, there is a sizable overhead of initial  cycles at the start of every new pattern set, and we want to take  this cost only once per loop condition. Having to loop SSN End  also slows down SDL loop speed as well.

A main challenge for LVP on at-speed and stuck-at test is  creating an exact trigger that aligns with the internal fast clocks  during testing. Generating a trigger from ATE is theoretically  possible for cases where PLL is used for clock generation. In  this scenario, the FA analysts must perform complex  calculations to synchronize the external trigger with the capture  clock perfectly. However, with an external trigger we still  cannot mitigate the slow loop speed due to the requirement of  running SSN END after each payload. Moreover, there is  preparation for wider use of Frequency Locked Loops (FLLs) during test and FA in the future. FLLs run independently from  ATE and external synchronization is impossible.

Fault isolation for shift fails using SSN LVx mode has been  discussed in detail by Endrinal et al. [5]. In this paper, we will

https://doi.org/10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2025p0175

focus only on our solutions for electrical fault isolation for  stuck-at and at-speed fails, in the context of SSN.

Experiment

We worked with DFT to develop a solution to print the targeted  load, capture and unload event 1000 times into one body  pattern, as shown in figure 1. In this approach, we loop 1000x  load, capture and unload events along with SSN End for LVP. This method is effective because we can generate valid triggers  for the LVP scope using chip internal signals.  Figure 2 shows  the chip internal clock- and trigger generation scheme.

Figure 1. (a) 1000x repeat of load, capture and unload pattern  with SSN END. (b) Zoom in of 1x capture Event.

ATE provides a reference clock signal to the chip internal  PLL/FLL as well as a bus clock signal to the Streaming Scan  Host (SSH).  Once the chain-load is finished, the SSH toggles  the Scan Enable (SE) signal and then starts the Test-Window (TWin) counter. The TWin counter defines the delay of when  the two fast test clock pulses are released, after SE goes low in  the capture phase of the pattern. The TWin output is  synchronized by a 3-stage synchronizer circuit into the fast  clock domain, which can be generated by PLL or FLL. The  output of this synchronizer circuit is called Fast-Step-Enable (FSE) and serves as our LVP trigger. FSE is the final chipinternal signal triggering the release of the fast-clock pulses for  at-speed test and is therefore always in perfect synchronization  with the fast-clock test pulses. Our DFT and Clock teams have  done extensive development to enable observability of the FSE  as well as other chip internal test signals like the SE for debug  and FA use cases.

Figure 2. Chip internal trigger generation scheme.

Results and Discussions

Our approach with IP specific retargeted pattern for FA reduces  dynamic power consumption by more than 80% given that most  of our products have >5 core IP blocks (some >15). Moreover, we are also able to utilize full SSN bandwidth for one IP, which  has made looping significantly faster. The fastest possible loop  for LVP would only include the necessary test cycles for chain  load and capture, which we would consider 100% looping  efficiency. The SSN loop has to include initial setup cycles and  the SSN-end, significantly reducing the efficiency when  including only one load, capture, unload. Our retargeted  patterns with 1000x subsequent load, capture events allow us to  achieve looping efficiency of >95% and significantly shorter  time to high SNR waveforms. The internal loop length (period  for one load + capture event) in SSN depends on the size and  complexity of the targeted IP. We have observed LVP loop  length in the range of 30us to 230us, which is on average ~3x  faster in SSN compared to our previous DFT architecture for  similar IP.  In our previous DFT architecture IOs were  hardwired to specific IP and targeting just one IP would not  improve loop speed. SSN allows dedicating the full bus  bandwidth for the targeted IP resulting in faster loop speed.

We experimented using both SE and FSE as chip internal  triggers in our LVP construct because FSE has not yet been  implemented in every IP of our current products, but SE is  observable in all IPs. The major benefit of using FSE as a  trigger is that waveforms have significantly sharper edges as  shown in figure 3. The 2-clk release is triggered directly by  FSE. SE goes through multiple synchronization stages on  different clock domains as shown in figure 2 and is less well  synchronized to the chip internal clock signals as a result. One  downside of using FSE as a trigger is that LVP may be limited  to the test clock event, in cases where shift-in and shift-out  periods of the test are not synchronized to the trigger signal well  enough to see sharp edges. The additional cost overhead for the  implementation of FSE observability was acceptable since FSE  was added to an existing high-quality clock-observation

muxing channel network which maintains the fast signal’s

integrity and fidelity.

Figure 3. Clock waveform with SE as a trigger vs FSE as a  trigger. Rise time of clock edge is ~200ps for clock waveform  with SE as trigger vs ~80ps for clock waveform with FSE as a  trigger.

Using SE as a trigger can only work for cases where test clock  is generated by PLL. This scheme also requires the FA analyst  to establish synchronization by changing the test-clock and PLL  programming to ensure that every bus-clock cycle includes an  integer number of fast-clock cycles and that the TWin counter  runs on the bus-clock frequency. This significantly adds to loop  setup time and complexity and only works if all relevant clock  signals and counters are understood and sufficiently  programmable by the FA analyst.  Figure 4 shows fast clock  waveforms in synchronized condition vs unsynchronized  conditions when using SE as a trigger.

Figure 4. Clock waveform of 2 fast clock pulses with and  without synchronization when using SE as a trigger.

For SDL on SSN based products, the classical  approach is to loop a retargeted pattern with one load, capture  and unload together with SSN End. SDL pass or fail signal is  generated by ATE and the pass or fail signal generation is based  on Advantest 93k’s matched loop construct [4] [6]. We have  observed SDL loop length of ~350us to ~1.5ms depending on  size and complexity of IP, which is fast enough for high volume  FA.

Our DFT team has enabled the observation of a  dynamic on-chip-compare signal called Compare Status, which  generates a short pulse for every chip internal mis-compare  during chain unload. Using the Compare Status as pass/fail  signal and the Scan-Enable signal as pixel-clock provides an  alternative solution that can significantly improve SDL speed, using the same 1000x subsequent load, capture, unload pattern  as used for LVP. The major challenge of this approach is that  the latch hardware of our existing fault isolation tool fleet is not  designed to work with fast, chip-internal signals for pixel-clock  and pass/fail latching. The chip-internal signals driven by  digital IOs only have a signal amplitude of ~500mV with 50  Ohm termination and the compare status signal pulse widths  can be as narrow as ~4ns at bus-clock frequency of 200 MHz, as shown in figure 5. Any pulse or burst of pulses detected on  the Compare Status signal indicates failures identified during  the unload phase of the retargeted pattern, whereas the absence

of pulses signifies that the retargeted pattern has passed  successfully.

Figure 5. (a) Scope shots showing Scan Enable and Compare  Status signals (b) Zoom in of 1 Compare Status signal.

To demonstrate SDL using chip internal signals, we used one  of our typical Burn-In fail cases with stuck-at Vmin behavior. The Vmin boundary for this stuck-at case was 820 mV at busclock frequency of 160 MHz. The software diagnosis for this  case calls out 4 logic cells and one net connecting these 4 logic  cells with 100% confidence.

Figure 6 shows the chip internal signals Scan Enable and  Compare Status signals for this case in failing condition of 800  mV while looping a retargeted 1000x load, capture and unload  events along with SSN End. There is one Compare Status pulse (~width of 9ns and amplitude of ~500 mV as shown in figure  6(b) during the unload phase of each 1000x load, capture and  unload event as shown in figure 6(b).  We used Stanford  Research Systems DG645 digital delay generator to trigger on  the rising edge of Scan Enable (end of capture window) to  create an amplified Scan Enable signal. We added a delay of ~30 us and created a pulse of width ~30 us and amplitude of 4V  to be driven into 50 Ohm impedance pixel clock channel of  SDL tool. Delay of ~30 us was added to condition the pixel  clock of the SDL port to latch the pass-fail signal. We used  another Stanford Research Systems DG645 digital delay  generator to trigger on rising edge of compare status signal. We  created an amplified Compare Status signal with pulse width of ~50 us and amplitude of ~2V to be driven into 50 Ohm  impedance Pass/Fail latch channel of SDL port of fault isolation  tool.

Figure 6. (a) Scope shots showing Scan Enable and Compare  Status signals at failing VDD, amplified Scan Enable and  amplified Compare Status signal (b) Zoom in of 1 Compare  Status signal.

The test condition was setup at 800mV VDD, 20 mV below the  pass-fail boundary. SDL was performed targeting Software  Diagnosis call out cells & nets using 1064nm laser and at a laser  power of ~700 uW. A clear fail to pass sensitivity was observed  in one of the Software Diagnosis call out logic cells as shown  in figure 7. The PFA call out for this case is the cell with fail to  pass spot and the net connecting the 4 suspect cells. The same  SDL results were observed using ATE matched loop  configuration looping one load, capture, unload event and SSN  End of retargeted pattern. The SDL speed was ~9x faster when  using chip internal signals vs using the ATE matched loop  approach.

Figure 7. (a) Raw and CAD overlay images of SDL with chip  internal signals.

Conclusions and Future Work

We have addressed one of the important challenges of failure  analysis in SSN based products, where traditional on the fly  loop setup using the production pattern set is not feasible for  LVP and SDL. We collaborated closely with DFT, clock teams  and Siemens to create a looping scheme based on 1000x repeat  retargeted pattern and utilization of chip internal signals for  LVP trigger. We observe significant reduction in dynamic  power consumption (>80%) and improved loop speed for LVP (3x compared to older DFT architecture for similar IP), high  looping efficiency (>95%) and significantly sharper LVP edges  due to the improved trigger quality. In our 1x SDL loop  construct for SSN, we can achieve loop length that is acceptable  for high volume FA. We have demonstrated that we can further  improve the loop speed by ~9x by utilizing chip internal San  Enable signals for pixel-clock and dynamic on-chip-compare  output signal for pass/fail generation rather than using 1x load, capture, unload followed by SSN End in Advantest 93K  matched loop configuration. We are working with DFT & Siemens to further optimize and streamline the pattern  retargeting flow for the necessary FA patterns, which is script  based und usually completes within less than 24h.

A Review of IO Debug Techniques in Chip-Level Failure Analysis: Case  Studies and Workflow

Thong Doan and Joy Y. Liao

NVIDIA Corporation, Santa Clara, CA USA

Abstract— Shrinking technology nodes and the adoption of  advanced packaging have significantly increased the complexity of I/O  debugging. Restricted physical access, signal integrity degradation, and limited fault isolation resolution collectively contribute to elusive  failure signatures. This paper presents a multi-technique, nondestructive Electrical Failure Analysis (EFA) strategy to address  complex I/O failures through real-world case studies. Techniques such  as Photoemission Microscopy (PEM) [8–11], Lock-In Thermography (LIT) [5–7], and Static Laser Stimulation with Lock-In mode (LI-SLS) [2–4] are evaluated in conjunction with circuit analysis and  schematic/layout signal tracing. The results demonstrate that no single  technique is sufficient; rather, an adaptive approach—built upon deep  circuit understanding and close collaboration between design and  Physical Failure Analysis (PFA) teams—is essential for accurate fault  localization and effective root-cause analysis.

Keywords— LI-SLS, PEM, LIT, IVCT, ATE, SIL, EFA, PFA, EFI, PPMU

I. INTRODUCTION

As semiconductor technology continues to scale into  advanced nodes, Input/Output (I/O) debug has become  increasingly complex. This complexity is driven by the  adoption of advanced packaging technologies—such as 3D,

3.5D ICs, and Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate (CoWoS). In  parallel, traditional Electrical Failure Isolation (EFI) techniques  face limitations in spatial resolution, signal sensitivity, and  effectiveness in high-density environments. These factors  contribute to a broad range of I/O-related failure modes, including leakage currents, electrostatic discharge (ESD) breakdowns, intermittent contacts, and ambiguous failure  signatures that are difficult to isolate and resolve.

To address these challenges, non-destructive Electrical  Failure Analysis (EFA) has become a critical step in identifying  and localizing faults without compromising the device. However, no single EFA technique can sufficiently address the  full spectrum of potential failure mechanisms. This paper  presents a multi-modal EFA approach that combines diverse  methodologies with schematic/layout CAD analysis tools. Three real-world case studies are presented, demonstrating the  application of Photoemission Microscopy (PEM) [8–11], Lockin Thermography (LIT) [5–7], and Static Laser Stimulation  with Lock-In mode, also known as OBIRCH with Lock-In  mode (LI-SLS) [2–4]. Each case illustrates how combining  EFA tools with detailed circuit analysis enables significantly  higher accuracy in fault localization, particularly in situations  where initial results were inconclusive or misleading. By  leveraging a flexible diagnostic strategy grounded in  engineering judgment and cross-functional collaboration with  I/O design and Physical Failure Analysis (PFA) teams, failure  analysts can effectively correlate observations, refine  hypotheses, and pinpoint root causes. Ultimately, this

integrated approach enhances the precision and efficiency of  PFA, accelerating time-to-resolution and enabling targeted  corrective actions in advanced semiconductor products.

II. CASE STUDIES

Figure 1 highlights three I/O debug case studies. The EFI  techniques used for all the case studies include Curve Tracer  Analysis (IVCT),  Photoemission Microscopy (PEM) which  includes: a) PEM in DC mode (direct DC biasing) and b) PEM  while running ATE vector with device powered-on; Lock-in  Thermography (LIT); Static Laser Stimulation with Lock In (LISLS) which includes a) LI-SLS with biasing I/O pins in DC  mode and b) LI-SLS with ATE biasing and looping the vector. Schematic and Layout analysis, Circuit Analysis, and  destructive Physical Failure Analysis (PFA) are also employed.

A. Failure Analysis of ESD Qual Failures

Techniques used: IVCT, LIT, PEM DC, LI-SLS DC

B. Failure Analysis of ESD receiver and transmitter pins Qual Failures

Techniques used: IVCT, LIT, PEM DC, PEM ATE, LISLS DC, LI-SLS ATE

C. Failure Analysis of JTAG Package Pre-Qual VIH/VOH Failures

Techniques used: IVCT, LIT, PEM DC, PEM ATE

CASE A. FAILURE ANALYSIS OF ESD QUAL FAILURES

A GPU device was submitted for FA after being subjected  to ESD testing —just enough to marginally induce ESD failures  in I/O pins to identify the weakest link in the GPU design. Multiple pins failed. One I/O pin was selected for further  analysis. EFA began with IVCT, which confirmed early diode  turn-on leakage between reference and failed devices in DC  testing (Figure 2).

Figure 2. DC IVCT of I/O pin of failed device (red) vs reference (green)

Next, LIT was performed while applying DC bias to the I/O  pin. LIT revealed a distinct anomalous hotspot when comparing  good and bad devices. However, LIT lacked the resolution  needed to pinpoint the exact circuitry associated with the  anomalous hotspots. To enhance resolution, PEM DC was  employed using higher magnification air-gap and solid  immersion (SIL) lenses. Under appropriate biasing, PEM DC  successfully reproduced the same anomalies previously  observed by LIT with greater clarity (Figure 3). Subsequently, DC LI-SLS was performed under identical bias conditions, precisely confirming the hotspot locations within the targeted  circuitry.

Figure 3.  LIT and PEM DC overlay hotspot images at different magnifications

Despite strong evidence from multiple EFA methods, a  critical question remains: Are these hotspot locations directly  linked to the failure mode (Figure 4)? The next phase involves  an in-depth schematic and layout analysis to trace the origin of  the hotspots and establish the connection to the initial ESD  qualification failure.

Figure 4.  CAD display of M1 and OD layers of I/O pad and hotspot locations

Schematic and layout CAD tools were utilized to manually  trace the signal from the bump pad to the hotspot locations. Leveraging CAD features, we aimed to establish a direct  connection from the failing I/O pin to the source of the failure. With continuous iterations of signal tracing analysis and  engineering judgment, a direct connection was established from  the failing I/O pin, going through Tcoil, impedance matching  network, and multiple I/O DAC circuitries (Figure 5(a)), to the  cells that were highlighted by the anomalous signal spots.  This  schematic tracing called out the M_MN_DRV and  M_MP_DRV transistors of TX_DAC_DRV circuitry as the  weak points on the I/O path (Figure 5(b)). Further layout  analysis suggested the output nets TX_DRVN and TX_DRVP, which connect to the internal driver transistors, originates at  metal layer M9 (Figure 5(c)).

Figure 5(a).  CAD Schematic shows the connection from I/O pad (Point 0) to  driver MN/MP_DRV transistors (Point 4) aligning with the hotspot locations

Figure 5.  CAD Layout and Schematic analysis display the entire connection from I/O pad (point 0) to driver Nmos/Pmos driver transistors (point 4) (a) and(b); overlayed hotspots of driver transistors and output net TX_DRVN indicate M9 being the start of the PFA (c)

After successfully pinpointing the failure locations with high  precision—at the MN_DRV and MP_DRV transistors, as well  as the metal layer for the output driver net M9—a PFA  instruction was carefully drafted (Figure 6) and (Figure 7). This  document, including full technical details, design instance paths, precise reference and failure locations of the transistors and nets  correlating with the hotspots, was provided to the PFA team to  continue investigation at the cell level.

Figure 6.  PFA instruction displays locations of the reference and failed  transistors impacted by the ESD event for the failing IO vs reference IO blocks

Figure 7. PFA instruction displays precise (X,Y) coordinates failed transistors  impacted by the ESD event for the failing IO

The PFA team was instructed to start further FI at M9 layer, the most top metal layer at which the transistors in the cell of  interest are still connected.  Nanoprobing revealed a leakage path at the output nets TXN/P_DRV<0> at M9; these data  correlated well with the EFI precise localization effort. Multiple  burnouts were observed at high-magnification SEM at M0 on  nets TXN_DRV<0> and TXP_DRV<0>

Further inspection at the Vd-Vg layer uncovered multiple  NMOS gate-to-drain shorts; no anomalies were found in the  corresponding PMOS drivers. Finally, TEM (Transmission  Electron Microscopy) cross-section analysis confirmed multiple  fin burnouts, which directly caused the NMOS gate-to-drain  shorts.

CASE B. FAILURE ANALYSIS OF ESD RECEIVER AND  TRANSMITTER PINS QUAL FAILURES

A GPU device was submitted to FA after failing receiver and  transmitter pins. The device was subjected to ESD failure. The  objective of the investigation was to identify the weakest link in  the I/O circuit design responsible for internal chip-to-chip  communication. The ESD failure signature on the device was  very subtle, making EFI particularly challenging. Initial IVCT  revealed very minimal leakage differences between the failed  and reference devices, offering limited insight (Figure 8).

Figure 8.  IVCT of Transmitter pin for failed device (red) vs reference (green)

181

Multiple EFI techniques were applied to the analysis. LIT, conducted at both low and high magnifications, revealed no  anomalous hotspots between the failed and reference devices. Similarly, PEM (DC and ATE modes), with SIL enhancement, revealed nearly identical emission sites between devices, all  appearing to originate from the ESD protection structures (Figure 9). Although I/O pin biasing indicated a measurable  leakage difference, the emission and hotspot locations did not  lead

to

any

conclusive

failure

sites.

Figure 9.  PEM ATE shows no emission difference between SN10(failed) vs  reference devices

To further investigate, LI-SLS in DC mode using a 1340nm  laser was utilized. This technique identified distinctive laser  sites; however, these findings did not provide high confidence  since lower intensity responses were also observed in the  reference device (Figure 10(b)). Subsequent high-magnification  analysis with SIL suggested that the anomalous sites  corresponded to NMOS and PMOS transistors located at the  input side of CMOSTX1 driver. Consulting EFI results with  design team confirmed that these transistors were on I/O path; however, they are not on the first output stages connected to the  external nets that are linked to the failing pin (Figure 11).

CMOSTX1 circuit

Figure 11(b). LI-SLS DC at SIL+CAD overlay shows SLS site at the input of  the CMOSTX1 circuit for SN10 (failed device)

Figure 11.  LI-SLS DC technique shows an indistinguishable site near the input  of CMOSTX1 for the ESD-failed device at SIL magnification (a) and (b)

In the continued effort to isolate the failure, an advanced  technique – LI-SLS ATE (Lock-In mode SLS with running ATE  leakage test) – was introduced (Figures 13(a), 13(b), 13(c)). This  method combines the lock-in mode of SLS using a 1340 nm  laser with an ATE-based environment to detect failures. An  external amplifier (FDx-SLS Remote Head via Meridian) biases  the I/O pin from the DUT input side during ATE execution. To  enable this feature, Per-Pin Parametric Measurement Unit (PPMU) instrument and AC relay (which typically connect the  I/O pin to the tester hardware and vector sequences) must be  electrically disconnected in the ATE “hardware perspective” (Figure 13(d)). Once isolated, an external bias voltage is applied  to the input of the I/O pin to achieve a similar leakage current as  seen before disconnecting AC relay and PPMU (Figure 13(e)). The area is scanned thermally using 1340nm laser to detect  resistive defects based on induced current and thermal  variations. A 600mV input voltage—representing logic “1”—was sourced from an external power supply to the FDx-SLS

remote head. The software configured the force voltage, current  limit, lock-in frequency, phase, and cycle count. This voltage  was applied to the DUT input pins to turn on the NMOS driver  to enable the IIH (Input High Leakage) path (Figure 12).

Using LI-SLS ATE with different Lock-In frequency and  phase mode settings for defect isolation, we identified a distinct  anomalous site with the failed device. Subsequent localization  and analysis at higher magnification revealed unique defect sites  within the NMOS transistors of the grs2_rx2_amp circuit

(associated with receiver) and the tx_pump circuit (associated  with transmitter). Leveraging CAD tools, circuit analysis, and  continuous signal tracing, a direct connection was established  between these identified sites and the failing pins. The failing  net RX2 which directly connects from the failing I/O pad to the  laser site was also identified.  The I/O design team further  confirmed that the Rx_amp and Tx_pump circuitries correspond  to the correct locations along the direct I/O path associated with  the ESD failure (Figure 14). After successfully pinpointing the  failure locations with high precision—Nmos driver transistors, as well as M19  metal layer for the output driver  net RX2.

PFA instruction was carefully drafted. This document, including full technical details, design instance paths, precise  reference and failure locations of the transistors and nets  correlating with the hotspots, was provided to the PFA team to  continue investigation at the cell level. The PFA team was  instructed to start further FI at M19 layer, the most top metal  layer at which the transistors in the cell of interest are still  connected. Nanoprobe revealed a metal short bridging at RX2 to  VDD power lane at M19. Further nanoprobe and TEM  investigation revealed silicon physical defect for Nmos driver  transistors M_MN1 as previously isolated by EFA.

CASE C. FAILURE ANALYSIS OF JTAG PACKAGE PREQUAL VIH/VOH FAILURES

Another GPU device family was submitted to FA after  failing a package pre-qualification at 1,000 thermal cycles. The  failure was observed during the bsr_jtag_vih_voh functional  test. By applying a scaling factor to the ATE DC levels setup to  isolate the VOH/VIH levels, the test engineer successfully  localized the issue to a single pin, which consistently failed the  VIH test. Shmoo plot showing functional pass/fail region of  Vmin and fmax is shown in (Figure 15).

Figure 15.  ATE Fmax vs Vmin shmoo for failed and reference devices

EFA process began with IVCT. In this case, IVCT did not  detect any DC leakage differences between the failed and  reference devices. Consequently, both LIT and PEM in DC did  not reveal any anomalous hotspots or emission sites at the failing  pin. The device was then placed on the ATE load board and  retested using the same Vih/Voh functional vectors as in the  original reliability qualification platform. Once the functional  failure was reproduced with the correct test vectors, PEM  detected an anomalous emission site in the I/O circuitry (Figure  16). Further magnification and localization revealed that the  emission originated from internal “main0/q_lat1” net that  connect to the common gates and drains of NMOS/PMOS  transistors within the gddr_u6_tx_latchlatch (latlat0) cell. This  cell drives multiple downstream components – such as inverters, multiplexers, and drivers – within the GDDR_TX circuitry that  ultimately connects to the external I/O pad.

Figure 16. PEM ATE with SIL enhancement between SN301(fail) vs reference  devices while running Voh/Vih functional vector. An additional strong emission  site for failed device was revealed.

emission site and the failing I/O pin, confirming the defect’s

III. DISCUSSION

As processing and packaging technologies advance—such  as backside power delivery (BSP), system-on-integrated-chip (SoIC), and co-packaged optics (CPO)—I/O debugging faces  growing complexity, particularly in high-speed datacenter  applications. To address these challenges, we are both  extending current tool capabilities and pursuing nextgeneration failure analysis methodologies. Emerging  methodologies include high-speed vector network analysis for  multi-GHz to THz I/O characterization, thermoreflectance  imaging for non-invasive thermal profiling, predictive  modeling for design-correlated debug, and integrated database  automation. Together, these approaches aim to build a scalable, future-ready I/O debug framework aligned with the  performance and integration demands of chiplet-based and 3Dintegrated systems. However, realizing this framework's full  potential depends on a strong foundation in established  electrical failure analysis (EFA) practices. This paper highlights  four critical pillars of successful EFA: (1) applying  complementary EFI techniques tailored to specific failure  modes; (2) replicating failures through controlled test setups;

(3) leveraging deep expertise in schematic and layout analysis; and (4) fostering collaboration between Design Engineering  and PFA teams. While EFI tools are essential for localizing  fault signatures, their diagnostic value is significantly amplified  when combined with test-mode validation, schematic tracing, and physical layout correlation. This integrated approach is key  to isolating root causes and avoiding misinterpretation from  secondary artifacts.

This paper reinforces the idea that data from EFI techniques  must not be viewed in isolation. Instead, it must be interpreted  through the lens of solid circuit understanding, engineering  judgment, and iterative hypothesis testing. Analysts must  evaluate whether anomalous findings are consistent with the  functional role of the I/O path and whether they trace logically  to an external symptom of the failure signature.

IV. CONCLUSION

We demonstrated that the synergy between advanced EFI  techniques, test mode setup, and expert-level schematic/layout  analysis is what enables high-precision fault localization and  effective root cause identification. By applying this rigorous  analytical approach, EFA analysts can significantly improve  PFA success rates, drives design/process improvements, and  accelerates delivery of robust products.

Figure 18 shows a complete I/O Debug Workflow designed  by our System Fault Isolation (SFI) team at NVIDIA. This  workflow was fully applied in all the cases presented in this  paper. It demonstrates all debug steps and techniques used for  shorts, leakage, and open cases. Due to the technical span and  focus of this paper, we only present leakage failures, ESD  debug, and VIH/VOH failure cases. Continuity-open or  intermittent failures were previously reported [1].

Enabling Volume Electrical Fault Isolation Workflow with Automation to  Enhance Throughput and Success Rate

D. Nagalingam, A.C.T. Quah, J.C. Alag, Y.H. Chan, P.K. Tan, C.Q. Chen

GlobalFoundries Singapore

Dayanand.nagalingam@globalfoundries.com

Abstract

Earlier studies have reported that static fault isolation (FI) methods such as NIR-PEM and TIVA could be utilized, in the  absence of software diagnostic or dynamic FI capabilities, to  localize subtle defects resulting in functional logic and memory  failures [1-3]. However, the success to this approach relied on  interrogating large samples of fail dies to chance upon “Golden” dies, where defect could trigger detectable weak  induced emission, from floating gate or bridging effects, from  nets that are connected to sensitive combinational logic [1]. This has resulted in long cycle time with current manual fault  isolation workflow in localizing these “golden” dies and  subsequently identifying the best candidate among these few  dies for physical analysis.

In this paper, for the first time, we described a novel volume  electrical fault isolation workflow tested on a new static fault  isolation system to perform semi-automated fault isolation. An  image recognition software was further employed to cherry  pick the best candidates for further analysis. Two case studies  were described to illustrate how volume fault isolation has  improved the success rate and cycle time with the identification  of the best candidates for subsequent physical failure analysis (PFA). This approach would be highly valuable to FA  community, especially foundries, to enlarge static fault  isolation coverage on functional logic failure in the absence of  diagnostic or dynamic fault isolation capabilities.

Introduction

Logic and memory defectivity improvements have been the  primary drivers of the yield enhancement roadmap of  International Roadmap for Devices and Systems (IRDS) for the  past few years. In IRDS 2023, logic was chosen to be the yield  technology driver due to its tighter pitch size, more metal layers  and higher complexity [4]. As the industry is trying to maintain  the yield with the advancements in technology by preventing, predicting and controlling the defects in the foundry, yield loss  due to logic and memory failures are still unavoidable. Failure  analysis (FA) community has been continuously utilizing  software-based test & diagnostics [5] and hardware-based fault

isolation solutions [6,7] to help the foundry maintain or recover  the yield. However, for mature technology nodes that lack these  debug approaches, foundries would still have to rely on static  fault isolation (SFI) methods due to their fast turn-around-time, simpler biasing, and their readiness to be applied to any  integrated circuit with limited information which is readily  available.

When it comes to isolating defects for logic and memory related  functional failures, it was commonly believed that static fault  isolation techniques are limited due to the inability to access the  defect through conventional power-gnd DC biasing of the  chip’s logic/memory blocks. However, earlier studies have  reported that SFI techniques can still be employed to localize  weak defect induced emissions or hotspots on logic and certain  types of memory failure modes [1-3]. In the case of powergated devices, it would require additional understanding of the  power management circuit layout routings to gain direct biasing  access to the power-gated logic and memory blocks for SFI  approach to be effective [8].

A major challenge in the above-mentioned approach is the low  success rate to chance upon these “Golden” dies due to several  factors as follows. Firstly, these defects induced emissions are  the result of marginal leakages from saturating transistors  which usually appear to be insignificant as compared to the  overall device logic and memory combined power-on  consumption leakage. As such, typical IV bench measurement  across power supplies would not be effective in distinguishing  these minute leakage differences and identifying these dies for  FI. Secondly, static-biased defect induced emissions are  observed to be localized from combinational logics that are  sensitive to floating gate effects or intermediately biased  voltage levels from resistive bridge between signal nets. These  sensitive logics include inverters, buffers, pass gate transistors  in memory or other logic gate configurations that could  effectively reduce to an equivalent inverter logic. Thus, only  dies encountering defects that have impacted these sensitive  signal nets would have a higher success rate in fault isolation. Lastly, successful SFI on logic and memory functional failures  is also dependent on utilizing highly sensitivity PEM cameras  with sufficient pixel resolution to effectively reveal these weak  emission spots from visual comparison [1].

With these challenges, it is evident that analyst would require  to interrogate large sample of fail dies before arriving with a die  with detectable exclusive hotspot. In more challenging cases, this probability can be 10 % or lower, 2 hits in 20 dies. In such  scenarios, PFA on each sample would become crucial with an  increased amount of analysis time in covering a large area of  inspection and applying various methods like PVC, EBAC and  nanoprobing to narrow down the defect location. To make  matters worse, PFA success would be low on dies with only  single exclusive logic spots found as they could be triggered by  middle or far back-end of line interconnect defectivities that are  not at the spot locations. Identifying a suspect failure net from  a single spot with approximately 1.5um CAD navigation  overlay error would be very challenging as it would constitutes  to multiple suspects. Applying SIL could alleviate but would  not remove this challenge, depending on the technology nodes  of the device.

Therefore, increasing the volume of fault isolation samples will  certainly increase the number of samples with hotspots thereby  increasing the flexibility to choose the best candidates for  physical analysis. To illustrate, when 100 samples are analyzed, probably 20-30 dies can be localized with hotspots from which  the best ones with hotspot signatures that correlate to suspected  defect type and layer could be selected for PFA. With the  existing workflow, which is fully manual driven, achieving  such a high fault isolation throughput is not practical. To  enhance the throughput, adopting an automated fault isolation  workflow will be an excellent solution. This paper puts forth a  novel static fault isolation system which incorporates an  automated workflow to analyze large numbers of samples in a  shorter duration to improve the overall success rate as discussed  above. Two case studies will be presented to showcase the  effectiveness of this approach.

Automated Fault Isolation Workflow

An Analytical Scanning Optical Microscope that has an  automated XYZ stage was used in the enhanced workflow. This  stage allows automated stepping of one die to another on the  wafer. Fig. 1 shows the automated workflow with three  segments namely system setup, auto analysis and post auto  analysis. Firstly, system setup is carried out to prepare the  system for precise navigation across the wafer and probe  landing on the correct die and biasing pads of interest. Probing  is performed using either micro-positioners or probe card and  the system stage has been designed to accommodate up to 10  micro-positioners. Wafer map setup step creates a software  readable version of the physical wafer map which allows the  user to navigate to the die of interest by clicking on the wafer  map. Next, a reference die is assigned for die-die matching of  XY co-ordinates of the wafer map and the physical wafer. Fig. 2 shows the software generated wafer map indicating the ref die  and an exclusion zone. For safe die stepping, an adjustable  exclusion zone at the wafer edge is marked out. Dies marked  with “X” within this zone are inaccessible during auto analysis. However, there is an alternate solution for accessing wafer edge  dies which will be discussed in the second case study later. Next  in the system setup is a rotation correction step to ensure the

wafer is perfectly aligned in horizontal and vertical directions. Subsequently, the system is trained on the physical dimensions  of the die.

Figure 1: Automated Fault Isolation Workflow

Figure 2: Software generated wafer map indicating ref die  and exclusion zone.

Once the setup is completed, the system is ready to perform  automated analysis to screen out the dies with hotspots. Firstly, select the dies to be analyzed on the wafer map. This can be  performed by manually selecting the dies of interest or  importing from the wafer sort map. Fig. 3(a) shows the colorcoded wafer sort bin map with each color representing a failure  bin. Import function in the software allows the user to select the  targeted failure bin for auto analysis. Fig. 3(b) shows the  orange-colored dies from wafer sort map being imported for  auto analysis. Next is a very critical step where the user instructs  the software on all the necessary analysis steps to be carried out  on the first die. For example, parameters like magnification, biasing voltage and current compliance, Photon Emission  Microscopy (PEM) or Thermal Induced Voltage Alternation (TIVA) analysis etc. are defined in this step. Next is to let the  software take control and repeat the analysis on all the selected  dies. Automated analysis is targeted only at the lowest  magnification objective to gain an overview on how many of

Figure 3: Wafer sort bin map and targeted bin map

Once the data collection is completed, in the post auto analysis  stage the large set of collected data is fed to an image  recognition software developed by GlobalFoundries Analytical  Labs to compare a set of good die signal images with all the bad  die signal images to classify the dies with and without hotspot. Fig. 4 shows the user interface comparing a good die EMMI  image on the left against a bad die on the right. Green box on  the bad die indicates the region of interest (ROI) for  comparison. The ROI is selected by the user on a good die and  the same ROI is used for comparison on the entire dataset. The  software identifies exclusive hotspots and highlighted them in  green circles. The comparison results are then tabulated and  further classified as single spot, multiple single spots, cluster  spots and no spot in a separate excel file. From these results, the  best candidates would be selected and subjected for 2nd round  of fault isolation, more effectively performed manually for this  round, at higher magnification. This is followed by layout  analysis and physical analysis which are similar to conventional  SFI workflow.

Subsequently, the steps are similar to conventional SFI  workflow where those dies with hotspots are subjected to  manual fault isolation process to collect the high magnification  images of the hotspot followed by layout analysis and physical  analysis.

Case Studies

This section will describe two successful case studies to  illustrate the effectiveness of the automated workflow. Both are  logic functional failures with no diagnostic support.

Case Study 1 :

A low yield issue affecting multiple wafers with logic  functional failure was investigated. Fig. 5 showed the affected  wafer with red patch representing the failed dies. Since the  device had no software diagnostic support and dynamic fault  isolation (DFI) capabilities, SFI had to be attempted to  determine the root cause by simply biasing the logic power  supply and ground. Preliminary manual fault isolation analysis  did not yield any exclusive PEM or TIVA signal from six  analyzed dies. Subsequently, automated analysis was  attempted. Following the automated workflow described in fig. 1, a total of 128 bad dies were analyzed from the failed patch. Fig. 6 highlighted the dies selected for analysis within the red  contour. 1x magnification PEM analysis was performed on 128  failed dies and 4 good dies to first identify those dies with  exclusive signal. It took a total of ~8 hrs with the initial setup  being carried out in the evening and the auto analysis was run  overnight without any supervision from the analyst and the data  was available for review the next morning.

Figure 5: Wafer Sort map  showing the failure patch in  red color

Figure 6: System Wafer

map showing the dies  selected for auto analysis.

Subsequently, the collected volume FI raw data was input into  the hotspot classification software. Each die was screened  through by the software to identify the dies with exclusive spot  and classify them as either single spot or cluster of spots. Fig. 7  shows an illustration of a set of raw data and a set of software  output images with exclusive spots being circled. 46 dies out of  128 dies exhibited exclusive signals as compared to reference  dies which constitutes about 36% of the total analyzed dies. Fig. 8 shows the summary of the different type of hotspots observed. 21% of the analyzed dies exhibited single spot, 10% showing  multiple single spots at different regions of the die, 5% showing  cluster spots signature and 64% of the dies were unsuccessful  with no exclusive spot. The best candidates for further analysis  would be those dies with cluster spots which were suitable for  layout analysis and potentially narrowing down the defect  location to increase the physical analysis success rate. As the  signals were defect-induced emissions, success rate on single  spot or multiple single spot dies would be considerably low.

Figure 7: Illustration of raw data and software output

Figure 8: Hotspot Classification result summary

Manual fault isolation was carried out on the 6 dies with cluster  spots. High magnification analysis indeed confirmed cluster of  spots on all those dies. Layout analysis was performed and

suspected failed nets were easily derived based on the spots. Fig. 9 shows the PEM overlay images of 4 bad dies, Bad 1 to  Bad 4, superimposed onto the failed nets. Bad 3 & Bad 4 had  two failure nets each with the backend metal 4 lines of each net  routing side by side indicating a possible metal 4 broken or  bridge defect. Bad 2 had similar signature with at least 3  suspected nets. Only 1 failure net could be localized for Bad 1, however based on other units the suspect was narrowed down  to the long metal 4 line. PFA on Bad 3 at the suspected location  revealed broken metal 4 as depicted in fig. 10. Defect was not  located at any of the cluster of spots. This proves that 31% of  dies with single spot would be unsuitable for physical analysis  as the defect would not be at the spot location and it will be  challenging to derive a suspected failed net based on the single  spot. Subsequently, PFA on Bad 1 also revealed broken metal  4 at the suspected location. With 2 dies showing consistent  defect and with the remaining dies also pointing to similar  defect, it was concluded that broken metal 4 was the cause of  this low yield issue.

Figure 9: 50X PEM overlay image with the suspected  failure net.

Figure 10: SEM image showing broken metal 4 along the  suspected net.

If this case had to be attempted through manual FI followed by  PFA, probably 1 day of FI on 10 – 15 dies could have identified  2 – 3 of those single spot dies. PFA at the spot location  including layer by layer inspection and nanoprobing would  require 2 – 3 days per sample. Since the emissions are defect  indued ones, likely PFA would be unsuccessful. In total 8-9  days effort would end up wasted completing all 3 samples. Even  if FI was lucky enough to identify 1 cluster unit, it is not  sufficient to narrow down to the defect layer or location. Likely  would still require a second round of FA to prove with more  cluster units. With automated FI workflow, there is so much  flexibility in choosing the right die for analysis and narrowing  down to the defect layer and location for faster defect finding  which incredibly improves the throughput and success rate.

Case Study 2 :

The second case study describes a case where the auto analysis  was performed on a partial wafer incorporating multiple  analysis steps on each die. Fig. 11 showed a low yielding wafer  with high logic functional failures at circled regions. Scattered  red-colored dies represented DC leakage failures which were  not the primary focus. Preliminary investigation based on ETest data revealed that contact layer resistance had drifted from  the baseline performance values; however, no failure was  detected. Similar to first case study, this chip also has neither  software diagnostics nor DFI capabilities. Therefore, SFI was  attempted. Since the region of interest also contained red  colored DC leakage dies, manual static fault isolation was first  attempted on those dies. I-V measurement confirmed high  leakage and exclusive PEM and TIVA signals were localized  on 4 out of 4 dies. However, physical analysis revealed defects  due to random defectivity not correlating with the suspected  contact resistance issue. One such dies found poly – contact  leakage though nanoprobing and cross-section TEM analysis  observed abnormal poly as shown in fig. 12.

Figure 11: Wafer map  showing 2 patches of logic  functional failure

Figure 12: Cross-section

TEM image showing

abnormal poly resulting in  poly – contact leakage.

As first round analysis on leakage failures turned out to be  futile, focus was shifted towards the logic functional failures. To achieve a higher success rate, auto analysis was attempted. The additional challenge in this case was that now the wafer is  already broken due to first round analysis, the masked-off  regions in fig. 11 were unavailable for second round analysis. The unmasked wafer piece had to be mounted on a 300mm  glass and all the setup and alignment had to be done on the

partial wafer. Each die was trained to capture 1x and 5x PEM  images and 5x TIVA images. Auto analysis was performed on  83 dies from the available piece of wafer. Total analysis time  was approximately 10hrs including the setup time. In total, 16  out of 83 dies exhibited exclusive signals with all of them being  single spot and no cluster. To summarize, 11 dies were  localized with TIVA spot, 4 dies with EMMI spot, 1 die with  both EMMI and TIVA spot and 67 dies comparable with good  die as depicted in fig. 13. As there is a higher percentage of dies  with TIVA spot, further higher magnification FI analysis was  targeted on them. Fig. 14 is a 50x TIVA overlay image showing  the exclusive signal. Manual FI followed by layout analysis on  the die with EMMI and TIVA spot identified a failure net with  the EMMI spot representing a defect induced emission  signature. Therefore, physical analysis was targeted on the  TIVA signal. Layer by layer delayering and SEM inspection did  not observe any anomaly until contact layer. Atomic Force  Probing (AFP) current imaging at contact level revealed a  suspected high resistance contact at the TIVA spot which was  later confirmed by probing analysis as shown in fig. 15 and 16  respectively. This finding correlated with the fab suspect. Further cross section TEM analysis confirmed partially landed  contact as depicted in fig. 17.

Conclusions

With automation playing a bigger role in the semiconductor  industry now than ever, we have taken the first step towards  automating the fault isolation workflow. In this paper, a novel  automated fault isolation workflow has been demonstrated for  the first time to enhance the overall effectiveness and success  rate of not just the FI workflow but the entire FA flow. The  ability to perform FI on a large number of samples within a  short span of time provided the analyst with greater insights  about the failure mode to confidently narrow down to the  suspected layer and defect, also gave the freedom to choose the  best candidate for physical analysis. Based on the first case  study, for the same analysis time, the automated FI approach  achieved a throughput of 128 samples versus 15 samples using  manual approach which is an 8-fold increase in FI throughput. Such amount of data was clearly useful in predicting and nailing  down a metal 4 defect with a 100% success rate. In the second  case study, apart from the throughput enhancement, volume  data was helpful in deciding whether to proceed with physical  analysis on samples with EMMI spot or TIVA spot. The  deciding factor was a greater number of dies exhibited TIVA  spot that too with the spot signature being the same on all dies.
