High-Precision Fault Localization in LSI Using Photo Emission Microscopy with  Logical State Consideration

Yasushi Oka

Renesas Electronics corp., FA Laboratory, Quality Assurance Division, 5-20-1, Josuihon-cho, Kodaira, Tokyo, Japan  E-mail: yasushi.oka.ak@renesas.com

Nakaba Matsui

Hamamatsu Photonics K. K., 812 Joko-cho, Chuo-ku, Hamamatsu City, Shizuoka, Japan

E-mail: nakaba.matsui@hpk.co.jp

Abstract

To improve the success rate of Failure Analysis (FA), it is  important to refine electrical troubleshooting processes. However, Electrical Fault Isolation (EFI) techniques face  serious challenges, not only with Critical Dimension issues but  also with excessive power consumption. Photo Emission  Microscopy, Soft Defect Localization [1], Electro-Optical  Probing, also called Laser Voltage Imaging [2], and Thermal  Frequency Imaging [3], are widely used. These major EFI  methods are usually performed under the ATE-driven operating  environment. Recent scan-designed LSIs consume a large  amount of current during tests, which never occurs in their  normal operation. This current can disrupt EFI operations. For  example, it could cause switching delays due to internal IR  drops, leading to unexpected malfunctions in logic operations. Moreover, it may damage the device. To mitigate this issue, minimizing the amount of switching activity during tests is a  widely adopted measure to reduce power consumption. However, when the switching activity is reduced, the total test  time becomes longer, and so does the looping period for EFI. This weakens every EFI detection signal, causing the 2D  location image to be less clear. To address this problem, a PEM  with halting at failing logic state was studied, which will not  cause excessive switching current. This static PEM method  proved effective, offering more accurate localization than  conventional dynamic EFI techniques.

Introduction

The structure of devices beyond the 16 nm process has  drastically changed from planar MOSFET to FinFET. Furthermore, the next-generation so-called Gate-All-Around (GAA) structure is expected to play a key role in the upcoming  2 nm technology. This rapid evolution presents significant  challenges for failure analysis. Device size is directly related to  Physical Analysis, which challenges the capability to produce  quality results, including sample preparation and observation. However, in this paper, we’d like to focus on Electric Failure  Analysis (EFA) or Electric Fault Isolation (EFI), because they  face fundamental problems. Small device sizes, low operating  voltages, and long test patterns all negatively impact the  accuracy of EFI. One of the major issues is that recent devices

consume a significant amount of supply current, especially  during a test or EFI with an ATE. The test of VLSI is optimized  through scan design, but during the application of test patterns  and observation of test results, large currents that would never  occur during normal operation flow. These large currents could  disrupt the operation of the device under test (DUT) or even  cause burnout of it. When performing EFI, the DUT is usually  set at room temperature without any heat dissipation  mechanisms, such as heat sinks. This increases the risk of  device burnout. Recent testing technology addresses this issue  by allowing test operations limiting each separated area to keep  the total current lower. This means test time will increase to  cover the whole area. EFI usually uses looping patterns  including the failure part. If the test becomes longer, the  duration of a loop increases, and the integrated signals detected  by EFI tools become weaker. This makes it more difficult to  find the defective location.

On the other hand, there are static EFI methods which are not  affected by excessive current problems. For example, if the  device has an IDDQ current abnormality, PEM or OBIRCH  analysis can be applied, halting at the abnormal IDDQ current  vector. Also, since the IDDQ current value changes according  to its current path created by logic states, this technique has the  potential to pinpoint the defect location inside a cell by  combining emission results and circuit simulation of the failing  logic states [4][5]. Additionally, there is the “External Trigger  Synchronous Lock-in Thermography” (ES-LIT) technique that  can provide the low-noise LIT images by subtracting the  thermal background images [6]. However, IDDQ abnormalities  are not used in latest devices because identifying IDDQ current  differences between normal and abnormal is getting hard. They  are usually hidden in a large amount of base current.

In this context, “Laser Logic State Imaging” (LLSI) [7], which  captures the logic state image during halting periods, is a good  suggestion. If the logic state of the scan failure can be set in the  same way as the IDDQ failure, it might be possible to  accurately identify the critical area using high-resolution tools. Therefore, this method was evaluated in the following  experiment. As a result, this simple method surpassed ordinary  test-looping EFI in terms of both defect pinpointing accuracy  and workflow simplicity. Considering this result, this method

Case Study

1. Sample information

⚫ Product: SOC assembled in BGA.

⚫ Process node: 7nm (FinFET).

⚫ Fail location: Burn-in screening.

⚫ Symptom: Scan failure with Vdd dependency.

2. General Electrical Fault Localization flow

The general EFI workflow using a dynamic test pattern is  shown in Figure 1. Firstly, fault diagnosis is applied to identify  the specific circuit or flip-flops. Then, EFI analysis described  from step 2 to step 5 in Figure 1 are applied. Note that this EFI  analysis uses a looping test pattern that includes the faulty part. When EFI detects a suspicious location that matches the  diagnosis results, Physical Failure Analysis (PFA), which is an  irreversible process, will be allowed.

Figure 1: Overview of the standard EFI workflow. Steps 2 to  step 5 utilize looping test patterns that include faulty logic, enabling emission-based localization prior to irreversible  physical analysis.

3. Fault Diagnosis

Fault Diagnosis is a tool used in semiconductor testing and  diagnostics to identify the root cause of chip failures. Figure 2  shows the results..

Figure 2: Fault Diagnosis result.

⚫ Suspect 1: Flip Flop 111 or its input or output nets. ⚫ Suspect 2: Flip Flop 112 or its input or output nets.

Designated candidates are two Flip-Flops (FFs) and their input  and output nets. It is common that the defect point is not  determined solely by fault diagnosis because there are many  possible points that can create an equivalent fail-log. EFI will  assist in the localization

4. Photo Emission analysis (PEM) with looping pattern

PEM analysis with SIL using a looping pattern was performed. Figure 3 illustrates a suspicious emission signal detected  between FF112 and FF113. Although the emission signal  corresponded to the suspected areas, its size encompassed the  entire flip-flop, making precise fault localization difficult.

Figure 3: PEM result showing widespread emission across  FF112 and the upper half of FF113. The signal spans entire  flip-flop regions, making precise fault localization challenging.

5. Soft Defect Localization (SDL)

F-V Shmoo plot is necessary to prepare the SDL analysis  settings. This faulty sample showed no operation region when  the supply voltage “Vdd” is below 1.08V.

Figure 4: Shmoo evaluation results. In good sample, a  sufficient operating region is secured, but in failing samples, no operating region is observed when Vdd drops below 1V.

The test conditions were established at the boundary of the  pass/fail region, and SDL analysis was conducted, as illustrated  in Figure 5.

Figure 5: SDL analysis result.

The red signal at the center represents the SDL response. It is  located at the border of FF112 and FF113, and still not  distinguishable which region contains the root cause.

6. Electro-Optical Frequency Mapping (EOFM)

Since this Scan Chain pattern was compressed by Embedded  Deterministic Test (EDT), this EOFM analysis was performed  with clock cycle instead of data cycle. EOFM image when Vdd  was 1.15V (pass condition) is shown in Figure 6, and that of  when Vdd was 0.80V (fail condition) is shown in Figure 7.

Figure 6: EOFM analysis result at a passing condition. A  strong signal was detected at the boundary of FF 112 and FF

113.  (clock rate: 90 ns, frequency: 11 MHz)

Figure 7: EOFM analysis result at a failing condition. Another strange signal was detected in FF 111

When Vdd was 1.15V (pass condition), a strong EOFM signal  at the border between FF112 and FF113 appeared. This position  is the same as the results of PEM and SDL. Since this EOFM  was seen in a passing condition, the strong signal does not refer  to a failing reason but rather indicates thermal generation, which EOFM often detects as a thermal frequency. So, it is sure  that there is a leakage defect there, but it is not sure if this  leakage caused this scan failure.

In contrast, the EOFM signal in the failure state appeared  separately from the other signals shown in Figure 7. PEM, SDL, and EOFM signal locations were summarized as shown  in the schematic of Figure 8. A strong EOFM signal in the pass  state is located near the border of FF112 and FF113, similar to  the positions of PEM and SDL. At this point, it is not clear why  EOFM (pass) is associated with PEM and SDL, while EOFM (fail) is independent.

Figure 8: Comparative schematic of emission signal locations  from PEM, SDL, and EOFM analysis. The EOFM results differ  between pass and fail conditions.

7. Electro-Optical Probing (EOP)

The aim of EOP analysis is to understand what is happening  between healthy and non-healthy points by observing their  waveforms changing during the propagation process. In this  analysis, the compressed scan test pattern was used. Some  simulations were performed around the capture time, and the  logical state of the FFs was extracted from these results.

Figure 9: EOP probing points. MUXs were set to pass the  signals from previous FFs.

Probing points were set at the Z-out of the MUXs, which were  set to pass through as shown in Figure 9. This is because the  design of the Q-out of each FF was too tight, causing EOP  signal mixing with neighboring signals.

Figure 10 shows the EOP result probed at the Z-out of MUX

181. When Vdd was 1.15V (pass), the signal was noisy due to  signal mixing from neighboring circuits. However, when Vdd  was 0.8V (fail), the signal was almost clear and healthy.

Figure 11 shows the EOP result probed at the Z-out of MUX

978. When Vdd was 1.15V (pass), the output waveform was  normal. However, when Vdd was 0.8V (fail), its signal showed  unusual behavior compared with that of pass condition. This  unexpected signal can explain why propagation error occurred  in its failing condition. These results indicate that the waveform  anomaly likely originated between the input and output of  FF112. Consequently, it is likely that the defect is associated  with FF112, not FF113.

In this case, the defect was successfully pinpointed to FF 112  without facing an overcurrent issue. However, this EFI method  would not provide the fundamental measure against the  overcurrent issue expected in the EFI analysis driven by scan  test pattern.

Figure 10: Result of EOP at the output of MUX 181.

This waveform represents the output behavior of FF113.

Figure 11: Result of EOP at the output of MUX 978.

This waveform represents the output behavior of FF112.

PEM considering logic states

To avoid the overcurrent issue, electrically static PEM analysis  is a recommended approach. Additionally, it is interesting to  see if it can enhance location accuracy compared to previous  results. The first step of this trial involves simulation to extract  the logical state when the fault is detected. This simulation is  performed with a compressed scan pattern despite the scan  chain failure, because it is impossible to perform simulation  with the compressed scan chain pattern and to extract the logic  state of the flip-flops (FFs). After these preparations, the next  step is to set the Test Vector corresponding to the failure logic  state using ATE and perform PEM analysis with the pattern  halt. This procedure is described in Figure 12 as a branch, highlighted in red. The steps (a.) and (b.) are expected to  replace the original steps (2.-5.).

FF113 Clock@Vdd=0.8V

MUX181/Z @Vdd=1.15V Pass (FF113)

MUX181/Z @Vdd=0.8V Fail (FF113)

FF112 Clock@Vdd=0.8V

MUX978/Z @Vdd=1.15V Pass

MUX978/Z @Vdd=0.8V Fail

Figure 12: Proposed static PEM workflow incorporating logic  state simulation. Red-highlighted steps (a and b) replace  conventional dynamic EFI steps (2–5), aiming to reduce  overcurrent and improve localization accuracy.

8. Experiment and results

Simulated waveforms on the most suspicious flip-flop FF112  are shown on the left side of Figure 13. The fault is estimated  to occur after the capture clock. To get the reference data, PEM  analysis on the pass state (before the capture clock) was  performed. The PEM result is shown on the right side of Figure

13. Under these conditions, the emission intensity was barely  detectable.

Figure 13: Simulated logic state of FF 112 (left) and Emission  analysis result on the ‘fail’ state (right). In the left figure “Emission” means emission detection timing.

Figure 14: The timing of emission detection was changed to the 'fail' state, and as a result, the emission intensity became  stronger than in the pass state. Both positions were the same as  in Figure 3.

Then, PEM analysis on the fail state (after the clock) was  performed. The result is shown on the right side of Figure 14. Under these conditions, the emission was stronger than in the  pass state. The emission signal appeared at the same location as  in Figure 3, as observed using SIL.

As shown in Figure 13 and Figure 14, the intensity of the  emission changed according to the logic states. Additional test  patterns were evaluated using the same PEM methodology. Table 1 summarizes the results performed with three different  patterns.

Table 1: Summary of the logic states and emission detection.

This table shows no relation between the logical states of MUX  in FF112 and emission intensity. On the other hand, the state of  the slave latch (Q) in FF112 has a strong relation with emission  intensity. From this result, it is concluded that the root cause  lies in the slave latch in FF112, as shown in Figure 15.

These findings demonstrate that PEM analysis incorporating  logical state information is highly effective because its  localization ability reached inside the flip-flop, surpassing  conventional dynamic EFI ability. Additionally, the workflow  becomes simpler even though it requires simulation to extract  logic states

Figure 15: Faulty slave latch in FF 112. Emission intensity  correlates with the Q output state of the slave latch in FF112. This finding pinpoints the defect within the latch structure, surpassing flip-flop level resolution.

Physical Failure Analysis

PFA was performed on the slave latch region, giving special  attention to the output (=Q). Plane view observation using SEM  and STEM confirmed a bridge path between MG (metal gate)

and MD (s/d contact layer) due to the abnormal extension of  MD material, as shown in Figure 16. This problem was  presumed to stem from some kind of manufacturing trouble in  the photo-lithography process

Figure 16: Plane view observation with S-TEM at the slave  latch in FF 112. A short circuit was confirmed.(between red  arrows)

Conclusion

This study introduces a refined PEM method that uses static  logic state extracted from a compressed scan pattern. The merit  of this method is that it can avoid the excessive supply current  issue expected in advanced scan-design LSI. This method also  has the potential to surpass the usual electrically dynamic  operation EFI in terms of localization accuracy. In this study, EFI using both dynamic and static methods with ATE was  compared. The dynamic method, which employed PEM, SDL, EOFM, and EOP, identified the defect at the level of a single  flip-flop. However, the static method outperformed it by  narrowing down the defect location to a slave latch within the  flip-flop, while also simplifying the workflow. Future research  could explore the application of this method to other types of  semiconductor devices and further refine the technique to  handle even more complex structures.

3.5D Package FA – The Challenges and Innovative Solutions to Successful Root  Cause Analysis

Wen Qiu, Bernice Zee, Shangyi Lim, Jingwen Chen

Advanced Micro Devices (Singapore) Pte Ltd, Singapore

Phone: +65 6796 9888, Email: wen.qiu@amd.com

Abstract

Advanced packaging technologies such as 3.5D are being  adopted to keep up with the demand for GPUs with large  compute power and memory bandwidth. This paper describes  the challenges involved in 3.5D advance package FA and how  this was overcome with the development of innovative sample  preparation flow and electrical characterization method to do  successful root cause analysis.

Introduction

High performance computing (HPC) and generative artificial  intelligence (AI) applications have driven the demand for  graphical processing units (GPUs) with large compute power  and memory bandwidth. To keep up with the demand, key  industry players have been adopting advanced packaging  technologies such as chip-on-wafer-on substrate (CoWoS) and  system on integrated chips (SoIC) to integrate more compute  and memory capacity into one component [1]. Figure 1 shows  the schematic drawing of a chiplet architecture GPU  accelerator, which adopts both 3D stacking and chip  disintegration [2, 3] in 3.5D advance packaging solution.

Figure 1: Schematic drawing of a chiplet architecture GPU  accelerator [2].

Such complex architecture poses several challenges when  performing failure analysis (FA), especially when finding  defects that are lowers in the stack, like in the interposer. For  power supply short failures, longer biasing times are needed for  thermal hotspot detection due to time delays. In the case of  signal pin opens, while detection is more straightforward by  using tools such as time domain reflectometry (TDR) and  electro optical terahertz pulse reflectometry (EOTPR), if the  defect is found to be in the back end of line (BEOL), subsequent  physical failure analysis (PFA) is generally challenging due to  large sample warpage, and the need to maintain the BEOL  integrity for further die level electrical fault isolation (EFI).

This paper discusses an innovative workflow used for doing  root cause analysis of interposer crack monitor (INTCKMON) failures. INTCKMON is structurally a wire ring around the  periphery of the interposer, and the failure mode associated  with it is either short/leakage or open. The function of  INTCKMON is to detect any defects at the interposer edge that  may pose reliability risk during field usage. Typically, when the  INTCKMON fails, the first step would be to do EFI to narrow  down the failure to a specific location along the trace, followed  by PFA. However, FA is not straightforward, and the  challenges will be discussed in detail in the section below.

FA Challenges

The size of CoWoS interposer is approximately 70 x 50mm, and INTCKMON has eight test pins to narrow down which  segment along the interposer periphery the defect is residing at, as illustrated in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Top view illustration of INTCKMON test points along  the wire ring.

However, the INTCKMON has no active circuitry such as  diodes or transistors, so the current-voltage (IV) curve only  shows a linear resistive curve. If there is a short or leakage  failure, the delta in measured current between a reject and a  reference unit is not significant, as compared to pins with active  circuitry as shown in Figure 3 (a) and (b). Hence, it is difficult  to determine if any marginal difference is caused by a real  defect or due to the unit-to-unit resistance variance.

November 16–20, 2025, Pasadena, California, USA

https://doi.org/10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2025p0199

(a)

(b)

Figure 3 (a): IV curve of INTCKMON pin biased with respect  to another INTCKMON pin (b): IV curve of an IO pin with  active circuitry biased with respect to VSS.

After IV characterization identifies a specific segment that has  resistance differences, further EFI needs to be done to pinpoint  a spot on the segment so that PFA can be performed to reveal  the defect.

For INTCKMON short/leakage failure, common techniques  such as photo emission microscope (PEM) and thermally  induced voltage alteration (TIVA) cannot be applied due to lack  of active devices in the interposer. Lock-in thermography (LIT) for localizing thermally activated on-die and embedded  semiconductor package defects can be used for INTCKMON  short/leakage fails [4]. However, as the heat generated by the  defect is very small (micro-Kelvin range), no hotpot is  detectable when the reject unit is in the fully stacked form.

For INTCKMON open failures, TDR and EOTPR can be used  to isolate a segment of the INTCKMON where the defect  resides nondestructively. However, it cannot pinpoint a specific  location for PFA. In this case, electron beam absorbed current (EBAC) technique is adopted to pinpoint the defect location

[5]. EBAC is widely used in silicon die FA to identify open  defects within the interconnect network. Typically, the area of  interest in silicon die applications is within a 200 µm x 200 µm  region, which fits comfortably within the field of view (FOV) of a scanning electron microscope (SEM). This allows the  entire process of positioning a nanoprobe on the interconnect  surface and obtaining the EBAC image to be conducted within

the same FOV. During the EBAC imaging process, the SEM’s

electron beam raster across the defined FOV. Acting as a

current source, the electron beam’s current is absorbed by the

interconnects, and flows towards the nanoprobe, which is either  biased or grounded. The EBAC amplifier, connected to the  nanoprobe, amplifies the small current. Any amplified current  above a certain threshold is considered an EBAC signal, correlated to the raster position of the electron beam.

If there is a breakage in the interconnect line, the EBAC signal  will be interrupted due to the high resistance impeding the  current flow towards the nanoprobe. Thus, any location with a  discontinuous EBAC signal path can be identified as the lateral  location of the defect. The EBAC signal penetration depth is  controlled by the electron beam accelerating voltage of the  SEM and generally limited to the topmost metallization.

Consequently, sample preparation is required to remove  stacked layers above the interposer to expose it to do LIT  measurement for short/leakage FA as well as EBAC for open  FA, this presents two significant challenges. The first challenge  is the silicon interposer exhibits considerable warpage. The  warpage of the stacked sample causes any form of planar  grinding and polishing to become uneven, making it difficult to  manually grind or use a computer numerical control (CNC) milling tool to achieve uniform deprocessing. Hence, to expose  the silicon interposer circuitry beneath, a precise combination  of grinding, wet and dry etching must be employed to achieve  uniform deprocessing.

The second challenge is the limited EBAC imaging range. This  limitation is primarily due to the FOV of the current SEM  system and the movement range of the probes (~25 µm). Accordingly, conducting EBAC on millimeter-long  interconnect lines is not feasible. These limitations hinder the  application of EBAC imaging on most interconnect lines on the  interposer.

Innovative FA Approaches

To address the above-mentioned challenges, an innovative  sample preparation flow and electrical characterization method  has been developed.

On the sample preparation side, the first step is to use a CNC  tool to grind the stacked chiplets materials as the sample  preparation flow illustrated in Figure 4. Once the micro bump  under bump metallization (UBM) layer of the interposer is  exposed, the second step is to use dry etching or mechanical  polishing to thin down the UBM layer to check for cracks or  physical damages that may contribute to the failure. Alternatively, wet etching can remove the UBM layer to expose  the bump pads and passivation layer of the silicon interposer if  no cracks or physical damages present.

The last step is to expose the redistribution layers (RDLs) of  interposer for electrical characterization and EBAC imaging by  using a CNC tool polishing. High surface uniformity can be  achieved using a combination of colloidal silica slurry and  polycrystalline diamond paste to expose the RDLs of interest, as shown as an example in Figure 5.

Figure 4: An innovative sample preparation flow (Crosssectional image extracted from ref [2].

Figure 5: Region of Interest (ROI) M4 metal line of silicon  interposer exposed for electrical characterization and EBAC.

As mentioned, conducting EBAC imaging on millimeter-long  interconnect lines is challenging with conventional  nanoprobing systems due to the limited SEM FOV and probe  movement range. To overcome this, a standard Kleindiek  prober shuttle had to be customized to create more space to  accommodate a large size sample.

Case Study Results and Discussion

Case Study 1: INTCKMON leakage failure

An INTCKMON leakage failure in a 3.5D stacked die unit was  reported after charge device model (CDM) testing. Curve trace  was performed by biasing each INTCKMON pin with respect  to VSS and comparing with a reference good unit to verify the  validity of the reported failure. Results are shown in Figure 6.

Figure 6: IV curve results by biasing 8 INTCKMON pins with  respect to VSS respectively.

To narrow down the failure location, further curve trace  analysis by biasing INTCKMON1 with other INTCKMON  pins found a slight difference when biasing INTCKMON1 with  respect to INTCKMON4 and INTCKMON5. Subsequently, curve trace analysis was performed by biasing INTCKMON3  with respect to INTCKMON 4, 5 and 6, INTCKMON4 with  respect to INTCKMON 5 and 6, and INTCKMON5 with  respect to INTCKMON6. A slight difference could be observed  in all IV curves as shown in Figure 7. Hence, the failure  location was highly suspected to be in the region between  INTCKMON4 and INTCKMON5.

However, TDR results performed at INTCKMON4 and  INTCKMON5 test pins showed no significant difference as  compared to a reference unit as shown in Figure 8.

Figure 7: IV curves by biasing INTCKMON3 with respect to  INTCKMON 4, 5 and 6, INTCKMON4 with respect to  INTCKMON 5 and 6, and INTCKMON5 with respect to  INTCKMON6.

Figure 8: TDR results of INTCKMON4 and INTCKMON5.

To proceed with further fault isolation using thermal camera, the innovative sample preparation flow outlined in the “Innovative FA approaches” section was utilized to remove all  the stacked chiplets on top of the interposer die until the microbump layer at the localized region of INTCKMON4 and  INTCKMON5 test pins was exposed. Thermal camera analysis  was performed and a long acquisition time of about 3 to 4 hours  was set to improve the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) to detect the  hotspot generated by the defect in a micro-Kelvin range. A  distinct hotspot was detected near/at the INTCKMON 5 test pin  in the reject unit by biasing INTCKMON 4 and 5 with respect  to VSS after the sample preparation respectively. The thermal  camera results are shown in Figure 9.

Figure 9: Thermal camera results of the failed unit by biasing  INTCKMON 3, 4, 5 and 6 with respect to VSS.

Optical and SEM inspection at the hot spot locations found an  underfill (UF) crack as shown in Figure 10. Progressive FIB cut  results shown in Figure 11 revealed copper extrusion in the  dielectric shorts INTCRKMON5 metal line and its upper metal  line. The FA results provided evidence that the failure was  likely due to mechanical damage.

Figure 10: Optical and SEM inspection results were performed  at the hot spot location.

Figure 11: Last FIB cut slice result performed at the hot spot  location.

Case Study 2: INTCKMON open failure case

Several

3.5D

stacked

die

unit’s

failed  DCM/INTERCRACKMON test for high impedance after  assembly was submitted for FA. Curve trace analysis was  performed, and the results revealed the failure to be in the  vicinity of INTCKMON5 as shown in Figure 12.

Figure 12: Curve trace results by biasing INTCKMON5 with  respect to VSS/INTCKMON 4 & 6 respectively.

TDR results shown in Figure 13 showed that the failure is close  to the INTCKMON5 test pin. Subsequently, to proceed with  further fault isolation using EBAC, the innovative sample  preparation flow outlined in “Innovative FA approaches” section was again utilized to remove all the layers on top of the  interposer die and expose the top AP layer of INTCKMON5  traces.

Figure 13: TDR results of INTCKMON5 pin.

Optical inspection done in the vicinity showed no significant  anomalies, as shown in Figure 14. EBAC result showed the  EBAC signal terminates near the INTCKMON5 trace junction  where it splits to INTCKMON4 and INTCKMON6 as shown  in Figure 15.

Figure 16 shows the FIB cross-sectional results performed at  the EBAC signal termination point. A manufacturing defect  due to missing via 2 was found.

Figure 14: Optical image after the UF layer above the  interposer is fully removed.

Figure 15: EBAC results by landing the probe at the  INTCKMON 5 M1 layer.

Figure 16: FIB cross-sectional results comparison at the  failure location and reference location.

Conclusions

This paper describes the challenges involved in 3.5D advance  package FA and how this was overcome with the development  of innovative sample preparation flow and electrical  characterization method to do successful root cause analysis. The two case studies discussed and demonstrated how  INTCKMON short/leakage and open failure defects in a  complex 3.5D package can be exposed with the right FA  workflow.

Failure from malformed via in an AC device

Wentao Qin1, Esteban Ortiz1, Raj Kabadi1, Brian Anderson1, and Al Merino1

1Failure Analysis Lab, Microchip Technology, 2355 W Chandler Boulevard, Chandler, AZ 85244, USA.

Abstract

The proper formation of vias is critical to device reliability. We  investigate a phase-locked loop (PLL) lock failure of a returned  unit. Through photoemission analysis and cross-sectional TEM  imaging, the failure was traced to corrosion/oxidation at the top  and bottom of a misaligned via. The misalignment caused  malformation of the via which led to moisture entrapment, and  promoted crevice and galvanic corrosion. During the bench  testing, the impedance from the corrosion/oxidation was low  and did not cause the failure initially due to the high frequency  of the phase lock. It was the temperature increase of the unit  that had elevated the via impedance to have eventually caused  the device to fail. Mitigation strategies are proposed to enhance  long-term device reliability.

Keywords: via impedance, latency, corrosion, crevice  corrosion, kinetics, fluorine.

Introduction

The reliability of semiconductor devices is dependent on the  proper formation of their interconnect structures, including vias  that connect different layers of a chip. One of the challenges in  this domain is the latent increase of via resistance induced by  fluorine (F)-assisted corrosion. Existing literature reports the  detection of F at the via bottom [1], and the attribution of the F  to the W CVD deposition [2]. Furthermore, F was stated to  cause high via resistance [2][3]. However, mechanisms of Finduced via resistance increase have not been studied. Mechanisms including galvanic corrosion and the transition  between corrosion and passivation to accompany the change of  the pH of the electrolyte had not been considered; instead, chemical equations to describe the F-induced corrosion were  actually F-induced passivation of the metal [3] [4]. Moreover, the role of corrosion in the latency of the via impedance  increase, and the impact of the operating frequency on the  impedance, have not been investigated and reported in  literature.

The aim of this paper is to explore these mechanisms in more  detail, providing insights into the chemical and physical  interactions at play. In addition, the via under investigation was  misaligned relative to both the superjacent and the subjacent  metal lines. The misalignment resulted in the corrosion of the  Ti glue layer and the Al layer, which contributed to the via  impedance increase. The mechanisms of the corrosion are

studied. Solutions and the interpretation of the impedance  variation over the operating frequency are presented.

Data and Discussion

Multiple units were returned from customer application due to  a Phase Lock Loop (PLL) failure. The PLL lock frequency was  programmed for a customer desired output frequency of 156.2  MHz. However, the output frequency would lose lock over time  and rail to either the highest or lowest voltage-controlled  oscillator (VCO) output frequency. The time from when  electrical bias was applied to device under test (DUT) to the  manifestation of the loss of PLL frequency lock ranged from a  few seconds to several hours from unit to unit. For one of these  units, this time was 3 seconds. The frequency shifted to a lower  value of 149.5 Mhz subsequently.

Backside photoemission data from the unit were taken before  and after losing the lock frequency, and presented in Figure 1. After losing the phase lock frequency, the photoemission at the  original sites within the feedback divider circuit block  disappeared, while new photoemission emerged at devices  within a different segment of the feedback divider circuit block. The feedback divider circuit block for this particular part type  operates at a very high frequency in the 3 GHz region and thus, was very sensitive to minor resistive and / or capacitive changes  that added parasitic RC delays to the switching path.  The DUT  operated at a supply current of approximately 250mA with a  supply voltage of 3.3V. This internal power dissipation within  the DUT was sufficient to cause self-heating and thus  negatively influenced the function of the feedback divider  circuit that was afflicted with one or more malformed vias. The  change in photoemission signature is thus a consequence of the  loss of a normal function caused by resistive vias within the  feedback divider circuitry. The change in photoemitting  locations is indicative of a different set of devices within the  feedback divider circuit block being activated as the PLL  continuously attempted, but failed to rectify the loss of  frequency lock. One of the new abnormal photoemission sites  was selected for progressive FIB/TEM in the even feedback  divider as shown in Figure 2.

Figure 3 displays a HAADF image of the contact-via stack (a), and higher-magnification STEM-BF image of crevice M (b) on  the malformed via A. On and above gate H, there is a redundant  contact and a redundant via 1, i.e. there are two contacts E and  G, and two via1s B and D, but there is only one via2 A. The

redundant contact and via are for the redundancy for reliable  electrical conduction.

Figure 1. Photoemission in the feedback divider circuit block before

(a) and after (b) losing lock. One of the new abnormal photoemission  sites selected for progressive FIB/TEM is marked with the white  arrow.

Figure 2. Image of the photoemission at the site marked with the white  arrow in Figure 1 overlaid on the layout. The TEM sample was  positioned at the center of the photoemission site. The two arrows mark  the TEM viewing direction.

Figure 3. HAADF image of the contact-via stack (a), and highermagnification STEM-BF image of crevice M (b).

The following are two misalignments that had caused an  increase of the serial impedance from gate poly H to metal2 Q.

1. The misalignment of A relative to Q, and the loss of Ti  along interface M at the top left corner of A. Both have  decreased the contact area between A and Q.

2. The misalignment of A relative to metal2 J, which has  caused A to fall off the edge of J. Oxygen and fluorine are detected at L, the interface between A and J.

There is a loss of Ti along interface M. Q was patterned with a  dry-etch that involves a physical component to sputter with Ar+ions and a chemical component to produce volatile products of  AlCl3 and TiCl4 that were pumped away from the etch chamber.

The top left corner of A was removed by the dry etch, which  exposed the metal stack along the left sidewall of Q to the wet  cleaning after the metal etch. Common wet cleaning solutions  include SC1, diluted (0.1 – 1%) HF acid, EKC265 and ozonated  water. The composition of EKC265, a proprietary wet chemical  cleaner, is confidential and not publicly disclosed. The wet  cleaning is followed by rinsing with de-ionized water and  drying. Finally, there is an optional dilute HF dip for oxide  removal followed by another DI water rinse.

Without the misalignment of A relative to Q, the sidewall of Q  is exposed to the wet cleaning. The exposed stack is Al/TiN/Ti. In the metal stack, TiN is the most inert material which makes  it the most cathodic. Al and Ti have the lowest and second  lowest EMF, respectively [5]. Both are therefore anodic relative  to TiN. However, the exposure area of Al is much larger than  that of TiN, while the exposure area of Ti is smaller than that of  TiN (since the Ti layer is thinner than the TiN layer). The  anode/cathode ratio difference causes the corrosion current  density of Ti to be higher than that of Al.

With the misalignment of A relative to Q, the exposed stack  now includes the tungsten (W) of the via, and becomes  Al/TiN/Ti/W. The EMF of Ti is lower than that of W, which  makes Ti anodic relative to W in addition to TiN. The Ti layer’s  being sandwiched between two cathodic layers exacerbates the  corrosion of the Ti. During the exposure to all the electrolytes  including the wet cleaner and DI water, Ti initially can be either  corroded or passivated per the associated Pourbaix diagrams. For example, a Pourbaix diagram of the Ti-F-H2O system at  25°C shows Ti is passivated in the pH range of 2-4 (and  corroded elsewhere) [6]. The following few factors can account  for the observed crevice corrosion of the Ti layer, regardless if  Ti is initially predicted to be corroded or passivated.

1. Ti being sandwiched between TiN and W caused the  Ti layer to be subject to crevice corrosion. Through the  crevice corrosion, the local pH inside the crevice  decreased. The acidification enhances the corrosion of  Ti if Ti was initially corroded in the electrolyte, and  shifted Ti into corrosion if Ti is initially passivated in  the electrolyte.

2. The galvanic effect and the anode/cathode ratio both  drove the Ti dissolution faster than that assumed by  the Pourbaix diagram, and the diagram does not  account for such effects.

3. The Pourbaix diagram in general assumes an ideal, defect-free metal surface, essentially treating the metal  as a perfect monolithic crystal rather than a real bulk  metal containing defects such as dislocations, grain  boundaries, or impurities. The Ti layer in contrast was  a thin film with defects (e.g., grain boundaries and  dislocations) and film-stress, which increased its  corrosion susceptibility.

4. At the W/Ti/TiN interfaces, lattice mismatches and  potentially Ti-W intermetallic compounds (IMCs)

205

could mechanically stress the Ti layer and create galvanic microcells. The mechanical stress weakened the Ti passivation, and the Ti-W IMCs would be subjected to microgalvanic corrosion. The Pourbaix diagram does not take such effects into account, either. In region L, via A falls off the edge of J. Figure  4  shows an HAADF image of the bottom right corner of A, and the associated elemental maps. The bottom right of A is no longer flat and horizontal, with not only TiN, but also Ti and Al exposed after the via etch. The via etch was time-controlled rather than end-point-controlled. There is SiO2 that embedded the Al of metal2 J left intact after the dry-etch as shown in Figure  4 . This SiO2 increased the impedance of L. In addition, the malformation of via2 A had the following effects in L.

1. The post-etch cleaning was locally impeded which increased the likelihood of residual F species' entrapment in L. The residual F species' were from the dry-etch and possibly the wet chemical cleaning.

Major gaseous products of the dry-tech to create the via and their boiling points are CO  (-191.5 °C)  and SiF4 (-86 °C). CO is more volatile than SiF4, which makes Si and F to be likely more abundant in the residue of the dry etch.

2. Vaporization of water in the duration between the via cleaning and the subsequent deposition of Ti/TiN(/W seed/W bulk) was impeded.

3. The TiN/Ti/Al stack in L was exposed to F species produced from the W bulk deposition, which can be described by the following equation

             6 (      ) + 3       2 (      ) = 6       (      ) + 6             (      ).

The Al-H2O Pourbaix diagram shows Al is passivated in the pH range of about 4 -9 [7]; however, with [F-]  = 0.0042 M, the passivation region is shrunk to pH = 8 -9. With [F-] = 0.042 M, the passivation region is entirely eliminated, and F-ions form stable complexes of AlF4 -, AlF4 2-and Al(OH)4 -  [8] . Both the passivation and corrosion of the Al elevated the electrical impedance. As shown in Figure  4 , the interface between the bulk W of via2 A and the metal2 J contains not only Si and O, but also F. The corrosion products in L are more resistive than the materials in a perfect stack of W/Ti/TiN/Al that would be present without the misalignment.

Overall, corrosion took place at the top and bottom of via2 A.

The kinetics of the corrosion determined the extent of the corrosion over time, and in turn the time it took to reach a level of impedance increase to cause failure in the PLLU lock. The problem can be solved with restoring the proper formation of the via2, by decreasing the via size, and/or properly aligning the via relative to the metal.

In the case described, crevice M and interface L had become effectively capacitors. Their impedances were low at the high frequency of 156.3MHz, which caused them both to be below detection by the ATE used for the final functional test. In the beginning of the bench test, they were similarly below detection; however, the failing unit temperature increased over time, which caused their impedances to rise and subsequently the phase lock to be lost. Based on the discussion, and from a theoretical standpoint, the latency of the via impedance cannot be proved electrically in this case. Nonetheless, the width of 93 nm of crevice M resulted from a gradual and lateral corrosion of the Ti layer, which still suggests a likely latency of the PLL loop failure.

 Conclusions

Conclusions

This study has demonstrated that via impedance increase can result from corrosion/oxidation caused by malformation of the via. The corrosion occurred both at the top and bottom of a misaligned via, driven by a combination of galvanic coupling, crevice effects and F-induced oxidation.

The latency of high impedance can arise from the kinetics of corrosion. The latency can cause the unit to evade detection by the final functional test. Over time, however, the degradation advances to a point where the impedance has become high enough to compromise circuit function. Field failures subsequently result. In the case presented, the latency cannot be proven electrically due to the decrease of the impedance of the corrosion crevice and interface at the high operating frequency in the beginning of the bench test. Nevertheless, the finite width of the crevice on the via resulted from a gradual and lateral corrosion of the Ti layer, which suggests a likelihood of the latency of the via impedance.

The study underscores the necessity of considering corrosion kinetics and structural geometry during both circuit design and process integration. Mitigation strategies include the control of via size and/or improving via-to-metal alignment, through which the long-term reliability of advanced interconnects can be improved, and the risk of latent via-related failures in the field can be reduced.

Comprehensive Fault Isolation Technologies for the Gate-All-Around Transistor  and Backside Power Delivery Paradigm Shifts

Mitchell J. Senger, Mauricio Posada, Christopher Morgan, Megan Knapp, Grace M. E. Khoo, Bathiya P.

Senevirathna, Praneeth Ranga, Ryan Fredrickson, MIR Tanjidur Rahman, Travis Williams, Samantha Lubaba  Noor, Manoj Devendhiran, Prasoon Joshi, Ashkan Abtahi, Kimberlee Celio, Joseph Basile, Eric Norum, Matthew  H. Kirsch, Miriam Cezza, Samia Rahman, Hasan Faraby, Joshua W. Kevek, Martin Von Haartman, Baohua Niu

Intel Corporation, Hillsboro, OR United States

Email: Mitchell.Senger@Intel.com, Phone: 503-309-8802

Abstract

Devices with backside power delivery and gate-all-around  transistors constitute new challenges for probe-based fault  isolation and device debug. We built a new fault isolation flow  that leverages next-generation probe technologies and methods, advanced device prep techniques, and enhanced electrical  diagnosis that is tailored for these new devices. The flow  extends fault isolation to integrated circuits with backside  power delivery and gate-all-around transistors, enabling  process yield improvement in this new device manufacturing  paradigm.

Section I: Introduction

Fault isolation (FI) technologies are integral for semiconductor  manufacturing development and integrated circuit (IC) debug. Backside power delivery (BSPD), an IC architecture that  sandwiches transistors between a metal grid designed to deliver  power on one side and metal signal traces on the other, is a  revolutionary device architecture that enables the continued  advances of Moore's Law IC scaling but dramatically alters the  landscape for FI flows aimed at improving semiconductor  device yield. BSPD architecture offers huge upside for device  performance and area scaling advantages for gate-all-around  transistor architecture, but routing metal on both sides of the  transistors makes traditional through-backside silicon optical FI  techniques commonly used in debug and fault isolation  extremely challenging [1]–[5].

Figure 1 shows comparative models of traditional flip chip (FC) and BSPD device architecture [1]. Semiconductor  manufacturers construct FC devices by patterning transistors on  a silicon wafer, building up metal interconnects for both power  delivery and signals routing on top of them, and finally  terminating the stack with solder bumps to enable packaging

[1]. This arrangement provides conventional optical fault  isolation (OFI) tools with direct access to the transistor layers  through the back-side Si layer.

With BSPD devices, the steps for transistors and signal metal  patterning hold, but the process changes from there. Manufacturing bonds a carrier wafer to the signal metal side of  the patterned wafer. Then, after removing backside silicon, more metal interconnect patterning on the backside forms the  BSPD power delivery network for the transistor layer [1], [3]. Finally, solder bumps terminate the BSPD network to enable  die packaging.

Figure 1: Transition from traditional frontside metal routing on  flip chip (FC) to backside power delivery (BSPD) [1], [4], [5].

Packaged BSPD dice have flipped die orientation relative to  their FC counterparts since the solder bumps are on the  backside of the transistor layer. For FC devices, the backside  silicon faces the probe when socketed on an FI tool. On the  other hand, with the new power delivery routing, the backside  of the transistor layer faces the package and socket for BSPD  devices, presenting a field of fine metal interconnects  underneath the residual carrier silicon on the frontside of the  device under test (DUT) to the probe under normal socketing.

In this paper, we present comprehensive technology and tool  innovations that enable FI for next-generation IC architectures  with buried transistors, including BSPD and 3D stacked chips. Our FI flows, diagramed in Figure 2, comprise industry-first  physical tools that leverage alternative processes to probe  transistors through blocking metal layers, sample preparation

https://doi.org/10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2025p0208
