www.asminternational.org

techniques that precisely expose buried regions of interest (ROI) for probing, and new software tools that diagnose  electrical failures with failure mechanism analysis (FMA). First, we analyze our electrical test data to identify possible  defective nets then corroborate the suspects with known failure  mechanisms, circuit schema, and circuit layouts to deliver a  small, but buried, ROI for our new set of physical FI techniques

[6], [7]. We utilize lock-in thermography (LIT), thermal  reflectance modulation (TRM), and through-package (3DFI) ebeam probing (EBP) to probe BSPD ICs to isolate failures with  high-resolution hotspot imaging, frequency mapping, waveform collection, and logic state imaging [4], [8]–[16]. Thermally assisted device alteration (TADA) and x-ray assisted  device alteration (XADA), techniques that temporarily shift  marginal transistor activity through the frontside metal stack, supplement traditional laser-based soft defect localization [17]–

[19]. To reduce ROI size even further, we developed first-ofkind SEM-based BSPD nanoprobing (nP) techniques to probe  suspect signal traces on the front side and suspect transistors  from the backside. 3DFI EBP and backside nP are revolutionary  probe techniques that require complete exposure of complex  device geometries from deep within BSPD devices and so  require equally complex device prep techniques to enable them. We engineered plasma focused ion beam (PFIB) prep recipes to  quickly remove the frontside and backside metal layers and  intra-layer dielectric that bury the FI ROI, wherever it is buried  in the BSPD device stack [10], [20], to prep devices for 3DFI  EBP and backside nP. Further, we will discuss the nuances of  each of the steps of our FI flow for devices with buried  transistors and show how these tools and techniques enable FI  on the forefront and future generations of semiconductor  devices and manufacturing process technologies.

Figure 2: Our BSPD/GAA FI flow encompasses electrical, optical, x-ray, thermal, and e-beam FI, die prep for physical FI, frontside  and backside nano-probing. Based on the defect’s ROI, as determined by diagnosis, we may run sites through direct FA (DFA) flows if  the ROI is small, or a full FI flow including thermal, optical, and e-beam FI techniques for large ROIs. All steps culminate in a ROI  small enough for planar or cross-section TEM imaging to provide a high-resolution image of the defect that caused the electrical failure.

Section II: Electrical Diagnosis with Failure  Mechanism Analysis

Volume scan diagnosis analysis is a critical tool for FI. It guides  subsequent physical FI steps to IC structures that are likely to  contain the defects causing failures detected in electrical  testing. As IC critical dimensions shrink with advancing  process technology, the number of diagnosis suspects per area

increases at every process node. Improving electrical diagnosis, by implementing methods to reduce the number of suspects and  more accurately predicting the physical structures  corresponding to an electrical failure, becomes more critical. Moreover, BSPD architecture buries defects further in metal  layers than for more traditional devices, increasing the number  of processing steps and overall throughput time of physical  device prep and FI flows. Determining a small ROI for these

physical steps is more critical for failure analysis than ever  before.

The scan diagnosis software takes the failing responses of  automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) patterns on a wafer  along with the logical and physical view of the design to  produce a diagnosis report that includes a suspect list of each  failing die and potential failure mechanisms. We use the  individual diagnosis reports to identify regions of interest for  further fault isolation and physical failure analysis (FIFA) of  scan failures. Subsequently, we use volume physical failure  analysis to obtain a defect pareto of a wafer and develop yield  improvement models. Such a large-scale FIFA is expensive and  is only possible on a small subset of wafers, which often  prevents finding the proper yield-limiting failure mechanisms.

Figure 3: a) Failure mechanism analysis flow. b) Region of  interest reduction following failure mechanism analysis  compared with diagnosed region of interest without failure  mechanism analysis.

New machine learning-based statistical analysis tools can find  a similar defect pareto that FIFA does by analyzing diagnosis  data from multiple lots and wafers. We implemented failure  mechanism analysis (FMA) to generate failure mechanism  pareto charts for large populations of diagnosis data, which  helps to identify the yield-limiting failing modes of the  population. FMA also helps to select dies with a specific/target  fail mode to perform FIFA, as shown in Figure 3a. Moreover, FMA produces die-level fail likelihood of suspects, resulting in  the pruning of diagnosis candidates for fault isolation [6]. For

one example (Figure 3b), FMA pruned the diagnosis from three  suspects to one, which in turn reduces the ROI from  65µm×35µm to 11µm×1.6µm and the reduces total number of  layers requiring inspection and nanoprobing. Therefore, FMA  reduces resource requirements on the expensive and timeconsuming physical FIFA steps for these innovative ICs.

Section III: Die Prep for Fault Isolation

The flipped geometry and frontside metal of BSPD devices  dramatically alter the FI DUT prep targets and outcomes. As we  will discuss in the following FI techniques sections (IV-VII), the various probe tools implemented for FI on BSPD devices  use different physical mechanisms to sense defects than were  used for FC devices. For the probe tools that can collect signals  through the metal layers of a BSPD device, we thin the carrier  wafer attached to the frontside signal metal (the frontside  silicon) to improve the optical transparency of the material  covering the frontside interconnects (Figure 4b). This is  analogous to backside silicon thinning prep for traditional FC  devices (Figure 4a).

Figure 4: Schematic DUT prep technologies used for probebased FI of FC and BSPD devices. The FI probe in this example  points at the die from bottom up. a) FC device prepped with  thinned backside silicon to enable sufficient optical  transparency for IREM, LVP, SDL. b) BSPD device prepped  with thinned frontside carrier wafer to enable sufficient optical  transparency for LIT and TADA. c) BSPD device prepped with  thinned frontside silicon and PFIB-exposed metal lines on the  surface of the die. d) BSPD device prepped for backside probing  with package drilling, etching, and backside PFIB milling. Socketing Si-down enables FI probe access to transistors  exposed on the backside through the package.

Other FI techniques, which are only sensitive to what signals  are fully exposed, require more precise removal techniques. The  frontside metal signals are essential to die functionality, therefore we do not use bulk removal techniques to expose  buried structures to FI probe tools. Doing so can introduce

massive electrical failures on the die and disrupt the electrical  test results used to characterize the defect. To fully expose metal  on the frontside, we first run the sample through a standard  polish to reduce the thickness of the frontside silicon to ~20 μm. Next, prep continues with a PFIB tool to mill the residual  material above the metal traces of interest [10], [20]. PFIB  offers a favorable removal rate (350 μm3/s for silicon and 100 μm3/s for copper) while also delivering a precise endpoint to  flatly expose all metal lines in the region of interest (ROI) without introducing line breaks. Chemically selective etching  further enables the tool to recess interlayer dielectric (ILD) material without breaking metal traces. We use selective  etching to expose metal lines in layers below the top metal  layer, again without introducing line breaks and electrical  failures. Figure 4c shows a schematic of a device under this prep  technique.

Prep flows for metal line exposures can dig only so deep into  the frontside metal stack before the layout geometry forces line  breaks. For highly localized defects on IC structures, with  electrical signals elevated only 1-3 metal layers above the  transistor layer, providing failure analysis flows with adequate  isolation requires probing the transistor layer. To expose the  transistor layer without inducing gross electrical failures, it is  easier to remove material from the backside power delivery  network than it is to mill through the frontside signal metal  layers. The frontside metal comprises electrical interconnects  that are critical to the unit function, and there is a low  probability of signal redundancy within the frontside metal for  most ROIs. The BSPD metal, on the other hand, comprises a  large, frequently redundant, power delivery network, so partial  backside line removal from one small ROI without disrupting  the electrical functionality of the DUT is possible. We have  demonstrated the viability of this transistor exposure technique  and probing in practice (see Section VI).

Figure 4d shows a cartoon of our backside DUT prep result. We  accomplish backside transistor exposure on packaged die by  first drilling the package with a tabletop CNC, then PFIB  milling the die on the backside through the package. After  drilling, we use a combination of selective etch techniques to  remove any metal or dielectric material from the drill box and  to smooth out the mechanical milling endpoint. Then, we use  PFIB to mill away redundant power lines and ILD to expose the  underlying transistor layer in a small window. However, we  must ensure that the package can still deliver power to maintain  functionality of the part and not alter the behavior of the circuits  in the ROI. Thus, we cannot fully remove the back metals, so  we leave the last layer(s) of metal lines in the ROI intact. We  use a selective etch to remove the ILD between the last metal  layer to expose transistors, which enables us to probe the  transistors with the electron beam. Prep engineers need input  from package and die design to identify critical traces in the  package and in the die to protect the ROI through this prep flow.

In addition to these new prep techniques, we have also  developed new die package design and manufacturing to  facilitate packaged FI and debug flows for BSPD devices. These packages have socket lands on their top and bottom sides  to enable die face up and die face down socketing and probing

[2], enabling one to probe the BSPD device on the front side  metal side, or through the package on the backside. Armed with  these packaging and prep techniques, we maximize signal  access and increase the efficacy of all available FI techniques  to localize defects in BSPD devices.

Section IV: Lock-In Thermography and Thermo  Reflectance for FI with Front-side Metal

Previous work has shown the efficacy of infrared photon  emission microscopy (PEM) to identify shorts and opens in  defective ICs on devices with conventional flip-chip  architecture [21]–[23]. OFI tools have continuously improved  over the past few decades, but they rely on the near-infrared  transparency window of silicon for direct probing of transistors. By leveraging solid immersion lenses (SILs), these OFI tools  achieve a spatial resolution of 200-500 nm. However, the  implementation of BSPD has blocked direct access to  transistors through the backside Si layer. In devices with BSPD, metal layers block most if not all the IR signal emitted at the  transistors layer. This compromises the usability and efficacy of  PEM for FI on devices with BSPD technology.

To fill the gap, we use thermal FI tools with high-speed cameras  sensitive to Mid-Wave Infrared (MWIR) radiation (wavelengths in the 3 – 5 µm range) and a frame-by-frame lockin demodulator to perform lock-in thermography (LIT) on  BSPD samples [8]. This technology relies on the ability of  thermal radiation to propagate through the stacks of metal and  dielectrics that make up the interconnects in BSPD  architectures. Figure 5a shows a schematic of an LIT tool. Instead of detecting NIR emissions, these tools leverage  thermal emissions from the sample to identify 'hot spots' generated by defective IC components. Here, we thin the DUT’s  frontside silicon (as shown in Figure 4b) to increase the  transmission of MWIR radiation from the buried IC features  and bring the defect closer to the die surface. We have  successfully implemented LIT for defect localization in  advanced ICs with BSPD technology and gate-all-around  transistors. This has effectively enabled a continuation of the  OFI activities for yield improvement on Intel’s latest  technologies. Figure 5b shows an example of amplitude and  phase shift maps collected on an Intel IC with BSPD. This  signal corresponds to emission generated at the transistor layer. We collected these LIT signals from the front side of the die, where the signal propagates through a full stack of front-side  interconnects. We used an MWIR-compatible SIL (NA = 2.6) to  improve the resolution of the tool.

We also developed thermal reflectance modulation technology  and tools (TRM) to further extend OFI with BSPD devices. In

TRM, we direct a visible or near IR laser to the surface of an IC  through thinned frontside silicon and monitor the reflected laser  intensity with a high bandwidth photodiode. Metal traces that  carry signals on the IC host periodic electric currents, which  periodically heat the surface traces at the frequency of the  signals they are carrying. A laser beam falling on the frontside  metal lines will be reflected with oscillating intensity because  the heat generated by the IC signals modulates the reflectance  of the metal [24]–[26]. Demodulating the photodiode’s output  at the frequency of a signal of interest with a lock-in amplifier  while rastering the laser across the DUT maps structures  carrying signals at the frequency of interest, generating a  frequency map. The frequency map reveals IC activity, or lack  of expected activity, which we can use to determine failure  boundaries for defects.

For our OFI based on LIT and TRM, we provide the device  under test (DUT) with a modulated signal with frequency Flockin. We choose Flock-in for the optical signal collection scheme we  are using based on the tool’s bandwidth capability. For LIT, signal collection bandwidth is roughly half of the framerate of  the thermal camera used on the tool [8] which, for state-of-theart thermal cameras that are sensitive to MWIR, have  framerates ~100 Hz. TRM, which leverages a photodiode in our  BSPD OFI, is limited to ~1 MHz while achieving hot spot SNR  needed for FI on BSPD devices. To accommodate these  bandwidth limits, we artificially slow DUT operations to  accommodate these bandwidth limits by developing special test  patterns targeted at the different blocks that make up our ICs. We have also implemented a solution in which we slowly  modulate selected power planes, enabling OFI for cases in  which data modulation is not effective based on preliminary  electrical characterization (e.g., boot failures). In both cases, the  tool references Flock-in to demodulate the captured camera  frames at the frequency of the signals of interest. These thermal  lock-in processes result in amplitude and phase maps of the  captured signals (Figure 5b). The amplitude provides an  indication of the magnitude of the thermal signal, whereas the  phase-shift provides information about the delay of the  measured signal relative to the excitation. Slight timing  variations detected in phase maps can help localize weaker  emissions in images with more than one signal generator. We  then use the results to identify abnormal ‘hot spots’ resulting  from the periodic excitation of defects (e.g., shorts to supplies).

Figure 5: Example schematic of an LIT tool and hotspot detection [8] on an Intel BSPD IC. A tester drives the DUT with a modulated  power supply and provides a synchronized reference signal to the LIT module onboard the tool for demodulation. A buried defect  generates heat which the thermal camera captures. The image processor integrates camera frames, demodulates each pixel according  to the tester reference, and outputs the lock-in component images. Images on the right side show an example amplitude and phase-shift  output, along with an overlay of the amplitude signal with the thermal image of the device.

Section V: Soft Failure Localization with  Backside Power Delivery

For devices with conventional flip-chip technology, FI has  extensively used visible and IR lasers for soft defect  localization (SDL). This technique, also called laser-assisted  device alteration (LADA), is an effective technique for isolating  IC failures [17], [18], particularly those causing weak passing  or failing test results. For LADA, an IR or visible laser is  rastered over a sample while a test pattern is running. The tester  continuously outputs a trigger signal corresponding to the result (e.g., high is pass and low is fail). Recording the test result  trigger and digitizing it into an image while rastering the laser  over the sample displays a map of areas with passing and failing  IC states.

For non-BSPD devices, SDL with a laser with photon energy  above the bandgap of silicon (E > 1.1 eV) generates  photoelectrons in the transistor channels by absorbing photons  from the incident laser beam, altering the conductivity of the  device under the beam. Using a laser with E < 1.1 eV produces  a similar conductivity change, but excess carriers are thermally  generated rather than optically generated. Removing the laser  beam from the device channel quickly returns the device to its  unaltered state.

Exposing a device with a marginal defect to the laser along the  raster path may switch it from a passing state to a failing state

(or vice versa). Precise electrical tuning of the circuit (via  operating voltage or frequency) can force the circuit into one  state for every raster pixel except where the laser alters the state  of the failing/passing device, causing the pass/fail image to  display an altered IC state only where the laser is landed on the  defective device. The result is a map that displays the location  of the weakly defective device in the IC, providing a pathway  to isolate soft failures.

As in the case of PEM techniques, BSPD implementation  impedes traditional laser-based SDL. The presence of metal  layers on both sides of the transistor layer blocks direct access  to the transistor layers by the IR or visible lasers that  conventional LADA techniques rely on.

As an alternative, we leverage temperature variations in the  transistor channels to alter the state of devices with soft defects  to perform thermally assisted device alteration (TADA). In  TADA, we accomplish transistor heating by rastering a highpower laser beam across the metal interconnects on a BSPD  device. Heating the top metal layer on the frontside of the die  induces a temperature increase that propagates through the  stack of metal and dielectric layers that compose the  interconnects in BSPD architectures. Top layer heating leads to  temperature changes to the transistors. Like LADA, the  pass/fail condition of the IC against the laser raster position  pinpoints the location of a soft defect in a BSPD device (Figure  6).

Figure 6: Example of TADA collection for soft fail detection on a representative Intel BSPD IC [17], [18]. Before running TADA, we  characterize the electrical failure on an electrical tester by tuning the device to the edge of its shmoo pass/fail boundary. The TADA tool  rasters an NIR laser across the frontside surface of the device, which heats the full material stack. The heat propagates to a soft failure  in the transistor layer. As the laser rasters, the electrical tester continuously evaluates the ROI for pass/fail state. A PC captures a  trigger indicating the pass/fail state and plots the result with the reflection image of the device. When heat from the laser is sufficient to  flip the pass/fail state of the defect, the TADA image records a change in the trigger output, which highlights the physical location of the  failure. In practice, TADA can identify the location of the failure to within three microns despite the obfuscating frontside metal lines.

There are key functional differences between TADA on BSPD  devices and SDL for FC devices. First, through-stack heating in  TADA requires more laser power than conventional SDL in FC  devices. Balancing the laser power, power supply voltage, device operating frequency, and device cooling against the  specific pass/fail threshold of the device is critical to producing  a deterministic TADA result. Damage to the top surface of the  DUT from rapid heating may occur if the laser heat delivery  exceeds the cooling capacity of testing set-up. Second, the size  of the TADA spot is larger than the laser spot itself due to lateral  heat spread through the stack on metal present in the ROI. Hence, besides the conventional diffraction limit to resolution, the lateral heat spread also limits resolution for TADA hits. Nonetheless, this technique has proven to be highly effective  for the isolation of soft defects in Intel’s latest technology  nodes.

We also use x-ray assisted device alteration (XADA) for soft  defect localization for SDL on devices with stacked chips or  with backside power delivery as an alternative to IR SDL  techniques [19]. This technique operates the DUT and tester  like LADA and TADA but leverages a focused x-ray beam, which readily transmits through metal and dielectric layers  obfuscating the devices, to alter the behavior of transistors on  the device under test [19], [27]. Figure 7 shows an example of  XADA data collection, revealing beam raster locations that  show increased IC pass/fail counts in response to the x-ray  beam.

Figure 7: Example of XADA soft defect localization. We scan  an x-ray beam over the DUT with a marginal failure, which  we electrically tuned to the marginality point. Pass/fail counts  are recorded during the beam scan, and the points where the  x-ray beam caused a shift away from marginality indicate the  location of the soft defect [19].

We find that TADA is sufficient for SDL for single die with  backside power delivery. XADA may offer additional upside  for SDL 3D stacked chips because obfuscating metal and  bonding layers between the device’s surface and the target  device layer in a stacked chip device weakens thermal  conductivity needed for TADA, but x-rays can transmit through  the full stack preserving XADA.

Section VI: High-resolution Failure Isolation  with E-Beam Probing

FI labs commonly leverage optical FI tools equipped with NIR  lasers to probe FC devices and localize defects. These tools map  active signals in the transistor layer using LVP (also referred to  as laser timing module, LTM, and active signal image mapping, ASIM) and capture waveforms from points of interest, enabling  both spatial domain and time domain signal sampling to track  down defective circuit elements [28], [29]. The resolution of  these optical FI techniques (using compatible solid immersion  lens (SIL)) is diffraction limited to ~0.25 μm. Unfortunately, shrinking process nodes are increasingly jamming devices into  the resolvable spot size of the NIR laser used to run LVP, rendering data collections less specific. Moreover, the  introduction of BSPD blocks laser access to the transistor layer  unless radical prep techniques are employed. Shrinking node  sizes and BSPD threaten the efficacy of laser-based signal  mapping and defect detection for next-generation process  technologies.

To enable signal mapping on devices with BSPD, we have  applied electron-beam probing (EBP) [10]–[12]. EBP is a  scanning electron microscope (SEM) with an electrical tester  loaded into/onto the SEM vacuum chamber. The tool can raster  the electron beam over the sample to determine the logic state  of static devices (logic state imaging, LSI) or generate ASIMs  of active devices by demodulating the electron detector signal  to a reference frequency provided by the tester. Alternatively, temporally averaging the detector in equivalent time relative to  a reference provided by the tester enables waveform collection [10], [29]. EBP for FI offers two distinct advantages over laserbased methods. First, EBP leverages voltage contrast to probe  signals of a DUT, which makes the probe sensitive to any  structure switching between high and low voltage, including  transistor components and metal traces [4]. This means we can  use EBP to probe BSPD devices in the front side signal metal  layers (Figure 8) and through-package to the transistors (Figure  9) with ASIM, waveform capture, and LSI (Figure 10). Second, EBP surpasses resolution limits of laser-based techniques. Modern scanning electron microscopes (SEMs) can easily  focus an electron beam to < 1 nm beam waist, offering hundreds  of times the resolving power of laser-based tools. It follows that  an electron beam gives better device localization for defect  detection on < 2 nm semiconductor device nodes than  traditional LVP tools.

Here, we present two test cases where we used EBP on devices  with BSPD. In one case, we probe the frontside metal to identify  a signal break within the metal stack (Figure 8). To probe  devices on the front side, we use PFIB to expose the top two  layers of metal lines in the ROI and socket the device Si-up on  the EBP tool (Figure 8a). We prep and probe two areas to  identify differences between a healthy reference area (Figure  8b) and the ROI (Figure 8c). High-magnification ASIM  imaging provides a map of active signals running on metal lines  in the ROI. In this case, a lack of signal at a specific metal line  determines the ROI for FA, isolating the defect to a couple  hundred nanometers across the ROI and within the top two or  three metal layers. Transmission electron microscopy imaging  of the EBP-determined ROI later revealed a broken, interlayer, metal interconnect that generated the failure.

Figure 8: BSPD device E-beam probing on frontside metal [9]. Comparison between ASIM images of reference and ROI  reveals broken traces in the ROI. FA results revealed an open  via beneath the exposed metal lines that caused the signal to  break.

In the second case, we isolated a more specific scan chain  failure with backside EBP. Here, we prepped the device with  the through-package drilling, etch, and PFIB milling according  to the description in the earlier DUT prep section. Socketing the  DUT on the tool with the die Si-down enables EBP on the

transistor layer (Figure 9a). With backside EBP, we have  demonstrated ASIM collections that show the location of active  signals at certain frequencies (Figure 9b) and waveform  measurements from specific points in the ROI (Figure 9c). To  isolate the failing scan cell, we collected ASIM at the data and  clock frequencies from exposed transistor components from  between the last layer of power delivery metal lines from scan  cells exposed in the backside prep. ASIM images of the data  path in the first failing scan cell in the chain revealed missing  data signals (red box in Figure 9b) while all clock signals are  accounted for, indicating the defect lies on the data path within  the cell. This failure isolation provided a ~150 nm ROI for  failure analysis flows to the root cause of the defect.

Figure 9: EBP on the transistor layer through the package on  an Intel BSPD/GAA IC from the backside [9], [11]. a) E-Beam  prober fault isolation tool setup. b) E-Beam prober data  showing active signal imaging maps of clock and data signals  running through a failing scan cell. Here, the signal collection  maps active signals as frequency maps in quadrature as inphase (black) or out of phase (white) with a tester reference. Missing data signals, revealing the fail boundary, are  highlighted in red. c) EBP waveform collection from a clock  node collected from the backside of a device with backside  power delivery.

Figure 10: EBP logic state imaging data from cache logic on a  BSPD/GAA device. A subtraction image taken from images of  the DUT in two states highlights devices that flip from 0 (red) to 1 (blue).

In cases where it is impractical or impossible for test content to  repeatedly stimulate a ROI based on the design and  implemented test hardware on the IC with an infinitely looping  pattern, backside EBP LSI is the preferred FI technique for high  resolution detection. LSI is useful because IC operation  information may be gleaned using static voltage contrast  imaging, without dynamic IC activity [10]. Figure 10 shows  SEM images of a functional cache logic circuit area on an active  Intel BSPD/GAA device. Here, we prepped the device through  the package to expose GAA transistors for EBP from the  backside. We then imaged the circuit in two static states. For  the first image (Fig. 10a), we wrote all zeroes (Write 0) into the  cache, then ran a read operation that was captured. Then, we  wrote all ones to the cache and ran another read operation, then  captured a second IC image (Fig. 10b). The EBP tool records  the secondary electron (SE) detector signal intensity for each  pixel as the tool rasters the primary beam across the circuit. The

state of each transistor feature in the image raster can be  determined in the captured images because the state of the logic  transistors controls SE voltage contrast. A careful analysis of  the SE signal differences between the two images reveals which  transistors are switched when reading after Write 0 and Write 1  operations. Figure 10c shows a subtraction image made by  subtracting Figure 10b from Figure 10a which was  subsequently filtered to improve signal to noise ratio. The  subtraction image highlights which feature switched from  bright (zero) to dark (one). While the lack of infinite looping  test content precludes ASIM capture for this circuit, LSI is  useful for generating maps of active signals based on the  comparison of images captured in two logic states.

Section VII: Nanoprobing for Devices with  Backside Power Delivery

Our FI flows for traditional FC devices heavily depend on nanoprobers (nPs) 1) to more precisely localize failures detected in  upstream beam-based FI probing (e.g., LVP, PEM, and SDL) and 2) to enable, when possible, direct failure analysis (DFA) flows that bypass the other probe-based FI techniques [7], [21]. We use DFA to provide fast, high volume, yield  characterization feedback to manufacturing. DFA requires high  sample throughput to be effective, and therefore the prep and  probing flows that underpin DFA must be simple, repeatable, and fast. We leverage frontside PFIB milling to expose the last  via above the transistor layer on FC devices to give nP access  to all the devices and their contacts within the ROI. Nanoprobers conduct traditional FC device probing by landing  probes on the contact layer (Figure 11a), which enables  independent control of source, drain, and gate voltage for all  transistors in the ROI while maintaining power and ground  isolation. Commonly, probers measure transistor source-drain  current as a function of gate voltage (ID(VG)) from all suspected  devices in an ROI, which are fully exposed in prep, to quickly  detect opens or shorts in the IC [21]. Figure 11b shows example  ID(VG) curves from a pair of transistors on a prepped FC device. The ID for the transistor with a weak gate open (T3, red line) is  weaker than for a healthy device (T1, black line) captured in the  same run.

Like other FI techniques presented here, BSPD's introduction  required innovation to maintain the defect localization efficacy  of nPs in these flows. nPs can only land probes on structures  that sample prep exposes at the device's surface, and the  insertion of BSPD technology removes access to source nodes  from the topside. Depending on defects, FI may target frontside  metal lines, the front end of the transistor layer, or the backend  of the transistor layer. Correspondingly, we have developed our  prep and probing methodologies to expose and probe target  structures in BSPD devices in all these locations.

Figure 11: Nanoprobing FC and BSPD devices. a) An Intel FC  IC exposed at the contact layer for transistor probing [7], [21]. b) Example ID(VG) characteristics from a healthy device (T1) and a device with a weak NMOS gate open (T3) on the unit  shown in 7a. c) Intel BSPD IC prepped on the frontside to  expose the contact layer. d) Example ID(VG) characteristics  from a healthy device (T1) exhibiting “U-shaped” curve and  the similar, but failing, device with missing PMOS channel in  7c. e) Intel BSPD IC prepped for backside nP. f) IGS(VGS) curves  captured from gate probing on the device shown in 7e.

To prep BSPD devices for frontside probing we leverage PFIB  delayering, which we previously developed for high volume FC  nP prep, to expose features. This prep only exposes the  transistor drains and gates because the BSPD layout routes  sources to the transistors from the backside. Mounting the  backside of the die on an nP sample holder electrically shorts  backside Vdd and Vss to one another and electrically shorts them  to the stage within the nanoprobing system. The BSPD network  and frontside metal routing convolutes the individual NMOS  and PMOS transistor characteristics of inverters since frontside  probe points share gate and drain nodes (Figure 11c). In this  configuration, two-point ID(VG) collections measure the PMOS  and NMOS in parallel and exhibit a “U-shaped" curve where  there is non-zero current for both positive and negative gate  voltage. Figure 11d shows ID(VG) characteristics take from a  healthy device (T1, black line) exhibiting a “U-shaped” ID(VG) while a similar, but defective, device with missing p-sided  diffusion (T3, red line) shows zero current for VG < 0. Twopoint inverter probing on BSPD devices enables faster site  throughput in high-volume probing flows for comparable sites  built on FC architectures. Probing shared NMOS and PMOS  transistors on FC architectures requires landing a minimum of  three probes on the nodes of each transistor. In BSPD frontside  probing, on the other hand, we can detect hard failures (opens  and shorts) within an NMOS and PMOS pair with a two-probe

measurement while leveraging the stage to bias the source. Here, the BSPD architecture allows two-thirds fewer probe  lands to screen the same number of devices as we needed on FC  devices.

In cases where FI on BSPD might require Vdd/Vss separation, fine access to transistor components, or (and) suspects a defect  in the frontside metal, we can leverage backside probing. For  DFA, where we bypass packaged FI flows, we PFIB mill the  die from the backside to expose the ROI. In backside nP prep, we remove the last layer of backside metal (closest to  transistors) to fully expose the transistor layer because the probe  tips deliver power directly to the devices under test locally. Backside nP prep for packaged die is the same, but we remove  the package before backside PFIB milling takes place. Figure  11e shows an example of a BSPD/GAA sample we prepped for  backside nP. This configuration restores independent control of  Vdd and Vss that is absent in frontside probing, and in the  example provided, gives exquisite access to the transistors. Figure 11f shows an example IGS(VGS) characteristic we  captured with one-point backside probing at the transistor layer. The characteristic for D3 (red line) identified a hard open in its  path to the driver, where D4 (black line) is healthy and the  expected output. Between these frontside and backside nP  schemes, we have extended DFA and non-DFA nP capabilities  to devices with next-generation architectures.

Section VIII: Conclusions

Improving yield for semiconductor processes with evershrinking device profiles and modern device architecture  requires FI flows to continue progressing. Semiconductor  manufacturing roadmaps driving node size to < 3 nm  simultaneously reduce the efficacy of traditional, laser-based, FI techniques. BSPD introduces an obfuscating layer of metal  to the backside of devices where we were, previously, able to  optically probe devices through backside silicon. To fill the FI  process gap that these innovative architectures introduced, a  comprehensive set of FI technique innovations to localize  defects on leading-edge ICs blossoms.

We developed and adapted LIT, TRM, TADA, XADA, EBP, and nP to isolate defects on devices with BSPD and GAA  transistors. Electrical diagnosis dictates the FI flow used for  defect detection. For IC failures with good electrical diagnosis, the DFA flow is fully enabled by frontside and backside nP. In  cases where diagnosis is poor, we can isolate large power  failures and shorts with LIT, soft failures with TADA, and  identify defects in specific IC structures with EBP. Through a  combination of these techniques, we have successfully bridged  the gap between electrical testing and failure analysis for yield  improvement for next generation IC architectures. We expect  these capabilities to provide full FI coverage for future process  nodes as well.

Package-level circuit editing of Copper Technology WLP Devices using PFIB

Benjoe A. Bayuga1 and Paul Hubert P. Llamera2

Analog Devices – Failure Analysis Department, Gateway Business Park, General Trias, Cavite, Philippines  Email: 1Benjoe.Bayuga@analog.com,  2PaulHubert.Llamera@analog.com

Abstract

Wafer level packaging has emerged as an advanced packaging  technique due to its size and lower cost compared to other  packaging. Due to the thick polymer layer found on the die, conventional circuit editing has been a challenge. Accessing the  top side of the die needs milling of the thick organic layer  covering it. The Focused Ion Beam (FIB) is known to be a  powerful tool in performing circuit editing (FIB-CE) and  delayering, etching of materials, isolation and disconnection of  metal interconnects. Recent years saw the emergence of the  Plasma FIB (PFIB) with faster and more precise milling. In this  study, the PFIB is utilized for package level circuit editing of  devices in WLP with copper metallization. Results showed that  the PFIB was able to etch top-down through polymer layers  with O2 precursor and use Dx gas chemistry to delayer and cut  copper metal interconnects in the lower layers, accomplishing  design simulations and keeping the packaging intact.

Introduction

Editing the internal circuitry of a die has been practiced in  failure analysis, design simulation and debug. The Focused Ion  Beam (FIB) is a widely used tool in physically altering the  circuit in the die, from FIB circuit editing (FIB-CE), FIB crosssectioning, and even the precise top-down FIB  deprocessing/delayering [1-3]. In FIB-CE, cutting metal lines  to disconnect one terminal from another to isolate problems in  the circuit or to simulate design is widely practiced with gasassisted milling, utilizing Gas Injection System (GIS). FIB can  come with a variety of gases which have their own applications  as to which material they can aid the FIB in milling [3].

Wafer-Level Packaging (WLP)

WLP is assembled using fewer resources and packaged as large  as the chip, smaller than other types of packaging [4]. It consists  of Redistribution Layers (RDL) connected to bumps serving as  external connections and is designed with a polymer layer [4-5] which covers the die on the bump side. Doing circuit editing on  the die top-down poses a challenge due to the thick polymer and  possible bump obstructions using the FIB equipment [6].

Fig. 1 design cross-sectional view of a 5-metal layer WLP

In a 2011 study, FIB was used to perform front side FIB-CE on  a unit in Wafer Level Chip Scale Packaging (WLCSP), a type  of WLP. FIB equipment V600 with IEE was utilized to etch  through the passivation materials and expose the metallization. This proved the feasibility of top-down FIB-CE on the package  level. [6]

Xenon Plasma FIB (PFIB)

The advent of the Xenon PFIB allowed more precise and faster  milling and delayering, and more accurate FIB end point  detection [7-9]. With an increased sputter rate, the PFIB is an  effective tool for milling larger areas, allowing package-level  circuit editing on WLP units to be more time efficient and more  controlled.

In this study, the Helios Plasma FIB UXe DualBeam is the  system used to do top-down FIB-CE by removing the polymer  and copper metal layers of devices in WLP. The PFIB comes  with polyimide etch precursor (Oxygen; O2) and Dx gas  chemistry in the MultiChem GIS. The Dx gas chemistry allows  uniform milling of Cu and dielectric oxides by slowing down  the etching of the oxides [10].

Case Studies

Case Study 1

A design simulation must be done on a 90nm 5-metal layer  copper technology WLP device by making a metal  disconnection at Metal 2 (Met2) layer.

Fig. 3 shows the layout indicating where to cut the Met2. The  metal should not have any obstruction above for this FIB-CE to  work.

Fig. 3 Layout image for the metal 2 (Met2)

Since this was a top-down FIB-CE on a WLP unit, the polymer  layer must be etched to access the die. The layout of the device  was integrated and superimposed with the PFIB equipment to  accurately locate the target area. With the PFIB sputter rate, regular delayering of a large area on top of the metal of interest  was successfully done.

Fig. 4 shows the SEM image of a three-stepped milling pattern  of the polymer layer, selectively exposing a portion of the  passivation above the metal to be cut. The first pattern was 40  microns x 40 microns in size. Multiple steps of the etching  pattern were made to avoid a deep trench and deformation.

Fig. 4 SEM image

The top metal (Met5) layer was partially exposed and was used  as reference together with the layout. The Dx gas chemistry was  then used to assist the etching of a smaller area on top of the  Met2 of interest.

Fig. 5 (a) shows the pattern of the Dx gas assisted etching, exposing the metal 3 (Met3) layer. Fig. 4 (b) shows the  exposure of the target Met2 to be cut.

The Dx gas chemistry was used to cut the Met2 of interest, resulting in disconnection.

Fig. 6 shows the SEM image of the cut Met2.

Fig. 6 SEM image

Tests were done by the design engineering team, and the  disconnection was confirmed resulting in successful simulation  and debug.

Case Study 2

A portion of the RDL of a 40nm 7-metal layer copper  technology device in WLP was cut to convert it from a 5-channel to a 4-channel device.

Fig. 7 shows the optical photo indicating which connection in  the RDL was cut.

Fig. 8 shows the SEM image of the partially exposed RDL as  seen using high accelerating voltage.

Fig. 8 SEM image

This resulted in a successful FIB job, helping the team understand the weight of the paths involved in  the hot plug test, leading to design improvement of the device.

Conclusions

Due to the complexity of WLP coupled with copper technology  fabrication, top-down FIB-CE gets more challenging. With the  design simulations needing the packaging to be intact and ready  for socket testing, etching through polymer layers poses  difficulty if done through conventional FIB-CE. The PFIB was  proven to be an effective tool in performing package-level  circuit editing on devices assembled in WLP at a faster and  more controlled approach, due to its precise and controllability  in FIB-CE and delayering.

Exploring Delayering Chemistries for Metal Removal  on advanced silicon technologies

Buxbaum, Alex; Vaghayenegar, Majid

Thermofisher Scientific, Fremont CA USA

Henry, Loic; Serre, David; Gounet, Pascal

STMicroelectronics, Grenoble France

Abstract

This paper addresses the challenges of delayering Cu metal  lines in a circuit edit instrument.  By choosing appropriate  focused ion beam (FIB) chemistry and gas delivery settings, FIB and chemistry were optimized by a series of DOE  experiments with factors including FIB energy, precursor type, and current density.  For this work, we study and compare two  gas precursors, SCM gas (water vapor) and Dx gas (proprietary  chemistry commonly used for delayering with Xe plasma  FIBs).

Introduction

Circuit Edit has proven to be an invaluable tool for shortening  the time between the IC design and the start of manufacturing. Following the initial design and test, the circuit can be modified  by circuit edit techniques and the modification can then be  validated by testing [1].  This approach circumvents the long  lead times associated with fabrication of masks and IC  manufacturing, enabling a faster time to market.

One of the main use cases for the modifications to the circuit  require revealing and rerouting of metal (Cu) signal lines.  To  access the appropriate metal lines, delayering steps are  employed by means of a dedicated circuit edit instrument [2].  Here, a focused ion beam in combination with the appropriate  gas chemistry is used to form an access hole in which the metal  lines can be rerouted or cut.  The desired layer is revealed with  minimal impact to the device functionality.  This typically  requires minimizing the size of the node access holes (NAH), while maintaining a uniform floor. The ideal access hole will  have a flat floor with minimal to no height variation. In nonideal settings, access hole floors have topography due to the  presence of both metal and dielectric materials [3].

Discussion

Instrumentation and Sample for Delayering

This study was carried out using a single beam Ga ion FIB, designed for Circuit Edit applications.  The ion column was  oriented top down, and capable of accelerating voltages ranging  from 30kV to 5kV.  Beam currents selected based on the access  hole size and gas chemistry and ranged from 1pA to 11nA.  A  dual-nozzle gas delivery system was used to introduce the gas  precursors, ensuring uniform gas flux from both sides of the  access hole.  Gas pressure, as defined in the recipe, was held at  a constant setpoint by closed loop control.

The delayering process was monitored in real time by both  imaging the patterned area (using the secondary electron signal  from the patterning process) and monitoring the endpoint graph  of secondary electron levels (gray levels) and current through  the sample to ground (stage current).

The experiments were conducted on 28nm node samples  containing 8 metal layers (M1→M8).  For the small access hole  experiments, the samples were mechanically polished to M4, leaving the lower level metals and transistors intact.  M4 was  removed with an established Xe Plasma FIB (PFIB) process, stopping on the interlayer dielectric (ILD) above M3.  The large  access hole experiments were conducted on the topmost metal  layer M8, coated with ILD.

Experimental plan

For this delayering study, we explored the following factors:  gas chemistry (SCM and Dx), accelerating voltage (low kV, medium kV and high kV), and beam current density (low and  high).  Furthermore, we examined these conditions on small  access holes (850nm x 850nm) and large access holes (25um x  25um), as summarized in Table 1.

The top surface for the small access hole experiments was the  ILD layer above M3, while the large access hole experiments  were conducted with M8 fully revealed.  With this experimental  setup, we explored conditions representing both backside edits (small access holes with relatively thin metal lines) as well as  top side edits with thick metal lines.

DOE Execution

A complete list of the settings for kV’s and currents used, as  well as the derived current densities are shown in Table 2.  Note  that the conditions for the SCM and Dx experiments are not  exactly the same, as the process space for each gas required  some adjustments to enable the milling and delayering to  succeed.

For each run, an endpoint monitor graph was acquired, showing  the progress of the delayering milling process.  For the small  hole experiments, the milling starts out on the ILD, which  shows a low secondary electron yield in the endpoint monitor  graph (Figure 1a), and then increases as the metal lines are  revealed by the beam and the gas chemistry. As the metal lines  are milled away, the endpoint graph shows a decrease in  secondary electron yield, eventually reaching an inflection  point where the slope decreases and flattens.  The milling  proceeds into an over etch regime and is manually stopped.  For  each gas in these experiments, we maintained a similar over  etch beyond the inflection point (as a percentage of dose to  inflection), namely 25% for Dx gas, and 50% for SCM.

For large access holes, the milling begins on the metal lines (M8) and starts with a high secondary electron yield in the  endpoint monitor graph (Figure 1b), and then decreases as the  metal lines are milled away.

Analysis approach

The floor of each milled small access hole was evaluated for  topography and planarity.  Ideally, the results would show no  topography (i.e. flat floor on the bottom of the milled area) and  flat (i.e. no slope or curvature) with no residual Cu on the ILD. Evaluating topography

To evaluate the topography, each milled area was imaged by  high resolution SEM microscopy in a dual beam FIB-SEM  system.  Images were acquired in backscattered electron mode, using a high sensitivity retractable annular BSE detector (a.k.a. ABS detector), all with the same image acquisition parameters (e.g. kV, current, dwell time, contrast, etc..).  In some cases, the  images showed residue / topography or residual Cu on the  bottom surface of the floor, as shown for a small access hole in

Following the M3 delayering, each milled region was evaluated for planarity with a dual beam FIB-SEM , as follows:

a. The milled area was capped with a protective layer of tungsten, by SEM deposition b. The ROI was cross sectioned by FIB and imaged by high resolution SEM in backscattered electron mode, using an In-Column Detector (ICD). c. The milled floor planarity (flatness) was evaluated by measurements of the range between the milled floor and the top of the metal layer below. An example of a cross section and the corresponding planarity measurements is shown in Figure  4 . For this study, we define planarity as follows:

                                                       = 2 [max(δ) -min (δ)] max(δ) + min (δ)

Surface quality evaluation for large access holes Large access holes were imaged after M8 delayering, by tilted view SEM and evaluated for surface quality. The results were binned into five categories as shown in Figure  5 .

For large access holes, the results of thick metal line delayering  were best with low kV’s, as seen in Figure 7.  The amount of  residual Cu on the surface was lowest for 8 and 5kV.   Evaluation of the surface quality in terms of the artefacts listed  in Figure 5, indicated that the best surface quality is seen with  Dx gas at a low accelerating voltage (8kV).  All other conditions  resulted in either residual Cu or surface artefacts.

The best results for the large access holes are seen by using low  kV’s and lower current densities.  In this case, as with the small  access holes, the best conditions tend to favor more chemistry  and less bombardment.   Here again, the conditions that enhance  chemical selectivity seem to play a key role in obtaining the best  results.  The root cause of the artefacts observed was not  investigated, however it is reasonable to assume that the pits  could be related to ESD events, the cracks to stresses from the fabrication process or oxide shrinkage, and the ripples could be  due to a non-incident ion bombardment.

Conclusions

Both Dx and SCM gas precursors can assist in ion beam  delayering of metal lines.  The study of both small and large  access holes shows the advantages of using low accelerating  voltages (5~8kv) over higher kV’s (16~30kV) both in terms of  surface quality and efficacy in removing metal lines.  Small  access hole floor planarity was best with low current densities  and with Dx gas, and topography was best with low kV and Dx  gas.  Large access hole delayering was best at low kV and lower  current densities with Dx gas. The combination of low kV, lower current densities and Dx gas provide good results for both  small and large access holes.

Leveraging Automation of TEM Sample Preparation for Increased Throughput  and Reproducible Results from Advanced Multimodal STEM Analysis of 3-nm  FinFET Transistors

Lukáš Hladík, Daniel Němeček, Maksym Klymov, Nithin Balaji Venkataraman Iyappan Shankar, Lukáš Omasta and Karel Novotný

TESCAN GROUP, a.s., Brno, Czech Republic

lukas.hladik@tescan.com, daniel.nemecek@tescan.com, maksym.klymov@tescan.com

Abstract

TEM sample preparation is increasingly challenging for  advanced semiconductor nodes due to complex architectures  and shrinking dimensions. In this work we present an AI-driven  automation package on the FIB-SEM which enables fully  automated in-trench preparation, lift-out, and low-keV cleaning  down to sub-100 nm sample thickness. We demonstrate its  results on TSMC 3-nm FinFET and Ti alloy samples. The  workflow produced four high-quality lamellae, with STEM and  EDS revealing detailed FinFET architecture and material  composition, including titanium-filled gates and ruthenium  layers. Batch testing on silicon trenches achieved a 96% success  rate. Automation reduced operator time by ~40% and supports  overnight system use, increasing throughput without  compromising specimen quality.

Introduction

The large semiconductor chip manufactures seek to improve the  yield of their production as well as to further drive the  development of the state-of-the-art and next generation logic  and memory technology nodes. To maximize the efficiency of  failure analysis as well as the pathfinding and process  monitoring stages, the nanometer-sized structures and thin  layers in devices must be quantitatively analyzed to understand  the root-cause of their failure [1]. The preparation of thin, electron-transparent specimens (lamellae) for high-resolution  imaging and analysis by Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) has therefore become the critical step in the failure  analysis process, which is now even more demanding as  modern materials, complexity and shrinking dimensions of  modern transistors require increasingly sophisticated  techniques to prepare high-quality, ultra-thin, artifact-free TEM  samples. The demand for TEM sample preparation is growing  also in automotive, display and power semiconductors, which  traditionally rely on less aggressive technology nodes and  bigger feature sizes.

Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) techniques are commonly used for physical characterization, compositional analysis, and failure analysis of semiconductor

device structures, especially when nanometer-scale resolution  and high sensitivity are required for the characterization of  critical dimensions of device structures, interfacial details, distribution of deposited layers and defects or flaws that arise  during the fabrication process. [2, 3, 4] Precise and clean  preparation of samples of the appropriate thickness for STEM  analysis is essential for precise and accurate determination of  the key sample characteristics without artifacts.

Commonly used thin TEM sample preparation methods aim to  produce electron-transparent regions (<100 nm) with minimal  damage. For metals and conductive alloys, mechanical thinning (grinding, dimpling) followed by electropolishing is used. Ion  milling with argon ions is widely applied to ceramics, semiconductors, and brittle materials, often at cryogenic  conditions to reduce damage. Ultramicrotomy with diamond  knives is commonly used for preparation of soft materials and  biological tissues. FIB lift-out has become the dominant  modern approach for site-specific TEM sample preparation in  microelectronics, nanostructures, and defect analysis, often  followed by low-energy ion polishing or plasma cleaning to  remove surface damage and contamination.

Ga⁺ FIB low energy milling techniques are routinely used to  prepare specimens for aberration corrected high resolution  electron microscopy [5,6]. Similar specimen preparation  methods can be also applied using Xe⁺ ions from a plasma FIB (PFIB) source for preparation of sample for TEM [7]. The  heavier mass Xe⁺ ions result in a larger sputter yield, but smaller  ion range, yielding fast specimen preparation of thin specimens  with reduced surface damage. Over the past decade, progressive  advancements in plasma focused ion beam (PFIB) technology  have significantly improved beam current density, leading to  reduced halo effects and smaller spot diameters — overcoming  the primary limitations for efficient PFIB-based TEM sample  preparation. In both cases, manual preparation involves  numerous navigation, deposition, milling, and sample  repositioning steps, requiring skilled operators to successfully  produce electron-transparent specimens using FIB equipment.

In this work we used a TESCAN SOLARIS FIB-SEM with  TEM AutoPrep Pro and an optional Ar+ broad ion beam cleaner (TESCAN Aura) attached directly to the main chamber. LiftCopyright © 2025 ASM International®All rights reserved.

STEM imaging was done on a TESCAN  TENSOR ― multimodal analytical STEM microscope  designed for high throughput of routine analytical STEM  measurements as well as advanced electron diffraction  techniques. [8, 9]. We demonstrate improved throughput and  consistent TEM specimen thickness, while minimizing  amorphization damage — an essential factor for achieving  optimal results in analytical STEM. AI-driven software solution  automates the entire TEM sample preparation workflow—including lift-out, 30 keV on-grid thinning, and final low keV  cleaning — ensuring high-quality sub-100 nm TEM samples  ready for TEM analysis.

Reproducibility of TEM sample preparations from various  devices and materials was assessed, while conventional  analytical STEM analyses (STEM imaging and EDS mapping) were performed to demonstrate the high quality of the final  analytical results.

Instrumentation

A standard approach of TEM sample preparation typically  involves navigation to ROI, creation of a carbon or platinum (Pt) protection cap over the ROI via electron or ion beam, coarse milling with 30 kV at high currents creating a lamella  attached to the bulk. The lamella is then cut free from the bulk  and transferred to a TEM grid with nanomanipulator. The  sample is further thinned using lower ion beam currents (e.g., 50 pA–250 pA) to reach a thickness of ~100 nm or less followed  by final low keV cleaning to reduce amorphization and  implantation damage. During the final thinning the SEM is used  for end-pointing to specifically target desired features. This  complex workflow is challenging and requires a high level of  skill, patience, and experience of the FIB operator to reach  satisfying success rate. Depending on the operators skill, TEM  sample size and end-pointing requirements such preparation in  manual regime can take between 25–90 minutes.

Considering these challenges, we designed the automation  package integrated on the Ga+ and Xe+ FIB-SEM platforms. The intermediate lift-out step is performed using the  nanomanipulator with rotational tip, which achieves lift-out of  top-down, plan-view, and inverted lamella geometries in a  single manipulation step. The system can optionally be  equipped with a 200 eV Ar⁺ broad ion beam enabling further  enhancement of TEM sample quality and ensuring suitability  for high-resolution TEM (HR-TEM) characterization. This  hardware and software solution delivers higher success rates  and automates routine steps across a broader range of sample  types compared to manual preparation. TEM sample  preparation typically requires around 29 discrete user  interventions, each involving precise parameter adjustments. Full automation streamlines this process by reducing operator  involvement to the initial setup. At the start, the user defines  preparation parameters, selects target areas, and specifies  sample placement on the TEM grid (Tab.1). The software

verifies these inputs and alerts the user to any missing or  inconsistent details.

Once setup is complete, the system executes the remaining  steps automatically. This approach reduces manual  interventions by approximately 75% and minimizes userdependent variability. The result is improved preparation  consistency and significantly lower risk of error.
