Automation also optimizes microscope usage and operator  efficiency. While manual preparation of multiple TEM samples — such as four in a single session — demands continuous  operator presence and is limited to laboratory hours, automated  systems can operate unattended, including overnight. Even  compared with semi-automated workflows, in which some  manual steps remain (e.g., TEM grid attachment and final  polishing), full automation can reduce operator time by  approximately 40%, enabling more effective scheduling of  microscope resources.

System Prerequisites for Automated Operation

Before initiating any automated TEM preparation process, it is  essential to ensure that the FIB-SEM system has properly  aligned user presets for both the FIB and SEM. Beam  parameters, including the high-voltage (HV) index and beam  current, must be optimized for the specific conditions applied  during each step of the lamella preparation process.

To address this requirement, the system integrates the Auto  Preset Tuner software, which performs automated FIB/SEM  beam alignments — such as beam centering, astigmatism  correction, and focusing — using a dedicated alignment  sample. This process can be executed during unattended  operation (e.g., overnight) to maintain optimal system  readiness. The module enables stable operation for users  without advanced FIB-SEM expertise, while still allowing  experienced users full control for manual fine-tuning of  parameters as needed for specialized workflows.

Lift-Out Needle Maintenance

The condition of the lift-out needle is another critical factor in  ensuring reliable automated TEM sample preparation.

Maintaining a sharp needle tip is essential both for geometric  precision during manipulation and for accurate detection by  automated recognition algorithms. As the needle broadens, AIbased recognition may fail to reliably locate the tip or determine  the nanomanipulator position during automated approach for  the initial welding step.

The automation package addresses this by incorporating an  automated self-cleaning function during lamella cutting Fig.1, which preserves needle sharpness for up to 35 lift-outs before  tip sharpening is required. When sharpening becomes  necessary, an integrated wizard guides the process. By  combining needle tip rotation with FIB-based cleaning, the  system restores the tip to its optimal geometry, ensuring  consistent performance in subsequent operations.

Figure 1: Comparison of the needle shape a) before and b) after 10x TEM sample lift-outs. The shape stays nearly  perfectly preserved due to well positioned cutting during the  process. c) If needle gets out of shape the incorporated tip  sharpening wizard reshapes the needle back to initial  conditions.

Setting up an Automated Process

At this stage, the FIB-SEM system is in a well-aligned state. The samples from which the target TEM lamellae will be  prepared are already mounted on the main microscope stage. Additionally, up to four Cu/Mo grid holders with fingertips—designed to hold the final TEM specimens (up to 8 lift-outs in  one run) for transport to the S/TEM—are also positioned on the  stage.

The software includes a recipe library containing pre-defined  recipes for common use cases (e.g., a 15 × 5 × 0.1 µm3 lamella  on silicon). These recipes streamline the process by eliminating  the need for manual definition of parameters such as lamella  dimensions, pre- and post-lift-out thickness, polishing offsets, sample pre-tilts, material type, and other adjustable settings.

Before starting the automated TEM lamella preparation  process, the following user inputs are required:

1. Lamella Geometry

• Define lamella shape (Fig.2a) and orientation: Topdown, inverted, or plan-view

• Specify target final thickness

2. Material Specification

• Select sample material from the built-in database

• Or define a custom material based on milling rate  calibration

3. Preparation Workflow

• Choose partial (guided) process (e.g., up to grid  welding for manual thinning)

• Or choose full process (sub-100 nm thickness to TEM  transparency, including low-keV polishing at  minimum 2 keV)

4. FIB/SEM Operating Parameters

• Load from recipe library or define manually for each  step:

o Deposition parameters

o Polishing parameters

o SEM imaging conditions

5. Grid Welding Points

• System automatically repositions stage to grid holders  and captures SEM/FIB images

• User marks welding positions in SEM and FIB views (Fig. 2b)

6. Lift-Out Site Selection

• Identify exact lamella extraction location on the  sample (or multiple samples)

• Use SEM/FIB images with embedded fiducial marks  for precise overlay positioning on ROI

7. Initiation of Automated Process

• Start process; system proceeds automatically

• If any issue occurs (technical fault, fiducial  recognition failure), the process pauses and waits for  user intervention

Figure 2: a) The automation package GUI showing the  interactive visualization of lamella objects. b) Definition of  grid welding points by the user, using the generated overlay  to align the nanomanipulator and lamella with grid.

Automation significantly enhances the user experience, streamlining TEM sample preparation and enabling the  production of high-quality TEM specimens from a wide range  of materials — even by users without extensive FIB-SEM  operational expertise. This democratization of the process  allows more operators to participate in sample preparation, thereby increasing throughput.

A consistently high success rate across diverse sample types is  achieved through AI-driven algorithms that optimize each stage  of the workflow, including trench milling, lift-out (Fig. 3a), grid  placement (Fig. 3b), and final polishing.

A major advantage of this solution lies in its precise detection  of critical objects such as the nanomanipulator tip, TEM sample  edges, and TEM grids. The AI also improves fiducial mark  recognition, even on challenging materials with complex  topographies (Fig. 3c). Notably, it can detect fiducial marks in  tilted images (Fig. 3d), in noisy or astigmatic images or partially  distorted marks — a task that can be difficult even for  experienced operators.

Figure 3: AI-assisted functionalities are utilized through all  the TEM sample preparation steps. a) Detection of the needle  tip during (blue) lift-out approach, b) detection of the grid (green) and attached lamella on the nanomanipulator (red), fiducial mark detection during preparation c) at top-down  geometry, d) at tilted geometry.

Statistical Reproducibility of TEM Samples

Consistency of results and the overall success rate are crucial  when using automation. Even when identical starting  parameters and processing methods are applied, several factors  can still introduce variability during the process:

1. Fiducial Mark Placement Precision – The user’s  alignment of fiducial marks to the exact target ROI in  the SEM image may vary slightly.

2. Variations in Sample Position – Slight positional  shifts can affect fiducial mark recognition, especially  in the presence of parasitic particles (e.g., smeared  debris from analytical systems) or background patterns

resembling fiducial marks (e.g., intersecting lines  forming cross-like features).

3. Surface Material Differences – Variations such as  delaminated passivation can alter e-beam/i-beam  deposition rates due to changes in secondary electron  yield, leading to thinner protective layers that may be  consumed faster during final thinning steps.

4. AI Detection Accuracy – Minor misalignments  during AI-based detection of edges, weld points, and  corners of FIB-milled structures can affect milling  precision. While the system has proven robust, failure  in fiducial mark detection remains the most common  cause of unsuccessful preparation in all existing FIB  automation solutions.

5. Lamella Stability – Internal stresses, thermal effects, and other material-specific behaviors can cause slight  variability in lamella stability during thinning, even  within the same sample region.

Despite the factors mentioned above that can affect the overall  success rate of the automated process, the solution was  developed with a target success rate of 95% for standard-size  lamellae (15 × 5 × 0.1 µm3) on stable materials such as silicon  wafers.

In approximately 5% of sample preparations, failures may  occur. In the case of batch TEM site preparations, the affected  site was automatically excluded from further processing, and  the system proceeded directly to the preparation of the  subsequent site. In contrast, during single lamella preparations, the system suspended operation and remained in a waiting state  until manual intervention was provided by the operator. At this  stage, corrective actions such as the manual identification of  fiducial markers or the adjustment of milling offsets could be  applied before the procedure was resumed.

To assess reproducibility, three lamellae from a titanium alloy  were prepared using a fully automated process, including liftout and final FIB 2 keV cleaning (Fig. 4a). A predefined library  recipe, optimized for producing 70 nm TEM specimens from Ti  alloy, was applied. The final lamellae quality was verified via  cross-sectional thickness measurements in the FIB-SEM and  TEM analyses. All specimens exhibited median thicknesses  between 68 nm and 71 nm (Fig. 4b), confirming the method’s  high reproducibility. This level of consistency ensures uniform  TEM specimen thickness, minimizing variability that could  otherwise impact data quality.

Figure 4: a) STEM Angular dark-field images of titanium  TEM samples prepared completely automatically, b) measuring cross section thickness of the three TEM samples  from a titanium alloy.

Similarly, we tested batch processing on silicon sample with  trenches to access success rate during long-time process (>10  hours). 29 out of 30 lamella sites was prepared successfully in  fully automated regime to electron transparency.

Figure 5: First 10 out of 30 in total lamellae samples  prepared in long process run. Each 5 keV SEM image taken  automatically after lamella welding step. Slight differences  between each site can be observed.

Preparation of Complex TEM Sample Geometries

With the advent of new device architectures and the increasing  3D complexity of modern transistors and memory cells, more  sophisticated TEM sample geometries are often required. These  geometries are tailored to align precisely with the internal  device structures of the target features — for example, planview preparations for 3D NAND stacks to assess channel filling  and cylindricity. Alternative geometries can also be employed  to mitigate curtaining artifacts and minimize internal stress. Inverted preparations, for instance, improve overall mechanical  stability and reduce the risk of bending, which is a common  limitation of standard geometries that use platinum protection  layers on top.

The nanomanipulator, positioned in-plane with the FIB column  in the main chamber, combined with a modified lift-out  geometry, enables efficient preparation of TEM samples with  advanced orientations — including inverted, plan-view, or  rotated geometries at non-orthogonal angles (e.g., 100°) —thanks to its full 360° rotation capability (Fig. 6). This is

achieved without the need for additional flipping devices, which could otherwise reduce the FIB-SEM system’s usability  for other applications or limit the number of samples that can  be mounted on the main stage.

Figure 6: Nanomanipulator positioned in-plane with the FIB  column  enables efficient preparation of TEM samples with  advanced orientations a) 180° inverted b) full 360° rotation.

Materials and Methods

Sample with 3-nm FinFET Transistors

As the source for TEM samples, we used Apple A17 Pro SoC,

manufactured using TSMC’s 3 nm FinFET technology,

extracted from a commercially available complete smartphone  device. After disassembling the device, the SoC was removed  from the main PCB, decapsulated, and mechanically polished  to expose the upper-level logic circuitry. Four electrontransparent samples were prepared from adjacent locations  within the logic section of the chip. Each TEM sample was  thinned to transparency, isolating a specific line of transistors. Sample preparation was performed automatically in-trench, including automated undercutting, automated lift-out and initial  thinning on the grid to ~300 nm thickness, followed by manual  high-keV polishing (FIB 30 keV @ 150 pA) and low-keV  cleaning (FIB 2 keV @ 50 pA) to precisely endpoint and isolate  specific lines in the fin-cut (Fig.7) and gate-cut orientations of  the FinFET devices.

TEM measurements of the prepared TEM samples were done  by the multimodal analytical STEM microscope.

Figure 7: Bright-field STEM overview image of an electrontransparent, fin-cut–oriented lamella prepared using  a combination of automated processing and manual FIB  polishing with manual end-pointing.

Figure 8: Bright-field STEM (top), dark-field STEM  (middle), and high-angle annular

dark-field STEM (bottom) detailed images of the fin-cut lamella. The images show high

contrast and quality of the polished central region of the lamella, exhibiting several

segments of cut FinFET devices. The relative contrast of the FinFET devices features

is given by the different, user-defined, data collection angles.

Figure 9: Bright-field STEM (left) and dark-field STEM (right) images of the fin cut   lamella, using user-defined data collection angles as indicated in the images.

Figure 10: Visualization of different metal layers of the 3-nm FinFET gates in the gatecut and fin-cut lamella by STEM EDS compositional analysis, while the ADF STEM image

(top left) shows the overall architecture in this gate-cut lamella.

The bright-field (BF) and high-angle annular dark-field (HAADF) STEM images were acquired at different  magnifications (fields of view). First, a sample overview image (3 × 0.6  µm2) with 1.46 nm/pix sampling, using 500 pA probe  current and 3 µs dwell time. Then, the detailed architecture of  FinFET devices was imaged in a smaller region of interest (750 × 375 nm2) with 0.37 nm/pix sampling, using 500 pA probe  current and 5 µs dwell time. The same region of interest was  subsequently analyzed by a proprietary dual windowless EDS  system with 2.0 sr collection solid angle. Beam current of 6.7  nA with 82 µs dwell time and 1.1 nm/pix sampling in 30 frames, which were aligned before averaging to compensate for any  possible sample drift during EDS data acquisition. No image  filtering or other post-processing of the EDX elemental maps  was applied.

Results

Compared to fully manual preparation of each lamella, incorporating automation into the process reduced preparation

time by at least 15 minutes per site. Using the automated

workflow, a lifted-out lamella attached to the grid was prepared  in a total time of approximately 25 minutes. A standard  10 × 5 × 5 µm³ silicon lamella recipe was loaded directly from  the recipe database without requiring modification of geometry  or milling depth parameters. In contrast, manual operation  requires the user to define milling objects and optimize the  recipe in multiple partial runs to ensure complete in-trench  release of the lamella while balancing milling speed and  damage minimization.

These manual adjustments typically consume additional tens of  minutes and increase the risk of errors during the lift-out  process. Manual lift-out and grid attachment are complex steps  that many users may struggle to perform without sample loss. In this case, the automation package successfully populated the  grid with four lamellae prepared from the 3-nm FinFET device, all ready for manual thinning, achieving a 100 % success rate.

The overview STEM images (Fig. 8) of the prepared TEM  lamellae clearly show the high quality and contrast of features  in the polished regions with several segments of FinFET  circuits. The difference in appearance of the bright-field (BF  STEM), dark-field (DF STEM), and high-angle annular darkfield (HAADF STEM) images originates from the different, user-defined, data collection angles for each type of the STEM  image and the corresponding image formation mechanism. While the BF STEM image is formed mainly by the difference  in electron transmissivity and phase contrast, the DF STEM and  HAADF STEM images are primarily given by electron  scattering from heavier atoms in the sample – ideal for  visualization of metal coatings in the device. The scattering  contrast in BF STEM and DF STEM images also reveals  crystallinity in the overlaying metallic layer and inside the gate  channels.

The zoomed in STEM images of the selected region of interest (Fig. 9) reveal more clearly the architecture and dimensions of

the 3-nm FinFET devices, including metallic layers, at subnanometer resolution. The standard CD metrology can be  performed directly on these images.

The EDS analysis (Fig. 10) of the same region of interest was  not compromised by hydrocarbon contamination from the  previous STEM imaging due to near-UHV (<10-6 Pa) conditions in the TEM microscope. The EDS analysis revealed  Al (aluminum) fill inside a TiN (titanium nitride) shell   typically used in contact and metallization structures, copper  connections with metallic layers on top of the circuit as well as  cobalt and ruthenium layers and surrounding silicon substrate. Light elements, such as oxygen and nitrogen, were clearly  visualized and can be clearly assigned to individual elements in  the device architecture.

Conclusions

The automated in-trench preparation process, combined with  automated lift-out and manual high-keV polishing, consistently  produced high-quality TEM lamellae from the Apple A17 Pro  SoC fabricated using TSMC’s 3-nm FinFET technology. This  approach enables less experienced operators to successfully  prepare TEM samples from advanced technology nodes and  increases laboratory throughput by allowing FIB-SEM  operation outside regular working hours.

A standard approach bright-field and dark-field STEM images  acquired at different signal collection angles clearly  demonstrated the high quality of prepared lamellas for STEM  analysis. The contrast and sharpness in the images was very  high, assuring accurate determination of measured dimensions  in downstream CD metrology. EDS analysis also clearly  revealed even very thin layers in the 3-nm FinFET device  architecture.

Advancement Towards FIB Active Auto Thinning (AAT) Process

Dr. Sang Hoon Lee, PhD, Dr. Xue Rui, PhD, Dr. Ning Lu, PhD, Mr. John Pittman, Dr. Qiang Jin, PhD, Mr. Joel Lebret, Mr. Robert Gifford, Mr. Tyler Lenzi

Micron Technology, Boise, Idaho, United States of America

Mr. Jaroslav Stárek, Mr. Viktor Švéda, Mr. Lukáš Hübner, Mr. Jakub Korgo

Thermo Fisher Scientific, Brno, Jihomoravský kraj, Czech Republic

Dr. Zhen Lian, PhD, Mr. Gabriel Woodworth, Mr. Davin Fast, Ms. Anne Kenslea

Thermo Fisher Scientific, Hillsboro, Oregon, United States of America

Abstract

In advanced DRAM and NAND structures, the feature size at  the targeted cut face during the Focused Ion Beam (FIB) process has been reduced to sub-ten nanometer scale. Even with  high-quality SEM resolution level scanned cut-face image data, determining the stopping point of the process remains a  significant challenge. To address this, Micron has successfully  implemented cut-face probability calculation and sliced image  data interpolation methods using machine vision image  artificial intelligence platforms (AIPs by Thermo Fisher  Scientific) for the Micron’s latest memory devices analysis.

This innovation enables machines to render a device’s threedimensional geometry, infer and predict the upcoming cut face  in SEM data points, and determine the stopping point in the FIB  thinning process using detector’s raw data signal extractions. This approach avoids signal post-processing and transformation  into visible light range for humans, thereby preventing  meaningful data loss. The new methodology surpasses human  eye detection limits, maximizes SEM resolution utilization, and  converts an automation system into an autonomous system  capable of deciding where to stop the FIB milling at each cutface, based on the sensory input of Micron wafer’s cut-face  analysis and learning algorithms.

This technology has been integrated into its associated FIB  platform, augmented by Open-AutoTEM, (iFast Extensibility). Micron defines this autonomous FIB thinning as active auto  thinning (AAT), distinguishing it from the conventional  fiducial-based FIB auto thinning, known as passive auto  thinning (PAT).

Introduction

Focused Ion Beam (FIB) auto thinning is the automated process  of thinning samples using a FIB system. This technique is  widely used in materials science and the semiconductor  industry for sample preparation, particularly for Transmission  Electron Microscopy (TEM) analysis. FIB auto thinning  enhances the efficiency and quality of sample preparation for  various analytical techniques by allowing the preparation of  multiple samples simultaneously or overnight. This  significantly increases efficiency and ensures more uniform  thinning, reducing variability between samples by minimizing  the risk of human error and damage to the sample. The process  can be monitored and controlled remotely, enabling unattended  operation. [1], [2]

Accurate calibration of the FIB system and tool-to-tool  parameter matching are crucial for reliable results. Additionally, optimal parameters for conventional autothinning processes may vary depending on the specific material  used in DRAM and NAND structures. Developing robust  automation routines can be challenging, especially for complex, fast-changing sample geometries in the semiconductor  industry.

To address these challenges, an innovative approach called  Active Auto Thinning (AAT) has been developed. This method  applies to the analysis of cutting-edge memory device  structures through AI (artificial intelligence) inference, utilizing  probability and interpolation algorithms. The newly developed  workflow is currently operational within the Micron laboratory  environment, as depicted in Figure 1.

Data Collection & Training

The first step is to collect multiple reference data of cut face  SEM images marching towards to the target cut face at every  1~5 nm steps, 150~1000 slices depend on the device’s pitch and  complexity of structure, shown in Figure. 2.

Fig. 2. An example reference cut face data collected from the  slice and view (S&V process). Multiple set of data is used for  the three-dimensional structure rendering.

Feature selection and extraction are followed by reference data  collection. The periodic repetition and selection of  distinguishable areas are key to successfully learning and  recognizing patterns for AI modeling. In fig. 3, the green boxed  area represents the AI model's region of interest (ROI). The  structure below the green boxes is not ideal for training and may  cause a hallucination effect [3], [4], [5].

(a)                                    (b)

Fig. 3. A schematic of (a) front and (b)rear cut face of target  ROI. Red lines are the detected device boundaries. Green  boxes are specific feature extraction area for AI process.

Probability & Interpolation

Once the target cut face of the sample is determined at the outset  of the active auto thinning (AAT) process, three lines of FIB  marks are added on the surface of the sample (Fig. 4). These  marks serve as anchor points to measure the sample's  orientation offset and align the sample's structure parallel to the  normal direction of the cut face. The ratio of distances 'a' and 'b' is calculated to correct the ion beam's scan directions, stopping  several hundred nanometers away from the target cut face.

(a)

(b)

Fig. 4. (a)Schematic of Anchor point FIB marks, three lines. Top view (left) and three-dimensional view (right). Black  arrows presents FIB milling directions. (b) a screenshot of  collected cut face SEM data including anchor point marks.

When the ratio of 'a' and 'b' reaches the set values, the system  switches to AI process mode to infer the probability and  interpolate real-time data to determine the current cut face  position (Y-axis). A larger trained model architecture is  employed for improved real-time SEM cut face monitoring and  to accurately calculate the distance between the FIB ion scan  and the sample target cut face.

The inference methodology can be selected based on the  characteristics of the feature extraction area, using techniques  used in image processing and computer vision, particularly in  the realm of feature extraction and object detection.

The first technique is the gradient-based edge detection filter in  image processing, designed to approximate the magnitude and  orientation of intensity gradients at each pixel location. The  output produced by this operator is an edge-enhanced image, wherein pixel intensities correspond to the strength of the  detected gradients—brighter pixels indicate stronger edges. Among its principal advantages are its simplicity and  computational efficiency, which make it suitable for real-time  and resource-constrained applications. However, the operator is  also characterized by certain limitations, including a  pronounced sensitivity to noise and a tendency to yield coarse  gradient approximations, particularly in areas with highfrequency intensity variations.

The second technique is for object detection and recognition  tasks. Its primary function is to characterize the shape and  appearance of objects by analyzing the distribution of gradient  orientations within localized regions of an image. The  algorithm begins by computing image gradients—often using  methods similar to the first operator—to capture edge  information. Its strengths lie in its robustness to minor  deformations and lighting changes, as well as its ability to  capture fine-grained structural details. However, it is not

inherently invariant to scale or rotation, and its computational  demands can be significant, particularly when applied to large  images or real-time systems.

Therefore, it is crucial to select suitable models and modify  them according to each device structure design.

During the image data training computation phase, the initial  step involves categorizing statistical image data without  assuming any intrinsic order. Following this, a mathematical  alignment procedure is applied to organize the image data  collection in preparation for subsequent interpolation and  visualization processes. This structured arrangement facilitates  the generation of a heat map representation, as illustrated in  Figure 5 and Figure 6.

Fig. 5. Real-time cut face data converted into the probability  calculation result, sorted by creation time, upper left is the  latest. The bottom right is from the first cut-face.

As illustrated in Figure 5 and Figure 6, the interpolation  algorithm is executed concurrently with the generation of the  probability map (heat map). This algorithm leverages real-time  heat map data to identify potential linear features and optimally  connect them into extended structures, akin to techniques  employed in advanced lane detection systems used in  autonomous vehicles. By compensating for missing data and  inaccuracies in cut placement—often caused by temporal  instability in the ion beam [1]—the algorithm enhances the  reliability of the process. As a result, it achieves a success rate  that surpasses that of highly trained human operators, effectively approaching a zero-failure threshold, a continuous  24/7 operational record of the solution has been maintained for  eight months, beginning in January 2025 in Micron. In the rendered image, fitting lines are  created, and their length measurements are used to mark the  distance from the target cut face. Once the targeted distance  from the endpoints is reached, the FIB milling stops, and the  same procedure is applied to the other side of the samples. The template script initiates the process by requiring an initial  set of 15 slices, which establishes the slope of the interpolation  line. This step also defines threshold values for probability  calculations and sets the thinning window width to 2.5 µm. Following this, the system proceeds to mill up to 200 slices, generating data for the interpolation fitting model. Milling  continues until the designated region of interest (ROI) is  reached. At this point, the system employs probability-based  algorithms to determine when to stop the milling process. The  expected stopping point is calculated to be approximately 57  nm from the target, or per memory device design, ensuring  precision in reaching the ROI. This structured approach allows  for controlled and accurate thinning, optimizing the  interpolation model while minimizing unnecessary material  removal.

FIB-SEM Data Validation

The final product of the FIB AAT process comprises three  major parts: the three anchor point marks area, the actual  thinning window area for TEM analysis, and the thinning  fiducial mark area (Fig. 7). It has been demonstrated that  machine vision (MV) aided AAT's sensitivity in detecting  surface morphology maximizes the utilization of immersion  mode SEM resolution to the limit (0.5 nm to 2 nm), surpassing  the detection capabilities of the human eye limited by SEM  image quality (Fig. 7 (b)). The final thickness is consistently  measured in the range of 10 nm to 20 nm for each trained model, completed with 2 kV ion acceleration voltage milling [7].

(a)

(b)

Fig. 7. In (a),  three anchor point marks,  thin window  area  thinning fiducial. (b)immersion mode SEM image of  target cut face.

Identifying the cut face SEM image and pinpointing the actual  cut face of the ROI with the quality of data shown in Fig. 7 (b)

has been the most challenging part of the manual FIB thinning  process. Common user errors include missing the target ROI  due to over-milling or under-milling, as the human eye can  process only about 10 to 12 data spots per second, whereas a  vision system can analyze thousands of parts in the same  amount of time. With the introduction of active auto thinning (AAT), the AIP-aided machine vision (MV) system  distinguishes and classifies objects on the cut face to predict the  next cut face and determine the ROI promptly, as shown in Fig.

7. Furthermore, low kV fine milling beam direction accuracy (X-, Y-, α tilt-, β tilt-, R-, and T-axes) within the thinning  window is achieved through segmented milling guided by a  real-time milling rate differentiation monitoring algorithm [8],

[9].

Discussions

TEM data evaluation confirms AAT's high-quality performance  on Micron's cutting-edge DRAM device nodes, providing crisp, clean metrology data as shown in Fig. 8. With precise thickness  control down to a sub-10 nanometer scale, the system delivers  metrology data free from 3-D effects, thanks to the machine  learning function combined with inference algorithms using  probability and interpolation calculation techniques to identify, distinguish, and classify every object signal to the detector in  the selected extraction area.

In contrast, human vision detects only visible light patterns  displayed on screen-filtered data from detectors, with a  significant latency, and then coordinates this data with the brain  to translate light into image data, limiting or partially missing  object recognition data.

(a) and (b) generated from one of AAT models in a device  node presents AAT’s higher endpoint definition control in  nanometer-scale. Red: Zero loss, Green: Si plasma, Blue: Micron materials.

Fig. 8 and Fig. 10 illustrate the results in memory device  applications. TEM data analysis was performed utilizing a suite  of specialized instruments, each selected for its suitability to  distinct analytical tasks. Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy

(EDS) was employed for elemental characterization, critical dimension measurements were obtained using precision metrology tools, and post-process visualization of sample thickness, integrated with EDS data, was conducted to assess structural integrity and uniformity. As shown in Fig.  8 , the probability fitting model provides precise stop-point control by predicting the next cut face morphology, proactively stopping the milling process to avoid destroying the ROI cut face and covering most milling parameter control scenarios. The cut surface shows an absence of overlapping three-dimensional features across the entire structure, enabling precise metrology analysis. The ratio of the trackable feature area to the unit area in the SEM image of the FIB-cut face significantly impacts the probability model and distance fitting accuracy. An elevated ratio significantly mitigates noise and improves the accuracy of ROI distance fitting within a sub-nanometer range ( < 1 nm). Conversely, a diminished ratio exacerbates noise and degrades distance fitting accuracy, exceeding the 3-nanometer threshold ( > 3 nm), as observed in the 16 nm-thickness autonomous FIB sample processing procedure.

As the low-kV fine milling process nears the final target endpoint, it transitions into segmented fine milling steps with approximately 1 µm-wide segments shown Fig,  12 . This approach enables localized milling within individual windows to compensate for ion beam scanning instabilities across the entire cut face, which spans approximately 3.5 µm in width. The system continuously infers the remaining distance to the endpoint in real time based on the current cut face profile and optimized training data. Milling is automatically halted approximately 7-8 nm before reaching the actual, non-visible target endpoint to ensure precision and prevent over-milling. As a result, the process produces a lamella with a thickness of approximately 14-16 nm, encompassing the endpoint plane, suitable for generating high-resolution TEM analysis data.

 Conclusions

Conclusions

The data inference algorithm for the autonomous FIB thinning step, built upon the fully automated FIB sample lift-out process, has been successfully validated and implemented on Micron's DRAM wafer data analysis. This meets the increasing demand for cost savings and reduced time-to-data throughput. Active auto thinning (AAT) is being implemented to replace the lab's current passive auto thinning (PAT) workflows, expanding its capabilities to other manual use cases by continually developing artificial intelligence platform (AIP) models for Micron memory device analysis applications. Moreover, this solution has enhanced the current lab environment, paving the way for the next steps towards an unmanned autonomous lab environment through data inference process and workflow automation methodologies.

Material Analysis of Cu End-Point Detection for Advanced Node PFIB Delayering Process Optimization

Or Haimson1, Thibaut Dessolier2, David Donnet2, Zdeněk Král2, Tzach Jaffe1, Hagit Sagi1

1 Annapurna Labs Ltd. an Amazon Company, Matam Scientific Industries Center, Building 19, Haifa  3508409, ISRAEL

2 Thermo Fisher Scientific, Achtseweg Noord 5, 5651 GG Eindhoven, the Netherlands

Introduction

As integrated circuits continue to scale down to ever-smaller dimensions and increased

complexity, traditional failure isolation & analysis (FA/FI), and sample preparation techniques face

significant limitations. The increasing density of modern semiconductor devices, now advancing beyond  3 nm technology nodes, presents unprecedented challenges in precise layer-by-layer analysis. Over the  past decade, Xenon (Xe) Plasma Focused Ion Beam (PFIB) gas assisted delayering has emerged as a

standard industry technique for precise layer-by-layer delayering of integrated circuits.

Recent studies have validated PFIB delayering as an effective sample preparation technique for

nanoprobing applications. Research on 14 nm FinFET devices in SRAM arrays has demonstrated the

technique's capability to provide clean, artifact-free surfaces suitable for atomic force nanoprobing (1). Furthermore, advancements in PFIB delayering have enabled successful nanoprobing of 5 nm node

devices (2), confirming its applicability to cutting-edge semiconductor technologies.

While previous studies have focused on electrical and topographical characterization of PFIB delayering (3,4), comprehensive material and chemical analysis of the delayering process remain crucial,

particularly for Cu interconnect end-point monitoring. This study addresses the chemical and structural  characterization of PFIB-delayered surfaces, with specific emphasis on the material properties of Cu

lines end-point detection.

This comprehensive characterization aims to optimize failure analysis protocols and establish

parameters for automated end-point detection.

Experimental

An advanced process node microprocessor was used for the scope of this investigation. The

whole sample was mechanically de-processed to the bottom of Via 4 as a starting point, over a cache

memory area of standard 6T SRAM cells. The PFIB delayering was carried out on a Thermofisher Helios 5  CXe PFIB tool.

Initially, a 20 by 20 um2 area was delayered by using a Dx gas flow of ~10-5 mbar; beam energy of 5 keV  and beam current equivalent to 1 nA. The PFIB beam parameters were chosen in accordance with

previous studies that validate them to be suitable for device nanoprobing with minimal electrical device  alteration while keeping good planarity over the region of interest (ROI) (4). The stage current was used  as the endpoint monitor as it allows the progress of the delayering to be monitored and clearly

distinguishes between vias and metal lines, thus making it a powerful tool for precise sample

preparation. The stage current for the delayering from via 4 down to the bulk silicon was used as a

reference (Figure 1).

Fig.1 Stage current end point monitor over a standard memory block.

As can be noted from the stage current end point monitor, and in agreement with previous studies

concerning PFIB delayering of Cu lines, these are common stage current based end point monitor plots (2,4).

In this work, we focused on the metal three layer. The metal three delayering dose is limited to the

region of roughly 0.82 to 1.1 nC/um2. Six different areas were delayered by specific dose using the

mentioned parameters (Figure 2). Each site was then protected by an electron beam W deposition of ~200 nm, at the center of the processed area. An additional non-delayered site was also prepared as a  reference to characterize the metal three stack and etch stop layer.

The peak stage current can be divided into two main regimes: the first at dose range of 0.81-0.91

nC/um2 with the stage current of around 1900 picoamperes (red area on Figure 2), and the second at  dose range of 0.98-1.1 nC/um2 of around 1780 picoamperes (blue area on Figure 2).

Fig.2 Metal 3 Stage current end point monitor indicating the different dose areas that were analyzed. Planar SEM images of the whole delayered areas were taken to correlate the stage current to the

uniformity of etching process.

Finally, seven cross lamellas were prepared using the Thermo Fisher AutoTEM and were analyzed using  HR TEM & EDS analysis. Each lamella was taken from the center of the delayered area.

Results

STEM images of the reference area lamella (Figure 3a) clearly show the Cu metal stack over the  6T SRAM cache area. High-magnification images (Figure 3b & 3c) reveal distinct layers including Al etch  stop, Co capping, and Cu metal 3 layers. The Al etch stop layer exhibits a distinctive dual-layer structure  with a thick upper layer and thinner lower layer separated by silicon oxide.

The low PFIB Dx etching dose of 0.85 nC/um2 indicates good uniformity across the processed area. We  note that the thick Al etch stop layer was delayered, but the thin Al etch stop layer and the Co capping  above the Cu metal 3 layer are intact.

Increasing the PFIB Dx etching dose to 0.88 & 0.91 nC/um2 slightly etches the thin Al etch stop layer and  starts to delayer the Co capping above the Cu metal. In addition, the planview SEM image indicates that  for the higher dose of 0.91 nC/um2, the whole processed areas starts to slightly lose uniformity and

there are areas where the Cu metal 3 layer is exposed (marked in orange in Figure 4a). Since the crosssection lamella was prepared at the center of each sample, this etch is not evident at the STEM & EDS.

We note that at these low doses, the stage current endpoint monitor indicates 30 picoamperes

fluctuations.

With the increase of the etching dose, the Cu metal lines are clearly etched until finally removed. The

planar SEM image shows the high uniformity of the PFIB Dx etching.

Discussion

The systematic analysis of PFIB delayering across multiple doses reveals critical insights into endpoint detection optimization. The observed stage current variations demonstrate a strong correlation

with specific layer transitions, particularly during Cu metal exposure. Most notably, the characteristic 30  picoampere fluctuations observed at doses between 0.88-0.91 nC/um2 serve as a reliable indicator for  approaching the Cu metal layer. This distinctive signal pattern provides a promising parameter for

developing automated endpoint detection protocols.

Further analysis reveals that 0.91 nC/um2 represents a critical threshold dose at which the delayering

process begins to expose the underlying Cu metal layer. Beyond this dose, we observe a systematic

progression of Cu metal removal, ultimately achieving highly uniform delayering across the processed

area at higher doses. This dose-dependent behavior suggests a two-stage approach for precise Cu layer  removal: an initial careful approach to the metal layer using the characteristic current fluctuations as

guidance, followed by controlled removal at higher doses to achieve uniform delayering.

Conclusion

This comprehensive material analysis of Cu end-point detection in PFIB delayering processes provides

crucial insights for advanced node semiconductor failure analysis. Our systematic investigation reveals  distinct correlations between delayering doses and material removal patterns. These findings establish  quantitative parameters for automated endpoint detection protocols for applications such as

nanoprobing (6)

The practical application of these findings is demonstrated through a case study on a logic area, where  precise dose control (Figure 5) proved essential for optimal passive voltage contrast imaging.

Fig.5 Stage current end point monitor over a reference logic area. The data labels indicate the ROI area  patterning dose used.

Initial delayering at 2.13 nC/um2 resulted in weak PVC signals and residual etch-stop layer material over  metal lines (Figure 6a). Increasing the dose to 2.3 nC/um2 significantly improved image contrast and

successfully removed residual materials (Figure 6b), highlighting the critical relationship between

delayering parameters and analytical outcome quality.

These results establish a framework for optimizing PFIB delayering protocols, particularly for advanced  node technologies where precise layer control is crucial. The combination of stage current monitoring

and dose-dependent material removal characteristics provides a robust foundation for developing

automated delayering processes. This approach can maintain consistency and reliability in

semiconductor failure analysis applications, paving the way for more efficient and accurate diagnostics  in increasingly complex integrated circuit architectures.

Implementation and Analysis of Open-Source Toolkit for rapid prototyping of  automated FIB-SEM workflows and 3D Tomography

Ishmam Iqbal, Yuyan Wang, Joseph Ziebarth, Ryan Meredith, Tyler Malone

Texas Instruments, Dallas, Texas

i-iqbal@ti.com

Abstract

Automation of FIB-SEM systems is a major point of focus and  an increasingly essential feature in modern tools for the  nanoscale imaging and analysis of semiconductor devices. As  semiconductor geometries gradually grow more complex, the  need is rising to automate progressive FIB cross-sections in  order to successfully reconstruct an accurate 3D model of dielevel features via FIB tomography. For most tools, automation  features could be purchased as complementary software. However, a more cost-effective approach for labs with budget  constraints, or for labs wanting to conduct a feasibility study of  automated scripts, is to utilize a set of open-source software in  order to perform automated progressive FIB cross-sections and  3D Tomography. In this paper, we introduce and analyze the  use of PyAutoGUI (an open-source Python library), ImageJ (open-source image processing software) and 3D Slicer (opensource 3D visualization and analysis software) to create a fully  open-source suite of tools for automating a progressive FIB  cross-section and tomographic reconstruction. Aside from 3D  Tomography, this approach could also be used to automate inFIB deprocessing and EDX analysis, which we are actively  investigating.

Introduction

A combined FIB-SEM system is designed to acquire SEM  images at each step of removing a slice of material with the  focused ion beam. After segmentation of the images, the virtual  slices can be extracted in any direction, and 3D surface  rendering of the structure with dimension data can be calculated

[1]. Commercial embedded software is costly and specific to its  own brand (e.g. Inspect3D and Avizo for Thermofisher Helios  G4 PFIB). In this paper, we introduce and analyze a suite of  open-source tools that can achieve rapid automated FIB-SEM  tomography workflows across a multitude of FIB-SEM  machines. Several case studies are also introduced in detail to  illustrate this pioneer method.

Automated FIB-SEM tomography can be broken down into 3  main steps (Fig. 1):

1. Automated image collection

2. Automated image alignment

3. 3D Reconstruction

For the purposes of automated image collection, most tools  have either built-in features or complementary automation  software. These features allow a FIB-SEM system to capture  images at specific intervals during a progressive FIB crosssection. For built-in features, the main limitations could include  gradual loss of focus/beam drift and image offset as we go  deeper into a progressive cross-section. These stem from the  fact that the features were not originally intended for  tomographic 3D reconstructions. Complementary software that  allow automation scripts and 3D reconstruction have to be  purchased separately as expensive add-ons to the tool.

Our solution to this problem is to utilize an open-source Python  package called PyAutoGUI. PyAutoGUI allows users to control  movements and actions of the mouse and keyboard through  Python scripts. Thus, these scripts can be used to automate  actions on the user interface of the FIB-SEM system. Built-in  image recognition also allows users to create scripts that can  check and detect conditions on the UI screen (beam off/on or  milling paused/running) and act accordingly. Furthermore, PyAutoGUI scripts can also be compiled into Windows  Executable files that can be run on computers without Python  installed. This means minimal interference/modification to the  actual tool PC.

Once images of multiple FIB cross-sectional planes are  collected, they can be stacked to generate voxel data (3D spatial  pixels) to be used in 3D reconstruction of the area of interest. Because the image plane gradually shifts laterally and vertically  during progressive cross-section cuts, the image slices need to  be repositioned to allow for accurate 3D reconstruction of the  area of interest. Due to this issue, alignment of slice data is  critical for accurate model construction. Utilization of  automated functions to carry out image alignments is a critical  need due to large datasets and high degree of precision required  for quality 3D model construction. This image alignment  feature could also be blocked behind expensive paywalls for  specific tools. Some FIB-SEM brands/models might not even  have any default capability of automated image collection and  alignment. In these scenarios, using open source  software/applications can prove to be valuable tools to  automate and enhance the capabilities of these machines.

So far, we have utilized and evaluated alignment algorithms  based in ImageJ – an open-source, Java-based image processing  and analysis software. For the purposes of FIB-SEM  tomography, linear stack alignment using SIFT (Scale Invariant  Feature Transform) proved to be an effective feature for image  alignment. This was also used in conjunction with the “Template Matching” plugin to obtain near-perfect image

alignment. More details on these algorithms are provided in the  Methodology section.

Once images are aligned, they need to be stacked together to  create a 3D volumetric reconstruction. Multiple 3D image  analysis software are available as open-source applications on  the web. For our purposes, we chose to use 3D Slicer due to its  extensive set of plugins and data analysis features, as well as its  robust segmentation and the capability to train our own  segmentation models via Machine Learning for semiconductor  FIB-SEM images [5-6].

Figure 1: 3 Main steps involved in typical FIB-SEM 3D  Tomography, and open-source tools used to achieve them in  our method.

Methodology

PyAutoGUI to automate UI controls

Python script using PyAutoGUI was tested out on our FIB-SEM  tool (Thermofisher Helios G4 PFIB UXe system). Although  this tool already had a built-in auto-image collection feature (iSPI – intermittent Switching between Patterning and  Imaging), we also incorporated auto-image collection features  in our script to confirm feasibility of this approach on other  FIB-SEM systems.

In order to setup the script, mouse coordinates were obtained  for different buttons/fields/elements that the script would have  to interact with, using the pyautogui.position() function. Image  snippets were also collected for different UI elements so that  the script could continuously check for these on the screen  during runtime, using the pyautogui.locateOnScreen(). For  example, the script would check whether the progress bar for  the current cross-sectional slice was nearly complete before  moving to the “Snapshot” button to capture an image. Another  approach is to determine the time needed for each crosssectional slice and hard-coding that time interval into the script, such that images are collected periodically at that specified  interval.

A major issue encountered in this process was the gradual loss  of focus on the images as the cross-section continued. Of  course, this could be adjusted manually at specific intervals, but

this would require constant pausing of the ion beam and close  monitoring of the user. To address this, autofocus capability  was added to the Python script. For this autofocus feature, the  script would adjust the SEM focus using mouse controls after a  set number of slices. For our tool specifically, focus was  adjusted by right-clicking and dragging the mouse cursor to the  right for a set distance after a set number of slices. This distance  was calculated via a series of experiments intended to determine  the change in focal point at a specific magnification for a  specific distance (Fig. 2). With this approach, the SEM image  needs to be zoomed out enough to capture the whole crosssection area. Another approach is to magnify the SEM image so  that it only captures the cross-sectional plane, then using a  Python script to periodically shift the beam upwards so that the  cross-sectional plane never drifts offscreen. The interval  between beam shifts and the magnitude of each shift can be  determined by knowing the distance of each cross-sectional  plane from the original/starting plane. In this case, it is  necessary to confirm beforehand whether the beam can shift  upwards enough to capture the whole area, as the lens might  have limited range of shift.

Figure 2: Calibration procedure for the autofocus script – determining magnitude of shift for the mouse cursor to shift  focus for a specific distance. This is later applied to the autoimage collection script.

A brief pseudocode of the automated image collection script  used in our previous tests is given below:

Start cross-sectional milling

Continuously check if progress-bar is complete (compare UI progress bar with image snippet of  complete progress bar)

If progress-bar is complete:

▪ Move cursor to “Snapshot” / “Save  image” button on UI and click

▪ Adjust focus / shift beam using  mouse control

Else:

▪ Keep waiting

The use of PyAutoGUI to automate the FIB-SEM UI also  extends to processes beyond just 3D Tomography. Using  python scripting, we were able to automate deposition of  tungsten caps and alignment markers on a specified area, creating the initial trench into the area of interest etc.

As our tool did not have pre-installed Python support and  because we did not want to modify the tool computer in any  way, all these scripts were first compiled and converted into a

Windows Executable file (using PyInstaller) and then run as an .exe program from a shared network drive, allowing us to  implement these features on the tool with virtually no changes  to the FIB-SEM computer.

Image Alignment using ImageJ

Once the series of FIB-SEM images were collected, they were  loaded into ImageJ as an image sequence. For our applications  we have been using FIJI, a version of ImageJ pre-packaged with  commonly used plugins [2]. By default, FIJI contains a  registration plugin for image alignment of a series of slices, labelled “Linear Stack Alignment with SIFT” [3]. This plugin  proved to be very effective at aligning well-defined, high  resolution FIB-SEM images as close as possible. The quality of  the alignment depended on the quality of the images, as well as  the nature and quantity of distinct features in each slice. We  discovered that using alignment markers, such as shallow  trenches in the overhead tungsten cap or deep cuts in both sides  of the cross-sectional plane, helped to get better alignment  results (Fig. 3).

Figure 3: Alignment markers used for linear stack alignment. Left – deep trench going through the side of the cross-sectional  plane. Right – shallow trenches embedded in the overhead  tungsten cap.

The SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) algorithm  showed consistently good performance in identifying features  through computer vision, but would still occasionally misalign  the images or not obtain perfect alignment. For this reason, another plugin called “Template Matching” was used to define  a certain feature on the cross-sectional plane (such as alignment  markers or an omnipresent feature in the cross-sectional slices) to be used as landmarks for alignment [4]. These 2 plugins were  used in conjunction, sometimes in multiple iterations, to get  proper image alignment for an accurate 3D reconstruction (Fig. 4). However, in some cases, final fine-tuning might require  manual alignment, where the user would have to manually  shift/reposition some of the images to get perfect alignment.

Figure 4: Overview of image alignment – cross-sectional plane  drifts upwards as the area is being cross-sectioned. Prior to 3D  viewing, all planes are required to be brought back to the  original XY coordinates of the starting plane.

3D Reconstruction in 3D Slicer

Once images are aligned, they can be imported into 3D Slicer  as a linear stack. The 3 default views on 3D Slicer allow the  viewing of the image stack from 3 angles. The angle of view  can also be manipulated to observe the image stack from any  other angle. The built-in Segmentation editor of 3D Slicer  allows 3D segmentation of the images via Contrast  Thresholding [7]. Thus, a 3D model can be created for different  features on the cross-sectional slices. Models for different  features can be viewed together to obtain a comprehensive 3D  reconstruction of the entire area. Volume manipulation can be  done to ensure the spacing between images match with the  thickness of each FIB cut, which increases the accuracy of the  3D reconstruction.

Segmented models rendered within the program can allow the  user to grab screenshots of stills or preset model rotations to  provide results of the 3D modeling without needing to output  an object file. Likewise, .obj or .stl files can be generated after  decimating the model to provide an actual 3D object file that is  an acceptably compact file size to be placed in Microsoft  Office, PowerPoint or other reporting programs.

Results

After successful alignment of images, loading them into 3D  Slicer can provide immediate viewing of top-down and  sideways reconstruction view, as shown in Figure 5. It is to be  noted that the 3D model is generated after a certain feature is  segmented (in this case, the metal interconnects were  segmented via Contrast Thresholding). Figure 5b also shows a  more detailed 3D model, where each metal layer is generated as  a separate, distinct segment.

Figure 5: (a) 3D Slicer UI after an aligned stack of images have  been imported and a feature segmented. Clockwise from topleft: cross-sectional view (XZ), 3D model of segment, sideways (YZ) view, top-down (XY) view. (b) 3D model generated from  multiple segments, with each segment corresponding to a metal  layer.

Apart from creating 3D reconstructions of a specific area of a  die, this approach and technique has also been used for 3D  characterization of die-level physical defects, providing more  thorough failure analysis data and expediting root cause  investigations. Some notable case studies where this open  source approach was used to successfully perform FIB 3D  tomographic imaging are given below.

Case 1 – Dielectric Cracking

In this case, optical inspection showed cracking in the dielectric  oxide above a metal layer. TEM imaging on sample 1 at the site  also revealed smaller cracking in the metal layer underneath. On sample 2 (which showed identical crack), progressive FIB  cross-section was done through the entire crack to characterize  it. 3D Tomography was done using our open source toolkit, which showed a comprehensive, three-dimensional view of the  crack progression on the top metal, as well as that of the  secondary, smaller crack on the lower metal layer (Fig. 6).

Figure 6: Clockwise from top-left: (1) TEM image showing  large crack above top metal, and smaller crack on lower metal,

(2) optical top-down image of crack, (3) cross-sectional view of  cracks (original SEM image), (4) top-down tomographic view  of upper crack (reconstructed image), (5) top-down  tomographic view of lower crack (reconstructed image), (6) sideways (YZ) tomographic view of cracks (reconstructed  image).

Case 2 – Silicon Pitting

In this case, stain etching and cross-sectional SCM revealed  abnormal edge profile at PBASE/NSD regions. Silicon pitting  was observed. 3D Tomography was done to create a 3D model  of the silicon pits showing its evolution and progression (Fig. 7).

Conclusions

We have presented a fully open-source workflow to implement  automated 3D tomography capability to a FIB-SEM dual-beam  system. This approach has already been used to perform  successful tomographic reconstructions for high priority failure  analysis investigations. Furthermore, this toolkit can be used  across a wide range of FIB-SEM systems, irrespective of brand  or model. Research is ongoing to implement similar automation  features for in-FIB deprocessing and EDX elemental analysis.

The biggest limitations to this approach currently are: compensation for beam drift, mitigating charging during SEM  imaging, FIB curtaining artifacts, time consuming image  alignment process (depending on quality of images and  alignment markers). To overcome these limitations, we are  currently exploring the use of AI algorithms and training  computer vision (CV)-based models on cross-sectional  features. Incorporating AI with the automation script could  potentially allow the tool to remain aligned after each FIB slice  during the entire period of cross-section, thus compensating for  beam drift and ensuring optimal focus.

 Optimized Ga FIB Lift-Out and Ar Ion Beam Milling for High-Quality STEM-EBIC TEM Specimens

Optimized Ga FIB Lift-Out and Ar Ion Beam Milling for High-Quality STEM-EBIC TEM Specimens

 Authors

 Abstract

High-resolution electrical characterization is critical for failure analysis of advanced semiconductor devices. Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy Electron Beam-Induced Current (STEM EBIC) offers a powerful solution by combining localized electrical property measurements with the highresolution structural and compositional data from transmission electron microscopy (TEM) techniques. Here, our methodology utilizes a Ga focused ion beam (FIB) system followed by post-FIB Argon ion milling, which effectively eliminates damage (amorphous and Ga-implantation) and enhances surface quality. We demonstrate the significant impact of specimen quality on STEM-EBIC contrast, successfully revealing the conductivity and interior electronic structure of multiple finFETs and dopant-related field contrast.

 Introduction

Introduction

Scanning transmission electron microscopy electron beaminduced current (STEM EBIC) is a technique for spatially resolved electrical characterization in semiconductor failure analysis, employing a focused electron beam to induce and measure local currents  [1, 2] . The electron-hole pair (EHP) separation mode of EBIC has been used to map electric fields in semiconductors since the 1960's [1][3]  most commonly in the scanning electron microscope (SEM). The related secondary electron emission electric-beam-induced-current (SEEBIC) mode [1] offers the potential for electronic contrast at atomic resolution [3]  due to the confined excitation volume, particularly in thin STEM specimens at high accelerating voltages. However, STEM EBIC measurements are vulnerable to artifacts introduced during specimen preparation. Ga focused ion beam (FIB) milling is a significant contributor to these issues as it can modify the specimen's electronic properties and surface topography, and therefore its secondary electron emission  [4] . Given the surface sensitivity of SE-based contrast in STEM EBIC, careful specimen preparation is crucial to minimize FIB-induced artifacts, particularly with conductive Ga ions. Previous works  [5, 6]  demonstrated the removal of Ga FIB-induced artifacts by combining Ga FIB preparation and controlled Ar ion beam milling for TEM specimen thinning. This study expands on our prior work  [8] [9] by further exploring how post-FIB Argon ion milling mitigates FIBinduced artifacts in STEM-EBIC. We evaluate its effectiveness across various FIB-prepared TEM specimen geometries, leveraging the common availability of Ga FIB systems. This approach broadens the utility of Ga FIB for preparing contamination-free STEM-EBIC specimens. We also emphasize STEM-EBIC's significant capability in the failure analysis of advanced semiconductors. Specifically, it excels at revealing complex conductivity networks and, crucially, provides a practical and convenient method for dopant-based contrast. Compared to more time-consuming or destructive techniques like atom probe tomography or conductive atomic force microscopy, STEM-EBIC offers a relatively convenient pathway to obtain doping profiles. Here, we further investigate STEM-EBIC's ability to generate dopant-related contrast and the impact of specimen orientation, which is influenced by the region of interest during FIB specimen preparation.

 Discussion

Discussion

Advanced 7 nm device  [TSMC]  with fin field-effect transistors (finFET) was depackaged; from this device, cross-section specimens were created using a Ga FIB tool. Bulk FIB milling was performed at 30 kV, followed by a final 5 kV polish. To investigate the influence of specimen orientation, a set of specimens was lifted out in top-down and inverted configurations and subsequently mounted onto a Si-based STEM EBIC-compatible biasing chip.

 Specimen preparation using the Ga FIB

Specimen preparation using the Ga FIB

A Scios  [Thermo Fisher Scientific]  was used to prepare crosssection TEM specimens. In this system, the electron and Ga ion sources traverse at 52°. Two types of specimens (Figure  1 ), topdown (Figure  1a ) and inverted (Figure  1b ) specimens attached to the Si-based biasing chip were prepared for STEM EBIC analysis.

 References

Figure 1: Scanning electron microscopy images after Ga FIB preparation of the TEM specimen lifted out and attached to Cu half-grid

(a) and the Si-based STEM EBIC compatible biasing chip (b).

The preparation of STEM EBIC specimens here was based on  previous works [8][9]. The same preparation method, on the  same STEM EBIC-optimized biasing chip, was applied to both  top-down and inverted specimens for STEM EBIC analysis. Modification of the top-down and inverted [10] FIB preparation  process was implemented for the specimens attached to the  STEM EBIC chip with most changes involving the extraction  and attachment of the specimen to the biasing chip.

Figure 2 illustrates the modified preparation steps for specimen  lift-out and attachment. As shown in Figure 2a, the biasing chip  was positioned vertically and secured with a clamp-type stub, similar to the orientation of the copper grid prior to specimen  attachment. Importantly, the eucentric position of both the  electron and ion beams was established using the biasing chip  electrodes, ensuring they were centered in the ion beam's view (as depicted in the magnified image of Figure 2a), rather than  aligning with the chip edge.

Following the "J-cut" procedure for specimen lift-out, the stage  was rotated to -15° (Figure 2b). Proper attachment of the  specimen to the biasing device is critical at this stage. Subsequently, the lift-out needle was introduced for specimen  attachment. It is essential to attach the needle to the top surface  of the specimen (Figure 2b) to prevent it from contacting the  biasing chip during subsequent steps. Once attached, the needle  was retracted. With the biasing chip in view and the stage  rotated to -15°, the needle was slowly lowered (Figure 2c) and  positioned so the specimen's right side aligned with the  electrode. As shown in Figure 2d, platinum (Pt) was then  deposited along the right side of the specimen. This ensured a  continuous electrical connection to the biasing chip. Once the  specimen was secure, the needle was cut free. The stage was  then rotated to +15° to prepare for Pt deposition on the  specimen's left side.

Figure 2: Scanning electron microscopy image (a) of the STEM EBIC biasing chip. The proper specimen attachment on the device  electrode using Pt depositions (gray boxes) is shown in (a, bottom). FIB specimen preparation lift-out and attachment steps are shown  as illustrations (b-e) from the electron beam perspective.

For both types of TEM specimens, FIB polishing included critical isolation cuts on specimens mounted on the biasing device. These cuts were made when the specimen thickness ranged from 500 to 900 nm. These isolation cuts are essential for the two-channel STEM EBIC analysis, as they allow for the independent isolation of the substrate and metal electrode connections. As depicted in Figure  3a -b, these connections provide access to the substrate and the top metal lines of the device, respectively. a rectangle milling box was used to perform two distinct cuts:

 Si cut: This cut extended through the FIB capping layer to the silicon (Si) substrate.  Metal line cut: This cut targeted a specific device layer, extending to the Si substrate.

For the top-down specimen, the metal line cut was made at the gate level of the device (Figure  3c ). Conversely, for the inverted specimen, the metal line cut was made on Metal line 1. The milling box on the metal line for the inverted specimen followed a diagonal path (Figure  3d ), reproducing the orientation of the device layer structure. The diagonal orientation of the device layers in the inverted specimen preparation resulted from rotating the specimen 180° before attaching it to the biasing device. Setting the milling direction using the rectangle milling box -Left to Right for the Si cut and Right to Left for the metal line cut -is important in creating a clean surface, preventing electrical shorts.

 Post-FIB milling using a concentrated Ar ion beam

Post-FIB milling using a concentrated Ar ion beam

The Ar ion beam milling system, which has a 600 nm diameter Ar ion beam, was used to thin the FIB specimens to electron transparency. The system includes a LaB6 electron source and electron detectors -a secondary electron detector (SED) and a STEM detector -that provide in situ imaging capability during ion milling. The biasing chip with the FIB specimens was mounted on a specimen holder compatible with the Ar ion beam milling system and the TEM.

The small, concentrated Ar beam was directed towards the top edge of the specimen (arrows in Figure  4a-b ) and milled in a raster pattern. Specimen tilting was performed in positive and negative directions to mill both sides of the specimen. The bottom part of the specimens (Figure  4a ) was milled at 20° with the Ar beam hitting the FIB cap layer. This tilt was selected to more effectively target the specimen, as line-of-sight was limited by the thickness of the chip's Si substrate. On the other hand, the top of the specimens was milled at the lowest tilt of -12° (Figure  4b ). A user-defined milling box of 10 x 5 µm (width x height) was placed in the top of the specimen for the specimens. Decreasing energies were employed from 700 eV to 500 eV for specimen thinning. Reduction in specimen thickness was observed in situ by the change in intensities from bright to dark intensities in the secondary electron detector (SED) images after Ga FIB (Figure  4c  and d ) and after Ar ion milling (Figure  4e  and f) of the top-down specimen and inverted specimens, respectively.

 References

High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) imaging (Figure  5 ) revealed distinct differences in specimen quality based on the milling technique used. The specimen prepared after Ga FIB milling was covered in dark particles on the Si substrate beneath the finFETs (Figure  5a ). In contrast, the Ar ion-milled specimen displayed homogeneous contrast (Figure  5b ), indicating a significant improvement in specimen quality. Further analysis using fast Fourier transform (FFT) corroborated these findings. The FFT acquired from the Si substrate after Ga FIB milling (Figure  5c ) showed a diffused halo in the background, an indicator of an amorphous structure. This suggests that 5 kV Ga FIB milling left behind an amorphous surface layer on the specimen. Conversely, the FFT from the Ar ion-milled specimen (Figure  5c ) lacked this diffused halo, confirming the absence of an amorphous layer. FFT images clearly resolve the Si lattice at the [011] zone axis, as notably confirmed by the measured intensity peaks on their FFTs.

 References

Ga implantation removal was confirmed using energy dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) and current-voltage measurements, as detailed in our previous work  [9] . Furthermore, single-contact SEEBIC images from our prior study  [9] , acquired after Ga FIB and subsequent low-kV Ar ion milling, provided direct evidence of surface Ga contamination removal. SEEBIC's sensitivity to electronic and topographic surface features, created or removed by ion milling, makes it an effective indicator of specimen surface quality.

Improvement in STEM EBIC conductivity and dopantrelated contrast with low-kV Ar ion milling Only one connection to the sample is necessary for obtaining SE contrast with SEEBIC. However, by using two channel connections, SEEBIC uniquely provides conductivity contrast, a feature not found in other TEM-based imaging techniques. This is achieved by monitoring current flow along multiple paths that holes created by SE emission might take to reach ground [1][5]  . In the double-contact STEM-EBIC method, two connections to the specimen (e.g., metal and substrate electrodes as in Error! Reference source not found.) are each hooked up to their own EBIC amplifier. As holes are produced at each pixel, the holes reach ground via one contact or the other, depending on the relative resistance of each path. This allows the resulting SEEBIC conductivity contrast to clearly differentiate the two possible current flow paths.

STEM EBIC effectively revealed conductivity and dopantrelated contrast in the top-down (previous works  [8][9] ) and inverted specimens prepared by Ga FIB, followed by Ar ion beam milling. The low magnification ADF-STEM and STEM EBIC images (Figure  6 ) were colorized to highlight regions which are better connected to either terminal: magenta for the top electrode and green for the substrate. The location of the isolating cut through the substrate into the metal layers (yellow line in Figure  6a  ) and the layout of the metal leads determine where the "conductivity watershed"  [1][5]  lies between the two device terminals. STEM EBIC images (Figure  6b ) revealed the conductivity boundary between the metal and substrate electrodes with the inverted specimen well connected to the metal electrode. Areas on the device, marked in STEM EBIC images (Figure  6b ), were analyzed at higher magnification.

For previously studied top-down prepared devices [8][9] , STEM EBIC measurements show that the device layer has a much stronger connection to the substrate than to the metal leads. In this case, electron-hole pairs generated by the beam in the device layer, even those adjacent to dopant-produced local electric fields, would recombine, resulting in no electric fieldbased EBIC current. In contrast, the substrate-measured STEM EBIC from the inverted Ar ion-milled specimen (Figure  6b ) reveals that this "watershed" of connectivity lies directly on the device layer. This is likely due to reduced surface leakage, as the inverted preparation prevents the redeposition of upper metal layers during milling. This inverted preparation enables efficient carrier separation, directing one carrier to ground via the substrate and its counterpart through the metal connection (each routed through an EBIC amplifier).

An area (marked in Figure  6b ) on the inverted specimen was analyzed at magnification. This area on the inverted specimen exhibits a repeating pattern of alternating bright and dark contrast (Figure  7a ) in the STEM EBIC signals. The observation of equal and opposite components of this repeating signal in both the metal and substrate EBIC channels confirms its origin in electron-hole pair separation, which is indicative of electric field-based EBIC contrast within the devices. We attribute this contrast to the electric fields present at the dopant interfaces of individual devices. Notably, a negative substrate EBIC signal, 18 to 27 nm wide (Figure  7b ), is measured below the source/drain contact at one of the most intense features, consistent with an NMOS device structure correlating to observations using nanoprobes in SEM EBIC  [19] .

 References

Figure 7: High magnification images (a) of a selected area in Figure 6b rotated 180°, showing repeating STEM EBIC contrast at the  source and drain across the device. STEM EBIC images (b), a magnified image from (a), showing black (left, STEM EBIC substrate  signal) and green (right, composite of ADF and inverted STEM EBIC substrate signal) contrasts indicative of measured electrons below  the source/drain contact of the device.

Specimen configuration for STEM EBIC conductivity and  dopant-related contrast

The configuration of a specimen significantly influences  electron-hole separation during STEM EBIC analysis, as  demonstrated by our findings. The secondary electron emission  mode of STEM EBIC, which provides conductivity contrast, is  virtually always present. For measuring the electric field within  a device layer using the "standard" (electron-hole pair  separation) STEM-EBIC mode, the conductivity watershed  should ideally be positioned at the device layer. This ensures  effective separation of electrons and holes, a principle  previously shown with nanoprobes in SEM-EBIC [19].

Observing electron-hole separation is critically dependent on  preparing specimens free from conductive surfaces that could  act as leakage paths. In top-down specimens, the presence of  multiple metal layers creates numerous such surfaces, demanding rigorous cleaning at low-kV and using inert ions by  Ar ion milling. While this approach allows for the observation  of dopant-related conductivity contrast (distinguishing between  electrically active and inactive fins), achieving clear fieldrelated contrast at dopant interfaces is difficult because the  metal layers sit directly above the gates, which can cause  redeposition of conducting material in the Si. Conversely, the  inverted specimen configuration simplifies this challenge  significantly; with only the Si substrate positioned above the  gate structure, there is just one layer to address, making the  removal of conductive surfaces straightforward via low-kV Ar  ion milling, as clearly demonstrated here.

Conclusion

We have shown that post-FIB Ar ion milling after Ga FIB  preparation improves the electronic quality of a specimen for  STEM EBIC analysis. The crucial post-FIB Ar ion milling step  effectively eliminates FIB-induced damage, particularly Ga  implantation, resulting in pristine surface quality as confirmed  by TEM and double-channel STEM EBIC results. An improved  preparation technique allowed for detailed revelation of  conductivity and interior electronic structure showing dopantrelated field contrast in the 7 nm finFET devices. Results show  that the inverted configuration proves superior for capturing

 dopant-related contrasts at gate structures, whereas the topdown approach from our previous work is suitable for analyzing localized conductivity variations
