In Situ Sample Preparation for Nano Probing Using SDB FIB

Jacob Fridburg, Yair Faiershtein, Guy Burg

Marvell Technology Inc., Yokneam, Israel   gburg@marvell.com

Abstract

Nano probing is critical for the design and optimization of  circuits. This high-precision measurement technique, widely  used in failure analysis, uses nanoscale probes to accurately  contact targeted regions, for measuring electrical characteristics  such as current and resistance. To undergo Nano Probing, samples must be subjected to some form of sample preparation, to remove surface layers and to expose the internal target  regions [1] [2]. Sample preparation process may involve  chemical etching and/or physical stripping techniques which  require precise control to avoid damage to the structure and  functionality of the circuit. In situ sample preparation using  Ga+ FIB has significantly advanced the field of nanotechnology  sample preparation. This approach enables the preparation of  accurate, site-specific samples directly within the FIB system, eliminating the need for multiple tools and reducing potential  contamination and handling errors. Additionally, dual beam  FIBs are extremely versatile machines that can perform a wide  variety of tasks. Utilizing an existing Ga+ FIB system would  offer significant cost and operational benefits compared to  purchasing a new Plasma FIB machine. This article presents the  methodology and highlights the benefits of using the SDB FIB  for in situ sample preparation for nano probing, particularly  over traditional mechanical polishing.

Introduction

Mechanical sample preparation has been around for decades. While it is a well proven technique, it is relatively hard to  control when advances technology node samples are being  processed. The ever-shrinking metal layers thickness, combined with the fact that mechanical polishing does not have  real time monitoring of the polished surface (but rather polish/ evaluate/ polish/ evaluate steps), makes it harder to stop the  process on the targeted layer. Focused Ion Beam (FIB) technology has been proven beneficial and successful before [3] for preparing samples for various types of nano probing  analysis. The use of FIB enables real time imaging of the  delayering process and thus providing a more controllable and  repeatable process. Many FA labs already have a Ga+ FIB inhouse. It is commonly used for failure analysis and for circuit  editing. This article details the in situ preparation process using  a standard Ga+ FIB, emphasizing the advantages of this method  over traditional mechanical polishing, and the benefits of using

an existing FIB system over investing in a new Plasma FIB  machine.

Overview of Ga+ FIB Technology

Ga+ FIB machines utilize a focused beam of gallium ions to  mill and image patterns at the nanoscale. This technology is  important for producing accurate, site-specific samples for  further analysis, such as Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM) or Atom Probe Tomography (APT). The Ga+ ions are  particularly effective due to their relatively high mass, which  allows for efficient sputtering of material from the sample  surface.

Proposed sample preparation steps of using Ga+

FIB for in situ sample preparation for nanoprobing:

Initial Sample Preparation:

a. Mounting the Sample: The sample is first mounted on a suitable holder, where a conductive adhesive is used to ensure stability and reduce charging during ion  beam exposure.

b. Coating: A thin layer of conductive material, such as platinum or carbon, is deposited on the sample surface to prevent charging and improve imaging quality.

In Situ Lift-Out Method:

Trenching: Using ion beam, trenches are milled  around the area of interest to isolate the suspected  failed circuit. This step requires precise control to  avoid damaging the region of interest.

Transfer and Attachment

a. Micromanipulator Attachment: A manipulator is attached to a specific location using deposition of Tungsten.

b. Lift-Out: The chunk is carefully lifted from the bulk sample and transferred to a TEM grid, as shown in Fig.

1.

Figure 1: – Silicon chunk containing suspected fail circuit

attached to Easy lift.

c. Thinning: After mounting, the grid is tilted 90 degrees  to allow parallel delayering. The sample is thinned to  isolate the failing circuit to transistor level (typically  stopping at the contacts level) using low ion beam  currents to minimize damage and amorphization as  shown in Fig. 2.

Figure 2: – Sample ready for probing on a TEM grid.

Key Considerations

a. Minimizing Damage:

• Ion Beam Energy: This has been a main  concern when using Ga+ FIB for years with  varying results. However, recent studies have  shown that the use of Ga+ FIB does not  significantly alter measured results SRAM  cells [5]. Furthermore, lowering the ion beam  energy during final thinning steps and, if  possible, the use of Ar. helps furthermore in  reducing damage and amorphization of the  sample [6].

• Beam Incidence Angle: Adjusting the angle  of incidence can help in minimizing the  introduction of defects and to improve the  quality of the prepared sample. Since the

process involves ion beam being parallel to  the sample surface and not perpendicular to  it, we believe it minimizes the Ga+ penetration and accumulation in a way the  affects the integrity of the measurements.

b. Contamination Control:

• Deposition Materials: Using tungsten for  deposition helps in securing the sample without  introducing significant contamination.

• Vacuum Conditions: Maintaining high vacuum  conditions during the FIB process is crucial for  preventing contamination and in ensuring the

integrity of the sample.

c. Versatility: The use of TEM grid enables further  modification of the sample. In our case, we proceeded  with FIB trimming of various areas of the circuit to  verify our test results. We performed this process  twice to make sure it yields the expected results while  maintaining the mechanical integrity of the sample as  shown in Fig. 3.

Figure 3: – Sample after further FIB trimming.

Benefits of In Situ Sample Preparation Using Ga+ FIB Over  Mechanical Polishing

1. Single-Tool Efficiency: The entire sample preparation  process is conducted within the FIB system, reducing the need  for multiple tools, and minimizing handling errors.

2. Reduced Contamination: In situ preparation limits exposure  to external environment, significantly reducing the risk of  contamination. Mechanical polishing often introduces  contaminants from handling and from the slurry itself.

3. Precision and Control: Use of dual beam FIB provides real  time SEM imaging and allows for precise control over the  milling and thinning processes, ensuring high-quality, sitespecific samples. Mechanical polishing can be less precise, leading to uneven surfaces and potential damage to the sample.

4. Time Efficiency: By consolidating the preparation steps  within one system, the overall time required for sample  preparation is reduced. Mechanical polishing is often more

272

time-consuming due to the need for multiple steps and cleaning  processes.

5. Minimized Mechanical Stress: FIB milling applies less  mechanical stress to the sample compared to mechanical  polishing. Mechanical stress can introduce micro-cracks and  other defects due to the abrasive nature of the slurry.

Benefits of Using an Existing FIB Over Buying a New  Plasma FIB:

1. Cost Savings: Utilizing an existing Helios FIB system may  eliminate the significant capital expenditure required for a new  Plasma FIB machine.

2. Operational Familiarity: FA engineers and technicians are  already familiar with the Helios system, reducing the learning  curve and the potential downtime associated with new  equipment.

3. Adequate Performance: For many applications, the Ga+ FIB  provides sufficient performance, making the additional  capabilities of a Plasma FIB unnecessary.

4. Maintenance and Support: Existing Helios systems already  have established maintenance routines and support networks, ensuring continued reliability and performance.

Benefits of Mounting the Sample to a TEM Grid:

1. Ability for repeated Delayering: The sample can be further  thinned and delayered for TEM analysis, allowing detailed  structural analysis at different depths.

2. Versatile Inspection: The mounted sample can be inspected  using various detectors such as Scanning Transmission Electron  Microscopy (STEM), Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDX), and Electron Energy Loss Spectroscopy (EELS), providing comprehensive material characterization.

3. Enhanced Stability: Mounting to a TEM grid provides a  stable platform for high-resolution imaging and analysis, reducing the risk of movement or damage during examination.

4. Improved Accessibility: The TEM grid format allows for  easy handling and transfer between different analytical  instruments, facilitating multi-technique analysis.

Discussion

Nano-probing has become the bread and butter of practically  every FA job. Adequate sample preparation may be, in many  cases, the defining factor between success and failure. As  described in this article, In situ sample preparation using FIB  machine offers significant advantages over traditional  mechanical polishing and provides substantial benefits when  utilizing an existing Helios FIB system compared to investing  in a new plasma FIB. Additionally, mounting the sample to a  TEM grid enhances the ability to continue delayering and  enables versatile inspection with various detectors. By  following the outlined steps and considerations, researchers can  effectively prepare high-quality samples for advanced  analytical techniques, facilitating new discoveries in  nanotechnology.

Our initial incentive in the research was to evaluate the  structural integrity of the sample and make sure it can withstand  the mechanical stress involved with nano probes placement and  measurements. What we have come to realize is that there are  additional substantial benefits to this method:

1. Increased throughput: since the probing itself can be done in  any SEM (or even optical microscope in some cases), the FIB  machine can be utilized to prepare the next samples  simultaneously with the probing process. In more advanced FIB  tools, software like Thermo-Fisher’s auto TEM can be utilized  to automatically prepare the samples overnight.

2. Different layer probing: since the preparation process is sitespecific, signals routed in different metal layers can be  measured. This enables characterization of “vertical” defects  such as resistive vias, which cannot be measured when the  entire sample is planar.

3. Increased e-measurement control: since the sample is  removed from the Silicon bulk, its grounding is controlled via  the TEM grid only. This allows grounding of the substrate (of  the sample only) or eliminating the P- substrate altogether and  connecting it to the grid via N-Well, enabling the verification  of the leakage path. Additional local circuit editing of the  sample can be done to farther investigate the failure.


Conclusions

In this work, the authors presented a novel way to utilize  existing equipment for new sample preparation approaches. We  have found this approach to be time and cost efficient, allowing  high throughput and controllability. This approach helps the  fault isolation on small size of samples. The main drawback of  this method is the upper limit on the sample size to be  processed. Using Ga+ FIB to extract chucks of silicon limits the  sample size to ~50µmX50µm. While bigger samples are harder  to delayer evenly across the entire sample, they allow for  specific delayering of each area so one can measure signals  routed in different metal lines. More work needs to be done to  assure that using Ga+ does not significantly affect the electrical  characteristics of the transistors. This may be addressed in  future research.

Comparison of Manual and Semi-Automated FIB Sample Preparation Techniques  for TEM Characterization of Semiconductor Devices

Jonas Wagner*, Shatadru Chakravarty, Norman R. Fong, Lina Gunawan, Narinder Kaur, Alexander Sorkin, Jie  Yang, Neerushana Jehanathan, Edson Bellido Sosa

TechInsights Inc., 1891 Robertson Rd #500, Nepean, ON K2H 5B7, Canada  *Corresponding Author: jwagner@techinsights.com

Abstract

This paper compares the strengths and weaknesses of a semiautomated dual-beam FIB workflow with a manual TEM  sample preparation process that involves mechanical polishing  and broad-beam ion milling. The two workflows are evaluated  based on TEM sample quality, site-specific targeting ability, and other operational aspects important for their application  within the semiconductor industry. For most devices, both  workflows produce excellent TEM samples that are comparable  with respect to TEM image quality and feature resolution. For  certain devices, however, one workflow can be superior to the  other. For example, the FIB workflow is preferred for devices  sensitive to mechanical damage. The superior targeting ability  achievable in the dual-beam instrument enables the production  of site-specific samples with single-transistor precision, which  is not possible with the manual process. Alternatively, manual  samples are advantageous if a large field of view or multiple  features within a singular cross-section plane with varying  degrees of sample thickness are required. In terms of  operational aspects, the FIB-based workflow is faster overall, allows for better site-specific targeting, requires fewer dies, reduces the amount of instrument operator time needed, and  requires less training time compared to the manual process.

Introduction

With advancing technology nodes, there is an ever-growing  need for high-quality, high-throughput TEM imaging and  TEM-based materials analysis of semiconductor devices for  failure analysis [1], [2], reverse engineering [3], and quality  control [4], [5]. This paper compares a semi-automated FIBbased workflow with a manual sample preparation process that  includes mechanical polishing [6] and ion milling [7], [8]. The  objective of this work is to highlight the strengths and  weaknesses of both techniques and provide guidance on  selecting the optimal approach for specific use cases, depending  on the target feature and device.

The sample preparation techniques are assessed based on TEM  sample quality, the ability to target a site-specific device  feature, and other operational aspects in the context of the  semiconductor industry.

A high-quality TEM sample is electron transparent and thin  enough to isolate the region of interest from overlapping  features when imaged in transmission. The introduction of  sample preparation artifacts, such as amorphization, ion  implantation, and redeposition, is to be minimized. Amorphization [9], [10], for example, manifests as reduced  contrast between adjacent features with originally different  crystal structures, or as contrast variation artifacts in the Si  single crystal substrate during TEM imaging. Moreover, the  diffraction pattern of the intact Si substrate lattice serves as an  important guide for orienting the target feature perpendicular to  the incident electron beam by adjusting the stage tilt in the TEM  in order to facilitate accurate metrology. Ion implantation can  affect compositional analysis by TEM-based electron energy  loss spectroscopy (EELS) and energy-dispersive X-ray  spectroscopy (EDS), especially where the ion species used for  milling is part of the device material, such as GaN power  devices prepared using a Ga+ FIB. Furthermore, TEM samples  should be flat and of uniform thickness without bending or  buckling, to allow for representative measurements of feature  dimensions. Thickness variations in the form of curtaining  artifacts [11] arise from different milling rates of features  oriented parallel to the incident ion beam. They are to be  reduced and redirected away from the principal regions of  interest (ROIs) to minimize their impact on the most critical  measurements.

The requirements for site-specific targeting depend on the  device and target feature characteristics, including size, repetition throughout the die, and reference points accessible  from the die surface. Targeting can be supported by ex situ  techniques and external information, such as through electrical  fault isolation, gate-level images, or a circuit floorplan. If the  precise target location is unknown, iterative milling and  imaging would be necessary to visually identify the target  feature or surrounding landmarks.

In terms of operational aspects, faster sample preparation  coupled with a reduction in failure rate and instrument operator  training time are essential for efficient TEM sample preparation  and TEM analysis turnaround in the semiconductor industry.

 Sample Preparation and Analysis Workflows

Sample Preparation and Analysis Workflows

The principal steps of the manual and FIB-based sample preparation workflows, as well as the main equipment and materials required for each of them, are detailed in Fig.  1 . It is assumed here that the die has been removed from any encasing and that the die surface is accessible. The manual sample preparation process starts with identifying the target region from the exposed die surface using an optical microscope. Next, a die fragment containing the target feature is cut from the intact die and sandwiched with epoxy glue between pieces of Si or glass. Following high-temperature epoxy curing, the resulting sandwich is cut into smaller pieces and mechanically polished using a sequence of abrasive films with decreasing roughness. The sample is then mounted on a grid for final milling using a broad-beam Ar ion mill (Fishione TEM Mill 1050/1051 or Gatan PIPS 691). For the FIB-based workflow, the sample is first prepared for SEM imaging by applying a conductive sputter-coating to reduce charging effects. The target area is then identified from an intact or mechanically polished die using SEM imaging, either directly from the die surface or from exploratory FIB cross-sections milled near the site where the target feature is expected. The lift-out and subsequent thinning of the lamella on the TEM grid post can be performed manually or automated. The state-of-the-art Helios 6 HD DualBeam FIB (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc.) and the AutoTEM v6.2.3 software used for this work feature improved automation capabilities for liftout, thinning, probe alignment, micro-manipulator maintenance, and grid management. This reduces the need for manual user intervention and increases overall sample throughput compared to previous FIB generations. Improved ion and electron columns enable intermittent high-resolution imaging during thinning, allowing for high-precision endpointing. Thinning at ion acceleration voltages of down to 500 V reduces amorphization and is essential for the preparation of sub-20 nm, damage-free TEM samples. An in-chamber flip stage mechanism enables the selection of the optimal lift-out strategy (top-down, inverted, or planar) for each site independently without the need to remove the sample from the chamber. After completing the steps shown in Fig.  1 , the TEM sample is ready for TEM imaging and analysis. The (S)TEM micrographs presented throughout this paper were acquired on ThermoFisher Talos F200E and FEI Tecnai G2 TF20 instruments operated at an acceleration voltage of 200 kV.  TEM Sample Quality

TEM Sample Quality

For most devices, both the semi-automated FIB and the manual workflow generate TEM samples of similar high quality that meet all their requirements in terms of TEM image field of view and sample thickness, the latter typically ranging between 15 to 100 nm, depending on the feature. This is exemplified in Fig.  2  showing cross-sectional TEM micrographs of the gate level of an advanced CPU die taken from a manual (Fig.  2a, b ) and a FIB (Fig.  2c, b ) sample. High-quality TEM images of the fin profile and the source/drain were obtained from both samples. Due to similar ion acceleration voltages routinely used in the final milling step (2.5 kV in the manual process, 2 kV in the FIB workflow), no significant difference in the amorphization layer thickness is apparent from the TEM micrographs. In the FIB workflow, additional low kV cleaning steps at ion acceleration voltages of 1 kV and 500 V can be employed to further reduce amorphization. Furthermore, ion implantation is not found to significantly affect image quality or materials analysis using either workflow.

 References

In addition to cross-sections, the dual-beam FIB enables the automated preparation of planar FIB samples from which planview TEM images can be acquired that exhibit the same high quality as images from manual samples. An example of this is provided in Fig.  3 , showing TEM micrographs of the top MESH of two DRAM devices prepared by the manual (Fig.  3a ) and the FIB-based (Fig.  3b ) workflow. For certain features, the FIB-based workflow produces superior samples than the manual process: For devices sensitive to mechanical damage, FIB samples show reduced cracking or delamination, as the strain imposed during mechanical polishing in the manual sample preparation process is avoided in the FIB-based workflow. A representative example is shown in Fig.  4 , where the wafer bonding interface between the CMOS image sensor (CIS) and the image signal processor (ISP) dies is delaminated in the manually prepared sample and intact in the sample prepared by FIB. FIB samples prepared using a parallel thinning strategy typically feature a more homogeneous thickness across the entire height of the sample compared to manual samples, where a gradually thicker base supports the thinner target areas. Such a thickness gradient can manifest in TEM images as a contrast gradient artifact for tall features and affect other microscopy techniques like differential phase contrast imaging. Different thickness gradients between manual and FIB samples are apparent in the cross-sectional TEM images of the DRAM capacitor array and metal layers shown in Fig.  5a-c . The thickness gradients were quantified from EELS spectra of the SiO2 dielectric layers acquired across the entire height of the samples, the result of which is shown in Fig.  5d . The FIB sample shown in Fig.  5c  features a relatively even thickness ranging from 110 nm at the top to 65 nm at the bottom of the sample. For FIB samples, the thickness gradient can be optimized by adjusting the overtilt angle during lamella thinning, where changes as small as 0.1-0.2° stage tilt can have a significant effect on the thickness gradient. In contrast, the manual sample in Fig.  5a  shows a stronger thickness gradient ranging from ~10 nm at the passivation to ~270 nm at the bottom of the array. Such an increase in sample thickness by about 250 nm for every 5 µm height distance from the sample edge is typical for manual samples. As a consequence of the stronger thickness gradients in manual samples, images of higher layers, such as the SiN layer of the passivation in Fig.  5a , need to be acquired from sections of the sample that are too thick to produce high-quality TEM images of features that are lower down in the sample, such as the edge of the capacitor array. In this case, higher magnification images of such lower features need to be taken from thinner regions of the sample where the upper features have been milled away (Fig.  5b ). Moreover, bending of thin areas is often less pronounced in FIB samples, as a wide variety of optional support structures can be employed to redirect sample load from thinner areas, an example of which is shown in Fig.  5c .

 References

Manual sample preparation is advantageous where overview TEM images of large device features are required. The cases detailed in the next figures include large Al metal processes, 3D NAND array, staircase, and staircase contacts, as well as the interconnects in a stacked die. Figure  6  shows TEM micrographs of a power device from a manual (Fig.  6a, b ) and a FIB sample (Fig.  6c, d ). Lowmagnification images including the large Al top metal (Fig.  6a ) as well as higher-magnification images of the gate level (Fig.  6b ) can be acquired from thicker and thinner regions of the same manual sample, respectively. The FIB sample of the same device (Fig.  6c ), however, is limited to a narrower region to achieve the thickness level and homogeneity required for a high-quality image of the gate level (Fig.  6d ).

Among the tallest device features routinely requiring TEM imaging and analysis are complete 3D NAND arrays for accurate layer counting and measurement. The TEM micrograph of the 3D NAND array acquired from a manual sample and shown in Fig.  7a  features a ~15 × 15 µm field of view. The metal layers both above and below the memory array are not significantly distorted by differential ion milling. Obtaining a similar overview TEM image from a FIB sample would be operationally impractical; instead, it is often more efficient to reduce the sample width to focus on a single vertical array segment during the FIB preparation (Fig.  7b ). In addition, the FIB sample is more homogeneously thin, allowing for highquality, high-magnification images across the vertical length of the sample, such as the contact to the array at the top (Fig.  7c ), and the inter-deck region at the center of the sample (Fig.  7d ). A shortcoming of the FIB sample in this case is the comparatively lower quality of the images acquired around the metal lines below the array, a region that is considerably affected by curtaining produced during the FIB sample preparation. Akin to the DRAM sample presented in Fig.  5a , the manual sample of the 3D NAND array exhibits a stronger thickness gradient than the FIB sample. While the sample region shown in Fig.  7a  is suitable for large overview images and micrographs from the thin region at the top of the array, it is too thick for high-quality, high-magnification images of the inter-deck region or the peripheral transistors. Instead, a gradually thinned region of the manual sample is required to take highmagnification images at individual locations with the desired thickness of the respective features. This exemplifies the advantage of manual samples having an electron-transparent region that is often more than 100 µm wide, allowing for the selection of the optimal imaging site for each device feature. Figure  8  illustrates how, over a width of ~80 µm, optimal regions are selected for imaging of the contact to the array (Fig.  8a ), inter-deck region (Fig.  8b ), and peripheral transistor (Fig.  8c ). This strategy is enabled by the combination of vertical (as demonstrated in Fig.  5d ) and lateral thickness gradients common in manual samples. Here, the sample thickness below the gate level laterally decreases from ~280 nm at location A to ~ 48 nm at location B (Fig.  8d ).

The staircase in  this 3D NAND device was imaged with a field of view of ~135 × 17 µm from a manual sample. This example illustrates  that, in certain cases, the most effective approach is to prepare  a manual sample with an extensive electron-transparent region  that cannot be achieved with FIB.

In summary, manual samples typically feature electrontransparent regions up to 100-250 µm wide and up to 10-15 µm  high, where the region within ~2 µm from the sample edge  reaches a thickness below 100 nm. While a shallower thickness  gradient can be achieved by adjusting the ion beam incidence  angle during the final milling stage, the likelihood of large  thinner sample areas bending and possibly covering  surrounding features is also increased.

Using parallel thinning, FIB samples about 3-5 µm wide and up  to 5-10 µm tall are routinely and efficiently prepared with a high  success rate. Increasing the width to about 10 µm increases the  likelihood of sample bending or buckling. Extending the sample  width to about 15 µm or the sample height to 15-20 µm during  parallel thinning usually requires a compromise in terms of  sample thickness; a thickness of 100 nm or less is likely not  achieved at all locations within the sample.

Employing wedge thinning (e.g., thinning with a higher overtilt  angle), the width of the FIB sample can be increased with  decreased likelihood of sample bending compared to parallel  thinning, as the thicker portion at the top of the sample serves  as a self-support for the thinner region at the bottom. The width  of wedge samples typically ranges between 8 and 12 µm but  can be extended to 20-30 µm. The height of the electrontransparent region, however, is significantly reduced in a wedge  sample compared to a sample prepared by parallel thinning. A  sample thickness below 100 nm is typically achieved in the  region within 1 µm distance from the sample edge, much like  what is attainable through manual preparation methods.

In addition to the required field of view, the presence of ion milling artifacts is an important consideration when selecting the optimal sample preparation strategy for a specific target feature. The manual preparation process often produces samples with fewer curtaining artifacts for devices where features with different milling rates are oriented parallel to the incident ion beam. Such curtaining-inducing features are often encountered in the back end of line (BEOL) structures, where lower milling rate materials, such as W, Cu, and Ta, are used for contacts, metals, and metal liners that reside within dielectric materials with higher milling rate, such as SiO2. Figure  10  compares the severity of curtaining artifacts found in typical samples of the BEOL of different semiconductor devices prepared using the manual (Fig.  10a, b ) and the FIBbased workflow (Fig.  10c, d ). For the manually prepared sample of the processor die (Fig.  10a ), curtaining is virtually absent from the first 11 metal layers, despite the stacked nature of the metals creating vertical "channels" of dielectric materials that are expected to be prone to curtaining. While the curtaining is more pronounced in the top-down FIB sample of the CIS die (Fig.  10c ) compared to the manual sample (Fig.  10a ), the overall severity of curtaining within the metal layers is low and does not impede the precise measurements of metal and dielectric layer dimensions. The comparison between Fig.  10c  and Fig.  10d  illustrates the importance of selecting the appropriate lift-out and thinning strategy during FIB sample preparation depending on the target ROI: While the metal layers show little curtaining, the gate level is more severely affected by curtaining in the sample prepared by top-down lift-out and parallel thinning (Fig.  10c ). In contrast, no curtaining at the gate level is apparent for the FIB sample prepared using an inverted lift-out strategy and wedge thinning (Fig.  10d ). Higher metals, however, are absent from this sample. Sample thickness variations due to differential ion milling are not exclusive to FIB samples, as both workflows employ ion milling as the final step. An example of curtaining-like artifacts in a manual sample is shown in Fig.  10b , where streaking is visible in the passivation of the DRAM die. The differential milling of the large Al top metal is exacerbated by the narrow gap between adjacent metal lines and the presence of voids due to incomplete filling of the gaps with dielectric material in the manufacturing process of the die. In this case, images with fewer artifacts could potentially be acquired from a FIB sample (compare Fig.  5c ). In addition, the FIB-based workflow offers the flexibility to cut off potentially curtaining-inducing features around the target area using FIB milling, if only a narrow field of view is required. TEM imaging and analysis of large contacts and interconnects are examples where manual sample preparation is advantageous, considering both the required field of view and their curtaining susceptibility, which is illustrated in Fig.  11 . The complete interconnect in the stacked die, together with the metal layers on both sides, was imaged from the manual sample (Fig.  11a ), while only a restricted field of view was practical for the FIB sample (Fig.  11c ). From the manual sample of the 3D NAND staircase region shown in Fig.  11b , several adjacent staircase contacts with heights up to 12 µm were imaged, in contrast to the one, ~5 µm high, contact in the FIB sample (Fig.  11d ). In both cases, the FIB samples exhibited significantly more curtaining at the bottom of their tall features due to their lower milling rate compared to the surrounding dielectric material and their parallel orientation with respect to the incident ion beam.

Site Specificity & Targeting Ability

Compared to the FIB-based workflow, site-specific targeting in  the manual sample preparation process is more challenging, as  the position of the sample cross-section relative to the die is  commonly observed only from the top and only using optical  microscopes during polishing. However, the targeting of feature  blocks at least 150 µm wide is routinely carried out; targeting  smaller feature blocks with a width of down to 50 µm is  possible, albeit associated with a higher failure rate. An  accuracy of 5-10 µm within a targeted block can be achieved  by iterative polishing and cross-section imaging. By preparing  the cross-section at a 1-2° angle with respect to the feature  orientation (e.g., word line direction in DRAM), features from  numerous subsequent planes in the target block are captured  within the same manual sample without noticeable effect on the  appearance of the feature in the TEM image. This is beneficial  for features that are difficult to identify from SEM images  during FIB preparation (e.g., targeting of PMOS vs. NMOS  transistors) or infrequent features whose location is unknown  and cannot be identified from the top metal or gate level die  image.

An example of the latter are resistors (Fig. 12), which are  typically found between intermediate metal layers where their  coordination with the surrounding features does not follow an  obvious repetitive pattern.

Figure 12: Example of infrequent features found in manual  samples. TEM micrograph of a resistor observed between  intermediate metal layers in a processor die.

Processed plan-view SEM images of (c) Metal 10 and (d) Metal 9 used to identify the location for the initial FIB crosssection cut. (e) Cross-sectional SEM image of the target area  exposed by FIB milling at the location marked by the blue line  in (c) and (d).(f) SEM image of the FIB sample prepared from  the target area. In contrast, the FIB-based workflow allows for easier sitespecific TEM sample preparation with single-transistor  precision. Figure 13 illustrates the targeting of a specific lownoise amplifier transistor (Fig. 13h) from the radio frequency  transmitter die shown in Fig. 13a. Precise stage movement in  the dual-beam instrument assists in getting closer to the target  area from any reference point on the die (e.g., die corner) with µm accuracy over a distance of several mm. High-resolution  SEM and FIB imaging enable precise positioning of the lift-out  area by measuring the distance of the target feature from other  features visible from the plan-view image of the die surface (e.g., top metal for an intact die). Iterative FIB cross-section  milling and SEM imaging can be beneficial to confirm the  correct lift-out position by referencing smaller unique features  from the exposed cross-section, such as recognizable patterns  of lower metals or transistor blocks. During final lamella  thinning, exact end-pointing is facilitated by high-resolution  SEM images, taken at regular intervals while milling.

Operational Aspects

The FIB-based sample preparation workflow has numerous  advantages in terms of operational requirements in the context  of the semiconductor industry. For example, the overall time for  the preparation of a TEM sample from start to finish is  significantly reduced. Manual samples require an average of  about 8 h, usually spread over two days to allow for thorough  curing of the epoxy glue, whereas a FIB sample is usually  prepared in less than half of this time. The automated lift-out  capabilities significantly contribute to this reduction in overall  sample preparation time, and further reduce the fraction of that  time during which an operator needs to be present. This allows  to increase throughput by automating multiple sites overnight  or operating the system remotely. The instrument has the  potential to further maximize productivity by fully automating  lift-out and thinning, with maximum benefits expected for the  repeated analysis of smaller features from multiple precisely  defined locations, potentially from different dies. In addition, the operator time spent on maintenance activities is  significantly reduced through automatic probe alignments and  automatic sharpening of the micromanipulator, the latter  reducing the frequency of needle exchanges.

Moreover, the FIB-based workflow has a reduced failure rate  compared to the manual preparation process. However, for both  methods, success rates are dependent on operator experience. A  contributing factor to the lower failure rate in the FIB workflow  is the ability to observe thinning in situ by SEM imaging, which  allows for stopping the milling as soon as the target area is  reached or at the first signs of reduced structural integrity of the  sample.

In addition, FIB samples are more robust and less prone to  breakage during handling and loading into the TEM holder. There is no pressure directly on the FIB sample when the TEM  grid is clamped due to the lamella being attached in one plane  with the grid posts. The manual sample, in contrast, is attached  on top of the TEM grid and thus exposed to the full clamping  pressure at its edges. Figure 14 shows typical damage in a  manual sample, where part of the thinned section has broken off  and a crack is present in the region above the staircase contacts,

making the sample susceptible to further mechanical damage  during handling.

While manual samples require significant portions of a die (about 2 × 3 mm on average), the beam damage to the die  surface during FIB lift-out is usually confined to an area within  less than 20 µm around the lift-out site, thus enabling numerous  lift-outs from the same die for repetitive target features. Together with the decreased failure rate, this reduces the  number of dies necessary for a reverse engineering project, which is particularly important for expensive or hard-to-source  devices, such as advanced AI servers.

Figure 14: Typical damage in a manual sample. TEM  micrograph of the staircase area from a 3D NAND die showing  a crack through the sample, and a section where the thinned  sample region has broken off.

As exemplified in Fig. 8, different features are often imaged at  different locations across the entire width of the manual  samples due to local thickness variations. If no sufficiently thin  region is found for a specific feature, the sample is re-milled  until the desired thickness is achieved at the required location. In this process, however, previously thin areas near the sample  edge are removed. If further analysis of features in those areas  is required at a later time, an entirely new sample needs to be  prepared. In contrast, iterative milling is not typically employed  for FIB samples, and analysis can be repeated at any time.

Furthermore, the training time to reach proficiency in sample  preparation is significantly reduced for the FIB-based  workflow. Without prior experience, FIB operators can reach  proficiency for a variety of samples within a few weeks to a few  months, while manual sample preparation requires training over  several months, and proficiency is reached after a year or more. Automation capabilities can be accessed without the need for  programming skills via the AutoTEM software, which features  an intuitive graphical user interface. In addition, expert training  and sample-specific advice are available from the instrument  manufacturer.

Operational advantages of the manual sample preparation  workflow are, in part, based on the larger thinned area that  allows for targeting different features more than 100 µm apart  within the same sample. This reduces the number of samples (and, therefore, the sample preparation and analysis time and

 Abstract

cost) for devices with several regions of interest that are located within a singular cross-sectional plane. In addition, the manual process involves lower capital equipment investment than the FIB-based workflow but requires a higher number of different instruments to be sourced and maintained (see also Fig.  1 ). The FIB-based workflow requires the dual-beam instrument and a sputter coater to apply a conductive coating, whereas the manual workflow employs a saw, hot plate, oven, polisher, ion mill, and optical microscope for visual inspection of the sample.

 Conclusions

Conclusions

The partially automated state-of-the-art FIB workflow allows for the high-throughput production of high-quality TEM samples, where the sample quality is generally on par with manually prepared samples using a traditional process consisting of mechanical polishing and ion milling. Compared to the manual process, the FIB-based workflow is overall faster, allows for better site-specific targeting, requires fewer dies, reduces the amount of instrument operator time needed, and requires less training time. For specific devices, particularly for those sensitive to mechanical damage, the FIB sample quality is superior compared to manual samples. The production of site-specific samples with single-transistor precision, not achievable in the manual process, is enabled by the superior targeting ability in the dual-beam instrument. Manual samples, however, are preferred if a large field of view or multiple features from the same cross-section plane with varying thickness requirements are needed. As a result of establishing the new FIB workflow, sample production at TechInsights Inc. shifted from primarily manual to a combination of FIB and manual processes, depending on the specific device and feature.

Identification of Counterfeit Integrated Circuits Using a Low-Cost  Near-Field Microprobe Scanning Setup

Michael Kögel, Sebastian Brand, Sebastian Tismer, Frank Altmann

Fraunhofer IMWS, Halle, Germany

Adrian Juwien

Deutsche Bahn AG, Halle, Germany

Abstract

The threat posed by counterfeit electronics has grown since the  2020 supply‑chain shutdown, increasing the necessity for a fast, non‑destructive method that flags suspect parts with high  confidence. This paper describes a custom, low‑cost, two‑dimensional near‑field‑scanning system that uses self‑built  electromagnetic probes and streamlined signal‑processing  software to identify relabelled or cloned integrated circuits by  their unique emission footprints. Case‑study measurements on  known relabelled and cloned samples of type STM32 and FTDI  with verification by X-Ray imaging demonstrate the setup’s  effectiveness and simplicity for routine counterfeit screening.

Introduction

Counterfeit Electronics

Counterfeit integrated circuits (ICs) permeate every tier of  electronics - from low-cost gadgets to life-critical medical and  defense systems [1]. These fake parts erode safety and  reliability while causing substantial financial losses. After a  brief dip in reported incidents during the COVID-19  supply-chain shutdown of 2020, ERAI data show that  submissions rose again from 2022 to 2024 - even though overall  semiconductor sales were trending downward [2].

Counterfeiters employ several tactics. The devices are merely  remarked, relabeled or recycled, while complete products get  fabricated as “clone” ICs: parts that imitate the form factor and  ostensibly, the function of a genuine device. Clone chips may  come from unauthorized fabs using stolen masks or from  opportunistic workshops that copy the package markings while  filling the package with inferior silicon. Lacking rigorous test  and quality-control procedures, these parts exhibit high failure  rates in the field [1], [3].

Detecting counterfeit devices involves a tiered sequence of  physical, electrical, and chemical tests. The process begins with  non‑destructive screening - visual inspection for sanding marks, black‑topping or poor legends [4], followed by X‑ray and  scanning‑acoustic microscopy (SAM) to reveal internal  package features and basic functional or electrical checks. If  suspicion remains, analysts escalate to destructive forensics

such as decapsulation, microscopic die inspection and advanced  materials analysis to confirm authenticity.

Standards such as SAE AS6171 and its European  counterpart IEC / EN 62668-1 and -2 define graded test flows  that let organisations match cost and rigour to the risk profile of  incoming parts [5], [6]. Independent distributors have expanded  on-site labs with X-ray, XRF, high-magnification optics and  automated handlers to keep pace. Yet traditional techniques still  fall short against high-fidelity clones whose die layouts deviate  only subtly or not at all, from authentic silicon. Destructive  approaches are slow and costly, making them impractical for  high-volume incoming inspection [7]. This motivates the search  for rapid, preparation-free, non-destructive methods that can  flag suspect parts with high confidence.

Electromagnetic Near‑Field Scanning

Electromagnetic near-field scanning (NFS) maps the reactive  E- and H-fields that exist within roughly λ⁄6 of active conductors and complete circuits. Because these fields are tightly coupled to on-die current paths, their spatial distribution is dictated by the chip’s metal stack, package geometry, and process technology. The resulting field map therefore acts as a persistent, layout-specific “fingerprint”, even when the device is fully over-moulded [7], [8], [9], [10]. Modern probes offer sub-millimetre footprints, enabling fine-grained images of the device under test (DUT). IEC TS 61967-3 (Surface Scan Method) standardizes probe transfer functions, calibration procedures, and reporting formats up to 6 GHz, ensuring data can be compared across laboratories [12].

Near-field scanning is well established for EMC compliance, silicon debug and hardware-security research; its use in  detecting counterfeits and clones has increasingly become  interesting [13], [14], [15], [16]. The near-field microprobe “fingerprints” the tiny magnetic- (H-) or electric- (E-) field that  leaks from active nets inside an IC. Because the exact geometry  of metal layers, vias, and transistors is unique to each layout (and to each foundry process), the field pattern forms a  reproducible signature. If a device is cloned, over-produced, or  remarked, subtle layout or process differences distort that  signature often enough to separate genuine from fake parts. Published case studies rely on commercial scanning platforms,

https://doi.org/10.31399/asm.cp.istfa2025p0284

whose integrated RF front ends and probes together cost well  over €10 000. Although references to lower-cost variants exist, none address the specific application of detecting counterfeit  electronics [17], [18], [19].

This paper introduces a low-cost near-field-scanning setup for  counterfeit detection that combines five self-built E- and  H-field micro-probes made from semi-rigid coax cables, off-the-shelf RF components, an inexpensive scanning rig with  a simple control software. In a single pass the system records  high‑resolution electromagnetic “fingerprints” of a device  under test. The probes are carefully designed and characterized  on custom demonstration structures to quantify lateral  resolution and signal‑to‑noise ratio. Finally, the complete setup  is validated on representative test targets, including cloned  STM32 microcontrollers and counterfeit FTDI USB‑to‑serial  converters, demonstrating a practical, non‑destructive first‑line  inspection tool for high‑volume workflows.

Methods and Samples

Electromagnetic NFS Setup

Two‑dimensional NFS measurements were carried out with a  custom system developed at Fraunhofer IMWS (Halle, Germany). The experimental setup, shown in Figure 1, included  an E-field or H-field micro-probe, a 50 Ω  pre‑amplifier/anti‑alias filter, a motorized three‑axis  positioning stage and a PC‑based data‑acquisition unit  controlled from MATLAB®. Probe positioning was  accomplished with a commercial XYZ scanner (ITK, Lahnau, Germany) driven by in‑house software for synchronized  motion. The probe was mounted on the Z‑stage so that its  field‑sensitive axis pointed normal to the sample surface. A  probe–sample gap of ~100  µm was maintained throughout the  non‑contact scans (Figure 2). The probe output was fed through  a 50 Ω micro‑coax line to a low‑noise amplifier (Mini‑Circuits, 38 dB gain). The amplified signal was digitized by an RF‑ADC  card (Spectrum GmbH, 5 GS s⁻¹, 8‑bit vertical resolution, 2 GHz analog bandwidth) installed in the host PC.

For cost estimation, the setup components were primarily  sourced from existing lab equipment, such as a  decommissioned XYZ stage from a scanning acoustic  microscope (SAM). Although such scanners can cost several  thousand euros, comparable results can be achieved using lowcost, open-source platforms like the MPCNC [20] (~€500). RF  amplification was integrated using commercially available lownoise amplifiers with 30–40 dB gain; suitable modules can be  acquired for under €200. For signal digitization, while we used  a high-performance ADC card from the SAM system, secondhand oscilloscopes or spectrum analyzers with sufficient  bandwidth (e.g., Tektronix TDS, HP Infinium) are available in  the €500–€700 range. Overall, a fully functional setup  including scanner, amplifiers, digitizer, cables and adapters can  be assembled for approximately €1500 - assuming no prior lab  infrastructure is available.

Each scan consisted of a 125 × 125 raster. At every pixel, the  system captured 1 × 10⁵ time‑domain samples at 0.625 GS/s.

Given the short per-pixel record length at the selected sample  rate, the probe did not need to dwell at each position: sampling  was performed in continuous-scan mode while the transducer  moved. Consequently, total scan time per map was on the order  of minutes, depending on scanner speed.

A Hann window was applied to the acquired signals, followed  by a transformation to the frequency domain using a Fast  Fourier Transform (FFT). The amplitude at a user‑selected  frequency bin was then mapped to a false‑colour image (scale  in dB) to visualise subtle spatial variations across the chip  surface. The procedure for generating a spectral image from the  sampled voltage values, along with a result from a test sample  containing a single trace excited by a Gaussian pulse to produce  a broadband field, is shown in Figure 3.

E-field and H-field microprobes

The micro-probes were fabricated from 50 Ω semi-rigid coaxial  cable terminated with SMA connectors, allowing them to  mount directly to the pre-amplifier located on the XYZ stage.

Figure 1: Photograph of the experimental setup. The XYZ-stage of a  repurposed acoustic microscope is used to position the near-field  sensor with an attached RF amplifier. The scanner’s trigger output  and the RF amplifier output are connected to the RF-ADC card in the  host PC for data acquisition.

Figure 2: Photograph of the measurement setup: a development board  containing an FTDI device under test is mounted on the stage, while  the H-field probe is held perpendicular to the scanning plane at a  constant height above the die surface.

The aluminimum outer conductor has a diameter of 3.5 mm  with an inner core diameter of 1.5 mm. The isolation barrier  between is made of Teflon. For the E-field sensor, the probe  acts as a monopole: approximately five millimetres of the outer  conductor and dielectric were stripped away, leaving the centre  conductor exposed. That length is close to one-quarter  wavelength at about 15 GHz, so the open-circuited tip sits near  resonance and couples the incident electric field capacitively  with maximum efficiency.

The magnetic near-field sensors were built as cylindrical  air-core coils, each wound from 200 µm enamelled copper wire  on a dedicated jig to control the loop diameter before being  hand-soldered to the coaxial feed. A larger loop area increases  both the inductance and the open-circuit output voltage, so the  probe intercepts more magnetic flux and delivers a higher  signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which in turn improves sensitivity  to weak emissions. The downside is greater susceptibility to  environmental interference, as the same sensitivity also couples  unwanted signals. Spatial resolution follows the opposite trend: in near-contact operation the lateral resolution is roughly  one-half of the coil’s inner diameter, making small loops  advantageous when imaging fine current paths. To measure the

Figure 3: Illustration of the spectral amplitude mapping process using  near-field H-field probe measurements. The top panel shows the timedomain voltage signal (in mV) acquired at a single pixel location. Applying a fast Fourier transform (FFT) to this signal yields its  spectral content. The bottom panels display spectral amplitude maps  at selected frequencies, where each pixel encodes the amplitude of the  corresponding frequency component. This approach enables  visualization of the spatial distribution of frequency-specific emissions  from the device under test.

vertically emitted field component, the coils were mounted  horizontally to measure field from current densities in lateral  direction of the DUT. In case of larger loops, it is necessary to  include a broadband impedance matching network to reduce the  large inductance at the sensor output and to reduce reflections  and increase the power transfer for better SNR.

Table 1 summarizes the five sensor tips - one E-field probe and  four H-field probes - whose differing tip geometries yield  distinct signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) and lateral resolutions.

Figure 4: Optical micrographs compare an STMicroelectronics  STM32F103CBT6 microcontroller (left) with a GD32F103CBT6  from GigaDevice (right), a pin-, peripheral- and largely  register-compatible clone that is sometimes illicitly remarked as an ST  part to command higher prices.

interfaces - features that have made it a staple in both industrial  and hobbyist designs. The GD32F103CBT6 from GigaDevice  is a register‑level, pin‑compatible drop-in replacement or clone  built on the same core but clocked at up to 108 MHz, with the  same nominal 128 kB flash and 20 kB SRAM. Because the  GD32 sells for roughly €0.97, compared with about €9.87 for  the ST part, it is sometimes illicitly remarked as an STM32  device and inserted into trusted supply chains to capture the  higher margin associated with the ST brand.

The microcontroller was soldered to evaluation boards  containing voltage regulators and additional necessary  peripherals for running the controller in the simplest possible  way. To isolate device-level electromagnetic signatures, both  microcontrollers were loaded with minimalist firmware that  forces a clock-only operating mode: the main oscillator (or PLL  reference) is enabled, but the CPU core is held in reset and all  peripheral inputs are fixed. In this state no instructions are  fetched; only the clock-distribution network and a handful of  always-on circuits toggle, yielding a clean, reproducible  emission baseline for comparative scanning.

Sample 2: STM32 F103C6T6A

The same measurement procedure was repeated using another  two devices from the STM32 product family (see Figure 5). The  STM32F103C6T6A from STMicroelectronics is a 32‑bit  ARM Cortex‑M3 microcontroller operating at up to 72 MHz. It  integrates 32 kB of flash memory and 10 kB of SRAM and  provides a rich set of peripherals including USB FS, CAN 2.0 B, multiple 12‑bit ADCs, and several serial interfaces, making it popular in cost-sensitive embedded applications.

The original part was purchased directly from  STMicroelectronics at a unit price of €8.70, ensuring a trusted  source. The potential counterfeit device was sourced from a  third-party vendor on AliExpress for €0.46. Optical inspection  of the latter revealed no suspicious signs of rework or  desoldering, such as solder residue or pin deformation, suggesting it is not a recycled component. Furthermore, the  packaging quality and marking precision appear comparable to  the original, making it unlikely to be a crude fake or low-cost  imitation. These observations point to the possibility of a  relabeled or cloned device, where an alternative microcontroller  has been rebranded to masquerade as the STM32F103C6T6A. Both devices were soldered to identical evaluation boards  equipped with voltage regulation and minimal peripheral

Sample 3: FTDI FT232RL

The third measurement sample focuses on the FT232RL, a  widely used USB-to-UART interface IC from Future  Technology Devices International (FTDI). This device serves  as a signal bridge between USB and serial protocols, supporting  up to eight data lines for serial communication and achieving  data transfer rates of up to 3 MBaud in both directions. An  internal quartz oscillator enables system clock frequencies of  6 MHz, 12 MHz, 24 MHz, and 48 MHz. Owing to its  widespread use in peripheral devices for PCs and embedded  systems, the FT232RL has become a frequent target for  counterfeiting, with numerous third-party clones and relabeled  devices circulating in the supply chain.

The Original part was purchased directly from FTDI at a unit  price of €5.26, while the Counterfeit device was acquired from  a vendor on AliExpress for €0.95 (see Figure 6). The counterfeit  is known to be a reverse-engineered reproduction of the original  chip, featuring its own microcode and requiring the use of a  generic USB CDC driver—commonly referred to as “Chinese  drivers.” The device is a well-documented clone, widely  recognized in hardware security and embedded systems  communities.

Both devices were mounted on identical evaluation boards for  testing. To stimulate measurable electromagnetic emissions, a  PC was connected to the USB interface of each board. Using

The RX  and TX pins were internally connected, enabling the transmitted  data to be echoed back to the PC. This setup ensured sustained  activity on the USB and UART interfaces, maximizing  switching events within the device’s internal logic and clock  domains and producing a robust electromagnetic signature  suitable for comparative near-field scanning.

Results and Discussion

In the measurements presented here, the magnetic near-field (H-field) probes provided the clearest insight. The electric-field  probe (Probe 1) was used to generate field maps, but its larger  footprint and higher susceptibility to ambient interference lower  the SNR. In contrast, the smallest H-field sensor (Probe 2) delivers the best spatial resolution and exhibits much better  noise performance. Therefore, most fingerprint comparisons  between original and suspect ICs that follow are based  primarily on data acquired with Probe 2. All scans used a 125 × 125 raster. At each pixel, 10 k timedomain samples were acquired at 0.625 GS/s. With the XYZ  stage employed, the total acquisition time per scan was at most  3 min. Each measurement was repeated with the same  configuration to confirm repeatability and to ensure the maps  were not affected by random ambient electromagnetic fields.

Sample 1: STM32 and GD32

Figure 7 compares the near-field scanning (NFS) data for the  two devices. Mapping the maximum amplitude across the entire  near-field spectrum reveals a distinct electromagnetic signature  aside from minor shifts caused by their different clock  frequencies. Since both parts were running identical clock-only  firmware - any observed differences in the amplitude maps can  be attributed solely to variations in silicon layout and package  construction. These differences provide a robust and  unambiguous basis for distinguishing the devices. Note that  both quantitative maps share the same colour scale (–70 dBV to -56 dBV), allowing direct visual comparison.

White circles in Figure 7 highlight regions where the field maps  differ significantly, indicating that the current density  distribution at the die level is markedly different. The two  devices therefore differ substantially at die level. If the  observed field variations were confined only to the edges, they  could be attributed to differences in IC packaging. However, since prominent differences also appear in the central die  region, it is evident that the silicon layouts themselves diverge  markedly.

For verification, X-ray images were taken and Figure 8 further  illustrates differences in package construction. Variations in  lead frame geometry and bond wire arrangements are clearly  visible, particularly in the GD32 device, where a notable  number of bond wires are concentrated toward the center of the  die.

Right column: corresponding maximum-amplitude  map for the GD32F103CBT6 (top) and the same map overlaid on an  optical micrograph of the device (bottom). The white circles indicate  general differences in the field maps.

To further substantiate these findings, Figure 9 presents die  photographs obtained from [19], showing the internal silicon  layouts of both devices. The Original STM32F103CBT6  features a monolithic die with a densely packed layout covering  nearly the entire die area. In contrast, the GD32F103CBT6  employs a stacked-die architecture: a larger die implements the  microcontroller’s functional blocks, while a smaller die, mounted on top, provides flash memory. The two dies are  interconnected via bond pads. These results confirm that the  GD32F103CBT6 is probably a reverse-engineered clone of the  STM32F103CBT6, with substantial silicon and package  differences that are detectable using the near-field scanning  method.

Sample 2: STM32 F103C6T6A

The same measurement procedure was repeated for two  STM32F103C6T6A microcontrollers sourced from different  suppliers and the resulting near-field emission maps are  presented in Figure 10. White circles highlight dominant  differences in the field intensity distributions, suggesting that  the underlying silicon designs differ substantially. Such  pronounced variations in the current density patterns and  resulting electromagnetic emissions are unlikely to arise from  packaging effects alone and instead point to significant  differences at the die level.

In contrast, differences in packaging between the two devices (Figure 11) appear to be minor. Variations are observed in the  geometry of the lead frames, while the bond wire configurations  are surprisingly similar, showing little deviation between the  two samples. Additional differences can be identified in the die  attach region, where variations in attachment methods or  materials may also contribute to subtle differences in the  thermal and electrical characteristics of the packages.

The pronounced variations in the near-field emissions strongly  indicate that the suspect device is not an original  STM32F103C6T6A. While external inspection revealed no  signs of rework or poor marking quality, the clear differences  in electromagnetic fingerprints suggest either a relabeled  alternative microcontroller or a functional clone with a  divergent die architecture. The findings highlight that even  visually identical parts can conceal significant internal  discrepancies, which the near-field scanning approach can  reliably detect.

Sample 3: FTDI FT232RL

Near-field emission measurements of the FTDI FT232RL  devices were performed using Probe 2 and subsequently  repeated with Probe 5 to address the low signal-to-noise ratio  observed with the high-resolution H-field probe. The reduced  SNR is probably attributable to the device’s low power  consumption and low operating frequency, which yield weak  electromagnetic emissions. To mitigate this, using a probe with  a larger loop area increases SNR at the expense of spatial  resolution in subsequent measurements.

The resulting field maps are shown in Figure 12. In contrast to  the STM32 samples, the near-field emissions of the Original  and Counterfeit devices appear remarkably similar. Only a few  localized differences, marked by white circles, are visible, suggesting subtle variations in current density distribution  rather than pronounced disparities in silicon or packaging  design. Measurements were repeated multiple times to ensure  that these differences are reproducible and not artifacts of  random fluctuations or environmental noise.

The near-identical emission patterns indicate that, at the  resolution of the near-field scans, no major differences in  internal circuit operation or clock distribution networks are  detectable. This observation is consistent with the Counterfeit  device being a reverse-engineered clone of the FT232RL, designed to mimic its functional behaviour closely.

Figure 13 provides X-ray images of both devices, revealing  differences in package construction. Variations are evident in  the lead frame geometry and the arrangement of bond wires. Notably, the die sizes also differ, inferred from the bond wire  connection points, suggesting significant differences in the  underlying silicon designs. These findings reinforce the  assumption that the Counterfeit device employs an  independently developed die architecture rather than being a  relabeled Original.

Although near-field emissions reveal only subtle variations, Xray imaging confirms notable die size and bond wire differences  consistent with a reverse-engineered clone of the FT232RL. This suggests that while the counterfeit device achieves a high  degree of functional mimicry - evidenced by near-identical  emission patterns - its underlying silicon and package design  diverge from the original. These results demonstrate the limits  of near-field resolution for high-fidelity clones and the  importance of complementary imaging techniques in  counterfeit detection.

Summary and Conclusion

This work has demonstrated a low-cost, preparation-free NFS  platform that employs five self-made electric- and magneticfield microprobes. By tailoring the probe geometries, we  achieved complementary operating points in signal-to-noise  ratio (SNR) and lateral resolution, enabling flexible inspection  of packaged integrated circuits without destructive preparation  or expensive commercial equipment.

Validation on three representative counterfeit scenarios  demonstrated the method’s practical relevance: near-field  amplitude maps and X-ray images for verification clearly  separated an authentic STM32F103CBT6 from its  GD32F103CBT6 clone; inconspicuous external markings  could not hide die-level discrepancies in a suspect  STM32F103C6T6A; and while a cloned FTDI FT232RL  reproduced the genuine emission pattern almost perfectly, structural imaging still exposed differences in die size and  bond-wire layout, revealing the present resolution limits of the  technique when confronting high-fidelity replicas. These  findings confirm that electromagnetic near-field scanning can  quickly flag suspect devices and distinguish genuine chips from  clones or relabels, although its selectivity decreases when  counterfeiters succeed in closely mimicking the authentic  electromagnetic footprint.

More broadly, the platform shows promise for a range of  failure-analysis and manufacturing applications. Short  measurement times, particularly when combined with a  multichannel probe array, enable in-line inspection of  electronic devices during production. Automatically generated  near-field maps can be compared against verified golden  references to detect anomalies or deviations indicative of  process variations or early-stage failures.

Looking ahead, the platform will benefit from an automatic  comparison engine that cross-correlates each measured  emission map with a verified golden reference, removing  subjectivity from the pass–fail decision. Embedding both the  sensor loop and a broadband pre-amplifier directly on a  dedicated PCB will shorten signal paths and ease integration  into production test handlers. Replacing the single-point  microprobe with a dense array addressed by multichannel  high-speed converters will reduce scan times dramatically and  enable true in-line screening. Finally, inserting a broadband  matching network between probe and amplifier will extend the  usable frequency range and raise the signal-to-noise ratio, further sharpening the electromagnetic fingerprint and  cementing the technique as a fast, non-destructive first-line  defence against counterfeit electronics.

Hardware Security Evaluation of Advanced Packaging

H.B. Kor, Q. Liu, C.L. Gan

Nanyang Technological University, School of Materials Science and Engineering,50 Nanyang Avenue, Singapore 639798.

Abstract

The increasing use of electronic products in IoT, SoCs, smart  appliances and automotive applications, etc. raises security  concerns, with hardware vulnerable to physical attacks using  failure analysis (FA) tools like microprobing, fault injection, and photon emission. This paper evaluates hardware security  on a system-in-package (SiP) device on a printed circuit board (PCB), with an embedded Electrically Erasable Programmable  Read-Only Memory (EEPROM), focusing on physical  inspection (X-ray) and sample preparation techniques such as  laser decapsulation, acid decapsulation, and microwave  induced plasma (MIP) etching to expose the EEPROM die or  stitch pads for signal probing. Techniques were also tested on  standalone SiP and dual-in-line (DIP) packages. After laser  decapsulation and MIP etching, the board functionality was  retained, and the EEPROM data was successfully read. This  enabled the electrical signal probing at both the chip and  package level for hardware security evaluation of advanced  packaging devices such as SiPs on PCBs.

Introduction

Hardware security is the basis of system security, providing  trust anchor or “root-of-trust” for other components of a  system that have close interaction with it. It not only focuses  on attacks, but also the protection of hardware [1,2]. Hardware  security and hardware assurance are important to ensure and  provide the confidence that electronic systems and devices can  work throughout their life cycle without being compromised.

Printed circuit boards (PCBs) and integrated circuits (ICs) are  vulnerable to not only software attacks, but also hardware  physical attacks [3]. Physical attacks or inspection tools and  techniques, which are commonly used in failure analysis (FA)

[4], aid in the assessment of data security in hardware security  evaluation. Physical inspection or attack techniques can be  non-invasive, semi-invasive or invasive [5,6]. Non-invasive  physical inspection or attack techniques include side-channel  analysis (SCA), fault injection, X-ray imaging or data  remanence. Semi-invasive physical inspection or attack techniques include optical fault injection, optical/photonic  emission side channel or optical probing. In invasive physical  inspection or attack, layout extraction can be carried out on  PCBs or ICs, or via the extraction of field-programmable gate  array (FPGA) bitstream or software. Electrical signal probing  and circuit edit are other invasive inspection or attack  techniques. In the hardware security evaluation of a system-inpackage (SiP) on a PCB, physical inspection such as X-ray  analysis and sample preparation techniques involving various

decapsulation methods to expose the critical metal connections  in both package and chip levels, were conducted for the data  security evaluation of the sample.

Experimental Details

Sample preparation techniques were studied on standalone  dual-in-line (DIP) package and system-in-package (SiP)containing electrically erasable programmable read-only  memory (EEPROM) to explore the decapsulation recipes, prior to decapsulation to expose the same EEPROM die or  stitch pads within a SiP on a PCB for electrical signal probing.

Sample preparation of standalone DIP containing  EEPROM

Standalone dual-in-line (DIP) packages (9 mm × 7 mm × 7  mm) containing an EEPROM die were sourced and studied, to explore the decapsulation recipe prior to decapsulation of standalone SiP and SiP on PCB containing the same embedded EEPROM die. 2D X-ray analysis of the DIP is shown in Fig. 1.

Figure 1: (a) Optical image of DIP, 2D X-ray analysis of DIP  showing (b) plan view, (c) cross-sectional view of entire DIP  and (d) magnified cross-sectional view of EEPROM die(indicated by arrow)

From the 2D X-ray analysis of DIP, bond wires with poorer  contrast are usually copper/palladium wires, as  copper/palladium is lighter than gold bond wires, which  exhibit high contrast in X-ray imaging.

For the DIP, laser and chemical decapsulation was carried out  to expose the EEPROM die and bond wires. The bulk of the

Sample preparation of standalone SiP with embedded EEPROM

A SiP (18 mm × 18 mm × 2 mm) ball grid array (BGA)) containing a power management integrated circuit (PMIC), a  double data rate 3 low voltage (DDR3L) dynamic randomaccess memory (DRAM), a microprocessor and an EEPROM  was studied next. Fig. 4 shows the plan and cross-sectional  views of the standalone SiP from 2D X-ray analysis.

Figure 4: 2D X-ray analysis of standalone SiP showing (a) plan view of entire SiP, (b) magnified view of EEPROM die  area (boxed in blue) and (c) SiP cross-sectional view

As observed from the 2D X-ray cross-sectional analysis, it  was challenging to locate the EEPROM die embedded within  the SiP package due to surrounding higher passive  components. Thus, computed tomography (CT) X-ray analysis  was carried out to confirm the location of the EEPROM die as  shown in Fig. 5.

Figure 5: CT X-ray analysis of standalone SiP showing (a) one slice view in XY plane (slice 968 out of 1904) of entire SiP  and (b) magnified image of slice 965 showing the EEPROM die stitch pads

In addition, 2D X-ray and computed tomography (CT) X-ray  analysis may not be able to confirm the material of the bond  wires. Thus, the standalone SiP was decapsulated to expose  the EEPROM die and EDX analysis was conducted.

The EEPROM die was exposed using a combination of laser decapsulation and MIP etching techniques. Chemical  decapsulation was not considered, due to the presence of  surrounding passive components near the EEPROM die which  may be vulnerable to acid attack and a lower success rate of  exposing the die without damaging the wires and the passive  components.

The bulk of the EMC was removed with laser decapsulation before MIP etching to further expose the die and bond wires.

The laser Z focus depth is 126.5 mm. The laser parameters  were similar to the standalone DIP, except that the standalone  SiP took 5 repeats of hatch style “hatch 3 times offset by 60°”(a total of 15 unidirectional repeats), less than the standalone  DIP. The high aspect ratio of the EEPROM die location within  the standalone DIP resulted in the increased depth and  narrower geometry around the die, which makes material  removal less efficient, thus requiring more laser repeats to  remove the bulk EMC.

Sample preparation to expose stitch pads of EEPROM die  embedded in the SiP on PCB for electrical probing

As the risk of touching or breaking the bond wires is higher  from the landing of microprobes on the bond pads for  electrical probing, sample preparation was also conducted to  expose just the stitch pads. Electrical probing

The EEPROM die pin layout obtained from the datasheet [12] is shown in Fig. 19. The signal of interest is the serial address  or data input / output (I/O) pin, also known as the SDA pin, circled in red.

Figure 19: (a) EEPROM die pin layout from datasheet [12];

(b) matching orientation of pin layout with decapped DIP, (c) SDA pin on exposed top stitch pads (circled in red) and (d) SDA pin on exposed die (circled in red)

The SDA pin is a bidirectional pin used to transfer addresses  or data into and out of the EEPROM. It may be

communicating with PMIC, DRAM or the microprocessor within the SiP on PCB. Since the SDA pin is connected to the  die bond pad and stitch pad, electrical probing was conducted  on the exposed stitch pad of the EPPROM die embedded in  the SiP on PCB.

A probe tip was made in contact with the stitch pad which is  connected to the SDA pin, while another probe tip is  connected to ground. The probe tips connected to the PCB were also directly connected to active probes and an  oscilloscope to capture the signal during electrical probing of  the EEPROM. Fig. 20 shows the electrical probing setup and  Fig. 21 shows the successful capture of the signal.
